\section{Vulkan Epyx Exploration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Playing Epyx Titles on the Native Vulkan Pipeline: Technical Exploration


This document outlines the design architecture to execute and display Epyx retro titles (e.g., \textit{Crush, Crumble and Chomp!}, \textit{The Temple of Apshai}) using our Yul-based EVM emulator and the native Vulkan rendering plugin (\texttt{tsfi\_vulkan.c}).


---


1. Graphics Pipeline: Assembling the Monsters


Unlike simpler games like \textit{Pong} which use single hardware sprites, Epyx games like \textit{Crush, Crumble and Chomp!} represent large entities (such as giant monsters: Glogg, Arachnis, or the Kraken) using multiple coordinated structures:


1. \textbf{Sprite Multiplexing}: \textit{ The monster is assembled from multiple overlapping C64 sprites to achieve rich multi-color details. } \textbf{Vulkan Resolution}: The host polling engine groups sprites \texttt{0}–\texttt{3} by tracking their relative coordinate offsets. Instead of rendering four independent textured quads, Vulkan combines them into a single instanced draw call using a unified model matrix: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{M\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{Monster\}\} = \textbackslash mathbf\{T\}(x\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\}, y\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\}) \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash mathbf\{S\}(w, h)\$\$ 2. \textbf{Custom Character-Cell Graphics}: \textit{ Map tiles (San Francisco, Tokyo) are composed of character cells in Screen RAM (\texttt{1024}–\texttt{2047}). } \textbf{Vulkan Resolution}: The Vulkan fragment shader samples a custom retro C64 font atlas texture. Character indices read from the EVM's \texttt{getScreenRAM()} function map directly to texture coordinates, rendering grid environments with a retro phosphor curvature filter.


---


2. On-Chain Collision \& Destruction Telemetry


In \textit{Crush, Crumble and Chomp!}, the player stomps on buildings, causing destruction:


\textit{ \textbf{Sprite-to-Background Collisions}: } Regulated via VIC-II register \texttt{\$D01F} (\texttt{53279}), emulated inside \texttt{cpu6502.yul}. \textit{ \textbf{Vulkan FX Overlay}: } When a collision between the monster sprite and a building character cell is flagged on-chain, the Vulkan render pass dynamically registers the event and overlays a particle explosion effect on the corresponding map coordinates. * Damage status registers are polled and displayed via a retro HUD panel rendered at the bottom of the viewport using text glyphs.


---


3. Real-Time Audio Synchronization (SID to OpenAL)


Sound effects for stomping, military sirens, and crushing structures are modulated via the virtual SID registers in the EVM contract:


- \textbf{Stomping/Sirens}: Synthesized via the low-frequency oscillators of Voice 1 and Voice 2 in [musicMaker.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/musicMaker.yul). - \textbf{Vulkan Synchronization}: The Vulkan rendering loop is locked to the audio callback rate (e.g., 60 FPS synced to a 48kHz audio buffer queue) to ensure visual explosions align perfectly with synthesized audio effects.


---


4. Run Command for Native Vulkan Visuals


Developers can run the native CLI visualizer with the Vulkan plugin loaded using the following test pipeline command:


``\texttt{bash (echo "LOAD plugins/tsfi\_vulkan"; sleep 1; echo "1.0 OPEN\_WINDOW"; sleep 10; echo "0.0 EXIT") ./tsfi2 --cli }``

\section{Comstar Printer Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Comstar T/F Printer: On-Chain Emulation \& Escape Sequence translation


This document outlines a design proposal to integrate emulation support for the popular \textbf{Comstar T/F (Tractor/Friction) dot-matrix printers} alongside our existing MW-302 parallel interface.


---


1. Historical Context


In the mid-1980s, Commodore users looking to avoid the high cost of official Commodore brand printers (like the MPS 801 or 1526) frequently bought third-party alternatives. \textbf{Comstar} (advertised heavily in retro magazines like \textit{RUN} and \textit{COMPUTE!}) offered affordable tractor/friction printers.


However, standard Commodore computers output text in \textbf{PETSCII} and communicate over the proprietary serial IEEE-488 bus, while the Comstar printers used standard Centronics parallel connections and expected \textbf{ASCII/Standard Escape Codes}. Users required an intelligent adapter (like the Micro World MW-302) to perform the signal and text translation.


---


2. Dynamic PETSCII-to-ASCII translation in Yul


To support standard Commodore software sending unmodified PETSCII streams directly to the emulated printer, we will implement an automatic translation table inside the Yul printer strobe logic (\texttt{54817}).


Character Mapping Rules: - \textbf{PETSCII uppercase (\texttt{0x41}–\texttt{0x5A})} maps to \textbf{ASCII lowercase (\texttt{0x61}–\texttt{0x7A})}. - \textbf{PETSCII lowercase (\texttt{0x61}–\texttt{0x7A})} maps to \textbf{ASCII uppercase (\texttt{0x41}–\texttt{0x5A})}. - \textbf{Carriage Return (\texttt{0x0D})} translates to both carriage return and line feed (\texttt{0x0D 0x0A}) to prevent overwriting the same line.


Proposed Yul Translation: ``\texttt{yul function translatePetsciiToAscii(c) -> out \{ out := c // Handle uppercase rotation if and(gte(c, 0x41), lte(c, 0x5A)) \{ out := add(c, 0x20) leave \} // Handle lowercase rotation if and(gte(c, 0x61), lte(c, 0x7A)) \{ out := sub(c, 0x20) leave \} \} }``


---


3. Emulating Comstar Escape Codes (Formatting)


Comstar printers supported standard dot-matrix control codes (often resembling Epson/Esc-P commands). We can parse these control characters inside our on-chain spooler to style the output logs:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Escape Sequence & Function & Spooler Interpretation \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC + 0x45} (\texttt{ESC E}) & Bold Mode On & Wrap subsequent text in HTML \texttt{<strong>} tags in the frontend console. \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC + 0x46} (\texttt{ESC F}) & Bold Mode Off & Close bold tags. \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC + 0x2D + 1} (\texttt{ESC -1}) & Underline On & Wrap subsequent text in \texttt{<u>} tags in the frontend console. \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC + 0x2D + 0} (\texttt{ESC -0}) & Underline Off & Close underline tags. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Event Staging Updates: When the strobe triggers, the character state machine parses sequences. The emitted \texttt{PrintLine} log contains structured rich-text formatting, rendering beautiful formatted printouts inside the frontend doc viewer.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Control Systems Peripheral Emulation}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Control Systems Modeling for On-Chain Hardware Peripherals


This document models the virtual hardware emulation of the \textbf{Comstar T/F Printer} and the \textbf{Centronics interface} from a discrete control systems perspective. Emulating hardware on an asynchronous, transaction-based VM (like the EVM) requires translating continuous-time physical handshakes into discrete-state transition matrices.


---


1. The Centronics Handshake State-Space Model


A physical Centronics interface relies on a closed-loop handshake between the host (C64/CPU) and the peripheral (Comstar Printer) using three primary control lines:


1. \textbf{\$\textbackslash text\{Data\}\$ (\$D\_0\$–\$D\_7\$)}: 8-bit output from host. 2. \textbf{\$\textbackslash overline\{\textbackslash text\{Strobe\}\}\$}: Active-low pulse from host indicating data is ready. 3. \textbf{\$\textbackslash text\{Busy\}\$}: Output from printer indicating it cannot receive data. 4. \textbf{\$\textbackslash overline\{\textbackslash text\{Ack\}\}\$}: Active-low pulse from printer indicating data is read and it is ready for the next byte.


1.1 State Transition Diagram


``\texttt{mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle Idle --> DataReady : Host writes Data DataReady --> Processing : Host asserts STROBE Processing --> Acknowledging : Printer processes character (Busy=1) Acknowledging --> Idle : Printer asserts ACK (Busy=0) }``


In the EVM, where time is quantized into transaction execution steps, we represent the state \$S\_k \textbackslash in \textbackslash \{0, 1, 2, 3\textbackslash \}\$ at step \$k\$:


\textit{ \textbf{\$0\$ (Idle)}: Default state. Ready for input. } \textbf{\$1\$ (DataReady)}: Data byte written to \texttt{\$D620}. \textit{ \textbf{\$2\$ (Processing)}: \texttt{\$D621} strobe asserted. \texttt{Busy} bit set in status register. } \textbf{\$3\$ (Acknowledging)}: Telemetry event logged. \texttt{Busy} bit cleared, \texttt{Ack} flag pulsed.


---


2. Emulating Stepper Motors \& Mechanical Paper Feed


Dot-matrix printers use stepper motors to feed paper via tractor pins. A line feed (\texttt{LF}, \texttt{0x0A}) advances the paper by a fixed increment (typically \$\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{6\}\$ of an inch).


2.1 Stepper Control Feedback Loop To simulate paper position \$y\_k\$ dynamically, the virtual printer maintains an accumulator register:


\$\$y\_\{k+1\} = y\_k + \textbackslash Delta y \textbackslash cdot u\_k\$\$


Where: - \$u\_k \textbackslash in \textbackslash \{0, 1\textbackslash \}\$ is the control signal triggered by parsing the \texttt{LF} character. - \$\textbackslash Delta y\$ is the step resolution constant. - If \$y\_k\$ exceeds the maximum page height \$Y\_\{\textbackslash text\{Max\}\}\$ (e.g., 66 lines for standard letter paper), a virtual \textbf{Paper-Out} interrupt flag is asserted:


\$\$x\_\{\textbackslash text\{Paper-Out\}\} = \textbackslash begin\{cases\} 1 \& \textbackslash text\{if \} y\_k \textbackslash ge Y\_\{\textbackslash text\{Max\}\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  0 \& \textbackslash text\{otherwise\} \textbackslash end\{cases\}\$\$


Asserting \$x\_\{\textbackslash text\{Paper-Out\}\}\$ raises the printer error line, mapping to a virtual CPU interrupt on-chain.


---


3. Simulating Asynchronous Physical Timing in Synchronous EVM Blocks


Physical printers process print jobs asynchronously over milliseconds. On the EVM, transactions execute instantaneously. To simulate physical processing latency and prevent spam:


1. \textbf{Block-Decayed Processing}: When the strobe trigger \texttt{\$D621} is written, the printer sets its \texttt{Busy} flag. Instead of clearing instantly in the same transaction, the \texttt{Busy} flag remains set until: \$\$\textbackslash text\{block.number\} \textbackslash ge \textbackslash text\{lastStrobeBlock\} + N\$\$ Where \$N\$ is the simulated block delay relative to data size. 2. \textbf{Buffer Backpressure}: If the host attempts to write a new character while \texttt{Busy} is active, the Yul code immediately reverts the transaction, simulating backpressure flow control.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Vulkan Multicolor Plotting}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Multi-Color Sprite Plotting in the Yul Emulator and Vulkan UI


This document details the architectural design and bit-decoding mechanics for emulating the Commodore 64's \textbf{Multi-Color Sprite mode} inside our Yul EVM graphics system and native Vulkan renderer (\texttt{vulkan\_logic.c}).


---


1. Multi-Color Sprite Control Registers


By default, VIC-II sprites are single-color: a \$24 \textbackslash times 21\$ bitmap grid where each bit represents either transparency (\$0\$) or the sprite's primary color (\$1\$).


In \textbf{Multi-Color Sprite mode}, the horizontal resolution is halved to \$12 \textbackslash times 21\$ pixels, where each pixel is represented by a \textbf{2-bit pair} to select from four color sources:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Register Address (Hex) & Register Address (Dec) & Function & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D01C} & \texttt{53276} & Sprite Multi-Color Register & Setting bit \$i\$ (0-7) to \texttt{1} enables multi-color mode for Sprite \$i\$. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D025} & \texttt{53285} & Sprite Extra Color 1 & Defines the RGB color mapped to bit pair \texttt{01}. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D026} & \texttt{53286} & Sprite Extra Color 2 & Defines the RGB color mapped to bit pair \texttt{11}. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D027 + i} & \texttt{53287 + i} & Sprite \$i\$ Main Color & Defines the RGB color mapped to bit pair \texttt{10}. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Bit-Pair Decoding Logic


In multi-color mode, the \$24\$-bit row pattern data is split into \$12\$ distinct pixel pairs (\$C\_0 C\_1\$) processed sequentially from left to right:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Pixel Color\} = \textbackslash text\{Decode\}(C\_0 C\_1)\$\$


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Bit Pair (\$C\_0 C\_1\$) & Color Output & Visual Transparency \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{00} & Transparent & Pass-through to background or underlying plane. \\ \hline
\texttt{01} & Sprite Extra Color 1 (\texttt{\$D025}) & Shared across all multi-color sprites. \\ \hline
\texttt{10} & Sprite Main Color (\texttt{\$D027 + i}) & Unique to the active sprite index. \\ \hline
\texttt{11} & Sprite Extra Color 2 (\texttt{\$D026}) & Shared across all multi-color sprites. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
C/Vulkan Decoding Routine: ```c // Extract multi-color enable mask uint64\_t multicolor\_enable = get\_register\_val(g\_graphics\_address, 53276); bool is\_multicolor = (multicolor\_enable \& (1 << sprite\_idx)) != 0;


uint32\_t extra\_color\_1 = c64\_palette[get\_register\_val(g\_graphics\_address, 53285) \& 0xF]; uint32\_t extra\_color\_2 = c64\_palette[get\_register\_val(g\_graphics\_address, 53286) \& 0xF]; uint32\_t main\_color = c64\_palette[get\_register\_val(g\_graphics\_address, 53287 + sprite\_idx) \& 0xF];


for (int r = 0; r < 21; r++) \{ uint32\_t row\_val = pattern[r]; if (is\_multicolor) \{ // Render 12 double-width pixels for (int c = 0; c < 12; c++) \{ // Extract 2-bit color code from left to right uint8\_t bit\_pair = (row\_val >> (22 - c * 2)) \& 0x03; uint32\_t pixel\_color = 0;


switch (bit\_pair) \{ case 0x01: pixel\_color = extra\_color\_1; break; case 0x02: pixel\_color = main\_color;    break; case 0x03: pixel\_color = extra\_color\_2; break; default:   continue; // 00 is transparent \}


// Plot double-width pixel on staging buffer plot\_pixel(sb, x + c \textit{ 2,     y + r, pixel\_color); plot\_pixel(sb, x + c } 2 + 1, y + r, pixel\_color); \} \} else \{ // Standard single-color mode: 24 pixels for (int c = 0; c < 24; c++) \{ if ((row\_val \& (1 << (23 - c))) != 0) \{ plot\_pixel(sb, x + c, y + r, main\_color); \} \} \} \} ```


---


3. Rendering Pipeline in Vulkan


The pixel plotting maps the decoded RGB values into the \texttt{StagingBuffer} (\texttt{sb->data}), which is copied to the Vulkan staging textures via \texttt{vkCmdPipelineBarrier} and uploaded to the GPU VRAM:


1. \textbf{Host-Side Blitting}: The CPU performs highly optimized bit-pair extraction (optionally vectorized using AVX-512 in \texttt{tsfi\_opt\_zmm.c} for multiple sprites simultaneously). 2. \textbf{GPU Texture Upload}: The updated staging buffer is synced to the Vulkan frame memory. 3. \textbf{Pipeline Draw Call}: A final quad shader renders the composite buffer, applying scanline offsets and retro CRT bloom shaders to produce vintage phosphor screen outputs.

\section{Rupert Report Cursor}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Dale Rupert's "Don't Curse That Cursor!" (Ahoy! Issue 1, Page 44)


Dale Rupert's inaugural column in \textit{Ahoy!} magazine details how to control cursor placement on Commodore systems.


---


1. Cursor Location System Registers


To position the cursor, Commodore systems maintain internal pointers tracking the current grid coordinate (row and column):


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Register (Hex) & Register (Dec) & Function & Range \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :---: & :--- & :---: \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D3} & \texttt{211} & Current Cursor Column & \texttt{0} – \texttt{39} \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6} & \texttt{214} & Current Cursor Row & \texttt{0} – \texttt{24} \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
\textit{   \textbf{BASIC Implementation:} A developer can manipulate these pointers in BASIC: ``\texttt{basic 10 POKE 214, ROW : PRINT : POKE 211, COL }`\texttt{ }Note: The intermediate }PRINT` triggers the Screen Editor to recalibrate to the target line.*


---


2. KERNAL PLOT Routine (\texttt{\$FFF0})


The standard, hardware-independent method for reading and writing the cursor coordinate is calling the KERNAL \texttt{PLOT} subroutine at address \texttt{\$FFF0} (65520).


Setting the Cursor Position: 1. Clear the Carry flag (\texttt{CLC} - opcode \texttt{\$18}). 2. Load target column (X) in the \textbf{X register}. 3. Load target row (Y) in the \textbf{Y register}. 4. Jump to Subroutine: \texttt{JSR \$FFF0} (opcode \texttt{\$20 F0 FF}).


Reading the Cursor Position: 1. Set the Carry flag (\texttt{SEC} - opcode \texttt{\$38}). 2. Call \texttt{JSR \$FFF0}. 3. Returns current column in the \textbf{X register} and row in the \textbf{Y register}.


---


3. EVM CPU Emulator Integration


Our CPU emulator (\texttt{cpu6502.yul}) maps addresses \texttt{211} and \texttt{214} into standard zero-page space. When custom programs execute \texttt{JSR \$FFF0}, the emulator intercepts the execution at PC \texttt{\$FFF0} to execute the native cursor PLOT update.

\section{Z Machine Onchain Design}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
On-Chain Z-Machine (Version 3) Design


We can implement a Z-machine (Version 3) interpreter directly in Yul. Version 3 (Z3) is the classic "Standard" interpreter used by \textit{Zork I-III}, \textit{Planetfall}, and \textit{The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy}. It is extremely space-efficient, fitting inside small memory bounds.


---


1. Z3 Memory Map Layout (On-Chain Slots)


The Z-machine uses a byte-addressable flat memory space. In Yul, we can store this inside dynamic storage slots namespaced to the user:


``` +------------------------------------------+ 0x0000


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Header (64 bytes) \\ \hline\hline
- Version (byte 0 = 3) \\ \hline
- High byte of High Memory (byte 4) \\ \hline
- Initial Program Counter (bytes 6-7) \\ \hline
- Dictionary address (bytes 8-9) \\ \hline
- Object table address (bytes 10-11) \\ \hline
- Global variables address (bytes 12-13) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Dynamic Memory (Read/Write) \\ \hline\hline
- Objects, Globals, Game State \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+ Base of Static Memory


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Static Memory (Read-Only) \\ \hline\hline
- Dictionary, Grammar tables \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+ Base of High Memory


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
High Memory (Instructions \& Strings) \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+ End of Story File ```


---


2. On-Chain Storage Mapping To prevent storage collisions between players or games, we map the Z-machine RAM to namespaced storage slots using our existing pattern: \$\$\textbackslash text\{StorageSlot\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(\textbackslash text\{userAddress\} \textbackslash parallel \textbackslash text\{gameId\} \textbackslash parallel \textbackslash text\{wordIndex\})\$\$


Each storage slot holds a standard EVM 32-byte word (representing 32 bytes of Z-machine memory).


---


3. Z3 Opcode Categories to Implement To run a classic Z3 story file, we must support: \textit{   \textbf{2OP (Two-Operand Instructions)}: \texttt{je} (jump if equal), \texttt{jl} (jump if less than), \texttt{jg}, \texttt{dec\_chk}, \texttt{inc\_chk}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{or}, \texttt{and}, \texttt{test\_attr}, \texttt{set\_attr}, \texttt{clear\_attr}, \texttt{store}, \texttt{insert\_obj}, \texttt{loadw}, \texttt{loadb}, \texttt{get\_prop}, \texttt{get\_prop\_addr}, \texttt{get\_next\_prop}, \texttt{add}, \texttt{sub}, \texttt{mul}, \texttt{div}, \texttt{mod}. }   \textbf{1OP (One-Operand Instructions)}: \texttt{jz} (jump if zero), \texttt{get\_sibling}, \texttt{get\_child}, \texttt{get\_parent}, \texttt{get\_prop\_len}, \texttt{inc}, \texttt{dec}, \texttt{print\_addr}, \texttt{remove\_obj}, \texttt{print\_obj}, \texttt{ret}, \texttt{jump}, \texttt{print\_paddr}, \texttt{load}, \texttt{not}. \textit{   \textbf{0OP (Zero-Operand Instructions)}: \texttt{rtrue} (return true), \texttt{rfalse} (return false), \texttt{print} (print inline literal string), \texttt{print\_ret} (print literal string and return true), \texttt{nop}, \texttt{save}, \texttt{restore}, \texttt{restart}, \texttt{ret\_popped}, \texttt{pop}, \texttt{quit}, \texttt{new\_line}, \texttt{show\_status}, \texttt{verify}. }   \textbf{VAR (Variable-Operand Instructions)}: \texttt{call}, \texttt{storew}, \texttt{storeb}, \texttt{put\_prop}, \texttt{sread} (read input line), \texttt{print\_char}, \texttt{print\_num}, \texttt{random}, \texttt{push}, \texttt{pull}, \texttt{split\_window}, \texttt{set\_window}.


---


4. Text Engine (ZSCII \& Z-characters) Z-machine text is heavily compressed: \textit{   Every character string is composed of \textbf{5-bit Z-characters} packed three to a 16-bit word. }   Uses three alphabets (A0, A1, A2) shifted dynamically using shift codes \texttt{4} and \texttt{5}. *   Supports abbreviation tables to reduce text size (perfect for on-chain gas optimization).


---


Next Steps 1. \textbf{Develop \texttt{zinterpreter.yul}}: Draft a clean Yul contract implementing the Z3 main execution loop, instruction fetch, decode, and stack operations. 2. \textbf{Write Z3 Test Script}: Create a script loading a tiny Z3 test story file to verify instruction execution.

\section{Zmachine Erc20 Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Integrating ERC-20 Tokens with the Z-Machine Object Table


To make Zork-like games that interact natively with on-chain assets, we can map ERC-20 token balances directly to objects in the Z-machine's Object Table.


---


1. Z-Machine Object Table Architecture


In a standard Z3 story file, the Object Table defines all "things", "rooms", and "actors". Each object has: 1.  \textbf{Attributes} (32 boolean flags representing state, like \texttt{is\_takeable}, \texttt{is\_lit}, \texttt{is\_worn}). 2.  \textbf{Parent, Sibling, and Child} pointers (establishing room/inventory hierarchies). 3.  \textbf{Properties} (custom variables like description, weight, or value).


``` +---------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Object ID (e.g. 50: "Gold Coin Token") \\ \hline\hline
- Parent: Player's Inventory (Object ID 1) \\ \hline
- Attributes: Takeable, Value-bearing \\ \hline
- Custom Property (0x20): ERC-20 Address \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+---------------------------------------------+ ```


---


2. On-Chain Binding (ERC-20 <-> Objects)


Instead of hardcoding static quantities inside the story file, we intercept properties or attributes of specific Object IDs:


\textit{   \textbf{Mapping Object Properties to Contract Calls}: If an object has a custom property (e.g., \texttt{TokenContractAddress}), the interpreter retrieves the player's balance dynamically from that ERC-20 contract instead of reading it from static memory. }   \textbf{Triggering On-Chain Mints/Transfers}: When the Z-machine processes actions like: \textit{   \texttt{take gold coin} -> Triggers an ERC-20 \texttt{transfer} or \texttt{mint} to the player's address. }   \texttt{drop gold coin} -> Triggers an ERC-20 \texttt{transfer} or \texttt{burn} from the player's address.


---


3. Implementation Workflow


1.  \textbf{Develop ZSCII Decoding Engine}: Write Yul functions to decompress 5-bit Z-characters into standard 8-bit UTF-8 strings. 2.  \textbf{Extend \texttt{zmachine.yul}}: Build the object property accessor functions, adding conditionals that execute dynamic \texttt{staticcall} or \texttt{call} operations to external ERC-20 addresses when querying specific object values.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Zmachine Erc20 Rewards And Payments}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Z-Machine ERC-20 Transaction Mapping


To allow Z-machine games to reward players with ERC-20 tokens or charge them for actions, we establish dynamic hooks in the opcode execution flow.


---


1. Interaction Mechanisms


We support two directions of ERC-20 interaction: 1.  \textbf{Rewards (Push)}: The contract transfers tokens \textit{to} the player when they achieve an objective (e.g., finding the Brass Lantern or solving a puzzle). 2.  \textbf{Payments (Pull)}: The contract collects tokens \textit{from} the player when they perform a purchase (e.g., buying a sword from a thief or paying a toll to cross a bridge).


---


2. On-Chain Binding in Yul (\texttt{zmachine.yul})


We define custom opcodes or intercept existing property modifiers in Yul.


Approach: Intercepting \texttt{put\_prop} and \texttt{set\_attr} \textit{   In the Z3 engine, altering object state is handled by opcodes like \texttt{set\_attr} (set attribute) or \texttt{put\_prop} (write object property). }   We reserve special attributes or property IDs to represent ERC-20 contracts and values.


Example: Buying an Item When the player buys an item: \textit{   The game code calls: \texttt{put\_prop Sword Price 10} }   Our Yul interpreter catches this modification. If the property being updated maps to an ERC-20 interaction: 1.  It queries the player's balance on the bound token address using \texttt{staticcall} (\texttt{balanceOf}). 2.  If the balance is sufficient, it triggers a \texttt{call} to \texttt{transferFrom} (pulling 10 tokens from the player to the game contract). 3.  If the transfer succeeds, the Z-machine updates the object's parent pointer to the player's inventory. 4.  If the transfer fails, the transaction reverts (or the game logic handles the failure state).


---


3. Dynamic Execution Flow (Yul Pseudo-code)


```yul // Inside the VAR:put\_prop execution handler function executePutProp(objId, propId, value, playerAddress) \{ // Check if this object maps to an ERC-20 token reward/payment hook let isTokenHook := getStorageHookFlag(objId, propId)


if isTokenHook \{ let tokenAddress := getTokenAddressForObject(objId)


switch getHookType(objId) case 1 \{ // REWARD: Transfer tokens to player let success := erc20Transfer(tokenAddress, playerAddress, value) if iszero(success) \{ revert(0, 0) \} \} case 2 \{ // PAYMENT: Collect tokens from player let success := erc20TransferFrom(tokenAddress, playerAddress, address(), value) if iszero(success) \{ revert(0, 0) \} \} \}


// Fallback: Perform standard Z-machine property write writePropertyToMemory(objId, propId, value) \} ```

\section{Advanced Infocom Technologies Blueprint}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Advanced Infocom Technologies Integration Blueprint


We will integrate all four advanced Infocom-inspired systems directly with our on-chain Z-machine ecosystem.


---


1. Rationale and Motivation


\textit{   \textbf{Gas Efficiency \& Data Overhead}: Packing game layouts into 5-bit ZSCII representations reduces dynamic storage writes, allowing complex narrative worlds to reside on-chain at a fraction of the cost of standard contract architectures. }   \textbf{Fully Decentralized Game States}: Emulating the Z-machine on-chain guarantees that game universes are permissionless, moddable, and resistant to server shutdowns. *   \textbf{Asset Interoperability}: Mapping ERC-20 balances directly to the virtual Object Table links standard DeFi assets dynamically to gameplay mechanics.


---


2. TSFi2 Core Component Compatibility


This Z-machine interpreter leverages the standard TSFi2 peripheral architecture:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Infocom Subsystem & Target Version & Compatible TSFi2 Contract / Tech & Interaction Channel \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{SID Synth Audio} & Z6 (YZIP) & [musicMaker.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/musicMaker.yul) & Intercepts \texttt{sound\_effect} opcodes; triggers note frequencies on voice registers. \\ \hline
\textbf{VIC-II Visuals} & Z5 (XZIP) & [graphicsSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/graphicsSystem.yul) & Intercepts window-split/draw calls; maps sprites directly to the canvas frame. \\ \hline
\textbf{ZILCH Compiler} & Z3/Z5 & Browser Compiler Engine & Compiles textual definitions directly to on-chain ROM storage. \\ \hline
\textbf{Invisiclues Hints} & Z3/Z5 & On-Chain Key-Value Registry & Interacts with [keySystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/keySystem.yul) to verify user signatures and release hint payloads. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Integration Architecture


Z6 Sound Engine (SID Synthesis) When a Z6 story file triggers \texttt{sound\_effect ID volume}: 1.  The interpreter maps the sound ID to specific ADSR envelope parameters. 2.  It executes a low-level call to the TSFi2 \texttt{MusicMaker} contract (\texttt{musicMaker.yul}). 3.  The SID registers generate the audio output dynamically.


Z5 Graphics Viewport Mapping When a Z5 file requests room rendering: 1.  The interpreter parses the room description offset. 2.  If the room has a graphic icon property, the interpreter extracts its compressed bitmap coordinates. 3.  It calls \texttt{graphicsSystem.yul} to draw the bitmap on-chain.


Token-Gated Invisiclues The player queries hints on-chain: 1.  The contract verifies payment using standard ERC-20 \texttt{transferFrom} calls. 2.  Once verified, the contract decrypts the progress stage text using the player's public address key via [keySystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/keySystem.yul).

> [!NOTE] > \textbf{ZILCH Compiler Memory Limits}: Processing complete ZIL syntax parsing tables inside browser memory can lead to out-of-memory errors on large game builds. > \textit{   }Mitigation*: We are streamlining tokenizers to parse text structures sequentially rather than building deep AST trees in memory.

\section{Cpu Banking And Timer Upgrades}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
On-Chain CPU Upgrades: Banking \& Jiffy Clock


We will implement bank-switching (6509 style) and an integrated cycle-accurate Jiffy timer directly into our Yul processor state.


---


1. Multi-Page Memory Banking (6509 Architecture)


To expand addressable memory beyond 64 KB, we map the banking registers to zero-page slots \texttt{0x0000} (bank select for index registers) and \texttt{0x0001} (bank select for accumulator / general instructions):


``` +------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Bank Select Registers (Zero Page) \\ \hline\hline
- 0x00: IND\_BANK (Indirect index bank) \\ \hline
- 0x01: ACC\_BANK (Accumulator data bank) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Bank Switching Mapping \\ \hline\hline
- Memory read/write routes data from the \\ \hline
active bank selected in 0x00 or 0x01 \\ \hline
instead of defaulting to Bank 0. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------------------------------+ ```


Yul Storage Key Calculation \$\$\textbackslash text\{StorageSlot\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(\textbackslash text\{userAddress\} \textbackslash parallel \textbackslash text\{bankId\} \textbackslash parallel \textbackslash text\{wordIndex\})\$\$


---


2. Integrated Cycle-Accurate Jiffy Timer


We store a 64-bit cycle counter (\texttt{cyclesExecuted}) inside the user's CPU state registers slot.


\textit{   Every instruction opcode has a standard cycle duration (e.g. \texttt{NOP} = 2 cycles, \texttt{LDA absolute} = 4 cycles). }   During step execution, we increment this counter by the exact instruction cycles. *   \textbf{On-Chain Jiffy Clock}: Games query this register at address \texttt{0xfffc} to execute timing loops (such as audio durations and graphics refreshes) without relying on block timestamps.

\section{Learning Source Hometax Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Learning Source, Inc. - Hometax Compliance Integration Blueprint


This document details the historical context of \textbf{Learning Source, Inc.} and outlines the integration blueprint for emulating their flagship product, \textbf{Hometax}, as an on-chain Yul tax calculation and compliance coprocessor for the TSFi2 platform.


---


1. Historical Context: Learning Source, Inc. \& Hometax


\textbf{Learning Source, Inc.}, active in California during the early 1980s, was an ambitious home software publisher and retail computer pioneer. Their defining software product was \textbf{Hometax}: \textit{ \textbf{The CP/M C64 Software Lifeline}: Originally compiled for CP/M-compatible Commodore 64 architectures, Hometax was one of the first home computer programs designed to guide users through the complex IRS Form 1040 layout using an interactive question-and-answer dialogue. } \textbf{hotline Support}: Learning Source, Inc. innovated by offering a toll-free 800-number support hotline and periodic calculation updates for a small subscription fee. * \textbf{IRS Review}: The program received positive recognition from the accounting firm Price Waterhouse and a benign nod from the IRS, establishing a precedent for automated consumer tax compliance.


---


2. On-Chain Hometax Coprocessor Memory Map (\$D6A0–\$D6AF)


To mirror the consumer financial calculation logic of Hometax at the protocol level, we introduce a Yul-based \textbf{Hometax Compliance Engine} remapped to the memory range \texttt{\$D6A0}–\texttt{\$D6AF} (54944–54959):


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Register Address (Hex) & Register Address (Dec) & Access Mode & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6A0}–\texttt{\$D6A3} & \texttt{54944}–\texttt{54947} & Read / Write & \textbf{Gross Taxable Income Pointer}: 32-bit value representing total accumulated tokens/gwei. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6A4} & \texttt{54948} & Read / Write & \textbf{Deductions Category Selector}: Selects standard deduction class (0x01: Single, 0x02: Joint, 0x03: Corporation). \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6A5} & \texttt{54949} & Write-Only & \textbf{Calculation Trigger Strobe}: Writing \texttt{1} initiates the on-chain tax calculation sequence. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6A6}–\texttt{\$D6A9} & \texttt{54950}–\texttt{54953} & Read-Only & \textbf{Net Taxable Liability}: 32-bit result register displaying calculated tax due. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6AA} & \texttt{54954} & Write-Only & \textbf{Tax Payment Release Strobe}: Writing \texttt{1} transfers calculated liability to the system treasury. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Dynamic On-Chain Tax Calculation Flow (Yul)


When the Calculation Trigger Strobe (\texttt{\$D6A5}) is activated with a non-zero write, the Yul operating platform executes the following logic:


1. \textbf{Read Gross Income}: Loads the 32-bit value stored across \texttt{\$D6A0}–\texttt{\$D6A3}. 2. \textbf{Apply Deductions}: Loads the category selector from \texttt{\$D6A4}. Deducts the standard allowance: \textit{ \textbf{Single (0x01)}: Deduct 1,000 OTRT. } \textbf{Joint (0x02)}: Deduct 2,000 OTRT. \textit{ \textbf{Corporation (0x03)}: Deduct 5,000 OTRT. 3. \textbf{Bracket Calculation}: } If Net Income \$\textbackslash le\$ 10,000 OTRT: Tax Rate is 10\%. * If Net Income \$>\$ 10,000 OTRT: Tax Rate is 15\%. 4. \textbf{Output Generation}: Writes the resulting calculated tax value to the read-only registers \texttt{\$D6A6}–\texttt{\$D6A9}. 5. \textbf{Clear Trigger}: Resets \texttt{\$D6A5} to \texttt{0}.


---


4. Bridge to COMTAX and Diyat Ledger Systems


The Hometax Coprocessor coordinates directly with the active TSFi2 systems:


\textit{ \textbf{COMTAX Synchronization}: Calculations made in the \texttt{\$D6A0} range can be imported by the \textbf{COMTAX} tax compliance coprocessor (\texttt{\$D590}–\texttt{\$D5AF}) to auto-verify capital gains ledger entries across distinct ERC-20 tokens. } \textbf{Platform Treasury Depositing}: Poking \texttt{\$D6AA} with \texttt{1} initiates an ERC-20 \texttt{transferFrom} equivalent from the user's mapped balance to the platform treasury (\texttt{0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111}), emitting the dynamic event log: ``\texttt{solidity event HometaxSettled(address indexed taxpayer, uint256 grossIncome, uint256 taxPaid); }`\texttt{ Topic1: }keccak256("HometaxSettled(address,uint256,uint256)")`. * \textbf{State Verification}: These events are parsed by Web3 dashboard consoles to show real-time audit receipts, ensuring that the emulated 8-bit application calculations are verifiable on the public ledger.

1. Emulated Sierra AGI Register Map (\$D6C0–\$D6CF)

2. Dynamic Room Boundary \& Interaction Logic (Yul)


Writing \texttt{1} or \texttt{2} to \texttt{\$D6C3} launches the AGI script interpreter to process position boundaries and object checks:


```yul case 54979 \{ // Sierra AGI Command Selector (\$D6C3) sstore(getUserSlot(54979), val) if val \{ // 1. Room Transition Check if eq(val, 1) \{ let x := sload(getUserSlot(54976)) let y := sload(getUserSlot(54977)) let room := sload(getUserSlot(54978))


let newRoom := room let changed := 0


// Exit West if lt(x, 5) \{ newRoom := sub(room, 1) sstore(getUserSlot(54976), 150) // Warp to East edge changed := 1 \} // Exit East if gt(x, 155) \{ newRoom := add(room, 1) sstore(getUserSlot(54976), 10) // Warp to West edge changed := 1 \}


if changed \{ // Excise 1 OTRT Diyat Game Tax on room transition let playTax := 1 if exciseOnChainTax(playTax) \{ log3(0, 0, 0x6e9f2cb42838841da92788e02012c2b71239e040f7b2291e5b200ac8c7c3b925, getContextUser(), playTax) \} sstore(getUserSlot(54978), newRoom) let flags := sload(getUserSlot(54983)) sstore(getUserSlot(54983), or(flags, 4)) \} \}


// 2. Parser / Interaction Check if eq(val, 2) \{ let itemID := sload(getUserSlot(54980)) let room := sload(getUserSlot(54978)) let success := 0


// Room 1 (Forest Cleave) -> Gold Key (ID: 10) at position X: [70, 90], Y: [90, 110] if eq(room, 1) \{ if eq(itemID, 10) \{ let x := sload(getUserSlot(54976)) let y := sload(getUserSlot(54977)) if and(and(gt(x, 69), lt(x, 91)), and(gt(y, 89), lt(y, 111))) \{ let inv := sload(getUserSlot(54981)) sstore(getUserSlot(54981), or(inv, 1)) // Get Gold Key success := 1 \} \} \}


// Room 2 (Castle Gate) -> Castle Door (ID: 20) at position X: [50, 70], Y: [120, 140] if eq(room, 2) \{ if eq(itemID, 20) \{ let x := sload(getUserSlot(54976)) let y := sload(getUserSlot(54977)) if and(and(gt(x, 49), lt(x, 71)), and(gt(y, 119), lt(y, 141))) \{ let inv := sload(getUserSlot(54981)) if and(inv, 1) \{ // Requires Gold Key (Bit 0) sstore(getUserSlot(54981), or(inv, 2)) // Castle Unlocked success := 1 \} \} \} \}


let flags := sload(getUserSlot(54983)) if success \{ sstore(getUserSlot(54983), or(flags, 2))


// Emit SierraAgiSettled event log mstore(0x300, room) mstore(0x320, itemID) log2(0x300, 64, 0xe11ca69da21867c2d5885c07342880a18413b63200ff9dfe8bc9c8be7ce68239, getContextUser()) \} if iszero(success) \{ sstore(getUserSlot(54983), and(flags, not(2))) \} \} sstore(getUserSlot(54979), 0) \} \} ```

:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline

\texttt{\$D6E1} & \texttt{55009} & Read / Write & \textbf{Right Margin}: Standard layout column margin (0–80, default 70). \\ \hline

---


2. On-Chain Print Preview Renderer (Yul)


When the Render Trigger Strobe (\texttt{\$D6E5}) is poked with \texttt{1}, the Yul operating platform performs the following:


1. \textbf{Clear Screen RAM}: Resets all C64 Screen RAM characters (addresses 1024 to 2023) to empty space (\texttt{32}). 2. \textbf{Draw Preview Page Outline}: \textit{ Draws a border representing a page on the screen. } Page coordinates: columns 10 to 30, rows 2 to 22. \textit{ Border character used: \texttt{160} (solid block) or similar graphic characters. 3. \textbf{Format \& Spool Text Preview}: } Reads margins and justification. \textit{ Translates the 0–80 margins into screen-relative coordinates within the page outline. } Distributes the text characters into layout rows. \textit{ Renders the layout blocks using character codes (e.g., solid blocks or hyphens) into Screen RAM. 4. \textbf{Deduct Spooling Tax}: } Deducts 2 OTRT units from the caller's balance, depositing them to the treasury. 5. \textbf{Emit Event Log}: ``\texttt{solidity event HomewordRendered(address indexed user, uint256 characterCount); }`\texttt{ Topic: }0x50fdb39d7be5a0438cf1dfba392019ff88d8b634882dfba51912bc5527e0291f`.


---


3. Register Definition in cpu6502.yul


```yul case 55013 \{ // Homeword Render Trigger (\$D6E5) sstore(getUserSlot(55013), val) if val \{ // 1. Clear Screen RAM (1024 to 2023) for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, 1000) \{ i := add(i, 1) \} \{ sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, i)), 32) \}


// 2. Draw Page Border // Top \& Bottom Border (rows 2 and 22, columns 10 to 30) for \{ let col := 10 \} lt(col, 31) \{ col := add(col, 1) \} \{ sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, add(mul(2, 40), col))), 160) sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, add(mul(22, 40), col))), 160) \} // Left \& Right Border (rows 3 to 21, columns 10 and 30) for \{ let row := 3 \} lt(row, 22) \{ row := add(row, 1) \} \{ sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, add(mul(row, 40), 10))), 160) sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, add(mul(row, 40), 30))), 160) \}


// 3. Format Spooled Text let left := sload(getUserSlot(55008)) let right := sload(getUserSlot(55009)) let just := sload(getUserSlot(55010)) let spacing := sload(getUserSlot(55011)) let len := sload(getUserSlot(55012))


if iszero(spacing) \{ spacing := 1 \} if iszero(right) \{ right := 70 \}


// Scale margins to 18 columns wide page boundary (columns 11 to 28) let pageLeft := div(mul(left, 18), 80) let pageRight := div(mul(right, 18), 80) if gt(pageLeft, 17) \{ pageLeft := 0 \} if gt(pageRight, 18) \{ pageRight := 18 \} if lt(pageRight, add(pageLeft, 2)) \{ pageRight := add(pageLeft, 2) \}


let lineWidth := sub(pageRight, pageLeft) let startRow := 3 let currentRow := startRow let currentCol := pageLeft


let textIdx := 0 for \{ \} lt(textIdx, len) \{ \} \{ if gt(currentRow, 21) \{ break \}


// Read character from buffer let char := and(sload(getUserSlot(add(55024, textIdx))), 0xFF) textIdx := add(textIdx, 1)


// Convert to PETSCII character line representation // We represent letters as horizontal dashes (45) or blocks to show preview layout let previewChar := 45 // Hyphen if eq(char, 32) \{ previewChar := 32 \} // Space remains space


// Justification offset adjustment per line could go here let colOffset := add(11, pageLeft) sstore(getUserSlot(add(1024, add(mul(currentRow, 40), add(colOffset, currentCol)))), previewChar)


currentCol := add(currentCol, 1) if eq(currentCol, lineWidth) \{ currentCol := 0 currentRow := add(currentRow, spacing) \} \}


// 4. Charge 2 OTRT Spooling Tax let tax := 2 if exciseOnChainTax(tax) \{ log3(0, 0, 0x6e9f2cb42838841da92788e02012c2b71239e040f7b2291e5b200ac8c7c3b925, getContextUser(), tax) \}


// Emit HomewordRendered event log mstore(0x300, len) log2(0x300, 32, 0x50fdb39d7be5a0438cf1dfba392019ff88d8b634882dfba51912bc5527e0291f, getContextUser())


sstore(getUserSlot(55014), 1) // Status: Success sstore(getUserSlot(55013), 0) // Clear strobe \} \} ```

\section{Mystery House Zengine Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Mystery House Vector Engine \& Z-Machine On-Chain Integration


This document outlines the design architecture and Yul implementation for bridging the \textbf{Z-Machine parser} and \textbf{Mystery House vector graphic engine} on-chain, rendering scenes to Vulkan staging textures.


---


1. Z-Machine Vector Interface: getVectorScene (\$2e06cbe8)


We introduce a dedicated graphical vector query method inside the on-chain Z-Machine interpreter:


``\texttt{solidity interface IZMachine \{ // Returns the vector drawing command stream for a specific adventure game room function getVectorScene(uint256 roomIndex) external view returns (bytes memory); \} }``


The returned byte array is structured as a series of 5-byte line drawing segments: \textit{ \textbf{Byte 0}: Start \$X\$ coordinate (0–255). } \textbf{Byte 1}: Start \$Y\$ coordinate (0–255). \textit{ \textbf{Byte 2}: End \$X\$ coordinate (0–255). } \textbf{Byte 3}: End \$Y\$ coordinate (0–255). * \textbf{Byte 4}: Line Color index (0–15).


---


2. Rendering Pipeline Coordination (Vulkan \& DeepSeek)


When the player navigates or enters a room: 1. The client queries the Z-Machine contract using \texttt{getVectorScene(roomIndex)}. 2. The returned bytes are parsed and drawn onto the C64 Doodle Graphics framebuffer via the Yul CPU emulator. 3. The Doodle framebuffer updates are uploaded to the GPU via Vulkan pipelines, synchronizing visual adventure rooms. 4. The transaction logs are hashed and verified against the DeepSeek consensus status bar to guarantee mathematical compliance.

\section{Zmm Zengine Rag Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Unified ZMM Z-Engine \& RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Architecture


This document outlines the system architecture to unite \textbf{AVX-512 ZMM Vector Registers}, the \textbf{Z-Machine (Z-Engine)} story interpreter, and \textbf{RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)} database scans on the TSFi2 platform.


---


1. Unified Architecture Overview


The system bridges the text parser of the 8-bit Z-Machine with high-dimensional AI vector space calculations executed on 512-bit ZMM hardware registers:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD User["Player Input ('look', 'take')"] --> Z3["Z-Machine (Z-Engine) Parser"] Z3 -->ZSCII Query StringHash["Vector Projection (ZMM0)"] Hash -->Cosine Similarity MatrixRAG["RAG Database (Zero-Copy Reservoir)"] RAG -->ZMM Register scanMLA["DeepSeek Multi-Head Attention (ZMM3)"] MLA -->Ranked Document MatchMemory["Z-Machine Story Memory (Dynamic RAM)"] Memory -->Render Game ScreenVulkan["Vulkan Native Visualizer"] }``


---


2. ZMM-Accelerated RAG Retrieval (C / AVX-512)


The RAG search queries the database of text blocks using parallel 512-bit registers via \texttt{tsfi\_registry\_scan\_zmm}:


```c \#include "tsfi\_opt\_zmm.h"


// Scans database blocks (512-bit wide chunks) for query cosine similarity matches LauMetadata\textit{ tsfi\_registry\_scan\_zmm(LauRegistryManifold }m, void \textit{query\_vector) \{ \_\_m512 q = \_mm512\_loadu\_ps((float})query\_vector); LauMetadata *best\_match = NULL; float best\_score = -1.0f;


LauMetadata \textit{current = m->head; while (current) \{ float }db\_vector = (float*)current->payload\_start; \_\_m512 d = \_mm512\_loadu\_ps(db\_vector);


// Dot Product similarity using AVX-512 \_\_m512 dot = \_mm512\_mul\_ps(q, d); float sum = \_mm512\_reduce\_add\_ps(dot);


if (sum > best\_score) \{ best\_score = sum; best\_match = current; \} current = current->next; \} return best\_match; \} ```


---


3. Z-Machine Integration (Yul)


The Z-Machine contract queries the ZMM-RAG backend when a player executes parser inputs. The matching ranked responses are loaded dynamically into Z-Machine object property slots:


```yul case 0xf1ba03f9 \{ // parseCommand(address player, bytes cmd) let queryHash := keccak256(add(cmd, 32), mload(cmd))


// Call RAG lookup registry contract (returns best-matching text object ID) mstore(0x300, shl(224, 0x5d5517bf)) // getVectorScene / RAG query selector mstore(0x304, queryHash) let success := staticcall(gas(), 0x4B4519ab516f2d209b3EFC25d7Eb5839615e49C4, 0x300, 36, 0x344, 32) let matchedObjectId := mload(0x344)


// Update Z-Machine Dynamic Memory Object Table directly writeObjectProperty(matchedObjectId, 5, 1) // Set property 5 (Active Room) to 1 \} ```


---


4. Vulkan Display \& DeepSeek Consensus \textit{ \textbf{Vulkan Render}: The Z-Machine's active room index triggers corresponding vector-graphic outline queries via \texttt{getVectorScene(roomIndex)}. These lines are drawn immediately to the Doodle Graphics buffer, rendering rooms dynamically inside the Vulkan visualizar window. } \textbf{DeepSeek Consensus}: Vector allocations and similarity metrics are compared against the active \texttt{acousticOracle} block validation registry to verify execution authenticity.

Broderbund Software Integration Blueprint

1. Game Mechanics \& Memory Map


A. Choplifter (Helicopter Rescue Simulation) Emulates flight mechanics, hostage rescue collision, enemy combat, and landing-pad scoring. \textit{   \textbf{Memory-Mapped Registers}: }   \texttt{\$D6E0} (55008): Player Heli X Coordinate (0-319) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6E1} (55009): Player Heli Y Coordinate (0-199) }   \texttt{\$D6E2} (55010): Helicopter State Flags: \textit{   Bit 0: Direction (0 = Left, 1 = Right) }   Bit 1-2: Speed/Thrust level (0-3) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6E3} (55011): Fuel Level (0-255) }   \texttt{\$D6E4} (55012): Hostages On Board (0-16) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6E5} (55013): Hostages Rescued (Score) }   \texttt{\$D6E6} (55014): Physics Tick Trigger (\$D6E6 = 1 updates Heli coordinates using current velocity and charges fuel tax)


B. Lode Runner (2D Grid Platformer) Emulates the 2D tile layout, collection of gold bars, guard tracking AI, and dig mechanics. \textit{   \textbf{Tile Definitions}: }   \texttt{0x00}: Empty space \textit{   \texttt{0x01}: Brick Wall (diggable) }   \texttt{0x02}: Solid block (undiggable) \textit{   \texttt{0x03}: Ladder }   \texttt{0x04}: Hand-rail / Rope \textit{   \texttt{0x05}: Gold Bar }   \texttt{0x06}: Dug Hole (temporary open space, refills after timer) \textit{   \textbf{Memory-Mapped Registers}: }   \texttt{\$D6EA} (55018): Player X Tile Position (0-39) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6EB} (55019): Player Y Tile Position (0-24) }   \texttt{\$D6EC} (55020): Action Trigger: \textit{   \texttt{1}: Dig Left (replaces wall tile at X-1, Y+1 with dug hole \texttt{0x06}) }   \texttt{2}: Dig Right (replaces wall tile at X+1, Y+1 with dug hole \texttt{0x06}) *   \texttt{3}: Collect Gold (scans current position for \texttt{0x05}, increments score, clears tile)


C. Karateka (Martial Arts Combat) Emulates combat states, collision checks for strikes (punch/kick), and health bar adjustments. \textit{   \textbf{Memory-Mapped Registers}: }   \texttt{\$D6F0} (55024): Player Stance Mode: \textit{   \texttt{0}: Normal / Running (vulnerable to instant defeat if hit) }   \texttt{1}: Combat / Stance \textit{   \texttt{\$D6F1} (55025): Player Attack Strike: }   \texttt{0}: Idle \textit{   \texttt{1}: Punch (short range, fast) }   \texttt{2}: Kick (long range, slow) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6F2} (55026): Enemy Stance Mode }   \texttt{\$D6F3} (55027): Distance between Player and Enemy (0-255) \textit{   \texttt{\$D6F4} (55028): Player Health (0-100) }   \texttt{\$D6F5} (55029): Enemy Health (0-100) *   \texttt{\$D6F6} (55030): Combat Tick Trigger (calculates hit registration based on distance and active strike)


---


2. Implementation \& Test Strategy


We will build emulations in the Yul CPU or as test scripts that write to simulated virtual registers to verify the math logic. \textit{   We'll start by implementing \textbf{Choplifter} physics tick mechanics and hostage collection checks on-chain. }   Then we'll implement \textbf{Lode Runner} digging mechanisms with tile replacement checks.

\section{Stuffed Animals Evolution}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\

3D Stuffed Animal Rendering \& Telemetry Evolution


The RAG node visualizer has been evolved from simple flat 2D shapes into interactive, rotating, 3D ray-marched stuffed animals rendered in real-time under a software-rendered Wayland compositor.


📐 Signed Distance Field (SDF) Architecture


To keep rendering lightweight and fast enough for software execution on the CPU, each stuffed animal is modeled using a collection of mathematically blended primitive shapes (ellipsoids, spheres, and cones) using a smooth minimum function (\$smin\$).


1. The 3D Teddy Bear (Baseline K0Rn) Formulated by combining ellipsoids for the body, head, snout, and ears: \$\$d\_\{\textbackslash text\{body\}\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{1.2x\textasciicircum 2 + 0.8y\textasciicircum 2 + 1.2z\textasciicircum 2\} - 0.35\$\$ \$\$d\_\{\textbackslash text\{head\}\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{x\textasciicircum 2 + (y-0.35)\textasciicircum 2 + z\textasciicircum 2\} - 0.25\$\$


2. The 3D Crow Uses custom wing ellipsoids and a sharp cone for the beak: \$\$d\_\{\textbackslash text\{beak\}\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{5(x-0.45)\textasciicircum 2 + 5(y-0.2)\textasciicircum 2 + 5z\textasciicircum 2\} - 0.1\$\$


3. The 3D Cat Employs pointy ear shapes and a tail sphere: \$\$d\_\{\textbackslash text\{ear\}\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{2(x-0.35)\textasciicircum 2 + 2(y-0.38)\textasciicircum 2 + 2z\textasciicircum 2\} - 0.05\$\$

🗺️ CompuServe Core Technologies \& Integration Vectors


1. VIDTEX Escape Graphics Protocol \textit{   \textbf{Historical Context}: VIDTEX allowed early microcomputers (Commodore, TRS-80, Atari) to render vector paths, cursor animations, and custom colors over dial-up terminals using specialized ESC sequences. }   \textbf{Wayland Integration}: \textit{   Map incoming raw character streams containing custom escape codes (e.g., \texttt{ESC ?} or custom control codes) to the existing \texttt{GfxPrimitive} overlay engine. }   Expand \texttt{gfx\_primitives} support to draw lines, run-length encoded (RLE) color blocks, and vector paths directly onto the framebuffer based on terminal shell output.


2. CompuServe GIF87a \& GIF89a (LZW Compression) \textit{   \textbf{Historical Context}: Developed in 1987 by CompuServe to exchange high-quality graphics over low-bandwidth modem connections using Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) lossless compression. }   \textbf{Yul CPU/VM Integration}: \textit{   \textbf{LZW Decoder}: Implement an on-chain or VM-native LZW decompressor in Solidity/Yul to decode graphic files stored in the smart contracts. }   \textbf{RAG Framebuffer Snapshots}: Compile frame telemetry and export static or animated RAG graphs into standard \textbf{GIF89a} formats directly from \texttt{tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c}. *   \textbf{Dracula Color Palettes}: Align the 256-color global palette of the GIF format with the Dracula palette currently used in the console.


3. CompuServe B+ Protocol \& Host-Micro Interface (HMI) \textit{   \textbf{Historical Context}: Reliable, error-free serial file transfer protocols supporting metadata queries and transaction headers, evolved to exchange files over noisy telephone line modems. }   \textbf{Workspace System Integration}: \textit{   \textbf{File Upload/Download}: Create a virtual serial link (\texttt{/dev/pts} / PTY) inside the Yul VM so the shell can execute \texttt{bget} / \texttt{bsend} commands. }   \textbf{IPC Telemetry Channel}: Implement HMI packet structures to exchange visual capturing telemetry (like \texttt{rag\_telemetry.jpg}) or 3D coordinate meshes between the background Yul VM processes and the Wayland terminal UI.


---


🛠️ Proposed Implementation Roadmap


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A["CompuServe Stream Reader"] -->Parse Escape SequencesB["VIDTEX Renderer (Wayland Overlay)"] A -->HMI TransactionsC["B+ Protocol File Transfer (PTY Virtual Modem)"] D["RAG Graph Telemetry"] -->LZW CompressionE["GIF89a Snapshot Exporter"] }``


1.  \textbf{Phase 1}: Add full parser support for \textbf{VIDTEX escapes} in the terminal emulator state machine, allowing Yul VM programs to draw vector lines directly onto the user's overlay screen. 2.  \textbf{Phase 2}: Write a lightweight LZW encoder to export RAG telemetry frame captures as animated GIFs directly from the software framebuffer. 3.  \textbf{Phase 3}: Implement a mock CompuServe Host-Micro Interface (HMI) responder to allow remote script control over terminal properties.

\section{Compuserve Protocols Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Deep Dive: CompuServe Terminal Protocols \& Subsystems


This document analyzes CompuServe's proprietary protocols and explores how they can be emulated or integrated into our current terminal design.


---


1. Vidtex (CompuServe Video Terminal) Escape Sequences Vidtex terminals supported specific escape sequences for local screen formatting, cursor positioning, and terminal feature negotiation.


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Sequence & Name & Description \\ \hline\hline
\texttt{ESC ESC d} & Clear Screen & Clears the terminal screen and resets cursor to home. \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC ESC c} & Query Terminal ID & Mainframe requests terminal capabilities (resolutions, color palettes, and local storage). \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC ESC g} & Graphics Mode & Triggers low-baud RLE vector/raster decoder. \\ \hline
\texttt{ESC ESC I} & Set Cursor & Position cursor at coordinates (X, Y) encoded as offset bytes. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. CompuServe B-Protocol (B, B+, and Quick-B) Designed to outperform standard XMODEM over early packet-switched networks (such as Tymnet or CompuServe's own network).


Key Architectural Advantages: 1. \textbf{Sliding Windows}: Allowed sending multiple packets before receiving an acknowledgment (\texttt{ACK}), mitigating high packet propagation delays. 2. \textbf{Variable Block Sizes}: Dynamic packet size adjustment (from 128 to 1024 bytes) based on line noise. 3. \textbf{Robust Resumption}: Supported checkpointing and resuming interrupted file transfers by checking file sizes and offset hashes. 4. \textbf{Metadata Exchange}: Packed filenames, creation timestamps, and target permissions directly into the initial handshake block.


---


3. Host-Micro Interface (HMI) Mainframe Protocol HMI was a structural payload system layered over B+ protocol frames, designed for front-end CIM (CompuServe Information Manager) applications:


\textit{ \textbf{Session Negotiation}: Programmatic login and encryption setup. } \textbf{Menu Serialization}: Transmitting structured navigation menus (tables, button lists, text widgets) in binary format instead of raw terminal ANSI text. * \textbf{Transaction Bundling}: Batching multiple mail reads, forum posts, or catalog requests to execute synchronously on the host mainframe.


---


Potential Integration Ideas: \textit{ \textbf{Option A}: Implement the \textbf{Vidtex Cursor Escape Sequence Parser} inside our console rendering pipeline. } \textbf{Option B}: Build a mock \textbf{CIS Menu Broker} that emulates navigation shortcuts (like \texttt{GO WAGE}, \texttt{GO WEATHER}) over our local shell interface. * \textbf{Option C}: Code the \textbf{B+ File Transfer sliding-window state machine} to allow native file exchanges with terminal hosts.

\section{Midwest Micro Superterm Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Midwest Micro Associates: SuperTerm Cartridge Emulation Design Blueprint


This document specifies the integration architecture to emulate the \textbf{SuperTerm} cartridge hardware, 80/132-column side-scrolling screen memory, offline text editing buffer, and parallel print interface ("Sprinter") from \textbf{Midwest Micro, Inc.} on our virtual Yul EVM platform.


---


1. Cartridge Port Hardware Interface Emulation


The original SuperTerm was distributed with a dedicated physical cartridge. The cartridge mapped custom control ROM banks and hardware expansions to C64 memory spaces:


- \textbf{EPROM Address Mapping}: Maps a 16KB system control ROM to standard cartridge locations \texttt{\$8000}–\texttt{\$BFFF} (8K/16K ROM Mode) configured by setting control lines \texttt{EXROM=0} and \texttt{GAME=1} inside the EVM's memory map control registers. - \textbf{Hardware Register Mapping}: - The cartridge incorporates custom memory-mapped IO registers at \texttt{\$DE00}–\texttt{\$DEFF} (C64 IO Address Space 1) to regulate hardware configurations: - \texttt{\$DE00}: Handshake register interfacing with the virtual terminal serial line (ACIA status emulation). - \texttt{\$DE01}: Side-scrolling offset register (controls window offsets for 80/132-column emulation).


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD subgraph C64 Memory Map IO1["IO1 Address Space (\$DE00 - \$DEFF)"] ROM16["Cartridge ROM Space (\$8000 - \$BFFF)"] end subgraph SuperTerm Emulator REG\_HS["\$DE00: Virtual ACIA Status/Data"] REG\_SCROLL["\$DE01: Viewport H-Scroll Offset"] ROM\_DECODE["EXROM/GAME Decoding Logic"] end IO1 --> REG\_HS IO1 --> REG\_SCROLL ROM16 --> ROM\_DECODE }``


---


2. 80-Column and 132-Column Side-Scrolling Framebuffer


SuperTerm supported displaying virtual 80-column and 132-column text widths on standard C64 40-column screens using interactive horizontal scrolling:


- \textbf{Virtual Grid Layout}: - Virtual text grids are sized to \$80 \textbackslash times 25\$ or \$132 \textbackslash times 25\$ characters in high-resolution memory. - \textbf{Side-Scrolling Renderer}: - The viewport position shifts left or right based on the cursor position or user command inputs. - The software renderer reads the offset register \texttt{\$DE01} to project a subset window onto the physical \$40 \textbackslash times 25\$ character grid (or our native 1280x720 Wayland screen space). - Intercepting the scrolling offset allows our Wayland client to automatically render the active portion of the wide text grid.


---


3. Offline Buffer Text Editor Integration


SuperTerm featured an offline text buffer editor storing up to 18.4KB of offline communications:


- \textbf{Buffer Mapping}: Mapped to RAM address space \texttt{\$1000}–\texttt{\$5800} in the EVM environment. - \textbf{Command Capture}: - Our Wayland terminal parser translates keystrokes to offline character buffers when the system enters offline mode (e.g. typing offline text edits). - Buffered content can be piped to the transmission channel using standard transfer protocol simulators (CBM, Xon-Xoff).


---


4. Midwest Micro "Sprinter" Printer Interface


The cartridge interface allowed connection to the "Sprinter" accessory to enable simultaneous logging to a parallel printer:


- \textbf{Printer Address Hook}: Emulates a parallel Centronics-compatible port interface mapped to user port registers (\texttt{\$DD01}). - \textbf{Printer Logging}: - Characters written to \texttt{\$DD01} are captured by our console logger and written directly to a local text file \texttt{artifacts/sprinter\_output.log}, simulating continuous print log output.


---


5. Deployment and Verification Command


To test the virtual Midwest Micro SuperTerm ROM boot sequence inside our terminal emulator, run:


``\texttt{bash ./bin/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell --load-rom plugins/superterm\_c64.bin }``

\textbf{VIP Terminal} & 80/106-column soft-rendered terminal & Integrated standard terminal width, software-based high-res font scaling \\ \hline
\textbf{VIP Calc} & Spreadsheet with mouse/keyboard control & Embedded VM utility \texttt{CALC} (currently mapped to basic expression parser) \\ \hline
\textbf{VIP Database} & Flat-file structured database manager & Yul VM state file indexer \& memory segment table explorer \\ \hline
\textbf{VIP Writer / Speller} & Word processor with unified visual commands & Embedded buffer text editor for script/Yul code generation \\ \hline
\textbf{VIP Accountant / Tax} & Ledger tracking and taxation calculation & Core bookkeeping simulation under the Yul gas/tax rules \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Technical Feature Integration


A. Soft-Rendered 80/106-Column Text Mode (VIP Terminal) The standard Commodore 64 display was restricted to 40 columns of text. Softlaw achieved 80 to 106 columns by bypass-rendering text in high-resolution graphics mode using custom 4x8 or 3x8 bitmapped fonts. * \textbf{Wayland Implementation}: In [tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c), we can use the software rasterizer (\texttt{draw\_debug\_text}) to switch dynamically between: - \textbf{Standard 80-Column Mode} (using an 8x16 font layout) - \textbf{Compressed 106-Column Mode} (using a custom 5x8 or 6x12 font layout) to maximize screen real estate when debugging large VM registers (like \texttt{zmm} vector registers).


B. Lisa/Xerox Star Icon \& Command Interface Softlaw applications unified their command sets around simple, visual menus and icons. * \textbf{Wayland Implementation}: Integrate a top menu bar or status line in the Wayland terminal displaying quick-action glyphs/icons for VM state controls (e.g., Run, Pause, Reset, Memory Dump, and Export).


C. Unified VM Expression Calc (VIP Calc) * \textbf{Wayland Implementation}: Expand the Yul VM's \texttt{CALC} terminal utility into a interactive command-line grid spreadsheet, enabling users to write formulas referring to memory addresses (e.g., \texttt{=MEM[0x1000] + MEM[0x1004]}).


---


3. Recommended Implementation Steps


1. \textbf{Font Extension}: Add a high-density font representation to \texttt{tsfi\_staging} supporting smaller glyph footprints for the 106-column VIP mode. 2. \textbf{Spreadsheet Subsystem}: Build a lightweight interactive sheet processor script running inside the Yul CPU environment to emulate \texttt{VIP Calc}. 3. \textbf{Database Register Inspector}: Create a database utility (\texttt{VIP DB}) to store and query compiled Yul contract metadata, function hashes, and call telemetry history.

\section{Ruleburst Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 07, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
RuleBurst-Style Natural Language Determinations Engine


RuleBurst (now Oracle Policy Automation / Oracle Intelligent Advisor) is a business rules engine (BRE) centered around \textbf{natural language inferencing}. Instead of traditional code, policy writers specify rules using structured sentences like: ``\texttt{text The citizen is eligible for assistance if the citizen is a resident and the citizen's income is less than 50000 }``


This document details the design of a lightweight, compile-to-Yul Determinations Engine running directly on our virtual CPU architecture.


---


1. Engine Architecture


The Yul-based Determinations Engine maps natural language rule declarations into operational memory locations and executable bytecode.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD NL[Natural Language Rules] --> Parser[Syntactic Lexer \& Data Dictionary] Dict[Data Dictionary / Schema] --> Parser Parser --> Compiler[Rule-to-Yul Compiler] Compiler --> Bytecode[Yul Bytecode] Bytecode --> VM[Yul CPU / ZMM VM] }``


Key Components: 1. \textbf{Data Dictionary}: Defines the layout mapping natural language concepts to VM memory offsets (e.g., \texttt{"the citizen's income"} \$\textbackslash rightarrow\$ offset \texttt{0x1020}, Type: \texttt{uint256}). 2. \textbf{Syntactic Lexer}: A C-based rules compiler running as a CLI utility that parses logic operators (\texttt{if}, \texttt{and}, \texttt{or}, \texttt{is less than}, \texttt{is greater than}, \texttt{is equal to}). 3. \textbf{Yul Codegen Engine}: Translates parsed logic trees directly into standard Solidity Yul IR code, which compiles to EVM-compatible bytecode executable on our CPU.


---


2. Syntactic Rules Grammar \& Mapping


We define a subset of RuleBurst-style grammar:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Rule Syntax & Logical Meaning & Translated Yul Code \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{[attribute] is true} & Boolean check & \texttt{mload(offset) // non-zero} \\ \hline
\texttt{[attr1] is less than [attr2]} & Comparison & \texttt{lt(mload(o1), mload(o2))} \\ \hline
\texttt{... if A and B} & Logical AND & \texttt{and(A, B)} \\ \hline
\texttt{... if A or B} & Logical OR & \texttt{or(A, B)} \\ \hline
\texttt{the outcome is [val] if ...} & Assignment & \texttt{if cond \{ mstore(o\_out, val) \}} \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Sample Rule Compiler Input ```text DECL: citizen\_income at 0x1000 uint256 DECL: citizen\_resident at 0x1020 bool DECL: citizen\_eligible at 0x1040 bool


RULE: the citizen is eligible if the citizen is a resident and the citizen's income is less than 50000 ```


Generated Yul IR Code ```yul object "determinations\_rules" \{ code \{ datacopy(0, dataoffset("runtime"), datasize("runtime")) return(0, datasize("runtime")) \} object "runtime" \{ code \{ // Load variables from memory mappings let income := mload(0x1000) let resident := mload(0x1020)


// Perform natural language inferencing let income\_check := lt(income, 50000) let eligible := and(resident, income\_check)


// Store outcome mstore(0x1040, eligible) \} \} \} ```


---


3. Benefits \& Practical Use Cases 1. \textbf{Readable Gas \& Tax Models}: We can model the \texttt{gas taxation} algorithms and accounting rules in readable English rules, compile them to Yul, and execute them on-chain or inside the VM. 2. \textbf{Interactive Simulation}: The Wayland terminal can feed input values into a virtual spreadsheet, execute the RuleBurst-style compiled contract, and instantly update the telemetry HUD with decision state trees.
