\section{Sega Saturn Vdp1}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Sega Saturn VDP1 Quad-Based Rendering Architecture


The \textbf{Sega Saturn VDP1} is a specialized coprocessor responsible for drawing sprites, lines, and polygons. Unlike modern 3D graphics processors that rely on triangle rasterization, VDP1 is designed entirely around \textbf{Quadrilateral-Based Rendering}.


---


1. VDP1 Command Tables


VDP1 executes drawing operations by parsing a list of commands stored in VRAM. This list is composed of \textbf{Command Blocks (CMD)}.


Command Block Layout (CMD) Each CMD block is 32 bytes wide and contains the following fields:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Offset (Bytes) & Name & Description \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{0x00} & \textbf{CTRL} & Control word (Determines sprite type: Normal, Scaled, Distorted, or Polygon) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x02} & \textbf{PMOD} & Plot Mode (Color mode: 4bpp, 8bpp, 16bpp high color, Gouraud shading flags) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x04} & \textbf{COLR} & Color/Palette address \\ \hline
\texttt{0x06} & \textbf{SRCA} & Source Texture address in VRAM \\ \hline
\texttt{0x08} & \textbf{SIZE} & Texture width and height (\$W \textbackslash times H\$) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x0A} & \textbf{XA, YA} & Vertex A Coordinate (\$X\_0, Y\_0\$) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x0E} & \textbf{XB, YB} & Vertex B Coordinate (\$X\_1, Y\_1\$) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x12} & \textbf{XC, YC} & Vertex C Coordinate (\$X\_2, Y\_2\$) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x16} & \textbf{XD, YD} & Vertex D Coordinate (\$X\_3, Y\_3\$) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x1A} & \textbf{GRDA} & Gouraud Shading Table address \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Quadrilateral vs. Triangle Rendering


Because VDP1 distorts textures to fit four arbitrary vertices (A, B, C, D), it maps textures using bilinear interpolation:


``\texttt{ A (X0, Y0) ────────────── B (X1, Y1) │                        │ │     P(x,y)             │ │    (Bilinear UV)       │ │                        │ D (X3, Y3) ────────────── C (X2, Y2) }``


During rasterization, the VDP1 spans horizontal lines between the edges \$AD\$ and \$BC\$, interpolating texture coordinates (\$U, V\$) along the way. If a quadrilateral is highly distorted or folded (concave), it can lead to visual artifacts (such as pixels missing or "texture tearing"), a signature characteristic of Sega Saturn 3D games.


---


3. Simulation Implementation


To demonstrate this system, we have created a simulator script: [test\_saturn\_vdp1.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/test\_saturn\_vdp1.js).


This script: 1. Simulates a VDP1 VRAM command stream containing Distorted Sprites and Polygons. 2. Implements a bilinear interpolator that computes \$X, Y\$ coordinate maps and texture \$U, V\$ parameters across a distorted quadrilateral. 3. Validates vertex mappings and bounding box boundary checks.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Yamaha Ym2612 Fm Synthesis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Yamaha YM2612 FM Synthesis Architecture


The \textbf{Yamaha YM2612 (OPN2)} is a six-channel frequency modulation (FM) sound synthesizer chip that gives the Sega Genesis its distinct, metallic, and punchy audio signature. This document details its 4-operator voices and the 8 algorithm routing configurations.


---


1. 4-Operator Voice Design


Each YM2612 FM channel is composed of \textbf{4 Operators (Op1, Op2, Op3, Op4)}. An operator is a digital sine wave generator modified by an envelope generator (controlling volume over time via Attack, Decay, Sustain, and Release).


Rather than simply mixing four audio waves, operators are routed so that the output of one operator modulates the frequency (phase) of the next:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Output\} = \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash phi + \textbackslash beta \textbackslash times \textbackslash text\{Modulator\})\$\$


Where \$\textbackslash phi\$ is the carrier phase, \$\textbackslash beta\$ is modulation strength, and \$\textbackslash text\{Modulator\}\$ is the signal from the preceding operator.


---


2. FM Algorithms (Routing Configurations)


The relationship between the four operators is determined by one of \textbf{8 Algorithms (0 to 7)}:


``\texttt{ [ Alg 0: Serial Cascade ]      [ Alg 4: Mixed Parallel ]      [ Alg 7: Pure Parallel ] ┌───────┐                      ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐            ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │  Op1  │                      │  Op1  │ │  Op2  │            │Op1│ │Op2│ │Op3│ │Op4│ └───┬───┘                      └───┬───┘ └───┬───┘            └─┬─┘ └─┬─┘ └─┬─┘ └─┬─┘ ▼                              │         │                  │     │     │     │ ┌───────┐                          └────┬────┘                  └─────┼─────┼─────┘ │  Op2  │                               ▼                             ▼     ▼ └───┬───┘                           ┌───────┐                        ┌─────────┐ ▼                               │  Op3  │                        │  Sound  │ ┌───────┐                           └───┬───┘                        │ Output  │ │  Op3  │                               ▼                            └─────────┘ └───┬───┘                           ┌───────┐ ▼                               │  Op4  │ ┌───────┐                           └───┬───┘ │  Op4  │                               ▼ └───┬───┘                          ┌─────────┐ ▼                              │  Sound  │ ┌─────────┐                         │ Output  │ │  Sound  │                         └─────────┘ │ Output  │ └─────────┘ }``


\textit{ \textbf{Algorithm 0}: Full serial cascade. Yields complex, highly distorted, metallic, and brassy synth sounds. } \textbf{Algorithm 4}: Op1 and Op2 modulate Op3, which modulates Op4. Good for pianos and bell attacks. * \textbf{Algorithm 7}: All operators run in parallel directly to the output. Useful for organ sounds or multi-tone mixing.


---


3. Simulation Implementation


To demonstrate this system, we have created a simulator script: [test\_ym2612.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/test\_ym2612.js).


This script: 1. Defines the structures for Operators (phase, frequency, envelope multipliers). 2. Implements operator phase modulation equations. 3. Simulates the 8 routing algorithms, generating output audio sample values based on operator configurations.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Sega Dreamcast Powervr2}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Sega Dreamcast PowerVR2 (CLX2) TBDR Architecture


The \textbf{Sega Dreamcast} graphics pipeline is powered by the \textbf{NEC PowerVR2 (CLX2)} GPU. Rather than using standard immediate-mode rendering, the PowerVR2 pioneered \textbf{Tile-Based Deferred Rendering (TBDR)}, which dramatically optimizes memory bandwidth and resolves overdraw constraints.


---


1. The TBDR Pipeline


``\texttt{ [ 3D Scene Geometry ] │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │  1. Tile Accelerator (Binning)    │ (Group polygons into 32x32 tiles) └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │  2. ISP (Image Synthesis Proc)    │ (Deferred Depth Test \& Z-Sort) └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────┐ │  3. TSP (Texture/Shading Proc)    │ (Shade only VISIBLE pixels) └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ [ On-Chip Frame Buffer ] }``


1.1 Tile Accelerator (Binning) The screen is divided into a grid of \textbf{\$32 \textbackslash times 32\$ pixel tiles}. During the geometry phase, the GPU's Tile Accelerator parses all polygons in the frame and bins them into local \textbf{Tile Lists} based on which tiles they intersect.


1.2 Image Synthesis Processor (ISP) For each tile, the ISP processes the binned polygon list. It performs hidden-surface removal (depth calculation) on a per-pixel level \textit{before} any texturing or shading occurs.


1.3 Texture and Shading Processor (TSP) Once the ISP determines exactly which polygon surface is visible for each pixel, the TSP applies textures, lighting, and mipmapping \textit{only} to those visible pixels. Overdraw is mathematically reduced to zero, maximizing pixel fillrate efficiency.


---


2. Simulation Implementation


To demonstrate this system, we have created a simulator script: [test\_dreamcast\_powervr.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/test\_dreamcast\_powervr.js).


This script: 1. Defines a scene with overlapping polygons at various depth (Z) levels. 2. Simulates the Tile Accelerator binning polygons into \$32 \textbackslash times 32\$ tiles. 3. Implements the ISP's deferred depth sorting, identifying the single visible polygon for a target coordinate. 4. Computes comparative statistics illustrating the fillrate savings of TBDR vs. immediate-mode rendering.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Sega Genesis Dual Cpu}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Sega Genesis Dual-CPU Bus Sharing Architecture


The \textbf{Sega Genesis} features a asymmetric multiprocessing layout containing a primary \textbf{Motorola 68000} CPU (running game logic) and a secondary \textbf{Zilog Z80} CPU (running sound drivers and controlling audio chips).


Because both CPUs share access to the system ROM and expansion ports, Sega engineers implemented a hardware handshake mechanism to prevent bus collisions.


---


1. The BUSREQ \& BUSACK Handshake


The Z80 operates on its own local 8KB RAM, but frequently needs to read audio data or sample streams directly from the main cartridge ROM.


To access the main bus: 1. \textbf{Bus Request (\texttt{BUSREQ})}: The Z80 (or main system controller) asserts the \texttt{BUSREQ} signal. 2. \textbf{Bus Acknowledge (\texttt{BUSACK})}: The 68000 finishes its current bus cycle, releases its control over the address/data buses, and asserts \texttt{BUSACK} to signal that the bus is free. 3. \textbf{Z80 Access}: The Z80 executes its read/write cycle over the main bus. 4. \textbf{Release}: The Z80 releases \texttt{BUSREQ}, the 68000 drops \texttt{BUSACK}, and the 68000 resumes executing game code.


``\texttt{ Z80 CPU                           68000 CPU ┌───────┐                         ┌─────────┐ │       │ ──── BUSREQ (Halt) ───► │  Busy   │ │       │                         └────┬────┘ │       │                              │ (Yield Bus) │       │ ◄─── BUSACK (Ack) ───────────┘ │       │ │       │ ──► [Read Cartridge ROM] │       │ │       │ ──── Release BUSREQ ──► [Resumes] └───────┘                         └─────────┘ }``


---


2. 68000 Control of Z80 Reset


To prevent the Z80 from accessing the bus during crucial memory operations, the 68000 can control the Z80 directly: \textit{ \textbf{Reset Register (\texttt{\$A11200})}: The 68000 can write \texttt{0x0000} to this register to hold the Z80 in a hard reset state (halting it), or \texttt{0x0100} to release it. } \textbf{Bus Request Register (\texttt{\$A11100})}: The 68000 can write \texttt{0x0100} to request the bus from the Z80, allowing the 68000 to write directly into the Z80's local 8KB RAM.


---


3. Simulation Implementation


To demonstrate this system, we have created a simulator script: [test\_sega\_dual\_cpu.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/test\_sega\_dual\_cpu.js).


This script: 1. Simulates memory-mapped control registers for \texttt{\$A11100} and \texttt{\$A11200}. 2. Models the state machine transitions of both the 68000 and Z80 during a bus request event. 3. Verifies that memory access blocks execute only when the proper lock conditions are met.

\section{Hardball Rendering System}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
C64 Hardball Wayland-Vulkan Presentation System


This document details the architectural layout of the C64 \textit{Hardball!} (1985) rendering simulator. The system uses a native \textbf{Wayland + Vulkan} presentation shell to display a C64-style retro baseball screen featuring the iconic pitcher's perspective.


---


1. Screen Layout \& Geometry


``\texttt{ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ SCOREBOARD:   VIS 0  HOME 2   INNING 5   S:0 B:1 O:2   │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │                                                        │ │                   / \textbackslash   Outfield Wall                   │ │                  /   \textbackslash                                  │ │                 /     \textbackslash   Infield Foul Lines            │ │                /   O   \textbackslash   Pitcher                      │ │               /    o    \textbackslash   Moving Ball                 │ │              /    / \textbackslash     \textbackslash                              │ │             /    O   O    \textbackslash   Catcher \& Batter          │ │            /  [Home Plate] \textbackslash                            │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ }``


The rendering grid mimics the 4:3 display ratio of standard CRT monitors: 1. \textbf{Scoreboard Header}: Static text and numbers tracking status. 2. \textbf{Perspective Foul Lines}: Screen coordinates projected from a focal vanishing point at the top center of the field down to the bottom corners. 3. \textbf{Player Sprites}: - \textbf{Pitcher}: Centered in the middle of the field (mound). - \textbf{Batter}: Standing to the left of home plate. - \textbf{Catcher}: Squatting directly behind home plate. 4. \textbf{Interactive Ball Path}: A particle vector shifting from the pitcher's hand towards the strike zone, scaling in size (z-depth simulation) per frame.


---


2. Compilation Target


The simulator is located at [test\_wayland\_hardball.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_hardball.c).


To compile and run it: ``\texttt{bash make tests/test\_wayland\_hardball ./tests/test\_wayland\_hardball }`\texttt{ \textit{Note: This utilizes our local }VulkanSystem` shell to hook into Wayland protocols and output frames directly into a presented presentation viewport.}


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Evm Memory Constraints}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Developing under Memory and Storage Constraints on the EVM


Like the 5 KB memory limitation of the Commodore VIC-20, the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) imposes severe constraints on memory, stack depth, and persistent storage. However, while retro computers were limited by physical hardware, the EVM is constrained by \textbf{economic gas costs} and \textbf{virtual architecture limits}.


This guide explains the EVM's memory, storage, and stack models, detailing how to optimize your code to build gas-efficient and functional smart contracts.


---


1. EVM Memory Architecture \& Constraints


The EVM has three main areas for holding data:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Memory Area & Persistence & Cost & Access Size & Characteristics \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Stack} & Ephemeral & Very Cheap & 32 bytes & LIFO stack, maximum depth of 1024 elements. \\ \hline
\textbf{Memory} & Ephemeral (Transaction lifetime) & Quadratic expansion & Byte-addressable & Linear, volatile memory array. \\ \hline
\textbf{Storage} & Permanent (On-chain) & Extremely Expensive & 32-byte slots & Key-value store mapping slots to values. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The Quadratic Memory Expansion Cost EVM memory is a linear, byte-addressable array initialized to zero. While writing to memory is initially cheap, the gas cost for memory expansion scales \textbf{quadratically} once you exceed 724 bytes (23 words).


The gas cost formula for expanding memory to \$N\$ words (32-byte chunks) is:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Gas\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{memory\}\} = 3 \textbackslash cdot N + \textbackslash lfloor \textbackslash frac\{N\textasciicircum 2\}\{512\} \textbackslash rfloor\$\$


> [!WARNING] > Because of the quadratic \$N\textasciicircum 2\$ term, large memory allocations (e.g., dynamically sized arrays, large string concatenations, or deep recursions) quickly become cost-prohibitive and can hit block gas limits.


---


2. Ephemeral Memory Optimization Patterns


Use \texttt{calldata} Instead of \texttt{memory} For read-only function parameters (especially arrays, structs, and strings), declaring them as \texttt{calldata} instead of \texttt{memory} avoids copying the data from transaction inputs into memory.


```solidity // Avoid: Copies array into volatile memory function processData(uint256[] memory items) external pure returns (uint256) \{ return items[0]; \}


// Preferred: Reads directly from transaction payload without memory expansion function processData(uint256[] calldata items) external pure returns (uint256) \{ return items[0]; \} ```


Memory Reuse \& Scratch Space In Yul assembly, the first 64 bytes (\texttt{0x00} to \texttt{0x3f}) are designated as \textbf{scratch space} for hashing methods. Using these slots for temporary operations avoids expanding the free memory pointer (located at \texttt{0x40}).


``\texttt{yul // Storing temporary variables in scratch space instead of expanding memory let temp := sload(someSlot) mstore(0x00, temp) let hash := keccak256(0x00, 32) }``


---


3. Storage Optimization \& Tight Variable Packing


Storage is the most expensive resource on the EVM. A single write (\texttt{SSTORE}) can cost up to 20,000 gas.


Tight Variable Packing (Solidity) Solidity groups sequential variables into the same 32-byte slot if their combined size fits. Always order variables to maximize packing density.


```solidity // Bad Layout: Takes 3 storage slots (3 x 32 bytes) struct UserBad \{ uint8 age;       // Slot 0 (1 byte) uint256 balance; // Slot 1 (32 bytes - cannot pack with uint8) uint8 level;     // Slot 2 (1 byte) \}


// Packed Layout: Takes 2 storage slots (1 slot saved!) struct UserGood \{ uint8 age;       // Slot 0 (1 byte) uint8 level;     // Slot 0 (1 byte) uint256 balance; // Slot 1 (32 bytes) \} ```


Transient Storage (\texttt{TSTORE}/\texttt{TLOAD}) Introduced in EIP-1153 (Cancun upgrade), transient storage behaves like normal storage but is cleared at the end of the transaction. It is perfect for reentrancy locks and passing data between separate calls in a single transaction without paying storage costs.


``\texttt{solidity // Reentrancy lock using Transient Storage (saves \textasciitilde 2,000+ gas compared to SSTORE) modifier nonReentrant() \{ assembly \{ if tload(0) \{ revert(0, 0) \} tstore(0, 1) \} \_; assembly \{ tstore(0, 0) \} \} }``


---


4. Overcoming the Stack Depth Limit (Stack Too Deep)


The EVM stack has a limit of 1024 slots, but instructions like \texttt{DUP} and \texttt{SWAP} can only reach the top \textbf{16 stack elements}. Attempting to access local variables deeper than 16 elements results in the infamous \texttt{"CompilerError: Stack too deep"} error.


Strategies to Bypass Stack Limits: 1. \textbf{Use Block Scoping:} Introduce internal scopes \texttt{\{\}} to discard variables from the stack as soon as they are no longer needed. 2. \textbf{Use Structs or Arrays:} Grouping local parameters inside a struct or passing them as an array uses a single stack reference (a pointer to memory) instead of allocating separate stack slots for each member. 3. \textbf{Encapsulate Logic in Helper Functions:} Breaking long functions into modular, focused helper routines keeps the active stack frame clean.

\section{Antic Cpu Terminal Improvements}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Improving the CPU Terminal with ANTIC Display Lists


The current Wayland CPU terminal shell ([test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c)) uses a monolithic, hardcoded rendering layout: a cyan divider line is drawn at a fixed coordinate (\$y=45\$), the header text is drawn at (\$20, 15\$), and characters are printed page-by-page via nested loops. Scrolling is implemented abruptly by shifting character row array indices.


By incorporating \textbf{ANTIC Display List} paradigms at the Wayland window level, we can fundamentally improve the terminal's architecture, adding support for \textbf{split-screen multi-pane layouts}, \textbf{smooth pixel-by-pixel scrolling}, and \textbf{zero-copy viewports}.


---


1. Architectural Enhancements


``` Monolithic Rendering (Current)              Display List Rendering (Proposed)


┌────────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  Status Header (Hardcoded) │              │  Mode 2 Instruction (Bar)  │ ├────────────────────────────┤              ├────────────────────────────┤ │                            │              │  Mode 4 Instruction (Text) │ │                            │              │  LMS: Point to Console RAM │ │   Text Console (Loops)     │              │                            │ │                            │              ├────────────────────────────┤ │                            │              │  Mode 8 Instruction (Diag) │ └────────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────────┘ ```


1.1 Dynamic Split-Screen Layouts (Multi-Mode Display Lists) Instead of hardcoding status bar divider limits, the terminal layout is defined dynamically as an array of ANTIC instruction structures: ``\texttt{c typedef struct \{ uint8\_t mode;             // Video rendering mode (Status bar text, Console text, 3D graphics) uint16\_t screen\_ram\_ptr;  // Memory source address (LMS pointer) uint8\_t line\_height;      // Number of scanlines for this band uint8\_t h\_scroll;         // Fine scroll offset \} TerminalDisplayInstruction; }`` By simply altering the Display List instruction array, the terminal can instantly add a split-screen debug window or display real-time graphics charts at the bottom of the screen, with zero changes to the underlying drawing loop.


1.2 Zero-Copy Viewport Control (LMS Pointers) Currently, scrolling the console requires iterating through characters and shifting row pointers in \texttt{g\_vram->grid}. * \textbf{Improvement:} The console text buffer is represented as a linear array. When the cursor moves past the visible screen limit, the terminal simply increments the \texttt{screen\_ram\_ptr} (LMS offset) of the active Display List instruction. This shifts the rendered console viewport instantly with \textbf{zero CPU cycles spent shifting characters}.


1.3 Smooth Sub-Character Scrolling (HSCROL/VSCROL) \textit{ \textbf{Current Limitation:} Text scrolling is discrete; it jumps character-by-character (18 pixels vertically or 10 pixels horizontally). } \textbf{Improvement:} Introduce \texttt{HSCROL} and \texttt{VSCROL} (0-7 pixel offsets). When the console receives input, the display engine increments the fine pixel scroll value. Once it reaches 8, it resets to 0 and increments the character offset pointer. This yields \textbf{smooth, modern pixel-by-pixel scrolling animations} for text consoles and files.


---


2. Display List Layout for the Terminal


Below is a proposed layout mapping the CPU terminal window:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Scanline Range & Mode ID & LMS Memory Pointer & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :---: & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{0–45} & \textbf{Mode 2 (Header)} & \texttt{\$0400} (Status RAM) & Renders the static title, system status, and cyan divider line. \\ \hline
\textbf{46–650} & \textbf{Mode 4 (Console)} & \texttt{\$0600} + Scroll Offset & Renders the interactive terminal character grid with fine vertical scrolling. \\ \hline
\textbf{651–720} & \textbf{Mode 8 (Gfx Graph)} & \texttt{\$2000} (Diagnostics) & Renders raw diagnostic line graphs showing real-time JIT compile cycles. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Verification Status


These architectural ANTIC paradigms are actively verified in our unified testing systems: - \textbf{Homeword/WordPac Tests}: Emulate zero-copy viewports, word wrapping, and line-split pointers. - \textbf{Automated Verification}: The automated exploratory suite [tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py) executes these emulations inside the terminal dashboard and validates the telemetry output and CPU state changes.

\section{Sega Hardware Innovations}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Sega Consumer Products — Hardware \& Video Architecture


Sega's hardware history is defined by highly modular, multi-coprocessor designs. From the 8-bit Sega Master System up to the 128-bit Dreamcast, Sega's engineering focused on massive sprite rendering and complex background scrolling plane layers.


This document details the video and audio mechanics of Sega's flagship systems: the \textbf{Sega Genesis (Mega Drive)} and the \textbf{Sega Saturn}.


---


1. Sega Genesis / Mega Drive VDP Architecture


The Sega Genesis Video Display Processor (VDP) managed graphics in parallel with the Motorola 68000 CPU.


1.1 Dual Scroll Planes (Plane A \& Plane B) Unlike simple tile layouts, the Genesis VDP supports two completely independent scrolling background layers: \textbf{Scroll Plane A} and \textbf{Scroll Plane B}. \textit{ \textbf{Window Plane}: A subset of Plane A can be locked as a non-scrolling Window (useful for HUDs/status bars) with zero CPU drawing overhead. } \textbf{Priority Mapping}: Each tile in Plane A or Plane B has a priority bit. When high-priority tiles are drawn, they cover sprites, allowing sprites to pass behind background elements (e.g. walking behind trees).


1.2 Line Scrolling (Raster Effects) The VDP allows changing the horizontal scroll offset of the background plane \textit{on a per-scanline basis}: \textit{ \textbf{Mode Selection}: Scroll values can be set for the entire screen, per tile row (8 pixels), or per individual scanline (1 pixel). } \textbf{Parallax Scrolling}: By offsetting each scanline slightly, games (such as \textit{Sonic the Hedgehog}) simulate complex 3D depth and parallax curves for horizons and water surfaces.


---


2. Sega Saturn: The VDP1 \& VDP2 Split


The Sega Saturn's architecture is famous for its complexity, relying on two distinct custom GPUs:


\textit{ \textbf{VDP1 (Sprite \& Polygon Processor)}: Renders sprites, textured quadrilaterals (Saturn does not use triangles), and wireframes into a dual frame buffer. } \textbf{VDP2 (Background Processor)}: An independent processor that composites the VDP1 sprite frame buffer with up to 5 background planes. VDP2 handles rotation, scaling, and perspective texture mapping on these planes (similar to Nintendo's Mode 7 but in multiple layers).


---


3. Sega Audio: Yamaha YM2612 FM Synthesis


The Genesis features the \textbf{Yamaha YM2612} Frequency Modulation (FM) sound synthesizer chip. \textit{ \textbf{Operators \& Channels}: 6 FM voices, each driven by 4 operators (sine wave generators that modulate each other's frequency). } \textbf{Feedback \& Algorithms}: Different configurations (algorithms) of these operators yield brassy, metallic, or synthesized waveforms. * \textbf{DAC Mode}: Channel 6 can act as an 8-bit DAC to play digital PCM samples (e.g. digitized speech like the classic "SEGA!" sound).


---


4. Emulation Verification


Our automated testing framework at [tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py) verifies these architectural models: - \textbf{Genesis VDP (SEGAVDP)}: Validates scrolling plane layout priority logic and scanline raster effects. - \textbf{Saturn VDP1 (SATURNVDP)}: Validates distorted quad rendering calculations and bilinear UV coordinates. These tests run successfully under mock CPU execution inside the terminal dashboard.

\section{Geos Operating System Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
GEOS (Graphical Environment Operating System) Architecture


Published by Berkeley Softworks in 1986, \textbf{GEOS} was a commercial marvel: a full, mouse-driven graphical operating system (complete with drop-down menus, windows, icons, and dynamic font selection) executing on a \textbf{1 MHz 6502 CPU} with only \textbf{64 KB of RAM}.


To achieve this, GEOS discarded the standard Commodore C64 KERNAL and implemented a sophisticated custom graphics kernel, an interrupt-driven input subsystem, and dynamic disk overlays.


This analysis details the low-level mechanics of the GEOS operating system and provides a Yul emulation mapping of its proportional font blitting engine.


---


1. Flagship Technical Innovations of GEOS


``\texttt{ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │                       64 KB RAM                        │ │   [\$0000 - \$0FFF]: Zero Page \& OS Buffers              │ │   [\$1000 - \$9FFF]: Active Application / Swap Space     │ │   [\$A000 - \$BF3F]: Hi-Res Screen Buffer (8 KB)         │ │   [\$C000 - \$FFFF]: GEOS KERNAL (Replaces Commodore)    │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ }``


1.1 Memory Overlays \& Swap Spaces Because the C64 RAM was capped at 64 KB, and the hi-res screen layout required 8 KB (\texttt{\$A000–\$BF3F}), GEOS apps had less than 40 KB of active heap space: \textit{ \textbf{Overlays:} Applications (like }geoWrite\textit{) were split into small, logical code segments. Opening a dialog box or selecting a menu option triggered an instant read from the floppy disk (or REU RAM disk) to load the necessary overlay code into memory, replacing the previous module. } \textbf{Disk Swapping:} When displaying dialog boxes, the OS saved the background bitmap pixels directly to disk or RAM expansion space, drawing the box, and restoring the pixels when closed.


1.2 Proportional Font Rendering Commodore’s standard text mode was strictly cell-based (8x8 pixel character grids). GEOS operated entirely in hi-res graphics mode (\$320 \textbackslash times 200\$), rendering proportional fonts: \textit{ \textbf{Font Strip Bitmaps:} Font characters were stored as tightly packed bitmap arrays. } \textbf{Software Blitter:} When rendering text, the KERNAL parsed the character width tables, read the character's bitmap pattern, and performed bit-shifting operations to align and draw the glyph at arbitrary pixel boundaries (not just 8-pixel character boundaries).


1.3 The GEOS KERNAL API GEOS replaced the Commodore KERNAL vectors with a rich suite of graphics and GUI control routines: \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{DrawString}:} Renders text using proportional font indices. } \textbf{\texttt{DoMenu}:} Automatically sets up mouse hot-spots, draws dropdown boxes, and listens for cursor clicks. * \textbf{\texttt{PromptBox}:} Draws standard user dialog boxes with custom button action vectors.


---


2. On-Chain Emulation: GEOS Proportional Font Blitter


Below is a Yul function demonstrating a software blitter loop. It emulates reading proportional character strips, calculating pixel alignments, and writing the shifted output directly to screen memory.


```yul // Method 24: simulateGeosFontBlit(characterAscii, xPixelOffset, yScanline, fontStripData, fontCharWidth) // Selector: 0xdc6b541a if eq(selector, 0xdc6b541a) \{ let ascii := calldataload(4) let xOffset := calldataload(36) let yLine := calldataload(68) let fontStrip := calldataload(100) let charWidth := calldataload(132)


if gt(charWidth, 16) \{ revert(0, 0) \} // Cap proportional width at 16 pixels


// 1. Calculate screen coordinates // C64 Hi-Res Screen is 40 columns x 25 rows of 8x8 character blocks. // Screen offset = (yLine / 8) \textit{ 320 + (xOffset / 8) } 8 + (yLine \% 8) let cellY := div(yLine, 8) let cellX := div(xOffset, 8) let lineInCell := mod(yLine, 8)


let screenMemoryOffset := add(add(mul(cellY, 320), mul(cellX, 8)), lineInCell)


// 2. Fetch shifted character pixels // Proportional characters can start at arbitrary bit boundaries. // We compute the bit shift needed within the target byte: let bitShift := mod(xOffset, 8)


// Shift the character strip right to align with the offset let shiftedStrip := shr(bitShift, fontStrip)


// 3. Blit onto target screen bytes (handling byte boundaries) // Read existing screen bytes from storage to perform transparent OR masking let byte1Offset := add(0x5000, screenMemoryOffset) // Virtual screen space starts at 0x5000 let byte2Offset := add(byte1Offset, 8) // Adjacent horizontal cell byte


let origByte1 := sload(byte1Offset) let origByte2 := sload(byte2Offset)


// Extract shifted bytes let drawByte1 := and(shr(8, shiftedStrip), 0xff) let drawByte2 := and(shiftedStrip, 0xff)


// Write blended pixel data back sstore(byte1Offset, or(origByte1, drawByte1)) sstore(byte2Offset, or(origByte2, drawByte2))


mstore(0x00, screenMemoryOffset) mstore(0x20, or(origByte1, drawByte1)) return(0x00, 64) \} ```


---


3. GEOS Performance Metrics (1 MHz 6502)


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
OS Operation & Time Taken & Mechanism \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Drop-Down Menu Draw} & \textasciitilde 0.15 seconds & Soft blit and background rectangle fill \\ \hline
\textbf{proportional Word Wrap} & Real-time typing & On-the-fly character width indexing \\ \hline
\textbf{Standard App Swap} & 3 - 5 seconds & Disk sector read (Track/Sector loading) \\ \hline
\textbf{REU RAM App Swap} & < 0.1 seconds & Fast DMA transfer via MOS 8726 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


4. Architectural Verification Status


The proportional font blitting and memory layout concept has been validated: - \textbf{Font Rasterization}: Validated via the custom terminal's UTF-32 styling and font engine. - \textbf{Continuous Memory Mirroring}: The automated testing suite [tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_terminal\_exploratory.py) verifies that the Yul CPU VM memory space (addresses starting at \texttt{0x4000}) continuously reflects the VRAM character grid, simulating the low-level screen overlays of GEOS.

\section{Ahoy Interrupt Music Maker}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
The Interrupt Music Maker/Editor (Ahoy! Issue 2, Page 39)


Pete Lobi's \textbf{Interrupt Music Maker/Editor} (IMM/E), published across Issues 1 and 2 of \textit{Ahoy!} magazine in early 1984, represents a classic milestone in background music driver design for the Commodore 64.


This document details the technical implementation, architectural design, memory layouts, and user command workflows of the software.


---


1. Architectural Design \& Interrupt Model


Unlike typical early 8-bit tracker software that locked the CPU in busy loops during sound execution, the IMM/E utilized the C64’s \textbf{Raster Interrupt (IRQ)} to modulate the Sound Interface Device (SID 6581) in the background.


``` +----------------------------------+

Main Editor Loop \\ \hline\hline
(Keyboard Inputs \& UX Render) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+----------------------------------+

\begin{table}[H]
\centering

\hline
IRQ Vector (\$0314/\$0315 Jump) \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+----------------------------------+


v +----------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Pete Lobi Playback Driver \\ \hline\hline
- Modulates Freq low/high \\ \hline

RTI (Return to Loop) \\ \hline\hline

+----------------------------------+ ```


1.1 Custom IRQ Hook The C64’s hardware interrupt vector at memory addresses \texttt{\$0314–\$0315} was redirected to point to the editor's machine language playback routine. Every raster screen tick (approx. 60Hz NTSC), the playback code: 1. Checked if the playback gate was active (\texttt{*P} mode enabled). 2. Advanced the internal note pointer. 3. Updated the 3 voice channels dynamically. 4. Jumps back to the normal kernel IRQ routine at \texttt{\$EA31} to handle the cursor blinking and keyboard scan matrix.


---


2. Command Set \& User Interface


On \textbf{page 39} of the February 1984 issue, Pete Lobi details the editor's key entry syntax, focusing on how voice parameters and commands are parsed:


2.1 Playback Command: \texttt{(\textit{P)} }   Typing *\textit{\texttt{(}P)}\textbf{ (with parentheses) triggers the }Play*\textit{ subroutine. }   Once triggered, the driver enables the IRQ gate, reading notes sequentially from memory blocks assigned to Voice 1, Voice 2, and Voice 3. *   Typing any key during playback returns the editor to interactive command mode.


2.2 Voice-Specific Registries Each note in the editor is stored as a character token. For example: \textit{   \texttt{C4} represents middle C. }   \texttt{T/S/P/N} specifies the voice waveform: \textit{   \textbf{T}: Triangle (Reg value: \texttt{\$11} / \texttt{17}) }   \textbf{S}: Sawtooth (Reg value: \texttt{\$21} / \texttt{33}) \textit{   \textbf{P}: Pulse/Square (Reg value: \texttt{\$41} / \texttt{65}) }   \textbf{N}: Noise (Reg value: \texttt{\$81} / \texttt{129})


---

4. Key Fixes in Issue 2 (Part II)


In the second installment of the article series, Pete Lobi resolved two significant bugs reported from the first release: 1. \textbf{The Exit Crash Bug}: The initial ML driver forgot to restore the default hardware vector at \texttt{\$0314} upon exit, leaving the CPU executing garbage memory when the user returned to BASIC. Part II added code to cleanly write \texttt{\$31} and \texttt{\$EA} back into the vector bytes before returning. 2. \textbf{Polyphonic Phase De-sync}: Voice 2 and Voice 3 envelopes sometimes fell out of sync due to clock division variances. The updated routine in Issue 2 synchronizes the gate-off ticks across all three channels.

\section{Synapse Software Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Synapse Software — Technical \& Physics Analysis


Founded in 1981 by \textbf{Ihor Wolosenko} and \textbf{Ken Grant}, \textbf{Synapse Software} was a premier developer of high-performance action titles for Atari 8-bit computers and the Commodore 64. Rather than focusing solely on arcade clones, Synapse became famous for pushing technical limits, implementing innovative physics models, and hiring legendary programmers like \textbf{Steve Hales} and \textbf{William Mataga}.


This document details Synapse's key mechanical milestones, specifically \textit{\textbf{Fort Apocalypse}} (1982) and \textit{\textbf{Shamus}} (1982), demonstrating how their 2D flight and state architectures translate to low-level assembly.


---


1. Flagship Technical Innovations


1.1 Helicopter Aerodynamics in \textit{Fort Apocalypse} (1982) Created by Steve Hales, \textit{Fort Apocalypse} features a multidirectional scrolling shooter where the player pilots a Rocket Copter: \textit{ \textbf{The Flight Model:} The game implements gravity and inertia vectors: - Vertical acceleration combines gravity (\$g\$) and variable rotor lift (\$F\_\{\textbackslash text\{lift\}\}\$): \$\$a\_y = F\_\{\textbackslash text\{lift\}\} - g\$\$ - Horizontal movement is governed by tilt-based thrust vectors: \$\$a\_x = F\_\{\textbackslash text\{lift\}\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash theta)\$\$ } \textbf{Landing Pad Detection:} To rescue hostages, the player must land flat on designated pads. Landing requires the helicopter to align its landing gear (yaw angle \$\textbackslash approx 0\$) and touch down below a maximum safe downward velocity threshold (\$v\_\{\textbackslash text\{safe\}\}\$) to prevent crashing.


1.2 Maze State-Tracking in \textit{Shamus} (1982) Developed by William Mataga, \textit{Shamus} is a maze action game featuring room-to-room navigation: \textit{ \textbf{Color-Coded Key States:} Progression is gated by locks of four distinct colors (Blue, Green, Yellow, Red). } \textbf{State Machine representation:} The program tracks the player's keys using a simple 4-bit register. Door openings query this register and clear the corresponding bit upon access.


---


2. On-Chain Emulation Schema: Helicopter Landing Physics


To model Steve Hales' flight and landing logic in Yul, we can evaluate coordinates, velocities, and orientation angles upon touchdown.


2.1 Physics Registers


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Memory Slot & Register Name & Data Range & Description \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{55400} & \textbf{Velocity X} & \texttt{-127 to 127} & Horizontal speed register \\ \hline
\texttt{55401} & \textbf{Velocity Y} & \texttt{-127 to 127} & Vertical speed register (negative is downward) \\ \hline
\texttt{55402} & \textbf{Helicopter Yaw} & \texttt{0 - 359} & Flight tilt angle (degrees, 0 is upright) \\ \hline
\texttt{55403} & \textbf{Pad Center X} & \texttt{0 - 320} & Landing pad horizontal center \\ \hline
\texttt{55404} & \textbf{Pad Top Y} & \texttt{0 - 200} & Landing pad vertical top boundary \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
2.2 Touchdown Collision Validator in Yul The following Yul function determines whether the copter successfully landed on the pad or crashed based on velocity thresholds, coordinates, and yaw offsets:


```yul // Validates helicopter touchdown physics on landing pad function checkLandingTouchdown(copX, copY, copYaw, vx, vy, padX, padY) -> landingState \{ // landingState outcomes: // 0 = In flight // 1 = Successful Landing (Safe state) // 2 = Crash (Velocity too high or tilted orientation)


// Check if helicopter base is at pad height (with tolerance of 2 units) let isAtPadY := 0 if and(iszero(lt(copY, padY)), lt(sub(copY, padY), 3)) \{ isAtPadY := 1 \}


if isAtPadY \{ // 1. Position Alignment Check // Copter center must align with pad center (width 32, i.e., distance < 16) let xDiff := 0 if gt(copX, padX) \{ xDiff := sub(copX, padX) \} if iszero(gt(copX, padX)) \{ xDiff := sub(padX, copX) \}


let aligned := lt(xDiff, 16)


// 2. Orientation (Yaw) Alignment Check // Copter must be upright (yaw offset < 10 degrees from 0/360) let upright := 0 if or(lt(copYaw, 10), gt(copYaw, 350)) \{ upright := 1 \}


// 3. Speed Check // Downward vertical velocity (vy) must not exceed safe threshold (e.g. -4) // Horizontal velocity (vx) must be negligible (absolute value < 3) let absVx := vx if lt(vx, 0) \{ absVx := sub(0, vx) \}


// vy is negative for downward flight; vertical speed must be between -4 and 0 let slowLanding := 0 // checks if vy >= -4 (in two's complement, greater than or equal is iszero(lt(vy, -4))) let vySafe := iszero(lt(vy, sub(0, 4))) if and(vySafe, lt(absVx, 3)) \{ slowLanding := 1 \}


// Evaluate conditions if and(aligned, and(upright, slowLanding)) \{ landingState := 1 // Safe Landing \} if iszero(and(aligned, and(upright, slowLanding))) \{ landingState := 2 // Crash \} \} \} ```


---


3. Synapse Electronic Novels \& The BTZ Parser


In 1984–1985, Synapse Software diversified from action arcade games into highly literary interactive fiction, coining the term \textbf{"Electronic Novels."}


3.1 The BTZ (Better Than Zork) Engine Written primarily by \textbf{William Mataga} and \textbf{Steve Hales}, the \textbf{BTZ engine} was designed to surpass Infocom's Z-machine parser capabilities: \textit{   \textbf{Sentence Complexity}: It supported compound sentences, nested clauses, and multiple direct objects (e.g., \texttt{TAKE ALL BUT THE BLUE KEY AND THEN PUT THEM IN THE BOX}). }   \textbf{Dynamic NPCs}: Characters in BTZ games possessed distinct schedules, moving independently through rooms and reacting dynamically to the player's conversation inputs rather than waiting for triggers. *   \textbf{Memory Paging}: Because C64 and Atari 8-bit RAM was limited to 64 KiB, the BTZ engine utilized an advanced virtual disk paging schema to pull text descriptions and vocabulary trees from floppy disk tracks on-demand.


3.2 Key Interactive Fiction Titles \textit{   }*\textit{Mindwheel} (1985)*\textit{: Written by U.S. Poet Laureate Robert Pinsky. The player travels through the minds of deceased historical figures (a poet, a musician, a dictator) to retrieve the "Wheel of Wisdom." }   **\textit{Brimstone} (1985)*\textit{: Based on Gawain’s dream journey, written by novelist James Paul. }   **\textit{Essex} (1985)*\textit{: A sci-fi space opera written by Bill Darrah. }   **\textit{Breakers} (1985)**: A dystopian cyberpunk story written by Rod Smith.


---

> [!TIP] > Steve Hales' \textit{Fort Apocalypse} implemented variable vector mechanics on an 8-bit 6502 CPU by caching local vector differences inside the zero page, freeing registers to update scrolling maps at high speeds.

Mercenary 3D Map, Room Objects, \& World Hollow Architecture


This document details the on-chain representation, 3D geometry engine, and interactive database structures modeling Novagen’s \textit{\textbf{Mercenary: Escape from Targ}} (1985) within the TSFi2 virtual ecosystem.


---


1. 3D Map Geometry \& World Hollow Coordinate Space


The planetary coordinate system for Targ and the subterranean complexes (such as the World Hollow/Central Complex) maps to a local 3D Cartesian space.


1.1 Emulated Vertex Map (17 Vertices) The 3D wireframe mesh representing the environment (ground grid, primary target building, and flying spaceship) is stored in Yul CPU VM memory slots starting at \texttt{55280} (\texttt{\$D7F0}):

\textbf{8–11} & \texttt{[-80, -45, -80]} to \texttt{[-80, -45, 80]} & Ground Coordinate Grid bounds & \texttt{55304 - 55315} \\ \hline

1.2 Line Connection Registry (24 Lines) Line connection mappings are stored starting at address \texttt{55536} (\texttt{\$D8F0}): \textit{   \textbf{Building Outlines (Lines 0–11)}: Front face, back face, and vertical columns. }   \textbf{Ground Outlines (Lines 12–15)}: Four lines defining boundary limits. *   \textbf{Spaceship Outlines (Lines 16–23)}: Base connections and apex struts.

2.2 Object Metadata Word Layout Each item in the Targ database is packed into a single 256-bit word at \texttt{2000000 + objId}: \textit{   \texttt{[0..7]}: Current Room ID (0 represents player inventory). }   \texttt{[8..23]}: Packed local X coordinate. \textit{   \texttt{[24..39]}: Packed local Y coordinate. }   \texttt{[40..55]}: Packed local Z coordinate. *   \texttt{[56..63]}: Interaction mask (e.g., \texttt{0x01} = collectible, \texttt{0x02} = keycard, \texttt{0x04} = energy source).


---


3. The Yul 3D Camera Projection Pipeline


The wireframe rendering pipeline uses trigonometric lookup tables and fixed-point math to project the 3D vertices onto the 2D C64 high-resolution viewport (320x200):


1.  \textbf{Yaw \& Pitch Rotation}: \$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} X' \&= X \textbackslash cos(\textbackslash text\{yaw\}) - Z \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash text\{yaw\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  Z' \&= X \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash text\{yaw\}) + Z \textbackslash cos(\textbackslash text\{yaw\}) \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$ 2.  \textbf{Perspective Division}: \$\$x\_\{\textbackslash text\{proj\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{X' \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{scale\}\}\{Z' + \textbackslash text\{depth\}\} + \textbackslash text\{offset\}\_x\$\$ \$\$y\_\{\textbackslash text\{proj\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{Y' \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{scale\}\}\{Z' + \textbackslash text\{depth\}\} + \textbackslash text\{offset\}\_y\$\$ 3.  \textbf{Rasterization Strobe}: Writing \texttt{1} to memory address \texttt{54966} triggers the GPU/ReBAR projection thunk. If successful, the engine stores the final screen line coordinates starting at \texttt{55800} and sets register \texttt{54967} to \texttt{1}.

\section{Zmachine Onchain Composition}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
On-Chain Z-Machine Engine Composition


The \textit{\textbf{ZMachine}} virtual contract (implemented in [\texttt{zmachine.yul}](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/zmachine.yul)) is composed as an on-chain virtual machine interpreter capable of parsing standard Infocom-style interactive fiction story files.


This document details how rooms, string parsing, and object states are structured and executed on-chain.


---


1. Core Structural Composition


``` +-------------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Z-Machine Story File \\ \hline\hline
- Header Data (Offsets to Object Table, Dictionary, etc.) \\ \hline
- Object Table (Rooms, Items, Parent-Child Connections) \\ \hline
- Z-String Data (Packed 5-bit text characters) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------------+


[Uploaded via uploadRomChunk] v +-------------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
EVM Storage Slots \\ \hline\hline
- Mapped starting at slot index 1000000 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------------+


[Evaluated by ZMachine Yul Core] v +-------------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Dynamic Command Parser \& Interpreter \\ \hline\hline
- decodeZString() -> Unpacks text descriptions \\ \hline
- readObjectProperty() -> Computes exits \& room states \\ \hline
- parseCommand() -> Coordinates interactive text loops \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------------+ ```


1.1 ROM Chunk Paging Because story files exceed typical transaction size boundaries, the Z-Machine uses segment paging: \textit{   \textbf{Method}: \texttt{uploadRomChunk(uint256 offset, bytes data)} (\texttt{0xf5a83724}). }   \textbf{Storage}: Each 32-byte chunk is stored sequentially in EVM slots starting at \texttt{1000000} + \texttt{div(offset, 32)}. *   \textbf{Access}: Low-level helper functions \texttt{readRom16} and \texttt{readRom8} retrieve bytes dynamically out of the storage slots on demand.


---


2. Dynamic Room \& Object Resolution


Rooms are represented as Z-Machine objects. Instead of hardcoding descriptions and exits, the interpreter parses the Z-object tables:


2.1 Object Entry Layout Each object entry inside the story file header contains a fixed structural schema: 1.  \textbf{Attributes}: Bitmask flags specifying object status (e.g. is it container, light source, open, closed). 2.  \textbf{Parent/Sibling/Child Pointers}: Defines room inheritance (e.g. is item \textit{inside} a container, or is container \textit{inside} a room). 3.  \textbf{Property Table Offset}: A 16-bit pointer to custom data attributes (e.g. room descriptions, navigation directions).


2.2 Property Parsing in Yul The Yul interpreter parses properties via \texttt{readObjectProperty(objId, propId)}: \textit{   It reads the object table base address from ROM offset \texttt{10}. }   It walks the property chain, checking property IDs (\texttt{id == propId}). *   If found, it returns the value (e.g. the room index or the Z-string text pointer).


---


3. Packed Z-String Text Decoder


Text descriptions in Z-Machine files are packed into 16-bit words containing three 5-bit characters each: \textit{   \textbf{Bit 15}: End-of-string flag (set to \texttt{1} on the final word). }   \textbf{Bits 14–10}: Character 1. \textit{   \textbf{Bits 9–5}: Character 2. }   \textbf{Bits 4–0}: Character 3.


3.1 Unpacking Logic (\texttt{decodeZString}) The decoder converts 5-bit codes into 8-bit ASCII characters by swapping alphabet tables: \textit{   \textbf{Alphabet 0}: Default lowercase letters (\texttt{a-z}). }   \textbf{Alphabet 1}: Uppercase letters (\texttt{A-Z}). \textit{   \textbf{Shift Characters}: Code \texttt{4} or \texttt{5} changes the alphabet state for the next character. }   \textbf{Output}: Unpacked bytes are stored directly in EVM memory and returned as a standard Solidity dynamic \texttt{string}.

\section{Platform Display Model}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Unified Platform Display Architecture \& Camera Models


To support different game genres (ranging from textual adventure interfaces to pseudo-3D racers and true 3D wireframe environments), this platform display model integrates multiple rendering modes and camera projection pipelines.


By utilizing our host-side Vulkan presentation engine, we can swap between these display styles and camera modes dynamically without rewriting core execution logic.


---


1. Multi-Style Presentation Layer


The Vulkan pipeline is structured to interpret the memory registers in several distinct \textbf{Design Styles}:


``\texttt{ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │     Vulkan Presentation       │ │     Host Display Engine       │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐ ▼                             ▼                             ▼ ┌─────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────┐ │  Terminal/Text  │           │  2D Tiled/Scroll│           │  Scanline 3D    │ │  - Char grids   │           │  - Sprites      │           │  - Pseudo-3D    │ │  - Status bars  │           │  - HSCROL/VSCROL│           │  - Road bend    │ └─────────────────┘           └─────────────────┘           └─────────────────┘ }``


1.1 Terminal \& Text Style (Interactive Fiction) \textit{ \textbf{Description:} A text grid rendering characters from a font map. } \textbf{Vulkan Pipeline:} Uses a character map texture as an index layer. The fragment shader resolves font glyphs directly from an ASCII character RAM buffer. * \textbf{Layout:} Typically a fixed grid (e.g., 40x25 or 80x25 characters) with status overlays and terminal prompt feedback.


1.2 2D Tiled \& Scrolling Style (Shamus / Rainbow Walker) \textit{ \textbf{Description:} Orthographic tilemaps with hardware-assisted sprite composition. } \textbf{Vulkan Pipeline:} Uses ANTIC-style Display List scrolling registers. The host binds specific texture atlases representing background grids and cycles colors dynamically. * \textbf{Scroller registers:} Fine horizontal (\texttt{HSCROL}) and vertical (\texttt{VSCROL}) offsets are applied in the vertex shader to shift the viewport without rewriting the map buffer.


1.3 Pseudo-3D Scanline Style (Pole Position) \textit{ \textbf{Description:} Linear horizontal shifting per scanline to project curved road planes and scaling lanes. } \textbf{Vulkan Pipeline:} Modifies the horizontal translation parameter dynamically in the vertex shader for each scanline band. By loading a curvature lookup table, the shader shifts scanline coordinates to simulate curves: \$\$x\_\{\textbackslash text\{render\}\} = x\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\} + \textbackslash Delta x\_\{\textbackslash text\{curve\}\}(y)\$\$


1.4 True 3D Wireframe Style (Mercenary) \textit{ \textbf{Description:} Vector graphics mesh renderer utilizing vertex buffers and camera transformation matrices. } \textbf{Vulkan Pipeline:} Performs real matrix transformations (rotation, translation, perspective projection) directly in the vertex shader or via fixed-point helper code. Renders wireframes using line list primitives (\texttt{VK\_PRIMITIVE\_TOPOLOGY\_LINE\_LIST}).


---


2. Dynamic Camera Model \& Matrix Pipeline


To handle different perspectives, the system implements a unified matrix configuration register set starting at memory slot \texttt{55100}:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Register Address & Name & Data Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{55100–55102} & \textbf{Cam Position \texttt{[X, Y, Z]}} & \texttt{int32} (Fixed-point 16.16) & Coordinates of the active camera \\ \hline
\texttt{55103–55105} & \textbf{Cam Rotation \texttt{[Pitch, Yaw, Roll]}} & \texttt{int16} (Euler Angles) & Orientation registers (degrees) \\ \hline
\texttt{55106} & \textbf{Camera Mode} & \texttt{uint8} & ID of active projection model \\ \hline
\texttt{55107} & \textbf{FOV / Scale} & \texttt{uint16} & Field of view angle or orthographic scale \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
2.1 First-Person Perspective Cam (Mode \texttt{0}) \textit{ \textbf{Use Case:} Cockpit view, flight simulators, or first-person exploration. } \textbf{Projection:} Perspective division projects 3D coords onto the 2D plane: \$\$x' = \textbackslash frac\{X \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{FOV\}\}\{Z\} + \textbackslash text\{Center\}\_x\$\$ \$\$y' = \textbackslash frac\{Y \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{FOV\}\}\{Z\} + \textbackslash text\{Center\}\_y\$\$


2.2 Third-Person Follow / Chase Cam (Mode \texttt{1}) \textit{ \textbf{Use Case:} Racing games (}Pole Position\textit{) and pseudo-3D jumpers (}Rainbow Walker\textit{). } \textbf{Projection:} The camera coordinates trace a target coordinate with a fixed distance (\$d\$) and elevation (\$h\$) offset: \$\$\textbackslash vec\{P\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{cam\}\} = \textbackslash vec\{P\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{player\}\} - \textbackslash vec\{D\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{facing\}\} \textbackslash cdot d + \textbackslash vec\{U\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{up\}\} \textbackslash cdot h\$\$ * The projection matrix applies dynamic tilt angles, making the camera lean in curves.


2.3 Orthographic Top-Down / Side Cam (Mode \texttt{2}) \textit{ \textbf{Use Case:} 2D mazes (}Shamus\textit{), maps, or tactical screens. } \textbf{Projection:} Maps coords linearly, discarding depth calculations to render orthographic views: \$\$x' = X \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{scale\} + \textbackslash text\{Offset\}\_x\$\$ \$\$y' = Y \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{scale\} + \textbackslash text\{Offset\}\_y\$\$


---


3. Implementation Blueprint in Vulkan Shaders


Our vertex shader pipeline dynamically handles these modes using the \texttt{CameraMode} register:


```glsl \#version 450


layout(location = 0) in vec3 inPosition; layout(location = 1) in vec4 inColor;


layout(push\_constant) uniform CameraBlock \{ vec3 camPos; vec3 camRot; uint camMode; float scale; \} camera;


layout(location = 0) out vec4 outColor;


void main() \{ outColor = inColor; vec3 pos = inPosition - camera.camPos;


// Apply Euler rotations (Yaw/Pitch) float cy = cos(camera.camRot.y); float sy = sin(camera.camRot.y); float cp = cos(camera.camRot.x); float sp = sin(camera.camRot.x);


// Yaw float rx = pos.x \textit{ cy - pos.z } sy; float rz = pos.x \textit{ sy + pos.z } cy; // Pitch float ry = pos.y \textit{ cp - rz } sp; rz = pos.y \textit{ sp + rz } cp;


if (camera.camMode == 0 camera.camMode == 1) \{ // Perspective Camera Modes (First \& Third Person) float zDepth = rz + 1.0; // Avoid division by zero gl\_Position = vec4((rx \textit{ camera.scale) / zDepth, (ry } camera.scale) / zDepth, zDepth / 1000.0, 1.0); \} else \{ // Orthographic Camera Mode (2D / Map) gl\_Position = vec4(rx \textit{ camera.scale, ry } camera.scale, 0.0, 1.0); \} \} ```


---


> [!NOTE] > By offloading projection decisions to the host shader using the \texttt{CameraMode} register, the guest game loop merely updates object coordinates in memory, completely bypassing CPU math bottlenecks.

\section{Razor Protocol Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
RazoR Protocol: Implementing Micro-Ware Concepts on-Chain


This document defines how the core concepts of \textbf{Micro-Ware Distributing, Inc.} (low-level nibble copying, uncopy signature protection, and serial/parallel bridging) map to a decentralized verification and oracle protocol (the \textbf{RazoR Protocol}) within our EVM/Yul context.


---


1. Concept Mapping Matrix


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Micro-Ware 8-Bit Concept & RazoR Protocol On-Chain Translation & Technical Implementation \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{The Clone Machine (Raw Nibbling)} & \textbf{Direct Storage Slot Verification} & Bypassing Solidity high-level getters to read raw EVM storage slots using \texttt{sload}. \\ \hline
\textbf{Uncopy (Disk Copy Protection)} & \textbf{Commit-Reveal \& Proof-of-Authenticity} & Cryptographic verification signatures protecting assets from simple replication/replay attacks. \\ \hline
\textbf{Parallel Printer Interface} & \textbf{Cross-Chain / VM Oracle Bridge} & Relaying inputs/outputs between the sandboxed ZMM-VM and EVM via standardized RPC logs. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Architectural Layout


``\texttt{ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │          RazoR Oracle Protocol               │ │      Decentralized Validation Gate           │ └──────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐ ▼                       ▼                       ▼ ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐ │  Raw Nibbler SLOAD│   │ Commit-Reveal Auth│    │ VM Oracle Bridge │ │ - Bypasses getters│   │ - Anti-replay    │    │ - Cross-VM logs  │ │ - Raw slot scans │   │ - Hash lock gates│    │ - Relays I/O     │ └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘ }``


---


3. RazoR Protocol Yul Engine Blueprint


The following Yul contract snippet implements the RazoR protocol. It enables: 1. \textbf{Raw Storage Nibbler (\texttt{0x11223344})}: Reads any raw storage slot directly, replicating low-level floppy drive bitstream extraction. 2. \textbf{Commit-Reveal Auth (\texttt{0x55667788})}: Assures the authenticity of digital assets by requiring a commit-reveal cycle to prevent copy replays. 3. \textbf{Bridge Relayer (\texttt{0x99aabbcc})}: Bridges data variables from the ZMM guest VM environment to the host EVM using event logs.


```yul object "RazorProtocol" \{ code \{ sstore(0, caller()) datacopy(0, dataoffset("runtime"), datasize("runtime")) return(0, datasize("runtime")) \}


object "runtime" \{ code \{ let selector := shr(224, calldataload(0))


switch selector


// 1. Raw Nibbler: Bypasses getter calls to read raw storage slots // Selector: 0x11223344 (nibbleRead) case 0x11223344 \{ let targetSlot := calldataload(4) let value := sload(targetSlot) mstore(0x00, value) return(0x00, 32) \}


// 2. Commit-Reveal Auth: Implements "Uncopy" protection gates // Selector: 0x55667788 (commitRevealCheck) case 0x55667788 \{ let player := calldataload(4) let committedHash := calldataload(36) let salt := calldataload(68) let revealedValue := calldataload(100)


// Verify if hash(revealedValue, salt) matches committedHash mstore(0x00, revealedValue) mstore(0x20, salt) let computedHash := keccak256(0x00, 0x40)


let valid := eq(computedHash, committedHash) mstore(0x00, valid) return(0x00, 32) \}


// 3. Oracle Bridge: Relays output between ZMM-VM and EVM via Logs // Selector: 0x99aabbcc (emitBridgeSignal) case 0x99aabbcc \{ let devId := calldataload(4)    // e.g. Port 1 printer let payload := calldataload(36)  // data byte


// Emit log indicating transaction/parallel output // log2(memOffset, size, topic1, topic2) mstore(0x00, payload) log2(0x00, 32, 0xbridgeSignalTopic, devId)


mstore(0x00, 1) return(0x00, 32) \}


default \{ revert(0, 0) \} \} \} \} ```


---


> [!TIP] > By mapping the physical 8-bit utility concepts (nibbling, hardware bridging, and copy prevention) into direct storage validation, cryptographic hash locks, and VM event logging, we align Micro-Ware's design model with the trustless standards of the RazoR protocol.

\section{Game Archetypes Spec}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Game Archetypes for Automated Vulkan Rendering Pipelines


This specification defines the coordinate registers, state databases, and graphics pipelines for \textbf{Candy Bandit} (2D Platformer/Maze style) and \textbf{Speed Racer} (Pseudo-3D Racer style).


These archetypes serve as a baseline model for developing automated presentation-layer rendering systems in our Vulkan framework.


---


1. Candy Bandit Archetype (2D Platformer \& Grid)


\textit{Candy Bandit} represents a classic multi-screen platform/maze action game. The state represents tile structures, player coordinates, and enemy motion vectors.


``\texttt{ Logical Viewport (320 x 200) -> Mapped to 40 x 25 Char Grid ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ [Score: 00240]                       [Candies: 04 / 08]│ │                                                        │ │     \#============================================\#     │ │     \#                                            \#     │ │     \#    + (Player)                              \#     │ │     \#                                            \#     │ │     \#                o (Candy)     X (Guard)     \#     │ │     \#============================================\#     │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ }``


1.1 Memory Register Layout (Storage Namespace \texttt{3000600+})


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Storage Slot & Name & Data Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{3000600} & \textbf{Player X} & \texttt{uint16} & Horizontal position (0–319 pixel space) \\ \hline
\texttt{3000601} & \textbf{Player Y} & \texttt{uint16} & Vertical position (0–199 pixel space) \\ \hline
\texttt{3000602} & \textbf{Player Action State} & \texttt{uint8} & \texttt{0} = Stand, \texttt{1} = Walk, \texttt{2} = Jump, \texttt{3} = Climb \\ \hline
\texttt{3000603} & \textbf{Active Score} & \texttt{uint32} & Total candy score accumulated \\ \hline
\texttt{3000604} & \textbf{Level Candy Count} & \texttt{uint8} & Remaining candies on the screen \\ \hline
\texttt{3000610–3000617} & \textbf{Candy Coords \texttt{[X, Y]}} & \texttt{uint8} packed & Coords of up to 8 active candy items \\ \hline
\texttt{3000620–3000635} & \textbf{Guard Databases} & packed \texttt{uint256} & 4 guards: Coords, facing direction, patrol limits \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
1.2 Automated Vulkan Rendering Mapping \textit{ \textbf{Background Tilemap Shader}: Parses a 1000-byte character RAM block. The vertex shader divides the viewport into a 40x25 grid, and the fragment shader overlays brick and ladder textures based on the byte values. } \textbf{Sprite Pipeline}: The automated system monitors slots \texttt{3000600} (Player) and \texttt{3000620} (Guards). It instantiates Vulkan billboard primitives at the calculated screen offsets, matching the current frame state (e.g. walk/climb frames) without CPU intervention.


---


2. Speed Racer Archetype (Pseudo-3D Scanline racer)


\textit{Speed Racer} models a high-speed racing environment utilizing a pseudo-3D scanning road layout.


``\texttt{ Horizon (Scanline 80) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── /\textbackslash   (Mountain background) /  \textbackslash  /    \textbackslash  /  \textbackslash  /   \textbackslash  /    \textbackslash   (Opponent vehicle) /     \textbackslash  /     [██]     \textbackslash  /       \textbackslash  /        \textbackslash  ──────────────/        /  \textbackslash         \textbackslash ──────────────────── /        /    \textbackslash         \textbackslash  /        /      \textbackslash         \textbackslash  }``

Storage Slot & Name & Data Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{3000700} & \textbf{Vehicle Speed} & \texttt{uint16} & Forward speed scaling factor \\ \hline

\texttt{3000702} & \textbf{Distance Traveled} & \texttt{uint32} & Metric distance along the active track \\ \hline
\texttt{3000703} & \textbf{Current Curvature} & \texttt{int16} & Target curve rate (negative is left, positive right) \\ \hline

2.2 Automated Vulkan Rendering Mapping \textit{ \textbf{Road Projection Shader}: Renders the road lines dynamically. Instead of pushing a static mesh, the shader reads the \textbf{Road Curve Lookup} buffer (\texttt{3000720+}) and the \texttt{VehicleSteerOffset}. } \textbf{Scanline Offset Shader}: For each scanline index \$y\$ representing the road region (scanline 80 to 239): \$\$X\_\{\textbackslash text\{center\}\}(y) = \textbackslash text\{Center\}\_x + \textbackslash text\{CurveLookup\}[y - 80] - \textbackslash text\{SteerOffset\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{scale\}(y)\$\$ The fragment shader renders alternating green/brown side grass bands and grey asphalt lanes relative to \$X\_\{\textbackslash text\{center\}\}(y)\$. * \textbf{Sprite Scaling}: Opponent cars are rendered as sprites. The system reads the opponent distance relative to the player, dynamically scaling the sprite scale in the vertex shader: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Scale\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash text\{SpriteScale\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\}\}\{\textbackslash text\{Distance\} + 1.0\}\$\$

> [!NOTE] > By mapping these structures to explicit storage slots, the host presentation system can implement optimized pipeline shaders specifically tuned for 2D platforming (scrolling billboard sprites) or pseudo-3D racing (scanline-curved road rendering).

\section{Onchain Database Manager}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
On-Chain Database Manager (Solidity \& Yul Hybrid)


This specification defines the architecture, storage layouts, and lookup schemas for a gas-optimized \textbf{On-Chain Database Manager} inspired by the 1980s \textbf{Mirage Concepts Database Manager} (incorporating free-form dynamic fields, custom calculated fields, and 16-bit indexing).


---


1. Storage Layout \& Mirage Packing Schema


To support the free-form structure of the Mirage Database Manager (which allowed up to 200 fields per record and multi-level calculations) while minimizing gas on the EVM, the Database Manager implements \textbf{Dynamic Field Allocation} rather than static struct layouts.


1.1 Record Header Layout (256-bit Control Word) Each record is indexed via a \texttt{uint16} identifier (supporting up to 65,535 records, matching Mirage's historical file limits). The first slot of a record acts as a Control Word:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Field Name & Bit Range & Data Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Record ID} & \texttt{[0..15]} & \texttt{uint16} & Unique record identifier (0–65535) \\ \hline
\textbf{Field Count} & \texttt{[16..23]} & \texttt{uint8} & Number of active fields in the record (max 200) \\ \hline
\textbf{Active Flags} & \texttt{[24..31]} & \texttt{uint8} & State flags (e.g. locked, synchronized) \\ \hline
\textbf{Field Offset Pointer} & \texttt{[32..255]} & \texttt{bytes28} & Packed offsets pointing to field text boundaries \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Dynamic Field Storage \& Calculations


Following the Mirage Concepts design, fields can be dynamically recalculated.


2.1 Calculated Fields Engine A dedicated Yul calculator allows field values to be computed on-the-fly using simple arithmetic formulas (e.g., \texttt{Field 3 = Field 1 * Field 2}).


``\texttt{yul // Calculates values dynamically for calculated fields in Yul function evaluateCalculatedField(valA, valB, operator) -> result \{ switch operator case 1 \{ result := add(valA, valB) \} // Addition case 2 \{ result := sub(valA, valB) \} // Subtraction case 3 \{ result := mul(valA, valB) \} // Multiplication case 4 \{ if valB \{ result := div(valA, valB) \} // Division \} \} }``


---


3. Hybrid Solidity-Yul Database Contract


The following blueprint demonstrates how Solidity manages interface definitions and access control, while inline Yul handles the raw bit-shifting for record packing and dynamic field lookups.


```solidity // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity \textasciicircum 0.8.20;


contract OnChainDatabaseManager \{ address public owner;


// Base storage slot namespace for records bytes32 private constant RECORDS\_SLOT\_BASE = 0xa31e7d2b8b9a10242801b070e92313f0c5d5d121235B13a2B87B10242801b070;


struct Record \{ uint16 recordId; uint8 fieldCount; uint8 flags; bytes32 fieldData; \}


modifier onlyOwner() \{ require(msg.sender == owner, "Not Authorized"); \_; \}


constructor() \{ owner = msg.sender; \}


/*\textit{ } @notice Pack and insert a record directly into EVM storage using Yul. */ function insertRecord( uint16 recordId, uint8 fieldCount, uint8 flags, bytes32 fieldData ) external onlyOwner \{ bytes32 targetSlot = getStorageSlot(recordId);


assembly \{ // Pack variables into a single 256-bit control word let word := recordId word := or(word, shl(16, fieldCount)) word := or(word, shl(24, flags)) word := or(word, shl(32, shr(32, fieldData)))


// Write to storage slot sstore(targetSlot, word) \} \}


/*\textit{ } @notice Retrieve and unpack a record directly using Yul. */ function getRecord(uint16 recordId) external view returns (Record memory rec) \{ bytes32 targetSlot = getStorageSlot(recordId);


assembly \{ let word := sload(targetSlot)


// Unpack fields mstore(rec, and(word, 0xFFFF))                       // recordId mstore(add(rec, 32), and(shr(16, word), 0xFF))       // fieldCount mstore(add(rec, 64), and(shr(24, word), 0xFF))       // flags mstore(add(rec, 96), and(word, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF00000000)) // fieldData \} \}


/*\textit{ } @notice Helper to calculate the record storage slot hash. */ function getStorageSlot(uint16 recordId) public pure returns (bytes32) \{ return keccak256(abi.encodePacked(RECORDS\_SLOT\_BASE, recordId)); \} \} ```


---


4. Advantages of the Mirage-Inspired Hybrid Approach


1. \textbf{Free-Form Dynamic Fields}: By using packed offset pointers rather than rigid Solidity schemas, users can define and resize fields dynamically (up to 200 fields), mirroring the flexibility of the original Commodore 64 application. 2. \textbf{On-Chain Calculations}: The arithmetic helper engine enables instant on-chain field calculations, bypassing the need to compute results in client-side code. 3. \textbf{Optimized 16-Bit Indexing}: Matches the 65,535 file record boundary of the original software, keeping key-indexing words compact and gas consumption light.

Music Utility System)}: A parser and interpreter for the custom macro-based music notation syntax published in the magazine. We will build a Yul-based AMUS parser extending our existing music notation system. }   \textbf{16-bit POKEY Audio}: Support combining POKEY audio channels (channels 1+2 or 3+4) for high-fidelity 16-bit pitch resolution.

\section{Analog Assembly Animation}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Technical Report: A.N.A.L.O.G. Assembly Animation Implementations


We have modeled and verified the core assembly animation methodologies popularized by \textit{A.N.A.L.O.G. Computing} magazine for the Atari 8-bit architecture. Below are the functional specifications and implementation paths for these techniques.


---


1. Player/Missile Graphics (PMG) Shift Loops


Atari PMG animation typically shifts bytes vertically in memory or swaps pointers to alternate graphics patterns.


We model this loop in assembly/memory spaces by simulating a 6502 pointer traversal over standard \texttt{\$D407} (\texttt{PMBASE}) page allocations:


``\texttt{ [PMBASE Page] --> [Offset + Y] --> [LDA (Sprite Frame A)] --> [STA (Target Address)] }``


Verification Logic: ```javascript function simulatePmgVerticalShift(pmgBase, spriteHeight, shiftOffset) \{ let memory = new Array(2048).fill(0); // Write initial sprite pattern (8 bytes) at offset 120 const pattern = [0x3C, 0x7E, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0x7E, 0x3C]; for (let i = 0; i < pattern.length; i++) \{ memory[120 + i] = pattern[i]; \}


// Simulate high-speed 6502 assembly shift loop // LDY \#8 (height) // LOOP: LDA mem, Y+offset -> STA mem, Y+offset+shift for (let y = spriteHeight - 1; y >= 0; y--) \{ const val = memory[120 + y]; memory[120 + y] = 0; // Clear old pixel memory[120 + y + shiftOffset] = val; // Shift down \} return memory; \} ```


---


2. Display List Interrupt (DLI) Color Animations


To change colors mid-scanline, the ANTIC processor sets the DLI interrupt bit. The CPU stops and modifies color registers in real-time.


``\texttt{ Scanline n: [PF0 Color: Blue] DLI -> WSYNC (\$D40A) -> Wait Electron Beam -> Write \$D016 (PF0 Color: Red) Scanline n+1: [PF0 Color: Red] }``


Verification Logic: ```javascript function simulateDliColorSwap(displayList, scanlineInterruptMap) \{ let activeColor = 0x02; // Default Blue let log = [];


for (let line = 0; line < 262; line++) \{ if (scanlineInterruptMap[line]) \{ // Trigger DLI: Wait for WSYNC and swap color register to Red (0x04) activeColor = 0x04; \} log.push(\{ scanline: line, color: activeColor \}); \} return log; \} ```


---


3. Page Flipping (Double Buffering)


Alternating between two separate display addresses during the Vertical Blank Interrupt (VBI) creates flicker-free transitions.


``\texttt{ VBI Triggered -> Check Frame Index -> Update ANTIC LMS Address (\$58/\$59) -> Swap }``


Verification Logic: ```javascript function simulatePageFlip(vbiEventCount) \{ const BufferA = 0x4000; const BufferB = 0x6000; let lmsPointer = BufferA;


for (let frame = 0; frame < vbiEventCount; frame++) \{ lmsPointer = (lmsPointer === BufferA) ? BufferB : BufferA; \} return lmsPointer; \} ```


---


4. Test Integration Summary


These simulation steps have been incorporated into the core architectural validation workflows, verifying coordinate offsets, register states, and transition timings during each frame rendering loop.
