\section{Entech Software Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
En-Tech Software — Technical \& Music Processing Analysis


Founded in 1983 in Arleta/Sun Valley, California, \textbf{En-Tech Software} (often stylized as \textbf{Entech}) was an early publisher and distributor of utility, educational, and music software for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20. Rather than focusing on graphical arcade titles, En-Tech specialized in user utilities, creating some of the earliest structural tools for C64 composers and database managers.


This document details En-Tech's signature products, mechanical pipelines, and low-level music transpose operations.


---


1. Flagship Technical Products


1.1 Studio 64: The "Word Processor for Music" En-Tech’s most successful release was \textbf{Studio 64} (1983), marketed as an advanced editor for SID musical structures: \textit{   \textbf{Block-Level Editing}: Inspired by word processor features like copy/cut/paste, it allowed composers to select blocks of notes (tracks) and execute operations such as transpositions, repetitions, or insertions without re-entering notes. }   \textbf{Dynamic Transposition}: It allowed shifting note pitches up or down by semitones. This was governed by logarithmic frequency scaling: \$\$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{new\}\} = f\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\} \textbackslash cdot 2\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash Delta\_\{\textbackslash text\{semitones\}\}\}\{12\}\}\$\$ \textit{   \textbf{Printing Integration}: Outputted formatted music lead sheets directly to early parallel/serial dot-matrix printers. }   \textbf{Contest Marketing}: To drive adoption, En-Tech hosted a nationwide "Songwriting Contest" in 1984, promising Hollywood studio recording time to the winner.


1.2 Data Base 64 A simplified database manager designed for home and small business use. \textit{   \textbf{Field Allocation}: Utilized static sequential files (SEQ) rather than relative records (REL), saving directory footprint at the cost of random-access speeds. }   \textbf{Memory Footprint}: Designed to fit in low-memory boundaries, allowing a full database structure to run alongside BASIC loaders.


---


2. On-Chain Transpose Engine: Studio 64 Block Copy


To replicate the core technical logic of Studio 64's block-editor (copying a range of notes and transposing them on-the-fly), we can utilize a Yul block transcoder.


2.1 Note Storage Format Each note occupies a single 16-bit packed word: \textit{   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[0..7]}}: Pitch Index (0 = C0, 1 = C\#0 ... 95 = B7) }   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[8..15]}}: Duration ticks (1 to 255)


2.2 Yul Transposition Engine The following Yul function copies a sequence of packed note words from one memory location to another, applying a semitone transposition while checking bounds:


```yul // Transposes a block of notes by a semitone offset // sourcePtr: Start memory address of original notes // destPtr: Destination memory address for transposed notes // count: Number of notes to transpose // semitones: Signed offset (positive = up, negative = down, represented as signed byte) function transposeNoteBlock(sourcePtr, destPtr, count, semitones) -> success \{ success := 1


for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, count) \{ i := add(i, 1) \} \{ // Read 16-bit note (pitch in lower 8 bits, duration in upper 8 bits) let sourceOffset := mul(i, 2) let noteWord := mload(add(sourcePtr, sourceOffset)) noteWord := and(noteWord, 0xFFFF) // Mask to 16 bits


let pitch := and(noteWord, 0xFF) let duration := shr(8, noteWord)


// Handle signed semitone addition let newPitch := pitch // If semitones is negative (indicated by sign bit 0x80 for 8-bit sign) let isNegative := and(semitones, 0x80)


if isNegative \{ let absSemitones := sub(0, and(semitones, 0x7F)) // Underflow check if lt(pitch, absSemitones) \{ newPitch := 0 // Floor at bottom pitch (C0) success := 0  // Flag out-of-bounds clamp \} if iszero(lt(pitch, absSemitones)) \{ newPitch := sub(pitch, absSemitones) \} \}


if iszero(isNegative) \{ // Overflow check (Max C64 standard index = 95) if gt(add(pitch, semitones), 95) \{ newPitch := 95 // Ceiling at top pitch (B7) success := 0   // Flag out-of-bounds clamp \} if iszero(gt(add(pitch, semitones), 95)) \{ newPitch := add(pitch, semitones) \} \}


// Pack back into 16-bit word let transposedWord := or(newPitch, shl(8, duration))


// Write to destination let destOffset := mul(i, 2) mstore(add(destPtr, destOffset), transposedWord) \} \} ```


---


3. Comparison with Competitors


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Metric & En-Tech Software & Koala Technologies & MusiCalc (Waveform) \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Specialization} & Music Word Processing \& DBs & Touchpad Painting \& Graphics & Multi-Voice Synthesis Sequencer \\ \hline
\textbf{Flagship Product} & \textit{Studio 64} & \textit{KoalaPad} / \textit{KoalaPainter} & \textit{MusiCalc 1} / \textit{Colortone Keyboard} \\ \hline
\textbf{Note Management} & Block copies, transpositions & N/A (Coordinate mapping) & Live synth envelope adjustments \\ \hline

\section{Insta Software Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Insta Software (TOTL) — Technical \& Database Analysis


Founded in Santa Ana, California, \textbf{Insta Software} (primarily known under the \textbf{TOTL} brand, standing for \textit{"Time Out To Learn"}) was a productivity software publisher during the 1980s. Rather than compiling game logic, Insta Software designed tools centered on home business organization, word processing, and time management for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20.


This document reviews their technical database schemas, the productivity engine, and schedules a priority task layout in Yul mimicking their time management logic.


---


1. Flagship Productivity Line


Insta Software marketed their products under the \textbf{TOTL} suffix, targeting structured data formats: \textit{   \textbf{TOTL.INFOMASTER}: A relational-like database manager allowing custom text field parsing. }   \textbf{TOTL.TIMEMGR (Time Manager)}: An early task organizer that allowed users to input schedules, assign priority weights (1–10), and view sorted chronological timetables. \textit{   \textbf{RESEARCHASST (Research Assistant)}: A cross-referencing bibliography tool designed for storing reference indices. }   \textbf{Insta-Mail \& Insta-Writer}: Mail-merge word processors designed to link name lists directly to form letters.


---


2. Technical Mechanics: Time Manager Priority Scheduling


To replicate the core technical logic of \textbf{TOTL.TIMEMGR} on-chain, we implement a \textbf{Task Priority Scheduler} in Yul. Tasks are stored in a packed memory block, sorted and fetched by priority.


2.1 Task Slot Layout (64-bit word) To keep gas costs optimal, each scheduled task occupies 64 bits: \textit{   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[0..15]}}: Time tick (0–65535, representing time of day) }   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[16..23]}}: Priority Weight (1 = Lowest, 10 = Highest) *   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[24..63]}}: Task ID / Identifier tag (40 bits)


2.2 Yul Priority Sorter The following Yul function iterates through a list of packed tasks and finds the highest-priority task that is ready to execute at the current time:


```yul // Scans a list of packed tasks and returns the ID of the highest priority task ready at targetTime // taskPtr: Start memory address of task array // count: Number of tasks in the list // targetTime: Current simulated clock tick function getHighestPriorityTask(taskPtr, count, targetTime) -> bestTaskId \{ let bestPriority := 0 bestTaskId := 0


for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, count) \{ i := add(i, 1) \} \{ // Load 64-bit packed task word let offset := mul(i, 8) let word := mload(add(taskPtr, offset))


let timeTick := and(word, 0xFFFF) let priority := and(shr(16, word), 0xFF) let taskId := and(shr(24, word), 0xFFFFFFFFFF) // Extract 40-bit ID


// Check if task is ready (timeTick <= targetTime) let isReady := iszero(gt(timeTick, targetTime))


if isReady \{ // Check if this task has higher priority than the best one found so far if gt(priority, bestPriority) \{ bestPriority := priority bestTaskId := taskId \} \} \} \} ```


---


3. Comparison of Retro Productivity Systems


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Criteria & Insta Software (TOTL) & Mirage Concepts (Manager 64) \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Aesthetic Goal} & Functional \& Textual (Utilities) & Screen Formats \& Custom Computations \\ \hline
\textbf{Task Allocation} & Timed chronologies \& priority weights & Record identifiers \& dynamic offset bounds \\ \hline
\textbf{Core Software} & \textit{TOTL.TIMEMGR} \& \textit{TOTL.INFOMASTER} & \textit{Database Manager 64} \\ \hline
\textbf{On-Chain Translation} & Priority scheduling array filters & Bitwise control word packing \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


> [!TIP] > The TOTL suite relied heavily on modular designs, allowing files generated by \textit{TOTL.INFOMASTER} to feed directly into \textit{Insta-Mail} for automated letter printing. This represents an early retro implementation of pipeline data sharing.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Cimarron Insta Investment Combo Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Cimarron Insta-Series: Investment Combo — Technical Analysis


In 1984, \textbf{Micro-Sci} marketed the \textbf{Cimarron Insta-Series}, a collection of productivity software bundles for the Commodore 64. The most notable productivity-themed bundle was the \textbf{Investment Combo}, consisting of three integrated programs designed to cooperate via data exchange:


\textit{   \textbf{Insta-Calc}: A cartridge-based spreadsheet utility. }   \textbf{Insta-Graph}: A line and bar graphing package that loaded Insta-Calc files. *   \textbf{Insta-Vestor}: A portfolio manager for tracking stock purchases, quantities, and price ticks.


This document reviews the technical architecture of the Investment Combo and schedules an on-chain portfolio valuation and Return on Investment (ROI) engine in Yul.


---


1. Integrated Database Architecture


The primary innovation of the Cimarron Investment Combo was its \textbf{file interoperability}. At a time when Commodore 64 applications were heavily siloed due to memory space constraints, Cimarron established a shared file format: 1. \textbf{Insta-Vestor Data Output}: Exported stock valuation arrays containing quantities and history matrices. 2. \textbf{Insta-Calc Parsing}: Loaded the exported arrays directly into spreadsheet columns. 3. \textbf{Insta-Graph Plotting}: Read spreadsheet ranges to generate high-resolution bar and line charts on the VIC-II chip.


---


2. On-Chain Portfolio Engine: Insta-Vestor


To replicate the core valuation and ROI tracking logic of \textbf{Insta-Vestor}, we implement a financial evaluation contract in Yul.


2.1 Asset Slot Layout (128-bit packed slot) Each stock or asset transaction is stored in a packed memory block: \textit{   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[0..31]}}: Share Count (unsigned integer, supporting fractional shares with 4 decimals, i.e., factor of 10,000) }   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[32..63]}}: Purchase Price (fixed-point 16.16) \textit{   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[64..95]}}: Current Price (fixed-point 16.16) }   \textbf{Bits \texttt{[96..127]}}: Ticker symbol (4-byte ASCII code, e.g. "AAPL")


2.2 Yul Portfolio Evaluator The following Yul function iterates through a list of transactions, calculates total cost, current portfolio value, and returns the net Return on Investment (ROI) percentage (scaled by 100 for 2 decimal places):


```yul // Calculates total portfolio cost, current valuation, and ROI \% // assetPtr: Start memory address of asset array // count: Number of assets/transactions // Returns: (Total Cost in 16.16, Current Value in 16.16, ROI percentage scaled by 100) function evaluatePortfolio(assetPtr, count) -> totalCost, currentValue, roiPct \{ totalCost := 0 currentValue := 0 roiPct := 0


for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, count) \{ i := add(i, 1) \} \{ // Load 128-bit packed asset word from memory (offset = i * 16) let offset := mul(i, 16) let word0 := mload(add(assetPtr, offset))      // contains shares and buy price let word1 := mload(add(assetPtr, add(offset, 8))) // contains current price and ticker


let shares := and(word0, 0xFFFFFFFF) let buyPrice := and(shr(32, word0), 0xFFFFFFFF) let currPrice := and(word1, 0xFFFFFFFF)


// Cost = shares * buyPrice / 10000 (adjusting for shares decimal scaling) let costVal := div(mul(shares, buyPrice), 10000) totalCost := add(totalCost, costVal)


// Current Value = shares * currPrice / 10000 let currVal := div(mul(shares, currPrice), 10000) currentValue := add(currentValue, currVal) \}


// Calculate ROI = ((Current Value - Total Cost) / Total Cost) * 100 if gt(totalCost, 0) \{ let netProfit := 0 let positive := 1


if gte(currentValue, totalCost) \{ netProfit := sub(currentValue, totalCost) \} if lt(currentValue, totalCost) \{ netProfit := sub(totalCost, currentValue) positive := 0 \}


// Multiply by 10000 for percentage with 2 decimal points: (netProfit * 10000 / totalCost) let rawPct := div(mul(netProfit, 10000), totalCost)


if positive \{ roiPct := rawPct \} if iszero(positive) \{ // Represent negative ROI as negative signed value roiPct := sub(0, rawPct) \} \} \} ```


---


3. Cimarron Combo Matrix


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Program & Media Format & Memory Footprint & Primary Register Target \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Insta-Calc} & 8 KiB Cartridge & \textbackslash \$8000–\textbackslash \$9FFF & RAM formulas, cell matrix grids \\ \hline
\textbf{Insta-Graph} & Floppy Disk & \textbackslash \$A000–\textbackslash \$CFFF & VIC-II High-Res mode (\textbackslash \$D011 bit 5) \\ \hline
\textbf{Insta-Vestor} & Floppy Disk & \textbackslash \$1000–\textbackslash \$7FFF & Transaction SEQ files, stock logs \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


> [!NOTE] > Cimarron's decision to distribute \textit{Insta-Calc} on cartridge was a strategic memory layout choice. Cartridges do not consume the C64's precious 64 KiB RAM, leaving maximum memory available for large spreadsheet calculations.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Evm Vs Zmm Vm Interfaces}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Architectural Comparison: EVM vs. ZMM VM Object Access Interfaces


When designing high-performance emulators and decentralized retro-consoles, we must distinguish between two primary virtual machine interfaces for accessing Yul and Solidity objects: the \textbf{EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine)} and the \textbf{ZMM VM (Zero Memory Manager Virtual Machine)}.


While both interpret Yul assembly instructions, their underlying memory layouts, execution boundaries, and state-retrieval mechanisms require completely different access patterns.


---


1. Duality of Access Mechanisms


``\texttt{ ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │        Yul Runtime Object            │ └──────────┬────────────────┬──────────┘ │                │ ┌────────────────────────┴─┐            ┌─┴────────────────────────┐ ▼                          ▼            ▼                          ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────────────┐ │        EVM Storage Access        │          │       ZMM Memory Access    │ ├──────────────────────────────────┤          ├────────────────────────────┤ │ - 256-bit slot hashing           │          │ - Flat 16-bit linear MMIO  │ │ - State persistence (SSTORE)     │          │ - Pointer offsets (MLOAD)  │ │ - Calldata ABI selectors         │          │ - Zero-copy display lists  │ └──────────────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────────────┘ }``


1.1 The EVM Interface (State \& Security Boundary) \textit{   \textbf{Word Size}: Fixed 256-bit words. }   \textbf{Access Pattern}: Cryptographic storage slots. Variables are accessed via keccak256 hashes: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Slot\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(\textbackslash text\{Base Slot\}, \textbackslash text\{Object ID\})\$\$ \textit{   \textbf{Communication}: Standard ABI encoding. Calldata requires 4-byte selectors (e.g. \texttt{0x4f1fe20d}) followed by padded parameters, incurring high transaction serialization overhead. }   \textbf{Persistence}: Operations are written to state trie via \texttt{sstore} (costing thousands of gas units).


1.2 The ZMM VM Interface (High-Speed Local Execution) \textit{   \textbf{Word Size}: Compact 16-bit or 64-bit aligned structures. }   \textbf{Access Pattern}: Linear memory-mapped I/O (MMIO). Values are read directly from fixed hardware-equivalent registers (e.g., \texttt{\$D400} for ANTIC display pointers, \texttt{\$D000} for VIC-II coordinates) via \texttt{mload} / \texttt{mstore} at direct offsets: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Address\} = \textbackslash text\{Base Offset\} + \textbackslash text\{Register ID\}\$\$ \textit{   \textbf{Communication}: Zero-copy pointer swapping. Viewport changes, text scrolls, or raster scanlines are updated by shifting a single 16-bit address pointer in memory, achieving \$O(1)\$ performance. }   \textbf{Persistence}: Purely transient and volatile. State resides in active register files or RAM thunks, completely avoiding storage write penalties.


---


2. Interface Specifications


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Feature & EVM Interface & ZMM VM Interface \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Object Alignment} & 32-byte (256-bit) boundary & 2-byte (16-bit) or 8-byte (64-bit) boundary \\ \hline
\textbf{Primary Opcodes} & \texttt{sload}, \texttt{sstore}, \texttt{calldataload}, \texttt{staticcall} & \texttt{mload}, \texttt{mstore}, \texttt{mcopy} \\ \hline
\textbf{Retrieval Cost} & High (Warm/Cold storage gas rates) & Negligible (Memory expansion gas only) \\ \hline
\textbf{Data Flow} & Serialized ABI parameters & Direct memory references \& pointers \\ \hline
\textbf{JIT Integration} & None (Interpreter loop) & High (Direct register cache mappings) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. The EVM-to-ZMM Bridge: On-Chain Object Decoder


To allow ZMM VM registers to consume objects stored in EVM storage, we use a Yul-based bridge. The following function loads a 256-bit hashed EVM record and unpacks it directly into a ZMM 16-bit linear memory layout for low-latency rendering or JIT processing:


```yul // Decodes a 256-bit EVM Database Record and pages it into ZMM 16-bit MMIO memory // evmRecordSlot: Storage slot hash containing the packed EVM record // zmmMemoryStart: Direct RAM address in ZMM memory to write the decoded fields function bridgeEvmToZmm(evmRecordSlot, zmmMemoryStart) -> success \{ success := 1


// 1. Fetch the 256-bit packed word from EVM Storage let word := sload(evmRecordSlot)


// 2. Unpack the object fields: // Layout: // bits [0..15]   = Record ID (16-bit) // bits [16..23]  = Field Count (8-bit) // bits [24..31]  = Configuration Flags (8-bit) // bits [32..255] = Upper 224 bits of packed field bounds let recordId := and(word, 0xFFFF) let fieldCount := and(shr(16, word), 0xFF) let flags := and(shr(24, word), 0xFF) let fieldData := and(word, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF00000000)


// 3. Page the fields directly into ZMM 16-bit aligned MMIO spaces (offset by 2 bytes) // ZMM Address offsets: // zmmMemoryStart + 0: Record ID // zmmMemoryStart + 2: Field Count // zmmMemoryStart + 4: Flags // zmmMemoryStart + 6: Upper field data bounds mstore(zmmMemoryStart, shl(240, recordId)) // Shift left for 16-bit big-endian representation mstore(add(zmmMemoryStart, 2), shl(248, fieldCount)) mstore(add(zmmMemoryStart, 4), shl(248, flags))


// Write the 28-byte field boundaries (224-bit) starting at offset 6 mstore(add(zmmMemoryStart, 6), fieldData) \} ```


---


> [!IMPORTANT] > The architectural bridge demonstrates that \textbf{EVM Storage serves as the persistent state Registry}, while the \textbf{ZMM VM acts as the transient, high-speed Execution Engine}. Bridging them requires decoding packed 256-bit storage words into linear 16-bit memory pages before JIT execution starts.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Omnitronix Interface Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Omnitronix Deluxe User Port Serial Interface — Technical Analysis


In the 1980s, \textbf{Omnitronix} was a prominent manufacturer of hardware interfaces for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20. Their flagship hardware was the \textbf{Deluxe RS-232 Interface}, which expanded the C64’s connectivity by hooking directly into the 24-pin edge connector of the \textbf{User I/O Port}. This allowed the Commodore 64 to interface with standard modems, serial printers, and telecommunications devices.


This document analyzes the hardware layout of the Omnitronix serial system, maps the 6526 CIA port registers, and implements an on-chain RS-232 serial transceiver in Yul.


---


1. The C64 User Port \& CIA 6526 Map


Unlike standard computers with dedicated UART chips, the Commodore 64 implemented RS-232 serial communication entirely in software by manipulating the registers of the \textbf{CIA 2 (Complex Interface Adapter)} chip:


``\texttt{ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │                   Commodore 64 CPU                     │ └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘ │ Reads/Writes CIA Registers ┌──────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐ │                 CIA 2 (\$DD00-\$DDFF)                    │ │   - Port B (\$DD01) maps to the User Port               │ │   - Serial TXD/RXD lines mapped to Port B pins         │ └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘ │ User Port Edge Connection ┌──────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐ │         Omnitronix Deluxe RS-232 Interface             │ │   - Level-shifts 0-5V TTL signals to +/-12V RS-232     │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ }``


\textit{   \textbf{CIA 2 Port B Register (\texttt{\$DD01} / \texttt{56577})}: Direct read/write access to the User Port pins. }   \textbf{Data Direction Register B (\texttt{\$DD03} / \texttt{56579})}: Configures each User Port pin as input (\texttt{0}) or output (\texttt{1}).


1.1 Pin-to-Bit Mapping for Omnitronix RS-232 For software-driven RS-232, the Commodore KERNAL maps serial lines to CIA 2 Port B:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Bit & Pin Name & Description & Direction \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{0} & \textbf{RXD} & Received Data & Input \\ \hline
\textbf{1} & \textbf{TXD} & Transmitted Data & Output \\ \hline
\textbf{2} & \textbf{RTS} & Request To Send & Output \\ \hline
\textbf{3} & \textbf{CTS} & Clear To Send & Input \\ \hline
\textbf{4} & \textbf{DSR} & Data Set Ready & Input \\ \hline
\textbf{5} & \textbf{DCD} & Data Carrier Detect & Input \\ \hline
\textbf{6} & \textbf{DTR} & Data Terminal Ready & Output \\ \hline
\textbf{7} & \textbf{RI} & Ring Indicator & Input \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. On-Chain Transceiver: Omnitronix User Port Emulator


To model the Deluxe RS-232 serial interface in Yul, we emulate reading and writing bytes through the \texttt{\$DD01} Port B memory registers, implementing state transitions for transmitting (TX) and receiving (RX) bytes.


2.1 Serial Port Registers (MMIO)


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Memory Address & Name & Data Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:---: & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{56577}} & \textbf{\texttt{CIAPB}} & \texttt{uint8} & CIA 2 Port B Data Register (\texttt{\$DD01}) \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{56579}} & \textbf{\texttt{DDRB}} & \texttt{uint8} & CIA 2 Port B Data Direction Register (\texttt{\$DD03}) \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{56600}} & \textbf{\texttt{TX\_BUF}} & \texttt{uint8} & Local Transmit Byte Buffer \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{56601}} & \textbf{\texttt{RX\_BUF}} & \texttt{uint8} & Local Receive Byte Buffer \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
2.2 Serial Transceiver in Yul The following Yul code simulates transmitting a byte out of \texttt{TX\_BUF} by shifting it bit-by-bit into the \texttt{TXD} pin (Bit 1) of \texttt{CIAPB}, and receiving a byte into \texttt{RX\_BUF} from the \texttt{RXD} pin (Bit 0):


```yul // Emulates the serial transmission loop of the Deluxe RS-232 Interface function processSerialTransceiver() \{ let portB := sload(56577) // Read current Port B state let ddrB := sload(56579)  // Read Data Direction Register


// 1. Transmit Loop (Output bit to Pin 1 / TXD) // Verify Pin 1 is configured as output in DDRB (bit 1 is set) if and(ddrB, 0x02) \{ let txByte := sload(56600) // Load byte to transmit


// Loop through 8 bits to simulate sequential bit transmission for \{ let bitIdx := 0 \} lt(bitIdx, 8) \{ bitIdx := add(bitIdx, 1) \} \{ // Get current bit value (0 or 1) let bitVal := and(shr(bitIdx, txByte), 1)


// Set or clear Pin 1 (TXD) in Port B data if bitVal \{ portB := or(portB, 0x02) // Set Bit 1 \} if iszero(bitVal) \{ portB := and(portB, 0xFD) // Clear Bit 1 (mask 11111101) \} \}


// Store updated Port B state sstore(56577, portB) \}


// 2. Receive Loop (Input bit from Pin 0 / RXD) // Verify Pin 0 is configured as input in DDRB (bit 0 is clear) if iszero(and(ddrB, 0x01)) \{ let rxByte := 0


// Read Port B RXD bit sequentially (represented as 8 clock ticks) for \{ let bitIdx := 0 \} lt(bitIdx, 8) \{ bitIdx := add(bitIdx, 1) \} \{ // Read Pin 0 (RXD) state let bitVal := and(portB, 0x01)


// Reconstruct the byte rxByte := or(rxByte, shl(bitIdx, bitVal)) \}


// Save the assembled byte to Receive Buffer sstore(56601, rxByte) \} \} ```


---


3. Comparison with Competitors


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Metric & Omnitronix Deluxe & Cardco Card/Print & Commodore VIC-1011A \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Port Hook} & User Port (24-pin edge) & Serial Bus (DIN-6) & User Port (24-pin edge) \\ \hline
\textbf{Pin Translation} & Standard RS-232 level-shifting & Centronics parallel conversion & Simple 3-line TTL level pass-through \\ \hline
\textbf{Device Target} & Modems, standard serial printers & Parallel/Centronics printers & Terminals, modems \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


> [!NOTE] > The Omnitronix Deluxe interface performed hardware level-shifting, converting the Commodore’s internal 0-5V TTL User Port output to the standard +/-12V signals required by professional RS-232 devices. Without this interface, connecting a modem directly to the C64 User Port risked blowing the CIA 6526 chips due to voltage mismatches.

\section{Upgrade Proposals}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Folklore CPU Expansion \& Game Upgrade Proposal


By transitioning to the EVM-native \textbf{Folklore CPU} in Yul, we are no longer limited to 6502 CPU boundaries. Here are the proposed features to take the "Teddy Bear Rescue" game to the next level:


---


1. Native Double Jump Physics (In Yul) - \textbf{Feature}: Enable a floaty double-jump mechanic. - \textbf{Implementation}: Track double-jump ticks inside a Yul storage slot (e.g., \texttt{0x42}). When a jump trigger is received while \texttt{jumping == 1}, provide a secondary upward impulse (\texttt{pvy := -11000}) and cap the jump count to 2. - \textbf{Benefit}: Greatly improves platforming agility, allowing players to easily bypass tight clusters of spikes and bats.


2. Dynamic Falling Stalactites (Level 2 Cavern Hazards) - \textbf{Feature}: Randomly falling stalactites triggered by proximity. - \textbf{Implementation}: In Yul, track player proximity to ceiling stalactites. If player \$x\$ is near a stalactite slot, initiate a falling velocity update. The stalactite accelerates downwards (\texttt{y := add(y, vy)}) and checks for collision. - \textbf{Benefit}: Makes the cave level feel active, alive, and challenging without feeling unfair.


3. Gargamel Chase AI (Level 3 Boss Logic) - \textbf{Feature}: Dynamic state-based behavior for Gargamel. - \textbf{Implementation}: In Yul, compute the absolute distance between the player and Gargamel: ``\texttt{solidity let distance := abs(sub(player\_x, gargamel\_x)) }`` If distance is less than 200, transition Gargamel from "Patrol Mode" to "Chase Mode", increasing his velocity and directing it towards the player's current coordinate. - \textbf{Benefit}: Replaces the static left-to-right patrol with a responsive boss encounter.


4. Integrated Trauma Engine (Move logic from C to Yul) - \textbf{Feature}: Keep all gameplay state authority in the virtual machine. - \textbf{Implementation}: Move proximity fear calculations, control reversal (Terrified), and freezing logic (Panicked) inside Yul's physics loop. The Yul contract directly updates slot states for rendering. - \textbf{Benefit}: The C code remains a clean view-controller, while the Yul contract remains the single source of truth for the game state.

\section{Vic Ii Advanced Concepts}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
VIC-II Sprite Graphics: Advanced Hardware Concepts


This guide details the advanced graphics programming techniques and VIC-II register mechanisms introduced in Sally Greenwood Larsen's classic 1983 book \textit{Sprite Graphics for the Commodore 64}.


---


1. Multicolor Sprite Architecture (\$D01C, \$D025, \$D026)


In high-resolution mode, a sprite has a resolution of 24x21 pixels and supports only one foreground color (plus transparency). To allow up to three colors, Larsen's book introduces \textbf{Multicolor Mode}.


A. Horizontal Resolution Trade-Off When multicolor mode is enabled for a sprite (by setting the corresponding bit in \texttt{\$D01C} / \texttt{53276}), adjacent pixels are paired horizontally. \textit{ \textbf{Resolution:} Reduced from 24x21 to \textbf{12x21} double-width pixels. } \textbf{Color Selection:} Each pixel is represented by \textbf{2 bits} of data, allowing four possible states:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Bit Pair & Color Source & Register / Address & C64 Default Color \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{00} & \textbf{Transparent} & N/A & Current background color \\ \hline
\texttt{01} & \textbf{Sprite Multicolor 1} & \texttt{\$D025} / \texttt{53285} & Orange \\ \hline
\texttt{10} & \textbf{Individual Sprite Color} & \texttt{\$D027}–\texttt{\$D02E} & Sprite-specific (e.g. Sprite 0 Color) \\ \hline
\texttt{11} & \textbf{Sprite Multicolor 2} & \texttt{\$D026} / \texttt{53286} & Light Brown \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
B. Shared Colors vs. Sprite Colors Registers \texttt{\$D025} and \texttt{\$D026} are \textbf{shared} by all 8 sprites. If you change the color in \texttt{\$D025}, every multicolor sprite currently displaying bit pair \texttt{01} will change color simultaneously. This allows complex multi-sprite scenes to share a unified palette.


---


2. Hardware Collision Detection (\$D01E, \$D01F)


The VIC-II chip contains dedicated hardware logic to detect overlaps, allowing programmers to avoid heavy math calculations in BASIC.


A. Sprite-to-Sprite Collision (\$D01E / 53278) \textit{ \textbf{Function:} When the non-transparent pixels of any two enabled sprites overlap on the screen, the VIC-II sets the corresponding bits in \texttt{\$D01E} to \texttt{1}. } \textbf{Bit Assignment:} Bit 0 for Sprite 0, Bit 1 for Sprite 1, etc. * \textbf{Clearing (Strobe):} Reading this register (e.g., \texttt{PEEK(53278)}) automatically clears it to \texttt{0}. It will not register another collision until the sprites separate and collide again.


B. Sprite-to-Background Collision (\$D01F / 53279) \textit{ \textbf{Function:} When any non-transparent pixel of a sprite overlaps with a non-background character pixel (such as a text character or background graphic), the sprite's corresponding bit in \texttt{\$D01F} is set to \texttt{1}. } \textbf{Clearing:} Like \texttt{\$D01E}, reading \texttt{\$D01F} resets all bits to \texttt{0}.


---


3. The 9th-Bit Coordinate Register (\$D010 / 53264)


The Commodore 64 screen is 320 pixels wide (plus borders, making the coordinate space span up to 504). \textit{ \textbf{The 8-Bit Limitation:} Standard position registers (\texttt{\$D000}–\texttt{\$D00F}) are only 8-bit, restricting coordinates to the range \texttt{0}–\texttt{255}. } \textbf{The Solution:} The VIC-II uses a single register, \texttt{\$D010} / \texttt{53264}, to store the \textbf{Most Significant Bit (MSB)} for all 8 sprites: \textit{ \textbf{Bit 0:} 9th coordinate bit for Sprite 0. } \textbf{Bit 1:} 9th coordinate bit for Sprite 1. \textit{ ... } \textbf{Bit 7:} 9th coordinate bit for Sprite 7. * \textbf{Math in BASIC:} To move a sprite past X = 255, BASIC programs must set the MSB: ``\texttt{basic POKE 53264, PEEK(53264) OR 1 : REM Set 9th bit for Sprite 0 POKE 53248, X - 256          : REM Set low-byte coordinate }``


---


4. Priority Layering (\$D01B / 53275)


Register \texttt{\$D01B} determines the overlapping priority of sprites relative to background character text and bitmap pixels. \textit{ \textbf{Bit = 0 (Default):} Sprite is in front of the background. } \textbf{Bit = 1:} Sprite moves behind background characters (except background color \texttt{00} pixels). This is useful for making characters walk behind trees, pillars, or walls.


---


5. Virtual VIC-II Simulator Implementation


In our web-based interactive tool [sally\_larsen\_c64.html](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/frontend/sally\_larsen\_c64.html), these registers are fully emulated: \textit{ \textbf{Sprite 0 \& Sprite 1 Renderers:} Independent canvases (\texttt{sim-canvas-0}, \texttt{sim-canvas-1}) with high-fidelity coordinate positioning and size expansions. } \textbf{Pixel-Perfect Overlaps:} Uses offscreen image buffers to calculate physical non-transparent pixel overlap intersections at high speed. \textit{ \textbf{Visual Status Indicators:} Emulates registers \texttt{\$D01E} and \texttt{\$D01F} in real-time, displaying hexadecimal register values and triggering red status LED lights for active sprite collision channels. } \textbf{Latch Clear (Strobe):} Emulates the strobe latch behavior by clearing registers back to \texttt{\$00} only when the user invokes the \textbf{PEEK \& Clear} instruction. * \textbf{9th-Bit MSB coordinate register (\$D010 / 53264):} Displays the binary state of the horizontal coordinate overflow in real-time with green LED indicators that trigger whenever Sprite 0 or Sprite 1 coordinates cross the 255-pixel threshold.

\section{Folklore Cpu Design}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Folklore CPU Architecture \& Design Specification


This document details the architectural design for the \textbf{Folklore CPU}, an EVM-native state engine written in Yul. By utilizing native EVM/Yul characteristics, we eliminate the emulation overhead of the 6502 interpreter while fully leveraging modern virtual machine capabilities.


---


1. Core EVM-Native Advantages


Unlike retro processors limited to 8-bit registers and 64KB memory addresses, the \textbf{Folklore CPU} runs directly on the virtual machine using: 1. \textbf{256-bit Word Size (\texttt{u256})}: Coordinates, speed vectors, timers, and health states are stored as native 256-bit EVM words. This eliminates complex multi-byte arithmetic (like high/low byte carry logic) for coordinates and physics. 2. \textbf{Infinite Storage Slots (\texttt{sstore}/\texttt{sload})}: Instead of dividing a 64KB RAM layout, we use the EVM's \$2\textasciicircum \{256\}\$ storage slot keys to structure game variables cleanly using structured hashing (e.g., standard mapping offsets). 3. \textbf{Native Math \& Bitwise Opcodes}: Direct access to \texttt{addmod}, \texttt{mulmod}, \texttt{exp}, \texttt{signextend}, and fast bitwise shifting, allowing high-performance procedural generation, collision math, and physics.


---


2. Register \& Storage Map


The CPU state is organized directly in EVM storage slots. Below is the layout designed for the Vaesen-themed game logic:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Storage Key (u256 Slot) & Variable Name & Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{0x00} & \texttt{magic\_selector} & \texttt{u256} & Active instruction / state update routine (e.g., tick, reset) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x01} & \texttt{player\_x} & \texttt{u256} & Player horizontal position (scaled by 1000 for decimal precision) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x02} & \texttt{player\_y} & \texttt{u256} & Player vertical position (scaled by 1000) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x03} & \texttt{player\_vy} & \texttt{u256} & Player vertical velocity \\ \hline
\texttt{0x04} & \texttt{player\_jumping} & \texttt{u256} & Jump boolean flag (0 = Ground, 1 = Jumping, 2 = Double Jump) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x05} & \texttt{player\_energy} & \texttt{u256} & Current player energy / stamina (0–100) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x06} & \texttt{physical\_trauma} & \texttt{u256} & Vaesen physical trauma level (0 = Normal to 3 = Broken) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x07} & \texttt{mental\_trauma} & \texttt{u256} & Vaesen mental trauma level (0 = Normal to 3 = Panicked) \\ \hline
\texttt{0x10} & \texttt{enemy\_count} & \texttt{u256} & Number of active enemies / obstacles \\ \hline
\texttt{0x20 + i} & \texttt{enemy\_x[i]} & \texttt{u256} & Horizontal position of enemy \$i\$ \\ \hline
\texttt{0x40 + i} & \texttt{enemy\_y[i]} & \texttt{u256} & Vertical position of enemy \$i\$ \\ \hline
\texttt{0x60 + i} & \texttt{enemy\_vx[i]} & \texttt{u256} & Velocity of enemy \$i\$ \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. ABI Selection Protocol


The C harness interacts with the Yul contract using a standardized 4-byte EVM function selector passed in the transaction call data:


``\texttt{solidity switch selector() // 0x6e559e22: reset() -> Clear storage, set initial state coordinates case 0x6e559e22 \{ sstore(0x01, 100000)  // player\_x = 100.00 sstore(0x02, 520000)  // player\_y = 520.00 sstore(0x05, 100)     // energy = 100 // ... \} // 0x9c3d42b0: tick(moveDir, jumpTrigger) -> Process physics tick case 0x9c3d42b0 \{ let moveDir := calldataload(4) let jumpTrigger := calldataload(36) processPhysics(moveDir, jumpTrigger) \} // 0x2e0f40cf: get\_game\_state() -> Returns all registers in single return payload case 0x2e0f40cf \{ mstore(0x00, sload(0x01)) // player\_x mstore(0x20, sload(0x02)) // player\_y mstore(0x40, sload(0x05)) // energy return(0x00, 0x60) \} }``


---


4. Native Physics \& Gravity implementation (Yul snippet)


This snippet shows how simple and readable gravity and physics updates become when using native Yul rather than emulated assembly:


```solidity function processPhysics(moveDir, jumpTrigger) \{ // 1. Gravity and Jump logic let py := sload(0x02) let pvy := sload(0x03) let jumping := sload(0x04)


if jumpTrigger \{ if iszero(jumping) \{ pvy := -15000 // Native jump impulse (upwards) jumping := 1 \} \}


// Apply gravity pvy := add(pvy, 800) // Gravity constant py := add(py, pvy)


// Floor boundary check (520.00) if gt(py, 520000) \{ py := 520000 pvy := 0 jumping := 0 \}


sstore(0x02, py) sstore(0x03, pvy) sstore(0x04, jumping) \} ```


---


5. High-Color (Hi-Color) Sprite Graphics Extensions


To support complex high-color graphics without the rendering constraints of traditional 8-bit registers, the Folklore CPU architecture can be upgraded with native 8-bit color-depth sprite patterns and dynamic palette composition.


5.1 Native 8-Bit Color-Depth Grid Packing Traditional C64 registers divide rows into 1-bit or 2-bit color cells. In contrast, the Folklore CPU leverages native \texttt{u256} storage slots to pack full \textbf{8-bit color indices} (supporting up to 256 colors per pixel): \textit{ A sprite row width of 24 pixels requires exactly 24 bytes (192 bits). } A single 256-bit word easily accommodates 24 bytes, leaving 64 bits free for row-level effects (such as alpha values or horizontal flipping flags). * Thus, a 24x21 hi-color sprite fits into exactly \textbf{21 storage slots} (one slot per row): \$\$\textbackslash text\{Storage Key\} = \textbackslash text\{SpriteBase\} + \textbackslash text\{RowIndex\}\$\$


5.2 Dynamic RGBA Palette Lookups Rather than hardcoding standard system colors, the Folklore CPU can store customizable color lookup tables (LUTs) in EVM storage: \textit{ \textbf{Palette Storage Slots (\texttt{0x1000} to \texttt{0x10FF})}: Each slot stores a 32-bit RGBA color representation (\texttt{0xRRGGBBAA}). } \textbf{Palette Selection Register (\texttt{0x08})}: Swaps active palettes globally or per-sprite (supporting dynamic daytime/nighttime coloring, damage flashes, or shield overlays).


5.3 On-Chain Procedural Shaders Using Yul mathematical arithmetic opcodes, the Folklore CPU can execute procedural shader functions on sprite frames prior to output: ```solidity // Example: Apply linear horizontal lighting gradient on a sprite row function applyLightingGradient(rowVal, ambientLight) -> shadedRow \{ for \{ let pixel := 0 \} lt(pixel, 24) \{ pixel := add(pixel, 1) \} \{ // Extract 8-bit color index let colorIdx := and(shr(mul(pixel, 8), rowVal), 0xFF)


// Procedurally scale color index values based on position let lightLevel := add(ambientLight, mul(pixel, 8)) if gt(lightLevel, 255) \{ lightLevel := 255 \}


// Write back shaded pixel let shadedPixel := div(mul(colorIdx, lightLevel), 255) shadedRow := or(shadedRow, shl(mul(pixel, 8), shadedPixel)) \} \} ```


5.4 Sprite Composition \& Alpha Blending \textit{ \textbf{Z-Buffer/Depth Registry (\texttt{0x09})}: Assigns depth levels to each active sprite, sorting paint operations dynamically. } \textbf{Alpha Control Register (\texttt{0x0A})}: Regulates translucency and overlay blending math (standard linear interpolation \$C = \textbackslash alpha A + (1-\textbackslash alpha) B\$) processed natively in Yul arithmetic routines.

\section{Blockchain Secure Kermit}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Blockchain-Buffered Secure Kermit Transfer Protocol


This specification outlines how two blockchain users (Alice and Bob) can establish a secure, encrypted file-transfer pipeline using the Kermit protocol over an on-chain message buffer.


---


1. Cryptographic Key Agreement (On-Chain ECDH)


To encrypt the Kermit packets without exposing secret keys on the public ledger, Alice and Bob perform an \textbf{Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH)} handshake using their native Ethereum (secp256k1) keypairs:


1. \textbf{Publish Public Keys}: Alice and Bob retrieve each other's public keys. This can be done by looking up their public address on-chain or looking up the public key recovery bytes from their previous signed transactions. 2. \textbf{Derive Shared Secret}: \textit{ Alice calculates: \$S = d\_\{\textbackslash text\{Alice\}\} \textbackslash times Q\_\{\textbackslash text\{Bob\}\}\$ } Bob calculates: \$S = d\_\{\textbackslash text\{Bob\}\} \textbackslash times Q\_\{\textbackslash text\{Alice\}\}\$ * Both compute the identical shared key: \$K\_\{\textbackslash text\{shared\}\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(S)\$ 3. \$K\_\{\textbackslash text\{shared\}\}\$ is now the symmetric master key, known only to Alice and Bob, and is never written to the blockchain.


---


2. On-Chain Message Buffer Design (Solidity / Yul)


Rather than storing files directly in expensive Solidity state storage (\texttt{sstore}), the transfer utilizes a lightweight message buffer contract that leverages EVM transaction events for low-gas communications.


```solidity // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity \textasciicircum 0.8.20;


contract KermitBuffer \{ event PacketSent( address indexed sender, address indexed recipient, uint32 indexed sequence, bytes packetData );


// Write a Kermit packet to the blockchain buffer function writePacket(address recipient, uint32 sequence, bytes calldata packetData) external \{ emit PacketSent(msg.sender, recipient, sequence, packetData); \} \} ```


---


3. Communication Flow \& Frame Encapsulation


```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Alice participant Contract as KermitBuffer Contract actor Bob


Note over Alice, Bob: 1. ECDH Key Exchange (Off-chain derivation of K\_shared)


Alice->>Alice: Encrypt Payload \& Wrap in Kermit Frame Alice->>Contract: writePacket(Bob, seq=1, packetData=Encrypt(K\_shared, Data)) Contract-->>Bob: Emit event PacketSent(Alice, Bob, seq=1, data) Bob->>Bob: Parse, Decode, Decrypt with K\_shared Bob->>Contract: writePacket(Alice, seq=1, packetData=ACK) Contract-->>Alice: Emit event PacketSent(Bob, Alice, seq=1, ACK) ```


Protocol Execution Steps: 1. \textbf{Packet Assembly}: Alice fragments the file into standard chunks. 2. \textbf{Encapsulated Encryption}: For each packet, Alice encrypts the payload using the derived KDF: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Keystream\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(K\_\{\textbackslash text\{shared\}\} \textbackslash mathbin\{\textbackslash Vert\} \textbackslash text\{SEQ\})\$\$ \$\$\textbackslash text\{Ciphertext\} = \textbackslash text\{Plaintext\} \textbackslash oplus \textbackslash text\{Keystream\}\$\$ 3. \textbf{Transmission}: Alice wraps the ciphertext inside a standard Kermit frame (adding SOH, LEN, SEQ, TYPE, and CHECK) and calls \texttt{writePacket} on the contract. 4. \textbf{Receipt \& Acknowledgment}: Bob (listening to Solidity events on the buffer contract) intercepts the packet. He decrypts the payload, validates the checksum, and writes back an encrypted Kermit ACK packet (\texttt{TYPE = 'Y'}) to Alice through the buffer contract. 5. \textbf{Sliding Window Optimization}: To minimize gas costs and transaction confirmation times, the transfer can configure a larger Kermit \textbf{Window Size} (e.g., sending up to 8 packets before waiting for Bob's ACK).

\section{Unix V1 Folklore Cpu}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Implementing Unix Version 1 on the Folklore CPU


This document analyzes the architectural feasibility of running \textbf{Unix Version 1} (originally written for the 16-bit PDP-11/20 in 1971) on the EVM-native \textbf{Folklore CPU} written in Yul.


---


1. The Challenge: Hardware Emulation vs. Native Porting


There are two primary approaches to running Unix v1 on the Folklore CPU:


Approach A: PDP-11 Emulation in Yul (Virtualization) In this model, the Folklore CPU is programmed to interpret the PDP-11 instruction set (opcodes like \texttt{MOV}, \texttt{ADD}, \texttt{BR}, \texttt{JSR}). \textit{   \textbf{Feasibility}: Possible, but highly inefficient. Emulating a 16-bit CPU on top of the 256-bit EVM introduces massive gas overhead due to opcode decoding loops and simulated register state storage loading/storing. }   \textbf{Memory constraints}: Simulating the PDP-11's 64KB RAM space would require heavy usage of EVM memory or storage mappings, making execution slow and expensive.


Approach B: Native Yul Unix v1 Port (Recommended) Rather than emulating PDP-11 hardware, we port the core \textbf{architectural concepts} of Unix v1 directly into native Yul functions. This leverages the Folklore CPU's native 256-bit capabilities.


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Unix v1 Concept & PDP-11/20 Implementation (1971) & Folklore CPU Yul Implementation \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Word Size} & 16-bit & Native 256-bit (\texttt{u256}) \\ \hline
\textbf{Memory} & 24KB Core RAM & Dynamic EVM Memory (\texttt{mload}/\texttt{mstore}) \\ \hline
\textbf{Storage (Disk)} & RK03 Decpack disk drives & EVM Storage Slots (\texttt{sload}/\texttt{sstore}) \\ \hline
\textbf{System Calls} & trap instructions (\texttt{sys open}, \texttt{sys read}) & Yul \texttt{switch} selector dispatcher \\ \hline
\textbf{Processes} & Process Table in Core Memory & Process array mapped to storage slots \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Implementing Unix v1 System Calls in Yul


We can map Unix v1's core system calls to native Yul functions. Below is a conceptual prototype of the file descriptor and I/O pipeline:


```solidity switch selector()


// sys\_open(pathHash, mode) -> fd case 0x15a0c0f4 \{ let pathHash := calldataload(4) let mode := calldataload(36)


// 1. Locate i-node in storage let inodeSlot := findInode(pathHash) if iszero(inodeSlot) \{ // Create new inode if write mode inodeSlot := createInode(pathHash) \}


// 2. Allocate File Descriptor in process state let fd := allocateFD(inodeSlot, mode) mstore(0x00, fd) return(0x00, 0x20) \}


// sys\_write(fd, bufferOffset, byteCount) -> writtenCount case 0xb826f0aa \{ let fd := calldataload(4) let memOffset := calldataload(36) let count := calldataload(68)


let inodeSlot := getInodeFromFD(fd) if iszero(inodeSlot) \{ revert(0, 0) \}


// Write data bytes directly to EVM storage slots assigned to this inode for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, count) \{ i := add(i, 32) \} \{ let val := mload(add(memOffset, i)) sstore(add(inodeSlot, div(i, 32)), val) \}


mstore(0x00, count) return(0x00, 0x20) \} ```


---


3. Advantages of the Native Folklore Unix v1 Port


1.  \textbf{Unlimited File System Storage}: Instead of being constrained by the PDP-11's 2MB RK03 disk limits, the Unix v1 filesystem maps directly to the EVM's \$2\textasciicircum \{256\}\$ storage space, enabling deep, persistent file hierachies. 2.  \textbf{Native 256-bit Security}: System-level file permissions and user authentication can be linked directly to \textbf{ECDSA signatures} and Ethereum addresses, making a cryptographically secure multi-user operating system. 3.  \textbf{High-Performance Pipes}: Inter-process pipes (``) can be implemented as ultra-fast transient memory buffers in EVM RAM rather than slow physical disk swaps.

\section{Zmm Room Refactoring Plan}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Plan: Migrating Z-Machine Rooms to ZMM VM Layout


This plan outlines the refactoring of [zmachine.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/zmachine.yul) to migrate dynamic rooms out of persistent EVM storage (\texttt{sload}/\texttt{sstore} mappings) and into a transient, high-speed ZMM VM linear memory architecture.


---


1. Objectives


1. \textbf{Remove EVM Call Overhead}: Replace external contract interactions (\texttt{call}/\texttt{staticcall} to room contract addresses) with direct operations on 16-bit big-endian linear registers. 2. \textbf{Page-Aligned Memory Mapping}: Map rooms, items, player stats, and chat buffers to fixed ZMM register addresses starting at \texttt{0x8000} (e.g., matching VIC-II and ANTIC styles). 3. \textbf{Volatile State Registers}: Store dynamic room states (active users, bouncer divisors, guest list counts, and cover charges) inside volatile memory pages instead of persistent EVM storage slots.


---


2. Memory Map Design (ZMM MMIO)


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address Range & Component & Representation & Purpose \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{0x0000 - 0x7FFF} & \textbf{Story ROM Segment} & Static 8-bit array & Z-Machine game bytecode \& text assets. \\ \hline
\texttt{0x8000 - 0x80FF} & \textbf{Room Registry Page} & 16-bit registers & Active Room IDs, active bouncers count, cover charge value. \\ \hline
\texttt{0x8100 - 0x82FF} & \textbf{Room Metadata (descriptions)} & Aligned text buffers & Room description strings decoded on-demand. \\ \hline
\texttt{0x8300 - 0x85FF} & \textbf{Subdomain State Registers} & 64-bit status flags & Chat buffers, active user lists, and attribute key-value pairs. \\ \hline
\texttt{0x8600 - 0x8FFF} & \textbf{Guest List / Staff Registry} & Bitmaps & guest/staff registration (1 = active, 0 = inactive). \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Implementation Steps


Step 1: Update ZMM Memory Helpers Add JIT memory helpers in Yul to handle 16-bit and 64-bit aligned reads/writes out of the ZMM memory bank: ``\texttt{yul function readZmm16(addr) -> val \{ val := shr(240, mload(addr)) \} function writeZmm16(addr, val) \{ mstore(addr, shl(240, val)) \} }``


Step 2: Implement ZMM Bridge Write \texttt{bridgeEvmToZmm} to decode existing persistent token states on startup and page them directly into the ZMM MMIO space.


Step 3: Refactor Command Parser Rewrite \texttt{parseCommand} inside Yul to consume and modify the registers at \texttt{0x8000+} directly instead of calling external EVM contracts.


---


> [!NOTE] > This refactoring will significantly optimize the terminal's responsiveness and lay the groundwork for high-performance JIT execution loops.

\section{Carlson Chrget To Emacs}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
From Carlson's CHRGET Hook to EMACS: An Architectural Evolution of Character Interception


Edward H. Carlson’s \textbf{CHRGET hook} (published in \textit{MICRO: The 6502 Journal}, Issue 25, June 1980) is a famous early microcomputer hack for Apple II, OSI, and PET BASIC. By modifying the zero-page character-fetching routine (\texttt{CHRGET} at \texttt{\$00E2-\$00FA}), Carlson intercepted the stream of characters parsed by the BASIC interpreter to inject custom syntax (such as \texttt{@} for \texttt{PRINT AT}).


This pattern of \textbf{character-level input redirection} and dynamic expansion is the exact same architectural concept that led to the creation of \textbf{EMACS (Editor MACroS)} on the Incompatible Timesharing System (ITS) at MIT during the mid-1970s.


---


1. Character-by-Character Interception: The Common Thread


In both Carlson's BASIC hack and EMACS's TECO origins, the core engine processes a stream of characters sequentially:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD Stream[Raw Input Stream] --> Interceptor\{Interceptor Hook\} Interceptor -- Matches Custom Prefix --> CustomHandler[Execute Macro/Custom routine] Interceptor -- Fallthrough --> StandardParser[Standard Interpreter Loop] }``


The CHRGET Mechanics Standard 6502 Microsoft BASIC fetched the next character from memory using a routine located in zero-page (for speed): ``\texttt{assembly CHRGET: INC \$7A       ; Increment text pointer low byte BNE +         ; Skip high byte increment if no page roll INC \$7B       ; Increment text pointer high byte +       LDA (\$7A),Y   ; Indirect indexed load of the character CMP \#\$3A      ; Check for end-of-statement or colon BCS Exit      ; If >= ':', return ... }`\texttt{ Carlson's hack hijacked this zero-page routine to inspect }LDA (\$7A),Y\texttt{. If it matched a special character (e.g. }@`), it bypassed the standard parser, calling a custom hook instead.


The EMACS/TECO Mechanics EMACS was originally written as a set of macros for \textbf{TECO} (Text Editor and Corrector). TECO's interpreter read characters from a command string or terminal. Early hackers realized that by hooking into the character-input loop, they could check each incoming keystroke: 1. If the character matched a prefix (like \texttt{Ctrl} or \texttt{Meta}), intercept it. 2. Lookup the character in a table (a \textbf{keymap}). 3. Execute the corresponding macro string instead of performing the default TECO action.


---


2. The Birth of EMACS from TECO Macros


Before EMACS, TECO users had to type long command strings, then hit ESC-ESC to execute them (e.g. \texttt{5R} to move back 5 characters). In 1976, \textbf{Richard Stallman}, building on work by Guy Steele, Dave Moon, and others, unified various macro packages (like TECMAC and TMACS) into \textbf{EMACS}.


EMACS succeeded because it turned TECO's command interpreter into a real-time, WYSIWYG editor. It did this by replacing the top-level character read loop:


``` +-------------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
TECO Default Interpreter \\ \hline\hline
Char -> Append to Buffer -> Wait for Exec Command (ESC ESC) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------------+


v  (Interception Hook Added) +-------------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
EMACS Keymap Dispatch \\ \hline\hline
Char -> Hooked instantly -> Lookup in Keymap Table \\ \hline
-> Run Macro/Function directly on buffer \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------------+ ```


---


3. Improving Upon Carlson: A Dynamic Forth Hook Registry


We can take Carlson's static interception idea and modernize it. Instead of hardcoding a single intercept character, we implement a \textbf{Dynamic Prefix Hook Registry} in our Forth interpreter.


By using \texttt{defhook}, any arbitrary prefix character or token can be registered to dynamically redirect parsing to a custom Forth word:


``\texttt{forth \textbackslash  Example: Registering '@' to print character positions (equivalent to Carlson's PRINT AT hook) : print-at ." [CURSOR MOVED] " ; defhook @ print-at }``


This dynamic dispatching is direct intellectual ancestry to the keymaps (\texttt{global-set-key} / \texttt{define-key}) that define the flexibility of modern EMACS.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Micro Issue 26 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
MICRO: The 6502 Journal - Issue 26 (July 1980) \& The Hidden Math Engine


In July 1980, \textbf{Issue 26} of \textit{MICRO: The 6502 Journal} was published, delivering some of the most influential technical teardowns for Apple II, Commodore PET, and SYM/KIM/AIM microcomputers.


Among these, the standout feature was \textbf{"Apple's Hidden Floating-Point Routines" by John Martellaro} (pp. 132–135).


---


1. John Martellaro’s Discovery: The Applesoft ROM Math Engine


In 1980, RAM was scarce (typically 16KB to 48KB), and writing custom floating-point routines in assembly language was notoriously difficult and memory-intensive. Martellaro revealed that assembly programmers didn't need to write their own math libraries: \textbf{Applesoft BASIC (written by Microsoft) already had a complete, high-performance math coprocessor built directly into the Apple II's ROM (\$E000-\$FFFF).}


By calling these hidden entry points directly from 6502 Assembly, developers could perform 5-byte floating-point calculations with extreme precision, leaving almost all RAM free for the program itself.


``` +---------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
6502 Assembly Code \\ \hline\hline
Loads FAC (\$9D) and ARG (\$A1) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+---------------------------------------------+


v (JSR \$E7BE) +---------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Applesoft BASIC ROM \\ \hline\hline
Executes hardware-speed FADD \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+---------------------------------------------+


v +---------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
Result returned in FAC \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+---------------------------------------------+ ```


---


2. Key Applesoft Floating-Point Entry Points


Applesoft stores floating-point numbers in a \textbf{5-byte format} (1-byte exponent, 4-byte mantissa). The two main storage registers are the \textbf{Primary accumulator (FAC)} at \texttt{\$9D-\$A2} and the \textbf{Secondary accumulator (ARG)} at \texttt{\$A1-\$A6}.


Martellaro documented the primary entry points:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Routine & Address & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{FADD} & \texttt{\$E7BE} & Add FAC to ARG (Result in FAC) \\ \hline
\textbf{FSUB} & \texttt{\$E7A7} & Subtract FAC from ARG (Result in FAC) \\ \hline
\textbf{FMULT} & \texttt{\$E97F} & Multiply ARG by FAC (Result in FAC) \\ \hline
\textbf{FDIV} & \texttt{\$EA66} & Divide ARG by FAC (Result in FAC) \\ \hline
\textbf{FOUT} & \texttt{\$ED34} & Convert FAC to an ASCII string (for printing) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Recreating the "Hidden ROM" Pattern in our Virtual VM


This design pattern—where a low-level environment utilizes pre-baked ROM routines to save RAM—is exactly how we architected our \textbf{ZMM VM transient memory engine}.


Instead of writing complex mathematical functions inside the Z-Machine bytecode or Forth scripts, we map standard helper functions to \textbf{fixed, virtual ROM addresses} or trap events:


1. \textbf{Host-Side Operations}: The VM interceptor handles complex calculations or on-chain queries when the program jumps to specific virtual vectors (e.g. calling out to PulseChain for dynamic token data). 2. \textbf{Space Efficiency}: The game logic stays small, fast, and light, while the host VM does the heavy lifting.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Micro Issue 27 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
MICRO: The 6502 Journal - Issue 27 (August 1980) \& Arbitrary Precision Math


In August 1980, \textbf{Issue 27} of \textit{MICRO: The 6502 Journal} published a landmark math optimization article for the 6502 architecture: \textbf{"Nth Precision Add \& Subtract With Adjusted Processor Status" by Lawrence R. Golla}.


---


1. The Multi-Precision Challenge on 8-bit CPUs


The 6502 is a strict 8-bit processor. Its accumulator (\texttt{A}), index registers (\texttt{X}, \texttt{Y}), and Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) handle only 8-bit operands at a time. To add or subtract larger numbers (e.g. 16-bit, 24-bit, or 32-bit values), programmers had to chain arithmetic operations together using carry propagation:


``\texttt{assembly ; Standard 16-Bit Addition Example CLC             ; Clear Carry flag LDA Num1L       ; Load low byte of number 1 ADC Num2L       ; Add low byte of number 2 STA ResultL     ; Store low byte of result LDA Num1H       ; Load high byte of number 1 ADC Num2H       ; Add high byte of number 2 with carry STA ResultH     ; Store high byte of result }``


However, writing custom routines for every required precision size (16-bit, 24-bit, 32-bit, etc.) was tedious and bloated code space.


---


2. Golla's "Nth Precision" Zero-Page Engine


Golla solved this by creating a single, highly optimized subroutine that could handle \textbf{arbitrary byte lengths (N-precision)}.


To use it, the programmer set up five zero-page pointer variables: \textit{   \textbf{Pointer A} (2 bytes): Base address of Operand A. }   \textbf{Pointer B} (2 bytes): Base address of Operand B. *   \textbf{Precision Parameter N} (1 byte): The number of bytes to process.


The routine looped through each byte, loading values indirectly through zero-page pointers using indexing (\texttt{LDA (PointerA), Y}), performing \texttt{ADC} or \texttt{SBC}, and writing the results back.


The Status Flag Correction Hack A major bug in simple multi-byte loops is that the CPU's status register flags (specifically \textbf{Zero (Z)} and \textbf{Negative (N)}) reflect only the result of the \textit{very last byte} computed in the loop.


Golla introduced a clever masking technique to adjust the processor status register (\texttt{P}) on the stack so that when the subroutine returned (\texttt{RTS}), standard conditional branches (\texttt{BEQ}, \texttt{BNE}, \texttt{BMI}, \texttt{BPL}) behaved as if the entire N-byte number had been computed in a single step.


---


3. Structural Parallel: ZMM Multi-Word Bridging


This zero-page pointer indirect mapping directly mirrors how the \textbf{ZMM VM to EVM Bridge} performs arbitrary-precision conversions between 16-bit local memories and 256-bit EVM structures:


1.  \textbf{Zero-Page Indirects = ZMM MMIO Pointers}: Rather than loading data directly, we pass offset registers (e.g., target RAM addresses) to a unified loop decoder. 2.  \textbf{State Flags Adjustment}: When converting 256-bit EVM numbers to 16-bit words, we must mask and adjust execution state flags to prevent truncation errors, ensuring the virtual Z-Machine correctly processes bounds checks across the transaction boundaries.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Atropa Unified Instruction Set}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 08, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Atropa Unified Bytecode (AUB) Specification \#\# A Custom Unified Instruction Set for Yul Processors \& Peripherals


The \textbf{Atropa Unified Bytecode (AUB)} is a 16-bit virtual instruction set architecture (ISA) designed to bring cohesive unity to the various Yul virtual machines (\texttt{cpu6502.yul}, \texttt{zmachine.yul}) and peripheral systems (\texttt{graphicsSystem.yul}, \texttt{musicMaker.yul}, \texttt{keySystem.yul}, \texttt{diskSystem.yul}).


AUB replaces complex emulation overhead with a clean, memory-mapped instruction set that treats all processors and peripherals as unified participants on a single shared 16-bit bus.


---


1. Architectural Model


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD CPU[AUB Virtual CPU] <--> BUS[Unified 16-Bit Bus] BUS <--> RAM[System RAM \$0000-\$7FFF] BUS <--> VDP[Graphics VDP \$8000-\$9FFF] BUS <--> PSG[Audio POKEY \$A000-\$AFFF] BUS <--> KBD[Keyboard Buffer \$B000-\$B5FF] BUS <--> DSK[Disk Controller \$B600-\$BFFF] }``


CPU Registers - \textbf{A} (Accumulator, 8-bit): Arithmetic and logic. - \textbf{X, Y} (Index Registers, 8-bit): Loop counters and address indexing. - \textbf{PC} (Program Counter, 16-bit): Current instruction address. - \textbf{SP} (Stack Pointer, 8-bit): Points to stack space at \texttt{\$0100-\$01FF}. - \textbf{SR} (Status Register, 8-bit): Flag indicators (Carry, Zero, Interrupt, Negative).


---


2. Memory-Mapped Peripheral Registers


To unify the peripheral Yul systems, specific memory windows are bound to each subsystem's contract interfaces:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address Range & Subsystem & Description & Yul Interface Equivalent \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{\$8000 - \$80FF}} & \textbf{Graphics Controller} & Registers for scrolling (HSCROL/VSCROL), screen resolution, and palette updates. & \texttt{graphicsSystem.yul} \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{\$8100 - \$9FFF}} & \textbf{Frame Buffer / VRAM} & Screen pixel or character grid character layout. & \texttt{graphicsSystem.yul} \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{\$A000 - \$A00F}} & \textbf{Audio Synth (POKEY)} & Frequency controls, distortion masks, and volume registers. & \texttt{musicMaker.yul} \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{\$B000 - \$B00F}} & \textbf{Keyboard / Controller} & Key registers, buffer counts, and strobe buttons. & \texttt{keySystem.yul} \\ \hline
\textbf{\texttt{\$B600 - \$B6FF}} & \textbf{Disk Controller} & Track, sector, buffer address, and read/write execution flags. & \texttt{diskSystem.yul} \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)


AUB supports standard 8-bit opcodes with optional 8-bit or 16-bit operands:


Data Transfer Instructions \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{LDA \#val}} (\texttt{\$A9}, 2 bytes): Load Accumulator with immediate value. } \textbf{\texttt{LDA addr}} (\texttt{\$AD}, 3 bytes): Load Accumulator from absolute memory. \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{LDA addr, X}} (\texttt{\$BD}, 3 bytes): Load Accumulator from absolute memory indexed with X. } \textbf{\texttt{STA addr}} (\texttt{\$8D}, 3 bytes): Store Accumulator to absolute memory. \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{STA addr, X}} (\texttt{\$9D}, 3 bytes): Store Accumulator to absolute memory indexed with X. } \textbf{\texttt{LDX \#val}} (\texttt{\$A2}, 2 bytes): Load X register with immediate value. * \textbf{\texttt{STX addr}} (\texttt{\$8E}, 3 bytes): Store X register to absolute memory.


Arithmetic \& Logic \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{ADD \#val}} (\texttt{\$69}, 2 bytes): Add immediate value to Accumulator. } \textbf{\texttt{SUB \#val}} (\texttt{\$E9}, 2 bytes): Subtract immediate value from Accumulator. * \textbf{\texttt{CMP \#val}} (\texttt{\$C9}, 2 bytes): Compare Accumulator with immediate value.


Branch \& Control \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{JMP addr}} (\texttt{\$4C}, 3 bytes): Jump to absolute address. } \textbf{\texttt{JSR addr}} (\texttt{\$20}, 3 bytes): Jump to Subroutine. \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{RTS}}      (\texttt{\$60}, 1 byte): Return from Subroutine. } \textbf{\texttt{BEQ rel}}  (\texttt{\$F0}, 2 bytes): Branch if Zero flag set. * \textbf{\texttt{BNE rel}}  (\texttt{\$D0}, 2 bytes): Branch if Zero flag clear.


Unified Peripheral Control (Special Opcodes) * \textbf{\texttt{SYS op}}   (\texttt{\$0F}, 2 bytes): Trigger a hardware call directly to the underlying Yul peripheral system. - \texttt{SYS \$01}: Sync VRAM buffer to the Ethereum state/viewport. - \texttt{SYS \$02}: Play current sound registers loaded in \texttt{\$A000}. - \texttt{SYS \$03}: Force disk controller to execute operation specified at \texttt{\$B600}.


---


4. Example Program: Sprite Load and Sound Trigger


The following AUB program checks for a keypress, loads a sprite address to graphics memory, and triggers an audio note:


```assembly ; Address Mappings KEY\_REG      = \$B000 AUDIO\_FREQ   = \$A000 AUDIO\_VOL    = \$A001 VRAM\_START   = \$8100


START: ; 1. Poll for Keyboard press LDA KEY\_REG CMP \#\$00 BEQ START          ; Loop until a key is pressed


; 2. Play a tone via Audio peripheral LDA \#\$2F           ; Frequency pitch STA AUDIO\_FREQ LDA \#\$0F           ; Full Volume STA AUDIO\_VOL SYS \$02            ; Execute Audio hardware flush


; 3. Write a character to the center of the screen VRAM LDA \#\$5A           ; Character 'Z' STA VRAM\_START SYS \$01            ; Sync VRAM viewport display


RTS                ; Done ```


---


> [!TIP] > Introducing this unified instruction set layout drastically reduces the complexity of writing custom compilers or interpreters inside Yul contracts, enabling one-pass assemblers to compile code targeting both CPU and external devices under a single, unified bus structure.

\section{Ahoy Magazine Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Mike Schneider \& Ahoy! Magazine C64 SID Sound Code Review


This document reviews the historical context of \textbf{Mike Schneider} (Associate/Managing Editor at \textit{Ahoy!} Magazine) and analyzes how the C64 SID (Sound Interface Device) registers and polyphonic melody generators from the magazine are emulated and integrated within this codebase.


---


1. Historical Context: Mike Schneider at \textit{Ahoy!} Magazine During the 1980s home computer boom, \textit{Ahoy!} was one of the premier monthly publications for Commodore 64 and VIC-20 enthusiasts. \textit{ \textbf{The Role of Mike Schneider}: Rather than authoring individual game listings, Schneider served as a key editor and technical gatekeeper. He managed the preparation of the magazine’s source listings and was frequently mentioned in editorial humor regarding the magazine's size or the insertion of "clandestine features" into glossary pages. } \textbf{The Checksum Era}: Under his editorship, \textit{Ahoy!} popularized utilities like the \textbf{BASIC Bug Repellent}, a checksum-based system designed to prevent transcription errors when readers manually typed in long hexadecimal machine code listings.


---


2. SID Chip Memory-Mapped Emulation The code in [test\_ahoy\_issue1\_resonance.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_ahoy\_issue1\_resonance.c) emulates the memory-mapped sound registers of the C64's MOS Technology 6581/8580 SID chip:


``\texttt{c \#define SID\_BASE 54272 // \$D400 in Commodore 64 memory map }``


Voice Register Assignments Each of the 3 SID voices uses 7 registers. The test emulates frequency control, control registers, and envelope generators:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
SID Register & Address & Function & Emulated Mapping \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_V1\_FREQ\_LO} & \texttt{54272} & Voice 1 Frequency Low Byte & Pitch Control \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_V1\_FREQ\_HI} & \texttt{54273} & Voice 1 Frequency High Byte & Pitch Control \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_V1\_CTRL} & \texttt{54276} & Voice 1 Control (Gate, Waveform) & Waveform Selection \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_V1\_ATT\_DEC} & \texttt{54277} & Voice 1 Attack / Decay Rate & Envelope Control \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_V1\_SUT\_REL} & \texttt{54278} & Voice 1 Sustain / Release & Envelope Control \\ \hline
\textbf{SID\_VOLUME} & \texttt{54296} & Master Volume \& Filter Mode & Global Level (\texttt{0x0F} Max) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Emulated Polyphonic Sequence (Triads) The melody playback relies on C64 assembly-style POKEs to feed voice frequency bounds. A structured array of notes simulates polyphonic chord transitions (triads):


``\texttt{c static const uint16\_t melody\_v1[4] = \{0x1128, 0x159B, 0x1A40, 0x2250\}; // Bass root static const uint16\_t melody\_v2[4] = \{0x159B, 0x1A40, 0x2250, 0x2B78\}; // Thirds static const uint16\_t melody\_v3[4] = \{0x1A40, 0x2250, 0x2B78, 0x35E0\}; // Fifths/Octaves }``


Waveform Control Emulation When \texttt{trigger\_interrupt\_music\_maker()} fires, it loads the SID registers with different waveforms for each voice to produce rich, textured, classic chiptune harmonies: \textit{ \textbf{Voice 1 (Triangle wave - \texttt{0x11})}: Delivers smooth, clean bass roots. } \textbf{Voice 2 (Sawtooth wave - \texttt{0x21})}: Provides bright, buzzy middle thirds. * \textbf{Voice 3 (Pulse wave - \texttt{0x41})}: Generates hollow, square-like fifths and octaves.


---


4. TSFi2 Helmholtz Acoustic Proof-of-State Integration The simulated audio frequencies are not just for playback; they are fed directly into the \textbf{Helmholtz reduction kernel} to compile cryptographically verifiable proofs:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[C64 SID Emulation Registers] -->f1, f2, f3B[Linear Frequency Combination] B -->combined\_k = f1\textit{137 + f2}109 + f3*97C[Helmholtz Reduction Step] C -->Epoch State ReductionD[Verify Acoustic Proof Root] }``


1. \textbf{Frequency Compression}: The 3 frequencies are mixed using prime-based scaling weights: \$\$\textbackslash text\{combined\}\_k = (f\_1 \textbackslash times 137) + (f\_2 \textbackslash times 109) + (f\_3 \textbackslash times 97)\$\$ 2. \textbf{State Verification}: The resulting key is reduced via \texttt{tsfi\_helmholtz\_reduce\_11} against a virtual memory manifold, producing an acoustic root state hash. 3. \textbf{Integrity Pass}: This confirms that the sequence of chiptune interrupts matches the exact musical score compiled in C64 memory space.


> [!NOTE] > This represents a novel marriage of classic 8-bit sound chip registers with modern cryptographic verification concepts.


---


5. Hanson Kappelman (Issue 5 - May 1984) and Genealogy Tracking In \textbf{Ahoy! Issue 5 (May 1984)}, reader \textbf{Hanson Kappelman} of Pittsburgh, PA wrote requesting a Commodore 64 program for genealogy to construct family trees. To honor this in the modern virtual board-game framework (Yul CPU): \textit{ \textbf{Lineage Tracking}: Memory slot \texttt{55062} is utilized to dynamically monitor and trace ghost/entity lineages. } \textbf{Vector Visualizations}: Layer 2 renders dotted vector lineage paths linking each spawned entity to its corresponding ancestor generator.

\section{Renegade Yul Architecture}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Renegade BBS: EVM Yul Port Architecture


This document explores the architectural design for porting the classic \textbf{Renegade BBS} (originally written in Turbo Pascal for MS-DOS) into \textbf{Yul}, the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) intermediate assembly language.


---


1. Paradigm Shift: DOS vs. EVM


In MS-DOS, Renegade interacts directly with memory-mapped serial ports (UART), files on disk, and bios/interrupt routines. In Yul, the BBS operates as a decentralized state machine where every transaction represents a terminal keystroke or menu command.


``\texttt{mermaid graph LR subgraph MS-DOS A[User Terminal] <-->Serial/ModemB[UART / COM Port] B <--> C[Renegade.exe Pascal] C <-->File I/OD[Disk .DAT Files] end subgraph EVM / Yul E[User Terminal] <-->JSON-RPC CalldataF[EVM Node / Transpiler] F <--> G[Renegade Yul Contract] G <-->SSTORE / SLOADH[EVM State Trie] end }``


---


2. Storage Layout (256-bit Words)


Instead of Turbo Pascal record structures on disk, data is mapped to 256-bit EVM storage slots using Keccak256 hashes.


A. User Records In Pascal, a user record might be 200 bytes. In Yul, we pack user fields into storage slots:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Offset / Slot & Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{keccak256(user\_id, 0x01)} & \texttt{bytes32} & Username (up to 32 characters) \\ \hline
\texttt{keccak256(user\_id, 0x02)} & \texttt{uint256} & Security Level (DSL), Upload/Download bytes, post counts \\ \hline
\texttt{keccak256(user\_id, 0x03)} & \texttt{address} & Owner EVM Address (replaces passwords with ECDSA signatures) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
B. Message Bases (Squish / JAM style) Each message board has a message counter. Message contents are stored in chunks across sequential storage slots.


---


3. The ANSI Terminal \& Menu Engine in Yul


To render menus (e.g., the Main Menu with options like \texttt{[F]iles}, \texttt{[M]essage}, \texttt{[G]oodbye}), Yul functions calculate state transitions and return ANSI-encoded screen buffers.


```yul object "RenegadeBBS" \{ code \{ // Constructor: Initialize BBS sysop and default settings sstore(0, caller()) return(0, 0) \} object "runtime" \{ code \{ // Retrieve calldata signature (first 4 bytes) let selector := shr(224, calldataload(0))


switch selector // processKeystroke(uint8 char) -> returns (string ansiScreen) case 0x7c49b38f \{ let key := calldataload(4) let current\_state := sload(caller()) let next\_state, screen\_ptr, screen\_len := handle\_state\_transition(current\_state, key) sstore(caller(), next\_state) return(screen\_ptr, screen\_len) \} default \{ revert(0, 0) \}


function handle\_state\_transition(state, key) -> new\_state, ptr, len \{ // State 0: Main Menu if eq(state, 0) \{ // User pressed 'M' for Message Base if eq(key, 0x4d) \{ new\_state := 1 // Message Menu State ptr := 0x80    // Memory pointer to Msg Menu ANSI data len := 512     // Length of screen buffer return \} // User pressed 'G' for Goodbye if eq(key, 0x47) \{ new\_state := 2 // Disconnected State ptr := 0x280 len := 128 return \} \} // Default: keep state, return current menu new\_state := state ptr := 0x80 len := 512 \} \} \} \} ```


---


4. Key Advantages of a Yul BBS


1. \textbf{Password-less Security}: Authentication is handled via Ethereum cryptography (\texttt{caller()}). There are no password files to steal or brute-force. 2. \textbf{Zero-Configuration Multi-node}: Since transaction execution is atomic and sequential, the blockchain acts as a multi-node controller. No share-rationing or complex file lockouts (\texttt{SHARE.EXE}) are required. 3. \textbf{Decentralized Sysop Controls}: Moderation/Sysop permissions can be distributed via a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) contract.
