\section{Msd Cbm Disk Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Micro Systems Development (MSD) vs. Commodore Business Machines (CBM)


This review covers the historical context of \textbf{Micro Systems Development (MSD)}, its relationship to \textbf{Commodore Business Machines (CBM)}, and how their legacy floppy disk drive commands are emulated inside our virtual [DiskSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/diskSystem.yul) contract.


---


1. Historical Background


\textit{ \textbf{Commodore Business Machines (CBM)}: Dominant maker of the Commodore 64, VIC-20, and PET. Their standard disk drives (like the CBM 1541) were notoriously slow due to serial bus protocols and a custom MOS 6502 processor executing CBM DOS on-board the drive itself. } \textbf{Micro Systems Development (MSD)}: Founded in 1982 in Dallas by former CBM engineers. MSD designed high-performance third-party alternatives. \textit{ \textbf{The MSD SD-1 and SD-2}: Released in 1983, these were the first major third-party drives for the C-64. } The \textbf{SD-1} (single drive) and \textbf{SD-2} (dual drive) featured both the Commodore serial (IEC) bus and the faster IEEE-488 parallel bus. * The dual-drive \textbf{SD-2} became legendary because it could perform ultra-fast sector-to-sector disk copies directly from Drive 0 to Drive 1 without sending data back and forth to the computer.


---


2. Command Channel Protocols


Both CBM and MSD drives communicated using a dedicated \textbf{Command Channel} (typically channel 15). Programmers opened channel 15 to send instructions as string command payloads:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Command & Name & CBM/MSD Behavior & \texttt{DiskSystem.yul} Emulation \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{R0} & Read & Read file contents sequentially. & Reads private sandboxed or global BBS files via Keccak256 hash routing. \\ \hline
\texttt{W0} & Write & Write file contents sequentially. & Appends (for global BBS) or overwrites (for private sandboxed partitions) via EVM storage. \\ \hline
\texttt{D0} & Duplicate & Copy files/disks (\texttt{D0:dest=src}). & Direct copy of storage slots from source base slots to destination base slots. \\ \hline
\texttt{U1} & Block Read & Read raw sector data (\texttt{U1 track sector}). & Extracts 256 bytes from a mapped track/sector storage key. \\ \hline
\texttt{U2} & Block Write & Write raw sector data (\texttt{U2 track sector data}). & Overwrites 256 bytes directly into a mapped track/sector storage key. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Implementation in Yul Assembly


Our virtual [DiskSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/diskSystem.yul) contract replicates these CBM and MSD commands using EVM storage:


A. Utility Block Operations (\texttt{U1} and \texttt{U2}) The contract parses tracks and sectors using \texttt{parseTrackSector()}: ``\texttt{yul // Block Read Command (U1) if eq(cmdType, 0x5531) \{ // ASCII "U1" let track, sector := parseTrackSector(68, cmdLength) ... let sectorKey := keccak256(0x00, 64) let sectorSlot := keccak256(0x00, 64) ... return(0x00, 320) // Returns the 256-byte sector data \} }``


B. High-Speed Duplication (\texttt{D0}) Mimicking the MSD SD-2's internal copying function, the \texttt{D0} parser copies file contents slot-by-slot on-chain: ``\texttt{yul // Duplicate Command (D0:destfile=srcfile) if eq(cmdType, 0x4430) \{ // ASCII "D0" ... let srcLen := sload(srcLengthSlot) sstore(destLengthSlot, srcLen) let numSlots := div(add(srcLen, 31), 32) for \{ let i := 0 \} lt(i, numSlots) \{ i := add(i, 1) \} \{ sstore(add(destBaseSlot, i), sload(add(srcBaseSlot, i))) \} \} }``


---


4. Modern Takeaways


By emulating CBM DOS and MSD commands in Yul: 1. \textbf{Developer Nostalgia}: Legacy 6502 codebases running in the virtual CPU (such as \texttt{cpu6502\_v18} or \texttt{FolkloreCPU}) can use standard BASIC/Assembly disk command syntax. 2. \textbf{On-Chain Sandbox}: Users get an isolated partition to store and copy virtual disk blocks (\texttt{U1}/\texttt{U2}) and files (\texttt{W0}/\texttt{R0}/\texttt{D0}) securely using their address namespace.

\section{Graphics Display Technologies}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Graphics Display Technologies Review


We have several graphics display technologies integrated across the workspace:


---


1. Virtual VIC-II Sprite Collision Engine Located inside [graphicsSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/graphicsSystem.yul), this system emulates the classic Commodore 64 \textbf{MOS 6567/6569 VIC-II} sprite control registers: \textit{ \textbf{Register Mappings}: } \texttt{53248} to \texttt{53263} (\texttt{\$D000} to \texttt{\$D00F}): Sprite X/Y coordinate storage for Sprites 0–7. \textit{ \texttt{53269} (\texttt{\$D015}): Sprite Enable Mask (active sprite states). } \texttt{53278} (\texttt{\$D01E}): Sprite-to-Sprite Collision register. * \textbf{Collision Logic}: A smart contract method \texttt{checkCollisions()} dynamically compares active sprite coordinate bounds using C64 24x21 bounding box rules: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Collision iff \} \textbackslash Delta X< 24 \textbackslash text\{ and \} \textbackslash Delta Y< 21\$\$


---


2. KoalaPainter (.koa) Multicolored Bitmap Decoder Also located inside [graphicsSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/graphicsSystem.yul), this module decodes raw Commodore KoalaPainter format files (\texttt{.koa}, 10003 bytes): \textit{ \textbf{Memory Map Parsing}: } \textbf{Bitmap Area} (8000 bytes): 40x25 character grid cells, 8 bytes per cell. \textit{ \textbf{Screen RAM} (1000 bytes): Holds primary and secondary cell colors (upper/lower nibbles). } \textbf{Color RAM} (1000 bytes): Holds tertiary cell colors. \textit{ \textbf{Background Color} (1 byte): The default fallback color. } \textbf{Pixel Resolver}: The contract extracts color indexes dynamically based on target \$(X, Y)\$ screen coords.

3. KoalaPad Analog Touch Input Emulation \textit{ Implemented in [graphicsSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/graphicsSystem.yul) and tested in [test\_koala.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/test\_koala.js). } Provides an interface \texttt{updateKoalaPad(uint8 x, uint8 y, uint8 buttonState)} to simulate analog touch pad input, mapping coordinates into retro pointer subsystems.

4. B-Graph (bGraph) Plotting \& Computational Geometry Located inside [bGraph.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/bGraph.yul), this module offers statistical graphics processing: \textit{ \textbf{Linear Regression}: Calculates slopes, intercepts, and \$R\textasciicircum 2\$ values for sets of coordinates. } \textbf{Bar Chart Coordinator}: Takes array inputs and computes scaled coordinate bounds (\texttt{X1, Y1, X2, Y2}) for plotting bars on a \$320 \textbackslash times 180\$ display layout. \textit{ \textbf{Decision Tree Classifier}: Computes options for classification tasks (such as the }Ahoy!* Issue 3 "What's My Job?" tree).

\section{Kinematic Rigging Phase}

\vspace{0.1in}

The prompt is fed back into Phase 1, closing the self-improving loop.

\section{3D Rendering Advancements Deepseek}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
3D Rendering Advancements — DeepSeek \& Soft Diffusion


Modern high-performance rendering architectures have evolved beyond the physical limits of raw polygon rasterization. Rather than relying on slow real-time ray-tracing or heavy ML neural models at run-time, advanced systems leverage an \textbf{Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) Tri-Model Compilation Matrix} (combining Vision-Language Models, DeepSeek-Coder, and Stable Diffusion) to synthesize photorealistic geometry.


This document details the transition from early 3D wireframe pipelines to hybrid neural-procedural rendering, focusing on \textbf{Phase 0 Offset Matrices}, \textbf{VLM bounding box discovery}, and \textbf{soft diffusion texturing}.


---


1. The Tri-Model AOT Compilation Pipeline


To achieve low-latency real-time rendering, heavy neural models are decoupled from the active frame loop and moved to the offline compilation stage:


``` [Phase 1: Stable Diffusion]              -> Generates Photorealistic Target Reference


[Phase 1.1: Orthographic Multi-View]     -> Synthesizes aligned front/side/top blueprints


[Phase 2: Moondream2 VLM]                -> Audits blueprints, extracts normalized bounds


[Phase 2.5: Kinematic Rigging \& Hulls]   -> Binds skeletons, sets Euler limits \& collision hulls


[Phase 3: DeepSeek-Coder]                -> Computes Phase 0 Offset Matrix \& outputs C-struct/Yul math


[Phase 4: Run-time Engine]               -> Renders wireframe geometry \& applies Soft Diffusion noise


[Phase 7: RAG Self-Improvement Loop]     -> Compiles runtime telemetry back to RAG (/lore) ```


1.1 Phase 0: The Primary Offset Matrix To prevent anatomical drift during bipedal animation, all coordinates are locked to a rigid hierarchy of relative offsets: 1. \textbf{Body Anchor:} The primary coordinate node \$(X\_0, Y\_0, Z\_0)\$ acting as the absolute origin. 2. \textbf{Offset Calculations:} Cranial and limb nodes are calculated strictly as relative offsets (e.g., \$X\_\{\textbackslash text\{head\}\} = X\_0 + \textbackslash text\{offset\}\_x\$, \$Y\_\{\textbackslash text\{head\}\} = Y\_0 + \textbackslash text\{offset\}\_y\$). 3. \textbf{Result:} Limbs and body features move as a single unified coordinate mass, guaranteeing structural integrity.


1.2 Bounding Box Discovery via VLM (Phase 2 \& 2.5) When the VLM collapses color analysis into normalized spatial bounding boxes (e.g., body bounds \texttt{[Y\_min, X\_min, Y\_max, X\_max]}), the system treats these coordinates as rigid boundaries to calculate the proportions of the wireframe model: \textit{ \textbf{snout coordinates:} Positioned directly below eye boundaries. } \textbf{ear offsets:} Derived from the top 10\% bounds of the body frame. * \textbf{Rigging Alignment (Phase 2.5):} These boundaries are mapped to joints (with explicit Euler rotation limits) and wrapped in collision primitives (spheres/cylinders) before compiling.


---


2. Soft Diffusion \& Procedural Texture Mapping


Running a 3GB Stable Diffusion tensor model at runtime is too computationally expensive for real-time 60 FPS performance. Instead, we implement \textbf{Soft Diffusion}:


2.1 Standard Deviation Extraction 1. Stable Diffusion is run offline to generate flat, macro-photography textures of the entity surfaces (e.g., matted fur). 2. The compilation pipeline extracts the \textbf{Standard Deviation (Variance)} of the RGB pixels. 3. This variance is compiled as a constant vector: \$\textbackslash sigma = [\textbackslash sigma\_R, \textbackslash sigma\_G, \textbackslash sigma\_B]\$.


2.2 Procedural Noise Simulation At runtime, the rendering engine simulates the physical roughness of the Stable Diffusion texture by passing the wireframe coordinates through a high-speed procedural noise function: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Noise\}(x, y) = \textbackslash text\{fract\}(\textbackslash sin(x \textbackslash cdot 12.9898 + y \textbackslash cdot 78.233) \textbackslash cdot 43758.5453)\$\$ The noise output modulates the base vertex color by the variance factor \$\textbackslash sigma\$, achieving organic "soft diffusion" textures with zero GPU memory overhead.


---


3. On-Chain Yul Implementation: Soft Diffusion Wireframe Shader


The following Yul function projects a 3D wireframe vertex to 2D screen coordinates and calculates a procedurally diffused soft texture color using fractional sine noise.


```yul // Projects a 3D vertex and computes a soft-diffusion color value based on coordinate noise function renderSoftDiffusedVertex(x, y, z, baseR, baseG, baseB) -> scrX, scrY, colorR, colorG, colorB \{ let scale := 1000


// 1. Isometric Projection Step let cos30 := 866 let sin30 := 500 let xOffset := 128 let yOffset := 96


let rotatedX := div(mul(sub(x, y), cos30), scale) scrX := add(xOffset, rotatedX)


let rotatedY := div(mul(add(x, y), sin30), scale) scrY := sub(add(rotatedY, yOffset), z)


// 2. Soft Diffusion Noise Generation // Noise algorithm: fract(sin(x \textit{ 12.9898 + y } 78.233) * 43758.5453) // Scaled to integer fixed point for Yul: let inputNoise := add(mul(x, 12989), mul(y, 78233))


// Pseudo-random sine approximation: sin(v) approx v \% 31415 let sinApprox := mod(inputNoise, 31415)


// Large multiplier for fractional extraction let noiseRaw := mod(mul(sinApprox, 43758545), scale) // returns 0 - 999


// 3. Texture Variance Modulation (Soft Diffusion) // Fur roughness variance coefficients: R\_var = 13\%, G\_var = 9\%, B\_var = 7\% let varR := 130 let varG := 90 let varB := 70


// Apply noise factor to the base color components colorR := add(baseR, div(mul(noiseRaw, varR), mul(scale, scale))) colorG := add(baseG, div(mul(noiseRaw, varG), mul(scale, scale))) colorB := add(baseB, div(mul(noiseRaw, varB), mul(scale, scale)))


// Clamp color outputs to standard RGB limits (0 - 255) if gt(colorR, 255) \{ colorR := 255 \} if gt(colorG, 255) \{ colorG := 255 \} if gt(colorB, 255) \{ colorB := 255 \} \} ```


---


4. Comparison of 3D Rendering Techniques


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Aspect & Early 3D Isometric (Quicksilva) & Modern Neural AOT Rendering \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Pipeline Strategy} & Single-pass Painter's algorithm & Tri-model (VLM + SD + DeepSeek) offline compilation \\ \hline
\textbf{Occlusion Handling} & Depth sorting and block drawing & Z-buffer with spatial bounding box anchors \\ \hline
\textbf{Texture Quality} & Flat color / dithering patterns & Soft Diffusion (variance-driven procedural noise) \\ \hline
\textbf{Computational Footprint} & Extremely low (3.5 MHz Z80) & Zero runtime overhead (AOT pre-calculated bounds) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


> [!IMPORTANT] > The architectural key of Soft Diffusion is translating massive offline neural assets (Stable Diffusion normal maps) into low-level procedural math (\texttt{fract(sin())}). This guarantees photorealistic organic graphics at compile-time performance limits.

\section{Mercenary Pipeline Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Improving the Mercenary Virtual World Engine via the AOT Pipeline


This document details how we apply our \textbf{7-Phase Tri-Model Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) Compilation Pipeline} to upgrade the classic \textit{Mercenary} 3D wireframe and room database engine, automating coordinate layout, physics bounding, and texturing.


---


1. Upgraded Compilation Matrix for Mercenary


``` [ Phase 1: SD (Reference) ] --> [ Phase 1.1: Multi-View Blueprints ]


[ Phase 2.5: Kinematic \& Hulls ] <-- [ Phase 2: VLM Object Discovery ]


[ Phase 3: DeepSeek Compiler ]   --> [ Phase 4: Runtime Shader \& Database ]


[ Phase 7: RAG Telemetry Loop ] ```


---


2. Phase-by-Phase Upgrades


Phase 1 \& 1.1: Asset Blueprinting (Stable Diffusion \& Multi-View) \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: Stable Diffusion generates 3D orthographic multi-view blueprints of the spaceships, room interiors, and building meshes (e.g. the central hangar or planetary bunkers). } \textbf{Benefit}: Ensures clean vector projections. We extract the exact depth profiles (\$Z\$-axis) of rooms and spaceships instead of using hardcoded cuboids.


Phase 2: Bounding Box Discovery (Moondream2 VLM) \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: The VLM scans the multi-view blueprints and isolates structural coordinates: } \textbf{Room Boundaries}: Wall, ceiling, and floor dimensions. \textit{ \textbf{Interactivity Zones}: Locations of doors, keycard readers, and energy portals. } \textbf{Benefit}: Automatically determines local \$X, Y, Z\$ positions, eliminating the need to manually program inventory coordinates.


Phase 2.5: Collision Hull \& Joint Rigging \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: Wraps room objects and walls in collision primitives (infinite planes for floors/walls, bounding box hulls for items). } \textbf{Joint Rigging}: Defines motion joints for opening doors, rotating spaceship wings, and elevator vertical slides. * \textbf{Benefit}: Calculates collision bounding zones before writing code, allowing the Yul engine to check player position against walls using simple primitive inequalities instead of complex vertex distance checks.


Phase 3: DeepSeek Database \& Code Compilation \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: Takes the rigged boundaries and automatically packs them into the 256-bit metadata slots (\texttt{2000000 + objId}) and generates the Yul rotation/projection routines. } \textbf{Benefit}: Auto-generates the database mappings and updates target vertex tables (\texttt{\$D7F0}–\texttt{\$D8EF}) without manual register writing.


Phase 4: Run-Time Engine (Soft Diffusion Textures) \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: The runtime engine renders the projected 3D coordinates. It applies the \textbf{Soft Diffusion} noise function (\texttt{fract(sin())}) to add visual texture to: } The planetary ground grid (simulating Targ's rocky desert terrain). \textit{ The walls of the Target Building (simulating matted concrete paneling). } \textbf{Benefit}: Achieves styled, detailed textures on a flat 3D wireframe grid with zero frame rate impact.


Phase 7: RAG Ingestion \& Self-Improvement Loop \textit{ \textbf{Operation}: Records player movement trajectories, frame rates, and room transition speeds. Telemetry is saved back to \texttt{lore/telemetry\_feedback.md}. } \textbf{Benefit}: If a player gets stuck or experiences frame rate drops in highly complex rooms, the next compile cycle reads the telemetry and automatically simplifies the vertex count or adjusts boundary collision scaling.

\section{Improved Rigging Supports}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Upgrading Phase 2.5: Advanced Kinematic Rigging Supports


This document specifies advanced improvements to our \textbf{Phase 2.5 (Kinematic Rigging \& Hull Generation)} pipeline, introducing Inverse Kinematics (IK) target solvers, hull elasticity deformation, and dynamic center-of-mass balance vectors.


---


1. Inverse Kinematics (IK) Solvers To allow entity limbs to reach for specific coordinates (e.g. the Teddy Bear reaching for an object, or feet conforming exactly to uneven planetary terrain in the \textit{Mercenary} engine), we implement a fixed-point \textbf{Analytical IK Solver} in Yul:


``\texttt{ [Shoulder Joint (0,0)] \textbackslash   L1 (Upper Arm) \textbackslash  [Elbow Joint] / /  L2 (Forearm) v [Hand Target (Tx, Ty)] }``


The Trigonometric Solver Using the Cosine Rule, the solver calculates the target interior elbow angle \$\textbackslash theta\_2\$ and shoulder angle \$\textbackslash theta\_1\$: \$\$\textbackslash cos(\textbackslash theta\_2) = \textbackslash frac\{T\_x\textasciicircum 2 + T\_y\textasciicircum 2 - L\_1\textasciicircum 2 - L\_2\textasciicircum 2\}\{2 L\_1 L\_2\}\$\$ 1. \textbf{Scaled Integer Math}: Standard float trig is converted to 1000-scaled fixed-point integer lookup tables. 2. \textbf{Angle Clamping}: If the hand target exceeds the boundary distance (\$T\_x\textasciicircum 2 + T\_y\textasciicircum 2 > (L\_1 + L\_2)\textasciicircum 2\$), the target is clamped to the maximum extension line, preventing joint dislocation.


---


2. Hull Elasticity \& Collision Deformation Rather than treating collision hulls as perfectly rigid shapes, we introduce \textbf{Soft Hull Elasticity}: \textit{ \textbf{Deformation Vectors}: When a collision hull (e.g., the Teddy Bear's torso cylinder) collides with a boundary wall, the engine computes a deformation offset based on overlapping depth: \$\$\textbackslash vec\{D\} = \textbackslash text\{penetration\textbackslash \_depth\} \textbackslash times k\_\{\textbackslash text\{elastic\}\}\$\$ } \textbf{Visual Representation}: The Phase 4 shader applies this deformation offset directly to the wireframe vertices falling within the collision quadrant. This creates a visible "squish" or impact recoil when hitting surfaces, simulating soft matted stuffing under pressure.


---


3. Center of Mass (CoM) \& Dynamic Balance Vectors To prevent unnatural walking cycles and tipping over, the rigging compiler tracks weight distribution: 1. \textbf{CoM Coordinates}: Derived by multiplying the vertex coordinates of each hull by its mass density, then taking the weighted average. 2. \textbf{Base of Support (BoS)}: The polygonal area formed by the entity's feet (leg end vertices) touching the ground. 3. \textbf{The Balance Rule}: \textit{ If the projection of the CoM falls inside the BoS, the entity is stable. } If it falls outside the BoS, the rigging engine triggers a fall state or offsets the torso coordinates in the opposite direction to restore balance.


``` (CoM) * (Stable: Projection falls inside feet)


[Torso] /     \textbackslash  /       \textbackslash  [Foot]===[Foot] (Base of Support) ``` This guarantees physically stable bipedal stand and walk-off cycles.

\section{Accumulator Vector Fields}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Building AI Systems Within Accumulator Vector Fields


This document specifies the architecture for embedding \textbf{Agentic AI systems} directly within \textbf{Accumulator Vector Fields} on the TSFi2 platform, combining cryptographic state accumulation (Keccak-based history tracking) with sensory potential fields to drive autonomous planning.


---


1. Concept: The Accumulator Vector Field


Unlike a standard potential field (which evaluates forces statically per tick), an \textbf{Accumulator Vector Field} maintains a running integral of historical forces, sensory inputs, and planning state transitions inside a single compressed state accumulator:


``\texttt{ [Sensory Potential Fields] ----\textbackslash  +---> [State Accumulator (Slot \$D6D0)] ---> [AI Planner / Decision] [Cryptographic Keccak Nonces] -/ }``


The Accumulation Math The system integrates incoming forces \$\textbackslash vec\{F\}(t)\$ and planning nonces over time: \$\$\textbackslash vec\{A\}(t) = \textbackslash alpha \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash vec\{A\}(t-1) + (1-\textbackslash alpha) \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash vec\{F\}(t)\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$\textbackslash vec\{A\}(t)\$ is the \textbf{Accumulated Decision Vector} (representing momentum, memory, and intent). } \$\textbackslash alpha \textbackslash in [0, 1]\$ is the memory-weight discount factor (governing how quickly past path decisions are forgotten).


---


2. Emulated Accumulator Register Map (\$D6D0–\$D6DF)


To implement this directly within the virtual CPU/VM memory space, we define dedicated accumulator registers:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address (Hex) & Dec Address & Access Mode & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6D0} & \texttt{54992} & Read-Write & \textbf{Accumulated Vector X (\$A\_x\$)}: Fixed-point integrated horizontal force. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6D1} & \texttt{54993} & Read-Write & \textbf{Accumulated Vector Y (\$A\_y\$)}: Fixed-point integrated vertical force. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6D2} & \texttt{54994} & Read-Write & \textbf{Memory Weight (\$\textbackslash alpha\$)}: Discount coefficient (scaled 0-255). \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6D3} & \texttt{54995} & Read-Only & \textbf{State Hash Accumulator}: Keccak256 hash of all state transitions and inputs, ensuring cryptographic proof of pathing history. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6D4} & \texttt{54996} & Write-Only & \textbf{Reset / Flush Strobe}: Writing \texttt{1} clears the accumulator vector registers. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. On-Chain Yul Implementation: Accumulator Integration


The following Yul code integrates the incoming force vector from the resolving potential field directly into the accumulator memory space:


```yul // Method 19: accumulateVectorField(baseWeight, elapsedTicks, incomingFx, incomingFy) // Selector: 0x8a924b11 if eq(selector, 0x8a924b11) \{ let baseWeight := calldataload(4)    // Alpha weight (0 - 255) let elapsedTicks := calldataload(36) let incomingFx := calldataload(68) let incomingFy := calldataload(100)


let scale := 256


// Load current accumulated values let currentAx := sload(54992) let currentAy := sload(54993) let currentHash := sload(54995)

// Apply Exponential Moving Average integration: // A\_new = (A\_old \textit{ baseWeight + incoming } (scale - baseWeight)) / scale let newAx := div(add(mul(currentAx, baseWeight), mul(incomingFx, sub(scale, baseWeight))), scale) let newAy := div(add(mul(currentAy, baseWeight), mul(incomingFy, sub(scale, baseWeight))), scale)


// Update registers sstore(54992, newAx) sstore(54993, newAy)

mstore(0x00, 1) return(0x00, 32) \} ```

4. AI Planning Integration


By embedding the AI system within this accumulator: 1. \textbf{Decision Momentum}: The AI doesn't react spasmodically to short-term noise. Because \$\textbackslash vec\{A\}\$ integrates forces over time, the agent exhibits physical momentum, continuing along its planned trajectory until a strong repeller or attractor forces an accumulation shift. 2. \textbf{Cryptographically Auditable Paths}: The \texttt{State Hash Accumulator} at \texttt{\$D6D3} creates a tamper-proof execution record of the path traversed. \section{Vector Field Query Tokenization}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Semantic Tokenization via Accumulator Vector Fields


This document specifies how \textbf{Accumulator Vector Fields} are utilized to optimize semantic tokenization, attention weights, and context routing during database and RAG queries within the TSFi2 ecosystem.


---


1. Concept: Semantic Attention Accumulation


When a user query is parsed, standard tokenizers treat words as discrete, isolated indexes. By integrating \textbf{Accumulator Vector Fields}, we treat incoming query tokens as dynamic "forces" that pull or push the active context accumulator in a semantic vector space:


``` [Query Input String] --> [Token Parser]


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
(Tokens mapped to Attractors/Repellers) \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
v [Accumulator Vector Field] ---> [Context Routing / RAG Query] (Integrated Attention State) ```


The Attention Integration Math As each token \$T\_i\$ is processed, it exerts a force vector \$\textbackslash vec\{F\}(T\_i)\$ based on its semantic embedding: \textit{ \textbf{Attractors (Topic Anchors)}: Nouns, keywords, and explicit user goals pull the accumulator toward specific document categories (e.g., \texttt{"SID"}, \texttt{"Z-Machine"}, \texttt{"rigging"}). } \textbf{Repellers (Negation/Exclude Tokens)}: Negation words (e.g., \texttt{"without"}, \texttt{"not"}, \texttt{"exclude"}) push the context accumulator away from matching categories.


---


2. Decaying Context \& Slit Windows


To prevent older parts of a long query or conversation from diluting the active focus, we apply the \textbf{decaying history buffer} model to token weights: \textit{ As new tokens are parsed, the attention force of past tokens decays at rate \$\textbackslash lambda\$: \$\$W\_\{\textbackslash text\{attention\}\}(T\_i, t) = W\_\{\textbackslash text\{max\}\}(T\_i) - \textbackslash lambda \textbackslash cdot (t - t\_\{\textbackslash text\{parsed\}\})\$\$ } This ensures that the context vector \$\textbackslash vec\{A\}(t)\$ remains highly focused on the active subject window, naturally handling topic shifts without hard context-window cutoffs.


---


3. Emulated Tokenizer Registers Map (\$D6E0–\$D6EF)


To run this semantic routing directly inside the virtual CPU memory map, we define the following interface:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address (Hex) & Dec Address & Access Mode & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6E0} & \texttt{55008} & Read-Write & \textbf{Semantic Centroid X (\$C\_x\$)}: Integrated topic coordinates. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6E1} & \texttt{55009} & Read-Write & \textbf{Semantic Centroid Y (\$C\_y\$)} \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6E2} & \texttt{55010} & Read-Only & \textbf{Active Category ID}: Resolved document namespace to query in RAG database. \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D6E3} & \texttt{55011} & Write-Only & \textbf{Parse Trigger}: Writing \texttt{1} updates the centroid coordinates with the next token word. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


4. Query Routing Application


By using these accumulator coordinates: 1. \textbf{Semantic Hashing}: The final integrated coordinate \$(C\_x, C\_y)\$ is mapped to a document hash sector inside the on-chain registry, retrieving the most relevant lore files in milliseconds. 2. \textbf{Context-Aware Deduplication}: Duplicate concepts in queries cancel out dynamically (forces balancing to net zero), preventing redundant RAG retrieval loops.

\section{Standun Controls Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Standun Controls — Historical \& Technical Architecture Review


Standun Controls (primarily active in the late 1970s and 1980s as an industrial control systems manufacturer) expanded into microcomputing hardware and software. Through its divisions, Standun Controls bridged the gap between custom hardware disk controllers and integrated office productivity software.


This review traces the architectural line from Standun Controls' hardware and software assets to our virtual on-chain emulation layers in [diskSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/diskSystem.yul) and [test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c).


---


1. The Standun Corporate Umbrella


In the early 1980s, Standun Controls managed two primary computer-oriented divisions: 1. \textbf{Micro-Sci}: Focused on disk drive manufacturing, offering alternatives to Apple's Disk II and Commodore's 1541, with custom controller cards optimizing data retrieval. 2. \textbf{Cimarron (InstaSoftware)}: Focused on business utilities, word processors, and spreadsheet cartridges designed to maximize free computer memory.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD Standun[Standun Controls] -->Hardware DivisionMicroSci[Micro-Sci Disk Drives / Controllers] Standun -->Software DivisionCimarron[Cimarron / InstaSoftware] MicroSci -->Emulated RegistryDiskSystem[diskSystem.yul / \$B600 controller map] Cimarron -->Terminal ViewInstaMode[MODE\_INSTAWRITER in terminal\_shell] }``


---


2. Micro-Sci: Hardware Disk Controllers \& Sector Optimization


Micro-Sci designed controllers that modified track layouts and sector-reading intervals to bypass standard OS disk delays.


Historical Comparison vs. Our Yul Emulation


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Feature & Physical Micro-Sci Controller (Apple II / C64) & On-Chain [diskSystem.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/diskSystem.yul) Emulation \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Interface} & Edge connector slots, custom PROM & MMIO Register Map (\texttt{\$B600 - \$B6FF} / Disk Controller space) \\ \hline
\textbf{Sector Access} & Stepper-motor tracking \& half-tracks & Direct storage offsets in state slots (\texttt{0x20}–\texttt{0x9F}) \\ \hline
\textbf{Command Set} & Disk II sector read/write loops & Fast block-read (\texttt{U1}) and block-write (\texttt{U2}) commands \\ \hline
\textbf{Performance} & Speed adjustment potentiometers & Block-decayed processing \& gas-optimized writes \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
In \texttt{diskSystem.yul}, sector reads bypass standard protocol bottlenecks by referencing namespaced database slots directly, reflecting the low-overhead hardware approach that Micro-Sci pioneered.


---


3. Cimarron / InstaSoftware: The Productivity Layer


To showcase Micro-Sci hardware capabilities, Standun marketed the \textbf{Cimarron Insta-Series} (such as \textit{Insta-Writer}, \textit{Insta-Calc}, \textit{Insta-Graph}, and \textit{Insta-Vestor}).


\textit{ \textbf{Insta-Calc (Cartridge)}: Avoided using RAM by running directly from the cartridge ROM space (\texttt{\$8000–\$9FFF}), leaving maximum system memory for spreadsheet cells. } \textbf{Insta-Writer}: A document processor that utilized clean text line wrapping, now emulated as \texttt{MODE\_INSTAWRITER} in the [terminal shell](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c).


Software Integration


Insta-Series programs exchanged data using a unified sequential file format written to disk. Our current VM shell supports this pipeline by allowing files downloaded via \textbf{Software to Go} to write directly to the caller's sandboxed disk namespaces.


---


4. Current Integration \& Diagnostics


\textit{ \textbf{Terminal Activation}: Typing \texttt{INSTA} in the Wayland terminal menu invokes \texttt{MODE\_INSTAWRITER}, rendering the Cimarron word processor environment setup. } \textbf{Virtual Storage}: Disk reads/writes map to the on-chain registry, verifying that data packets adhere to the sandboxed storage boundaries. * \textbf{Build Check}: Verified that all C modifications in \texttt{test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c} compile cleanly under the project's strict \texttt{-Werror} rule.

Writing here triggers the virtual speech output engine, deducting a \textbf{Diyat Speech Tax} (1 OTRT token) on-chain. }   \textbf{\texttt{\$D608 - \$D609} (\texttt{54792 - 54793})}: TMS5220 Command/Data interface, mapping to a 16-byte internal FIFO buffer inside the Yul memory layout.

Writing a file index here deducts the \textbf{Diyat Library Tax} (2 OTRT) and pulls down file sectors directly into the caller's namespaced disk registry (\texttt{diskSystem.yul}).


---


3. Benefits of Virtual MMIO Architecture


1.  \textbf{Instruction-Set Portability}: Legacy 6502 binaries interact with hardware as if they were running on real silicon, while the underlying Yul engine converts these interactions into secure EVM state updates. 2.  \textbf{Explicit Resource Sandboxing}: User RAM registers are completely isolated from peripheral control registers, preventing any malicious overflow of execution boundaries. 3.  \textbf{Low-Overhead Call Execution}: Bypasses traditional Web3 JSON-RPC polling by allowing retro hardware loops to query data dynamically using PEEK and POKE instructions.

Bob Lloret's "Air Assault" — Historical \& Technical Review


First published in \textbf{Ahoy! Magazine Issue 5 (May 1984, page 45)}, \textit{Air Assault} is an action shoot-'em-up game designed by \textbf{Bob Lloret}. The game places the player in command of a ground defense cannon, fighting off waves of descending enemy aircraft.


We have fully integrated a virtualized emulation of \textit{Air Assault} into our terminal emulator shell ([test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c)), mapping it alongside our Cimarron spreadsheet interfaces.


---


1. Historical Gameplay Mechanics


In the original C64 version, Bob Lloret utilized sprite matrices and character custom fonts to render the descending helicopters: \textit{   \textbf{Player Cannon (\texttt{=\textasciicircum =})}: Placed at the bottom scanline, moving horizontally. }   \textbf{Enemy Aircraft (\texttt{v})}: Slowly sweep left-to-right and step down vertical scanlines. \textit{   \textbf{Missiles (``)}: Fired upwards, clearing out enemy lines upon collision detection. }   \textbf{Shield Integrity}: The player has 3 shield units. If an enemy reaches the bottom, shield strength is reduced.


---


2. Technical Integration in the Wayland Terminal Shell


We translate Bob Lloret's game loops and sprite collisions into a dedicated console mode (\texttt{MODE\_AIRASSAULT}):


2.1 State variables \textit{   \texttt{g\_air\_player\_x}: Canon offset column (1 to 48). }   \texttt{g\_air\_missile\_x} \& \texttt{g\_air\_missile\_y}: Missiles active on the coordinate grid. *   \texttt{g\_air\_invaders\_x[5]} \& \texttt{g\_air\_invaders\_y[5]}: Position states of descending enemy units.


2.2 Gameplay Actions \textit{   \textbf{Left / Right Movement}: Keys \textbf{\texttt{A}} and \textbf{\texttt{D}}. }   \textbf{Laser Missile Fire}: \textbf{\texttt{Spacebar}}. *   \textbf{Invader Update Loop}: Updated every 25 game ticks, moving enemy units down. When an enemy hits the baseline, it regenerates at the top and reduces player shields by 1.


---


3. Spreadsheet Synchronization (Cimarron Interop)


Reflecting Cimarron Corporation's historic focus on file pipeline interoperability under the Standun Controls umbrella, we have wired the active score metrics directly into the spreadsheet engine.


\textit{   When playing }Air Assault\textit{, the game score is updated in memory. }   Upon entering the \textbf{Insta-Calc} spreadsheet (command \texttt{CALC}), the current score and telemetry values are loaded from registers directly into row 4 cells, allowing developers to analyze performance data or write spreadsheet formulas using active game stats!

\section{Unreal Vaesen Mystery House 6502 Rocm}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Unreal Vaesen Mystery House: 6502 \& ROCm Hybrid Architecture


This specification outlines the hybrid integration of the \textbf{MOS 6502 Emulator} (running the core game state and player trauma logic) and the \textbf{ROCm (AMD HIP) GPU Accelerator} (powering parallel RAG database scans and real-time vector coordinate projection). By bridging these two architectures, we achieve authentic retro interactive fiction execution coupled with state-of-the-art high-dimensional AI story mapping.


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{/home/mariarahel/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/d40269bc-efcf-4529-8437-83e04f19b8b8/vaesen_mystery_house_1781025201147.png}
\caption{vaesen\_mystery\_house\_1781025201147.png}
\end{figure}
---


1. System Topology Overview


The hybrid game engine splits execution between the sequential 8-bit registers of the 6502 and the parallel GPU compute wavefronts of ROCm:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD Input["Player Command"] --> CPU6502["MOS 6502 Emulator (CPU)"] CPU6502 -->1. Write Trauma State to RAM \$D400RAM["6502 System RAM"] CPU6502 -->2. Trigger Vector RAG SearchBridge["EVM/HIP Bridge (\$D560)"] Bridge -->3. Transfer Query HashROCm["ROCm HIP GPU Kernel"] ROCm -->4. Parallel Cosine Similarity SearchRAG["Gothic Story Vector Embeddings"] RAG -->5. Return Ranked MatchRAM RAM -->6. Render wireframe linesDoodle["Doodle Graphics Buffer"] Doodle -->7. Upload FramebufferVulkan["Vulkan Staging Texture"] }``


---


2. 6502 Memory Map \& Vaesen Trauma Registry


Core player parameters, game screens, and retro sound cues are mapped into the Zero Page and specialized memory-mapped I/O zones:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Memory Address (6502 hex) & Registry Name & Type & Description \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$0010} & \texttt{PLAYER\_ROOM} & \texttt{byte} & Active room index (0 = House Exterior, 1 = Foyer, 2 = Parlor, 3 = Portal) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D400} & \texttt{PHYS\_TRAUMA} & \texttt{byte} & Vaesen physical trauma level (0 = Normal, 1 = Exhausted, 2 = Battered, 3 = Broken) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D401} & \texttt{MENT\_TRAUMA} & \texttt{byte} & Vaesen mental trauma level (0 = Normal, 1 = Shaken, 2 = Terrified, 3 = Panicked) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D402} & \texttt{JOYSTICK} & \texttt{byte} & Joystick state inputs mapped diagonally \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D560} & \texttt{HIP\_CALL\_TRIGGER} & \texttt{byte} & Writing \texttt{\$01} triggers high-speed ROCm compute dispatch \\ \hline
\texttt{\$D561}–\texttt{\$D57F} & \texttt{HIP\_QUERY\_HASH} & \texttt{32 bytes} & Keccak-256 hash of the parser query to project into ROCm vector space \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. ROCm (HIP) Parallel Cosine Similarity Kernel


The ROCm GPU parallelizes the search across thousands of story nodes and gothic dialogue options. A query vector (generated from the player's text command) is compared against pre-loaded story embeddings using dot-product similarity:


```cpp \#include <hip/hip\_runtime.h>


// HIP Kernel to perform parallel dot-product cosine similarity searches \_\_global\_\_ void roc\_story\_rag\_similarity( const float\textit{ \_\_restrict\_\_ query\_vector, const float} \_\_restrict\_\_ db\_vectors, float\textit{ \_\_restrict\_\_ scores, const int vector\_dim, const int num\_story\_nodes ) \{ int node\_idx = blockIdx.x } blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; if (node\_idx >= num\_story\_nodes) return;


float dot\_product = 0.0f; int offset = node\_idx * vector\_dim;


// Unrolled vector processing for AMD wavefront execution (64-wide) for (int i = 0; i < vector\_dim; i++) \{ dot\_product += query\_vector[i] * db\_vectors[offset + i]; \}


scores[node\_idx] = dot\_product; \} ```


---


4. 6502 Assembly Interface \& Game Loop


This assembly snippet shows how the 6502 game loop updates player coordinates, writes trauma states to RAM, and polls the ROCm/HIP accelerator:


```assembly ; ======================================================== ; UNREAL VAESEN MYSTERY HOUSE - MAIN CORE STATE LOOP ; ========================================================


* = \$C000               ; Start assembly execution


START   JSR INIT\_ROOM    ; Initialize starting room LOOP    JSR READ\_JOY     ; Read Zero Page joystick values LDA \$D401        ; Load Mental Trauma Level CMP \#\$03         ; Is player Panicked? BEQ PANIC\_SHIVER ; If yes, skip to panic jitter handling


UPDATE  JSR PHYS\_UPDATE  ; Apply fatigue delay JSR DRAW\_SCENE   ; Draw the vector wireframe JMP LOOP         ; Loop infinitely


PANIC\_SHIVER JSR RANDOM\_JIT   ; Calculate rapid screen jitter coordinates JSR DRAW\_SCENE JMP LOOP


; --- Trigger GPU Dispatch --- TRIGGER\_ROCM LDX \#\$00 WRITE\_HASH LDA HASH\_BUF, X  ; Load hash segment STA \$D561, X     ; Write to GPU communication area INX CPX \#\$20 BNE WRITE\_HASH


LDA \#\$01 STA \$D560        ; Write 1 to launch ROCm kernel RTS ```


---


5. Visual Rendering Coordination


> [!NOTE] > All coordinates are represented as 5-byte packed structures (\texttt{fromX, fromY, toX, toY, colorCode}).


1. \textbf{Vector Projection}: The active room index from Zero Page \texttt{\$0010} is loaded. If a ROCm scene update is active, the GPU transforms room coordinates (applying rotation/scaling matrices in parallel) and writes the results back to the C64 Doodle framebuffer. 2. \textbf{Consensus Synchronization}: The C host verification harness reads the generated frame, hashes the frame using AVX-512 registries, and validates it against the active EVM transaction block to ensure consensus.

Ahoy! Magazine Issue 6 (June 1984) — Technical \& Historical Review


Published in June 1984, \textbf{Issue 6 of Ahoy! Magazine} captured a major turning point in the home computer market, detailing Commodore's new hardware direction and featuring advanced program listings designed to push character-graphics memory layouts to their limits.


This review details the magazine's key highlights and aligns them with our on-chain Yul and terminal-shell emulation architecture.


---


1. Page 4: "A View from the Bridge" (Editorial Column)


Page 4 contains the editor's column \textbf{"A View from the Bridge"}, introducing the June 1984 issue's main focus: \textbf{programming tools, generators, and column debuts}.


1.1 Orson Scott Card's Debut Column \textit{   \textbf{Announcement}: The debut of a new recurring column, }Creating Your Own Games\textit{ for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20, written by renowned author \textbf{Orson Scott Card} (who was formerly a Senior Editor at }COMPUTE! Books\textit{). }   \textbf{Focus}: Card's column aims to guide hobbyist developers through the mechanics of interactive game design, coordinate movement, and state variables in game development.


1.2 Code and Program Generators *   \textbf{Article Previews}: Introduces features on program generator applications by Joe Rotello and Bernhardt Hurwood. They evaluate C64 code generation utilities that write BASIC files automatically, highlighting the shift from raw code entry to algorithmic automation.


1.3 VIC-20 Sound and Memory Management \textit{   \textbf{Audio Features}: A.J. Kwitowski introduces simplified sound registers concept, while Morton Kevelson's }Memory Management on the VIC and 64 (Part II)* details the internal RAM expansion layouts.

The cover story of Issue 6 reviews the upcoming \textbf{Commodore 264 and 364 series} (which would launch as the \textbf{Plus/4} and \textbf{C16}). \textit{   \textbf{Integrated Software}: Unlike the Commodore 64, which relied on external cartridges (like Cimarron's }Insta-Calc\textit{) or floppy disks, the 264 series featured built-in productivity software in ROM: a word processor, spreadsheet, database manager, and graphing package. }   \textbf{Our Emulation Alignment}: This built-in software concept mirrors our terminal shell menu, where typing commands like \texttt{WORDCRAFT}, \texttt{INSTA}, \texttt{CALC}, or \texttt{APPLEPANIC} dynamically switches between word processing, dynamic spreadsheets, and games, all operating inside a single unified Wayland environment.

2. Program Listing: "Slinky" by David L. Lindsell


One of the most popular game listings in Issue 6 was \textbf{Slinky}, an isometric action puzzle game where the player guides a spring-like toy down a pyramid of 3D-appearing blocks, changing each block's color upon landing (heavily inspired by arcade \textit{Q}bert*).


``\texttt{ /\textbackslash  /\_\_\textbackslash  /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash  /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash  /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash  /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash  /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash   /\textbackslash  /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash /\_\_\textbackslash  }``


2.1 Isometric Character-Mapping Mechanics To render the 3D pyramid on a standard character grid, David Lindsell utilized custom character sets (redefining the C64's character generator RAM at \texttt{\$3000}–\texttt{\$37FF}). Left-diagonal and right-diagonal slopes were drawn in custom glyph tiles and combined to represent the edges of the isometric blocks.


2.2 On-Chain Coordinate Verification To implement \textit{Slinky}'s isometric physics and collision checks on-chain, we can represent the pyramid structure as a triangular matrix in a packed Yul array: \textit{   \textbf{Pyramid Row \$R \textbackslash in [0..6]\$}: Row index of the block. }   \textbf{Pyramid Column \$C \textbackslash in [0..R]\$}: Column index of the block within that row. *   \textbf{Grid Vertex Calculation}: \$\$x = X\_\{\textbackslash text\{offset\}\} + (C - \textbackslash frac\{R\}\{2\}) \textbackslash times \textbackslash Delta X\$\$ \$\$y = Y\_\{\textbackslash text\{offset\}\} + R \textbackslash times \textbackslash Delta Y\$\$


This maps standard 2D array offsets directly to the 3D-skewed coordinates on the terminal renderer.

Technical Proposal: Hurwood Code Generator Optimization \& Integration


This document reviews advanced upgrades for the \textbf{Hurwood Code Generator} suite (\texttt{HURWOOD [MAZE SOUND SPRITE CHARSET RASTER JOYSTICK]}), focusing on dynamic compilation, execution bridges, and integration with \texttt{YULBUILD}.


---


1. Dynamic Frequency Calculations (\texttt{SOUND} Parameterization)


Currently, \texttt{HURWOOD SOUND} outputs a static envelope for C-4. We can calculate the exact register values dynamically based on target frequencies:


\textit{   \textbf{SID Frequency formula}: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Register Value\} = \textbackslash text\{Frequency (Hz)\} \textbackslash times \textbackslash frac\{16777216\}\{f\_\{\textbackslash text\{clk\}\}\}\$\$ Where \$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{clk\}\} = 1022727\textbackslash text\{ Hz\}\$ (NTSC clock rate). }   \textbf{Implementation}: A CLI input like \texttt{HURWOOD SOUND --freq 440} will compute: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Value\} = 440 \textbackslash times 16.405 = 7218 \textbackslash implies \textbackslash text\{High Byte\} = 28, \textbackslash text\{Low Byte\} = 50\$\$ Generating the customized line: \texttt{30 POKE 54273, 28: POKE 54272, 50}


---


2. Compaction \& Optimization of BASIC Listings


To fit resource-constrained emulators and save cycles, the generator should pack statements using standard Commodore 64 BASIC shortcuts:

\hline
Original Template & Optimized Structure & Memory Saved \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{10 POKE 53280,0}<br>\texttt{20 POKE 53281,0} & \texttt{10 POKE 53280,0:POKE 53281,0} & 5 bytes (combines lines) \\ \hline
\texttt{10 FOR I=832 TO 894}<br>\texttt{20 POKE I,255}<br>\texttt{30 NEXT I} & \texttt{10 FORI=832TO894:POKEI,255:NEXT} & 9 bytes (removes spaces, optional variable in \texttt{NEXT}) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Direct Memory Injector Bridge


Rather than just displaying the text, a \texttt{--stage} flag can write the generated code directly to RAM starting at the BASIC limit pointer (\texttt{\$0801}):


``\texttt{mermaid graph LR Command["HURWOOD SOUND --stage"] --> Tokenizer["BASIC Tokenizer"] Tokenizer --> RAM["VM Memory Space (\$0801)"] RAM --> VM["Run / List instantly"] }``


*   \textbf{Poking Tokenized Lines}: The C code parses the text representation (e.g. \texttt{10 PRINT "HI"}) and converts keywords to Commodore 64 tokens (\texttt{PRINT} = \texttt{\$99}, \texttt{POKE} = \texttt{\$97}) and writes them directly into the emulated RAM.


---


4. Cross-Tool Integration with \texttt{YULBUILD}


We can add a bridge so that generating code outputs assembly routines readable by \texttt{YULBUILD}:


\textit{   \textbf{Syntax}: \texttt{HURWOOD [SCHEMA] --asm} }   \textbf{Result}: Outputs standard 6502 assembly formatting instead of Commodore BASIC: ``\texttt{assembly LDA \#\$0F STA \$D418 ; Max volume LDA \#\$0F STA \$D405 ; ADSR }`\texttt{ *   \textbf{Piping to Editor}: }HURWOOD SOUND --asm --edit\texttt{ copies these assembly statements directly into the }g\_yulbuild\_asm\texttt{ editor buffer, allowing the user to immediately debug or step through the generated audio routine inside }YULBUILD`!

\section{Memory Injector Security}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Technical Assessment: Direct Memory Injector Bridge (Benefits \& Security)


This assessment reviews the architectural advantages, threat model, and mitigation strategies for introducing the \textbf{Direct Memory Injector Bridge} (staging generated C64 BASIC/assembly bytes directly into virtual RAM \texttt{\$0801}).


---


1. Architectural Benefits


Direct injection bypasses manual keyboard entry buffers to write structured code blocks directly into the VM memory space:


\textit{   \textbf{Frictionless Developer Testing}: Eliminates typing overhead for large register arrays (e.g., custom VIC-II character sets or complex SID envelope tables). }   \textbf{Deterministic Pointer State}: The C host automatically adjusts the C64 pointer registers (\$45/\$46 end of variables, \$2B/\$2C start of BASIC, and \$2D/\$2E end of program) to reflect the exact injected size, avoiding "Out of Memory" or pointer desync errors. *   \textbf{Gas \& Call Optimization (On-Chain)}: Tokenized BASIC bytes are up to 60\% smaller than ASCII text. Compressing listings into binary structures before pushing them to the Yul EVM minimizes calldata overhead.


---


2. Security Implications \& Threat Model


Bypassing keyboard input loops opens direct pathways to the memory core. The following table highlights key risks:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Threat / Risk & Target Vector & Severity & Mitigation Strategy \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Buffer Overflow / Memory Corruption} & Overwriting Zero Page (\$00–\$FF), Stack (\$0100–\$01FF), or System Vectors (\$0300–\$03FF). & \textbf{High} & Strictly validate that injection targets do not overlap system-reserved boundaries. Enforce \texttt{\$0801} as the lower bounds limit. \\ \hline
\textbf{Arbitrary Code Execution (Emulator Escape)} & Injection of malicious machine language payloads targeting host system resources. & \textbf{Medium} & The emulator VM is sandboxed inside the EVM/Yul context. Enforce strict type validation on poked addresses and prevent direct injection of unauthorized binary payloads. \\ \hline
\textbf{Spectral VAE DNA Drift} & Raw injection bypassing normal parser audit chains, causing structural consensus drift. & \textbf{Medium} & Couple the injection routine with \texttt{lau\_audit.c} combinatorial validation, triggering VAE resets if resonance feedback exceeds boundaries. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


3. Sandboxing \& Memory Protection Schema


To prevent memory clashing and emulator crashes, the injector should implement a validation mask before committing pokes:


``` +-------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
0x0000 - 0x07FF: System Reserved (Zero Page, Stack) & -> BLOCK WRITE \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
0x0801 - 0x2FFF: Permitted BASIC Space & -> ALLOW WRITE \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
0x3000 - 0x3FFF: Custom Character Matrix (ROM/RAM) & -> READ-ONLY / WARN \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
0xD000 - 0xDFFF: Memory-Mapped I/O Registers & -> Vetted writes only \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------------------------------------------+ ```


Validator Rule: ``\texttt{c bool is\_injection\_safe(uint16\_t addr, size\_t size) \{ uint32\_t end\_addr = addr + size; // Prevent system-area clashing if (addr < 0x0801) return false; // Prevent wrapping or over-writing past custom matrix zone if (end\_addr > 0xC000) return false; return true; \} }`` Using this validation mask guarantees that direct memory injections cannot crash the interpreter or destabilize the emulated operating system state.

\section{Vic20 Yul Upgrades}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Technical Proposal: Yul CPU Upgrades for VIC-20 Emulation


To support authentic VIC-20 hardware programs (such as A.J. Kwitowski's \textit{Sound Concept}) natively on-chain within the Yul-compiled \texttt{cpu6502.yul} contract, several memory and peripheral address upgrades should be considered.


---


1. VIC-I (MOS 6560/6561) MMIO Space Mapping


Currently, the Yul CPU emulator intercepts Commodore 64 registers (VIC-II at \texttt{\$D000} and SID at \texttt{\$D400}). To run VIC-20 code, we must map the VIC-I registers:


\textit{   \textbf{Address Range}: \texttt{\$9000}–\texttt{\$900F} (36864–36879 decimal). }   \textbf{Registers to Intercept}: \textit{   \texttt{\$9000}–\texttt{\$9003}: Screen columns, rows, character size, and horizontal/vertical raster offsets. }   \texttt{\$9004}: Current raster line. \textit{   \texttt{\$900A}–\texttt{\$900D}: Bass, Tenor, Soprano, and Noise voice registers (the target for the Kwitowski-Harris }Sound Concept\textit{). }   \texttt{\$900E}: Auxiliary color and master volume. *   \textbf{Yul Code Upgrade}: In \texttt{cpu6502.yul} memory writes, implement address routing: ``\texttt{yul if and(gte(addr, 0x9000), lte(addr, 0x900F)) \{ // Store in dedicated VIC-I state variables/storage keys sstore(add(VIC\_I\_STORAGE\_OFFSET, sub(addr, 0x9000)), val) leave \} }``


---


2. VIC-20 RAM Expansion Layouts


The standard VIC-20 has only 5K of RAM. Upgrading memory configurations to support external RAM cartridges requires adding bank-switching boundaries in Yul memory lookups:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
Memory Blocks & Function / Cartridge Slot \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{\$0000}–\texttt{\$03FF} & System Areas (Zero page, Stack, Vector maps) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$0400}–\texttt{\$0FFF} & 3K RAM Expansion (Block 0) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$1000}–\texttt{\$1FFF} & Standard User BASIC RAM (without expansions) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$2000}–\texttt{\$7FFF} & 8K RAM Expansion Blocks (1, 2, and 3) \\ \hline
\texttt{\$A000}–\texttt{\$BFFF} & 8K ROM Expansion (Game Cartridges) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
*   \textbf{Upgraded Lookup Logic}: If a RAM expansion is active, the \texttt{cpu6502} load/store logic must map addresses dynamically based on configured registers, allowing standard assemblies to run without clashing with the basic zero page.


---


3. Dual MOS 6522 VIA (Versatile Interface Adapter) Timers


The VIC-20 relies on dual 6522 VIAs at \texttt{\$9110}–\texttt{\$912F} for timers and keyboard interrupts.


*   \textbf{On-Chain Decrementing Timers}: Implement decrementing counters based on the VM step cycles. For example, during every \texttt{step()} execution block in Yul: ``\texttt{yul let timer\_a := sload(VIA1\_TIMER\_A) if gt(timer\_a, 0) \{ timer\_a := sub(timer\_a, 1) sstore(VIA1\_TIMER\_A, timer\_a) if eq(timer\_a, 0) \{ trigger\_via\_interrupt() \} \} }`` This achieves deterministic timer interrupts directly on-chain without requiring external clock synchronization from the host system.

\section{Ahoy Issue 6 Gameplay Improvements}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Ahoy! Magazine Issue 6 (June 1984) — Gameplay Improvements Guide


Based on the technical review of \textit{Ahoy! Magazine} Issue 6, there are several key game design and implementation principles that can be integrated to improve gameplay mechanics within our emulated software suites.


---


1. Orson Scott Card's Game Design Axioms


Orson Scott Card's debut column \textit{"Creating Your Own Games"} outlines foundational rules for establishing highly engaging, responsive gameplay on 8-bit architectures:


1.1 Clear Goal Structures and Feedback Loops - \textbf{Objective Clarity}: The player must understand their objective immediately without complex manuals. In \textit{Slinky}, the goal of coloring every block is visually obvious. - \textbf{Dynamic State Mappings}: Visual cues must immediately reflect state transitions. Highlighting cells or playing audio notes (e.g. using the Kwitowski sound driver) upon successful action reinforces the feedback loop.


1.2 Fluid Coordinate Movement and Inertia - \textbf{Proportional Bounds Checking}: Rather than immediate grid stepping, game physics should check boundary coordinates with small fractional increments or strict diagonal vectors to prevent clipping and make traversal feel natural. - \textbf{Decoupled Input Scans}: Input scanning (from Joystick CIA registers or raw keyboard queues) must run independently from the graphics frame rate.


---


2. David L. Lindsell's Isometric Diagonal Mappings


Lindsell's \textit{Slinky} solves the problem of mapping 2D inputs onto a 3D isometric block pyramid by establishing a dedicated diagonal key binding system:


2.1 Isometric Control Mapping By default, 2D arrow keys do not align with a 3D pyramid. To align inputs with the visual coordinate axes: - \textbf{\texttt{I} (Up-Left)}: Moves the player diagonally up-left. - \textbf{\texttt{O} (Up-Right)}: Moves the player diagonally up-right. - \textbf{\texttt{K} (Down-Left)}: Moves the player diagonally down-left. - \textbf{\texttt{L} (Down-Right)}: Moves the player diagonally down-right.


Implementing this layout in emulators (like our \texttt{SLINKYBEAR} and \texttt{SLINKYPANIC} modes) dramatically reduces player frustration and matches visual motion directly to keyboard triggers.


---


3. Recommended Actions for Our Codebase 1. \textbf{Unify Key Bindings}: Apply \texttt{I}, \texttt{K}, \texttt{L}, \texttt{O} diagonal jump bounds to our interactive \texttt{SLINKY} modes to match the original \textit{Slinky} mechanics. 2. \textbf{Dynamic Highlights}: Ensure screen writes use high-contrast color codes from the C64 palette (such as white or light blue highlights) to emphasize state changes immediately upon collision.

\section{Ahoy Issue 6 Pages 38 40 Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Ahoy! Magazine Issue 6 (Pages 38-40) — Sound Concept for the VIC 20


On pages 38-40 of \textit{Ahoy!} Issue 6 (June 1984), author \textbf{A.J. Kwitowski} published the seminal article \textbf{"Sound Concept for the VIC 20"}. This article introduced a simplified register assignment mapping model to standardise multi-channel audio synthesis on the VIC-20's VIC-I chip.


---


1. Technical Register Mappings (Pages 38-39)


Kwitowski detailed the three primary voice registers and the noise channel located within the VIC-I (\$36864–\$36879) address block:


\textit{   \textbf{Voice 1 (Bass/Alto)}: Memory address \textbf{\texttt{36874}}. Controlled low octave registers (\texttt{128–255} pitch ranges). }   \textbf{Voice 2 (Tenor)}: Memory address \textbf{\texttt{36875}}. Controlled mid-range frequencies. \textit{   \textbf{Voice 3 (Soprano)}: Memory address \textbf{\texttt{36876}}. Controlled high octave frequencies. }   \textbf{Voice 4 (Noise/Static)}: Memory address \textbf{\texttt{36877}}. Used for percussive sounds or retro explosions. *   \textbf{Master Volume}: Memory address \textbf{\texttt{36878}}. The lower 4 bits (\texttt{0–15}) set global amplitude.


---


2. Playback Queue Layout (Page 40)


To play notes programmatically, the article standardises a \textbf{3-byte data cell structure} staged in memory: 1.  \textbf{Byte 1 (Voice Index)}: Maps to register offsets (\texttt{10} for Voice 1, \texttt{11} for Voice 2, \texttt{12} for Voice 3, \texttt{13} for Voice 4). 2.  \textbf{Byte 2 (Frequency)}: Represents the raw pitch code (\texttt{128–255}). 3.  \textbf{Byte 3 (Duration)}: The gate length in ticks.


This data is queued in sequential memory rows and read by the assembly player thunk (SYS Hook \texttt{\$0D00}) or BASIC driver loop.


---


3. Emulation Integration Our \texttt{HURWOOD CONCEPT} program generator (which outputs C64/VIC-20 BASIC code) maps this exact 3-byte structure, utilizing a sentinel row \texttt{DATA -1, 0, 0} to terminate execution cleanly.

\section{Ahoy Issue 6 Page 63 Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Ahoy! Magazine Issue 6 (June 1984) — Page 63 Code Review


Page 63 of the June 1984 issue of \textit{Ahoy! Magazine} features Dale Rupert's recurring column \textbf{"Commodares,"} where reader-submitted solutions to previous programming challenges are showcased.


The code samples printed on this page present elegant, optimized, and creative implementations in C64 BASIC. Below is a technical analysis of the main listings.


---


1. Challenge \#5-4: The Letter Triangle This challenge required generating a triangle of alphabetical characters where each letter is repeated according to its alphabetical position (A once, B twice, C thrice, up to Z).


BASIC Listing: ``\texttt{basic 10 FOR L = 1 TO 26 20 FOR N = 1 TO L 30 PRINT CHR\$(L + 64); 40 NEXT N 50 PRINT 60 NEXT L }``


Analysis: \textit{ \textbf{Nested Loops}: The outer loop cycles through the 26 letters of the alphabet (\texttt{L}). The inner loop repeats \texttt{L} times to print the character. } \textbf{Character Mapping}: \texttt{CHR\$(L + 64)} maps the loop index \texttt{L} (1 to 26) to the uppercase ASCII/PETSCII values for A–Z (\texttt{65} to \texttt{90}). * \textbf{Formatting}: The semicolon \texttt{;} at the end of line 30 prevents printing carriage returns between matching letters, while line 50 forces a new line at the end of each row.


---


2. Problem \#2: Reversals The task was to take an input word or phrase and output it in reverse order. The shortest solutions were optimized down to a single BASIC line.


Shortest One-Liner (Dino Russo): ``\texttt{basic 1 INPUT "WORD OR PHRASE"; W\$: FOR L = LEN(W\$) TO 1 STEP -1: PRINT MID\$(W\$, L, 1);: NEXT }``


Centered Screen Variation (S. Gaudet): This variation centers the reversed string horizontally on the C64's 46-column screen: ``\texttt{basic 1 INPUT N\$: L = LEN(N\$): FOR X = L TO 1 STEP -1: PRINT TAB((20 - LEN(N\$)) / 2) MID\$(N\$, X, 1);: NEXT }``


---


3. Right-to-Left Typing (Ken Buskirk) This creative solution prints characters onto the screen from right to left in real-time as the user types them.


BASIC Listing (Paraphrased): ``\texttt{basic 10 X = 39: B\$ = CHR\$(32): C\$ = CHR\$(13) 20 GET A\$: IF A\$ = "" THEN 20 30 X = X - 1: PRINT SPC(X) A\$ "\{CURSOR\_UP\_LEFT\}" 40 IF A\$ = B\$ AND X <= 10 THEN X = 39: PRINT 50 IF X = 0 THEN X = 39: PRINT 60 IF A\$ = C\$ THEN X = 39: PRINT 70 GOTO 20 }``


Analysis: \textit{ \textbf{Interactive Buffer}: Uses \texttt{GET} to capture single keypresses asynchronously instead of blocking on \texttt{INPUT}. } \textbf{Dynamic Spacing}: Employs \texttt{SPC(X)} and terminal cursor controls to reposition the characters backwards, giving a reverse-typing visual effect.


---


4. Palindrome Solver (Mark Nekic) A palindrome solver determines if a word is spelled the same forwards and backwards. Mark Nekic submitted the shortest program using a single line:


BASIC Listing: ``\texttt{basic 1 INPUT N\$: L = LEN(N\$): FOR X = 1 TO L: IF MID\$(N\$, X, 1) = MID\$(N\$, L + 1 - X, 1) THEN NEXT: PRINT "YES" }``


Analysis: \textit{ \textbf{Symmetry Check}: Compares character \texttt{X} from the beginning with character \texttt{L + 1 - X} from the end. } \textbf{Implicit Loop Logic}: The loop continues using \texttt{THEN NEXT}. If any character mismatch occurs, the condition \texttt{IF ... THEN NEXT} fails, the loop halts, and "YES" is skipped, indicating it is not a palindrome.

\section{Ahoy Issue 7 Code Listings Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Ahoy! Magazine Issue 7 (July 1984) Code Listings Review


This document reviews the architecture, memory layouts, and algorithmic design of the program listings published in \textit{Ahoy!} Issue 7 (July 1984) for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20.


---


1. Math Defender (VIC-20 \& C64) — Andy Van Duyne An educational arcade action game where mathematical equations fall down columns, and the player must input the correct answer before the equations reach the bottom of the screen.


1.1 Architectural Flow \textit{   \textbf{Game Loop}: Operates on a vertical gravity tick. Every \$N\$ frames, the active equation moves down by one row. }   \textbf{Input Handling}: Maps keys \textbf{\texttt{F}} and \textbf{\texttt{J}} to navigate left/right columns, and the number row to input numerical answers. *   \textbf{Equation Generator}: Dynamically constructs random math pairs: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Value\}\_1 \textbackslash times \textbackslash text\{Value\}\_2 = \textbackslash text\{Target\}\$\$ Difficulty registers scale the maximum operand size from single-digit integers up to double-digit products.


1.2 Sound \& VIC Registers (VIC-20 version) \textit{   \textbf{Voice Registry}: Writes to the middle voice generator at address \texttt{36876}. }   \textbf{Siren Effect}: Decrements voice frequency value from 240 down to 130 inside the game-over loop to simulate a failing defense warning. *   \textbf{Border Color}: Set via \texttt{POKE 36879, 238} for high contrast (Green background, black border).


---


2. Renumbering Utility (C64) — Anthony Wood A system utility written by a teenage Anthony Wood (later founder of Roku) designed to re-index BASIC line numbers.


2.1 BASIC RAM Structure Manipulation In C64 BASIC V2, programs are stored as a singly linked list starting at \texttt{\$0801} (2049): \textit{   \textbf{Link Pointer} (2 bytes): Points to the memory address of the next line. }   \textbf{Line Number} (2 bytes): Big-endian line index. *   \textbf{BASIC Tokens}: Null-terminated stream of tokens and values.


``` +------------------+------------------+------------------+------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Link Pointer LSB & Link Pointer MSB & Line Number LSB & Line Number MSB \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+------------------+------------------+------------------+------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
<---------------- 2 Bytes ---------> & <---------------- 2 Bytes ---------> \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```


2.2 Algorithm Design 1.  \textbf{Pass 1 (Address Collection)}: Traverses the link pointers starting at \texttt{2049}, mapping the old line numbers to their memory addresses and new target line numbers. 2.  \textbf{Pass 2 (Line Renumbering)}: Overwrites the 2-byte line number fields with the new linear progression sequence. 3.  \textbf{Pass 3 (Link Resolution \& GOTO Update)}: Decodes tokenized statements looking for \texttt{GOTO} (\texttt{\$89}), \texttt{GOSUB} (\texttt{\$8D}), and \texttt{ON GOSUB} token sequences, modifying the target line numbers in-place based on the Pass 1 mapping.


---


3. What's My Job? (C64) — B.W. Behling A dynamic database game demonstrating a \textbf{Binary Decision Tree} for classification.


``\texttt{ [ Has fur? ] /        \textbackslash \textbackslash  (Yes)       (No) /            \textbackslash \textbackslash  [ Bark? ]        [ Slithers? ] /     \textbackslash \textbackslash           /         \textbackslash \textbackslash  (Dog)    (Cat)   (Snake)      (Fish) }``


3.1 Memory \& Data Serialization \textit{   \textbf{Nodes Array}: Stored in a flat table representing parent-child linkages: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Node\} = \textbackslash \{ \textbackslash text\{Text\}[64], \textbackslash text\{LeftChildIndex\}, \textbackslash text\{RightChildIndex\} \textbackslash \}\$\$ }   \textbf{Dynamic Learning}: When a guess is incorrect, the program prompts the user: 1.  \textit{What is the correct job?} 2.  \textit{Provide a distinguishing yes/no question.} 3.  Splits the current leaf node into a question node with two new leaves (the old guess and the new job). *   \textbf{Disk/Tape Storage}: Writes sequentially to disk via device 8: \texttt{OPEN 1, 8, 2, "0:JOB DATA,S,W"}


---


4. Bug Repellent V2 (C64 \& VIC-20) The magazine's proofreader tool to prevent typos when entering code.


\textit{   \textbf{Logic}: Hooked into the C64's \textbf{\texttt{CHRGET}} routine at memory address \texttt{\$0073}. }   \textbf{Checksum Verification}: Sums the character values of the currently typed line, performs an XOR check, and outputs a 2-letter alphabetic proof code. The reader compares this code against the published tables to check for spelling mistakes.

On-Chain Emulator Integration Specification


This document details the hardware mapping, register layouts, and software hooks required to bridge retro BASIC and machine language applications from \textit{Ahoy!} Issues 7, 8, and 9 to our simulated 6502 Yul CPU (\texttt{cpu6502.yul}) and peripheral contracts.


---


1. Memory-Mapped I/O Maps


The emulator utilizes namespaced storage mapping to simulate Commodore 64 and VIC-20 memory layout structures:


``` +-------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address Range & Subsystem / Function & Yul Target Slot / Helper \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\$0000 - \$00FF & Zero Page (Registers) & Private Storage / getUserSlot \\ \hline\hline
\$0400 - \$07E7 & C64 Screen RAM & graphicsSystem.yul Screen Buffer \\ \hline
\$0801 - \$9FFF & BASIC Program Area & RAM Emulation \\ \hline
\$D000 - \$D02F & VIC-II Display Registers & graphicsSystem.yul config \\ \hline
\$D400 - \$D41F & SID Sound Synthesizer & musicMaker.yul Voice registers \\ \hline
\$D800 - \$DBE7 & VIC-II Color RAM & graphicsSystem.yul Color mapping \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+-------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+ ```


---


2. KERNAL Hook Trapping (Disk DOS System)


To support utilities like \textbf{Directory Assistance} and \textbf{DOS}, we intercept standard Commodore KERNAL ROM entry points within \texttt{cpu6502.yul}:


2.1 Vector Trap Setup \textit{   \textbf{LOAD (\texttt{\$FFD5})}: Trapped at PC address \texttt{65493}. }   \textbf{SAVE (\texttt{\$FFD8})}: Trapped at PC address \texttt{65496}.


When the PC hits these vectors, the emulator suspends native execution and pulls arguments from Zero Page registers: \textit{   \texttt{\$B7} (183): Filename length. }   \texttt{\$BB-\$BC} (187-188): Pointer to filename string. *   \texttt{\$BA} (186): Current device number (usually 8 for disk drive).


2.2 Sector-Level Directory Traversal Yul procedures query the \texttt{diskSystem.yul} contract by formatting calldata targeting Track 18 Sector 0 (Block Availability Map) to retrieve the directory chain: 1.  Read Track 18, Sector 0: Extract the first directory block coordinates (Track 18, Sector 1). 2.  Traverse Directory Blocks: Read sector data, offset 3–18 for filenames, and offsets 21–22 for block sizes.


---


3. SID Audio Register Mapping


For \textbf{Sound Explorer}, register offsets are translated in real-time to generate raw audio output:

Register Offset & Name & Synthesizer Mapping \\ \hline\hline

\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\$D400 / \$D401 & Voice 1 Frequency (LSB/MSB) & Frequency = (MSB * 256 + LSB) / 16 \\ \hline\hline
\$D405 / \$D406 & Voice 1 Attack / Decay & ADSR Envelope parameters \\ \hline
\$D404 & Voice 1 Control Register & Waveform select (Noise, Pulse, etc) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
+--------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+ ```

4. VIC 40 Column Display Upgrade (Completed)


We have implemented the software-rendered display columns expansion technique: *   \textbf{Grid boundary trapping}: When \texttt{COLS 40} is selected, screen rendering wraps/clips at column 40 inside the Wayland display loop, successfully simulating the custom character font layout conversion.


---


5. PTE Word Processor Architectural Integration Pathway


To fully integrate the \textbf{PTE Word Processor} into our emulator workspace, we establish a dedicated editor mode (\texttt{MODE\_PTE}) utilizing a modular architecture:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD Input[Keyboard Event] -->Raw KeystrokesRouter\{Editor Mode Router\} Router -->MODE\_PTEPTE[PTE Control Engine] PTE -->Ctrl+M: Set MarginsLayout[Page Wrap Engine] PTE -->Insert/Delete CharBuffer[Line Buffer Array] PTE -->Ctrl+P: Save FileFloppy[diskSystem.yul SEQ Handler] Layout -->Reflow TextRender[graphicsSystem.yul screen RAM] }``


5.1 Memory Layout \& Wrap Boundaries \textit{   \textbf{Text Buffer}: Allocated as a sequence of linked text lines in memory (\texttt{\$0801} upwards). }   \textbf{Boundary Margins}: Stored at registers \texttt{\$02} (Left Margin) and \texttt{\$03} (Right Margin). The Wrap Engine queries these boundaries during insertion to shift text segments dynamically.


5.2 Disk I/O Bridge (On-Chain Storage) \textit{   When a print or save operation (\texttt{Ctrl+P} / \texttt{Ctrl+S}) is issued, the control engine converts the line buffers into a standard Commodore Sequential (\texttt{.SEQ}) file stream. }   This stream is written block-by-block to the on-chain Yul Floppy controller (\texttt{diskSystem.yul}) by raising a virtual disk interrupt.

\section{Ahoy Issue 12 Page 48 49 Review}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 09, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Ahoy! Issue 12 (December 1984) — Pages 48–49 Review


On pages 48 and 49 of \textbf{Issue 12 (December 1984)}, \textit{Ahoy!} magazine details the design and application of its signature \textbf{type-in proofreading utilities}, highlighting how hobbyists verified large BASIC programs.


---


1. Technical Context: The "Bug Repellent"


Type-in program listings in the 1980s were notorious for syntax errors introduced during manual keyboard entry. To mitigate this, \textit{Ahoy!} utilized two specialized validation tools:


1. \textbf{The Bug Repellent}: \textit{ A small machine language utility loaded into memory before typing the target program. } Whenever a user completed typing a line of BASIC and pressed \textbf{RETURN}, the utility calculated a checksum of the line's bytes and printed a 3-character verification code on the screen. * Users compared this code with the printed values in the magazine's column margins. A mismatch immediately flagged a typing error.


2. \textbf{The Line Total System}: \textit{ Provided a static table at the end of program listings. } Summed the ascii values of each line's instructions.


---


2. Page 48–49 Operational Guide


The text on pages 48 and 49 breaks down the workflow for using these checksum proofreaders:


\textit{ \textbf{Relocation}: The Bug Repellent machine code was designed to reside in a safe memory location (typically starting at \texttt{\$C000} / \texttt{49152} decimal) so that it would not be overwritten by the BASIC program being entered (which starts at \texttt{\$0801} / \texttt{2049} decimal). } \textbf{Control Characters}: The pages detail the bracketed notation used to represent Commodore graphics characters (e.g. \texttt{\{SC\}} for clear screen, \texttt{\{BL\}} for blue text color, or \texttt{\{CR\}} for carriage returns). Because standard printers could not easily print these proprietary Commodore PETSCII symbols, the bracketed labels served as translation guides.

\textbf{Gameplay \& Mechanics} \textit{ \textbf{Command}: Type \texttt{TOWERS} in the terminal, or select it from the \texttt{BOOTER} menu. } \textbf{Controls}: \textit{ Press \textbf{\texttt{A}}, \textbf{\texttt{B}}, or \textbf{\texttt{C}} to select the source peg. } Press \textbf{\texttt{A}}, \textbf{\texttt{B}}, or \textbf{\texttt{C}} again to select the destination peg. \textit{ Press \textbf{\texttt{ESC}} to return to the shell. } \textbf{Visualization}: Rendered with dynamic height block representation (\texttt{\textit{} characters indicating disk sizes) on retro-styled pegs. } \textbf{Rules}: Standard Hanoi rules (larger disks cannot be placed on smaller ones).
