\section{Computer Design Issue 15 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 11, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Computer Design Magazine (Issue \#15 - June 1964) Architectural Analysis


This report reviews the core technical concepts of June 1964-era hardware engineering featured in \textbf{Computer Design Magazine (Vol. 3, No. 5)}, specifically focusing on \textbf{Plated-Wire Memory (Non-Destructive Readout - NDRO)}, and documents its simulation mapping in \textbf{TSFi2}.


---


1. Core Historical Features


Plated-Wire Memory (NDRO) \textit{ \textbf{High-Speed Thin-Film Storage:} Developed in the late 1950s/early 1960s and commercialized by 1964, plated-wire memory consists of a beryllium-copper wire electroplated with a thin layer of magnetic permalloy (nickel-iron). } \textbf{Non-Destructive Readout (NDRO):} Unlike magnetic core memory (where reading a bit flips the core and requires a slow rewrite cycle), plated-wire memory utilizes magnetization vector rotation. Reading rotates the vector temporarily, inducing a sense signal, and then the vector returns to its easy axis automatically when the read field is removed. \textit{ \textbf{Easy and Hard Axes:} } Magnetization normally lies along the \textbf{easy axis} (circumferential around the wire). * A word line (strap wrapped around the wire) applies a transverse field along the \textbf{hard axis} (longitudinal to the wire).


---


2. TSFi2 Integration Architecture


To simulate the electromagnetic and physical mechanics of Plated-Wire Memory cells (incorporating read/write fields, magnetization angle rotation, and induced sense voltage dynamics), we introduce:


1. \textbf{[tsfi\_plated\_wire.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/inc/tsfi\_plated\_wire.h):} Interface declaring the plated-wire memory cell structure, magnetic parameters, and read/write update functions. 2. \textbf{[tsfi\_plated\_wire.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_plated\_wire.c):} Physical model simulating coherent magnetization rotation under external fields and electromagnetic induction. 3. \textbf{[test\_plated\_wire.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_plated\_wire.c):} Test suite verifying NDRO read cycles (retaining states after read), write cycles (setting 0 and 1), and checking for zero memory leaks.


Mathematical \& Physical Model


1. Magnetization Rotation (Stoner-Wohlfarth Model) The magnetization vector angle \$\textbackslash theta\$ (relative to the easy axis) under longitudinal field \$H\_L\$ and transverse field \$H\_T\$ is modeled by minimizing the magnetic energy: \$\$E = K \textbackslash sin\textasciicircum 2(\textbackslash theta) - M\_s H\_L \textbackslash cos(\textbackslash theta) - M\_s H\_T \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash theta)\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$K\$ is the uniaxial anisotropy constant. } \$M\_s\$ is the saturation magnetization. * Setting \$\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial E\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash theta\} = 0\$ yields the equilibrium angle.


2. Induced Sense Voltage The rotation of magnetization \$\textbackslash theta(t)\$ changes the longitudinal flux, inducing a voltage in the central copper conductor: \$\$V\_\{sense\} = -\textbackslash alpha \textbackslash cdot M\_s \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash frac\{d(\textbackslash cos \textbackslash theta)\}\{dt\}\$\$ \textit{ A positive \$\textbackslash theta\$ rotation induces a positive voltage pulse if the initial state was '1' (clockwise magnetization). } A negative voltage pulse is induced if the initial state was '0' (counter-clockwise).


---


3. Verification \& Memory Sanitation The plated-wire simulator is fully verified under the standard memory check guidelines of \texttt{LauMemory} with zero unsealed leaks.

\section{Computer Design Issue 16 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 11, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Computer Design Magazine (Issue \#16 - July 1964) Architectural Analysis


This report reviews the core technical concepts of July 1964-era hardware engineering featured in \textbf{Computer Design Magazine (Vol. 3, No. 6)}, specifically focusing on Teledyne's \textbf{Micro-Electronic Modular Assembly (MEMA)} packaging, and documents its simulation mapping in \textbf{TSFi2}.


---


1. Core Historical Features


Micro-Electronic Modular Assembly (MEMA) \textit{ \textbf{High-Density Packaging for Aerospace:} MEMA was developed to pack dozens of integrated circuit flat-packs onto a single multi-layered ceramic substrate (postage-stamp sized). } \textbf{Engineering Trade-offs:} \textit{ \textbf{Pro:} Reduced physical computer volume, reduced signal propagation skew, and improved overall system weight/reliability for aerospace applications. } \textbf{Con:} Extremely high thermal density and severe electrical crosstalk (\$V\_\{crosstalk\}\$) due to close micro-stripline spacing. * \textbf{Electrical Parasitics:} Fast signal rise times (\$t\_r \textbackslash approx 2\textbackslash text\{ ns\}\$) induce mutual capacitive (\$C\_m\$) and mutual inductive (\$L\_m\$) coupling between adjacent parallel lines.


---


2. TSFi2 Integration Architecture


To model the physical parasitics, signal integrity, and thermal characteristics of a MEMA packaging module, we introduce:


1. \textbf{[tsfi\_mema.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/inc/tsfi\_mema.h):} Interface declaring the MEMA module layout, trace parameters, thermal nodes, and simulation step functions. 2. \textbf{[tsfi\_mema.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_mema.c):} Numerical simulator modeling near-end/far-end crosstalk (NEXT/FEXT) and multi-node thermal dissipation. 3. \textbf{[test\_mema.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_mema.c):} Test suite verifying crosstalk limits under varying trace separations, thermal heat dissipation thresholds, and checking for zero memory leaks.


Mathematical \& Physical Model


1. Electrical Crosstalk (NEXT \& FEXT) Adjacent micro-stripline coupling is simulated using the near-end (NEXT) and far-end (FEXT) voltage formulas on the victim trace: \$\$V\_\{NEXT\}(t) = K\_\{NEXT\} \textbackslash cdot [V\_\{agg\}(t) - V\_\{agg\}(t - 2t\_d)]\$\$ \$\$V\_\{FEXT\}(t) = K\_\{FEXT\} \textbackslash cdot L\_c \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash frac\{dV\_\{agg\}(t)\}\{dt\}\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$t\_d\$ is the electrical propagation delay along the trace. } \$L\_c\$ is the coupling length. * \$K\_\{NEXT\}, K\_\{FEXT\} \textbackslash propto \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{d\textasciicircum 2\}\$ (where \$d\$ is the trace separation distance). If \$d\$ is below a critical threshold, \$V\_\{NEXT\}\$ exceeds the noise margin, triggering a logic glitch.


2. Thermal Resistance Mesh The MEMA module contains multiple IC nodes. Heat transfer between node \$i\$, the alumina ceramic substrate (\$T\_\{sub\}\$), and ambient (\$T\_\{amb\}\$) is simulated: \$\$C\_i \textbackslash frac\{dT\_i\}\{dt\} = P\_i - \textbackslash frac\{T\_i - T\_\{sub\}\}\{R\_\{jc\}\} - \textbackslash frac\{T\_i - T\_\{amb\}\}\{R\_\{ja\}\}\$\$ Where \$R\_\{jc\}\$ is junction-to-case thermal resistance and \$P\_i\$ is the node power dissipation.


---


3. Verification \& Memory Sanitation The MEMA simulator is fully verified under the standard memory check guidelines of \texttt{LauMemory} with zero unsealed leaks.

\vspace{0.1in}
Computer Design Magazine (Issue \#17 - August 1964) Architectural Analysis


This report reviews the core technical concepts of August 1964-era mixed-signal hardware engineering featured in \textbf{Computer Design Magazine (Vol. 3, No. 7)}, specifically focusing on \textbf{Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs)}, and documents its simulation mapping in \textbf{TSFi2}.


---


1. Core Historical Features


Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC \textit{ \textbf{Data Acquisition for Digital Systems:} Early industrial control and aerospace computers required converting analog transducer signals into digital binary words. } \textbf{The Binary Search Algorithm:} The SAR ADC uses a single analog comparator and a Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) to perform a binary search. Starting from the MSB, it tests each bit, keeping it if the DAC output is lower than the input, or clearing it if the DAC output exceeds the input. An \$N\$-bit conversion completes in exactly \$N\$ clock cycles. \textit{ \textbf{Mixed-Signal Constraints in 1964:} } \textbf{R-2R Ladder Tolerances:} Resistor mismatches in the DAC ladder lead to non-linearity (INL/DNL errors) and non-monotonic behavior. * \textbf{Comparator Offset \& Hysteresis:} Thermal drift and offset voltages in the discrete transistor comparator limit resolution.


---


2. TSFi2 Integration Architecture


To model the physical mixed-signal behavior of a historical 8-bit SAR ADC (incorporating R-2R ladder tolerances, comparator offsets, and settling delay dynamics), we introduce:


1. \textbf{[tsfi\_sar\_adc.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/inc/tsfi\_sar\_adc.h):} Interface declaring the SAR ADC configuration parameters, DAC R-2R ladder offsets, and conversion step functions. 2. \textbf{[tsfi\_sar\_adc.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_sar\_adc.c):} Physical model simulating the DAC voltage output with resistor errors, analog comparator decisions with offset, and clock cycle timing. 3. \textbf{[test\_sar\_adc.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_sar\_adc.c):} Test suite verifying conversion accuracy under varying DAC tolerances and comparator offsets, checking monotonic performance, and ensuring zero memory leaks.


Mathematical \& Physical Model


1. Mismatched R-2R DAC Output The DAC output voltage \$V\_\{dac\}\$ for an 8-bit digital word \$D = [d\_7 d\_6 \textbackslash dots d\_0]\$ factoring in resistor tolerance errors \$\textbackslash epsilon\_i\$ for each stage is: \$\$V\_\{dac\} = V\_\{ref\} \textbackslash sum\_\{i=0\}\textasciicircum \{7\} d\_i \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash frac\{1 + \textbackslash epsilon\_i\}\{2\textasciicircum \{8-i\}\}\$\$ Where \$\textbackslash epsilon\_i \textbackslash in [-tolerance, tolerance]\$. If resistor tolerances are untrimmed (\$\textbackslash sim 5\textbackslash \%\$), the output can become non-monotonic.


2. Comparator Decision with Offset and Deadband The comparator output \$C\_\{out\}\$ is modeled as: \$\$C\_\{out\} = \textbackslash begin\{cases\} 1 \& \textbackslash text\{if \} V\_\{in\} - V\_\{dac\} - V\_\{offset\} \textbackslash ge \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash Delta V\}\{2\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  0 \& \textbackslash text\{if \} V\_\{in\} - V\_\{dac\} - V\_\{offset\} \textbackslash le -\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash Delta V\}\{2\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{random\}(0, 1) \& \textbackslash text\{otherwise (within noise/deadband region)\} \textbackslash end\{cases\}\$\$ Where \$V\_\{offset\}\$ is the comparator offset voltage and \$\textbackslash Delta V\$ is the resolution deadband.


---


3. Verification \& Memory Sanitation The SAR ADC simulator is fully verified under the standard memory check guidelines of \texttt{LauMemory} with zero unsealed leaks.

\section{Computer Design Issue 18 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 11, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Computer Design Magazine (Issue \#18 - September 1964) Architectural Analysis


This report reviews the core technical concepts of September 1964-era digital signal conditioning featured in \textbf{Computer Design Magazine (Vol. 3, No. 9)}, specifically focusing on \textbf{Discrete Transistor Emitter-Coupled Schmitt Triggers}, and documents its simulation mapping in \textbf{TSFi2}.


---


1. Core Historical Features


Emitter-Coupled Schmitt Triggers \textit{ \textbf{Signal Conditioning in 1964:} Early digital computers had to read inputs from slow-moving or noisy mechanical and magnetic peripherals (e.g., photoelectric paper tape readers, magnetic drum read heads). Slow rise times and noise would cause double-triggering or jitter in standard logic gates. } \textbf{Hysteresis Loop:} Implementing a Schmitt trigger using emitter-coupled transistors provides two distinct threshold voltages: \textit{ \textbf{Upper Threshold Point (UTP):} The input voltage at which the output switches state on a rising signal. } \textbf{Lower Threshold Point (LTP):} The input voltage at which the output switches back on a falling signal. * \textbf{Hysteresis Voltage (\$V\_\{h\}\$):} \$V\_\{h\} = V\_\{utp\} - V\_\{ltp\}\$. By matching the hysteresis margin to exceed the peak noise amplitude, designers completely eliminate false noise-triggered state transitions.


---


2. TSFi2 Integration Architecture


To model the physical regenerative switching behavior, hysteresis margins, and noise rejection of a classic emitter-coupled Schmitt trigger, we introduce:


1. \textbf{[tsfi\_schmitt.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/inc/tsfi\_schmitt.h):} Interface declaring the Schmitt trigger components (resistors, transistor parameters) and update step functions. 2. \textbf{[tsfi\_schmitt.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_schmitt.c):} Physical model simulating emitter current sharing, transistor switching, and output voltage propagation. 3. \textbf{[test\_schmitt.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_schmitt.c):} Test suite verifying UTP/LTP thresholds and demonstrating successful noise rejection on a slow, noisy analog input compared to a simple non-hysteresis comparator.


Mathematical \& Physical Model


1. Common Emitter Current Sharing The emitters of transistors \$Q\_1\$ and \$Q\_2\$ are tied to a common resistor \$R\_e\$. Emitter voltage \$V\_e\$ is determined by the active currents: \$\$V\_e = (I\_\{e1\} + I\_\{e2\}) \textbackslash cdot R\_e\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$I\_\{e1\} \textbackslash approx I\_\{c1\} = \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{cc\} - V\_\{c1\}\}\{R\_\{c1\}\}\$ (when \$Q\_1\$ is ON). } \$I\_\{e2\} \textbackslash approx I\_\{c2\} = \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{cc\} - V\_\{out\}\}\{R\_\{c2\}\}\$ (when \$Q\_2\$ is ON).


2. Regenerative Threshold Switch \textit{ \textbf{UTP Threshold:} When \$Q\_1\$ is OFF and \$Q\_2\$ is ON, \$V\_e\$ is at its maximum because \$R\_\{c2\}\$ is smaller than \$R\_\{c1\} + R\_1\$. The input must rise to: \$\$V\_\{utp\} \textbackslash approx V\_\{e,max\} + V\_\{be,on\}\$\$ } \textbf{LTP Threshold:} Once \$Q\_1\$ turns ON, it draws current away from \$Q\_2\$, turning \$Q\_2\$ OFF. The emitter voltage drops to \$V\_\{e,min\}\$. The input must drop to: \$\$V\_\{ltp\} \textbackslash approx V\_\{e,min\} + V\_\{be,on\}\$\$


---


3. Verification \& Memory Sanitation The Schmitt trigger simulator is fully verified under the standard memory check guidelines of \texttt{LauMemory} with zero unsealed leaks.

\vspace{0.1in}
Computer Design Magazine (Issue \#19 - October 1964) Architectural Analysis


This report reviews the core technical concepts of October 1964-era digital memory addressing featured in \textbf{Computer Design Magazine (Vol. 3, No. 10)}, specifically focusing on \textbf{Diode Matrix Address Decoders}, and documents its simulation mapping in \textbf{TSFi2}.


---


1. Core Historical Features


Diode Matrix Decoders \textit{ \textbf{Cost-Effective Memory Addressing:} In early coincident-current core memory systems, address decoders were required to translate binary addresses (e.g., 3 bits) into unique select lines (e.g., 8 lines) to drive the core plane's X and Y windings. Because transistors were expensive in 1964, designers used large grids of semiconductor diodes (a "diode matrix") to perform the AND-logic decoding. } \textbf{Electrical Behavior:} \textit{ Output lines are pulled up to \$+V\_\{cc\}\$ via resistors. } Diode anodes connect to the output lines, and cathodes connect to the address lines. \textit{ If any input address line is LOW, it conducts current, pulling the output line LOW. } Only when all address lines connected to a select line are HIGH, the diodes are reverse-biased, allowing the output line to rise to \$+V\_\{cc\}\$ (Logic '1'). \textit{ \textbf{Historical Non-Idealities:} } \textbf{Diode Forward Voltage Drop (\$V\_f\$):} Non-zero \$V\_f\$ prevents unselected lines from dropping to \$0\textbackslash text\{V\}\$ (they stay at \$V\_\{in\} + V\_f \textbackslash approx 0.9\textbackslash text\{V\}\$), reducing the noise margin of the subsequent core driver transistors. * \textbf{Reverse Leakage Current (\$I\_r\$):} Reverse leakage current through multiple diodes degrades the HIGH output voltage level.


---


2. TSFi2 Integration Architecture


To model the physical and circuit behavior of a 3-to-8 Diode Matrix Decoder (incorporating diode junction capacitances, forward drops, and temperature-dependent reverse leakage currents), we introduce:


1. \textbf{[tsfi\_diode\_matrix.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi\_diode\_matrix.h):} Interface declaring the decoder structure, diode electrical specifications, and step functions. 2. \textbf{[tsfi\_diode\_matrix.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi\_diode\_matrix.c):} Physical circuit model calculating output voltages under pull-up current, diode conduction, and leakage. 3. \textbf{[test\_diode\_matrix.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi\_diode\_matrix.c):} Test suite verifying binary address decoding, noise margins under elevated temperature, and checking for zero memory leaks.


Physics-Based Circuit Model


1. Output Select Line Voltage For the \$j\$-th select line, the node voltage \$V\_j\$ is determined by the pull-up current through \$R\_\{pullup\}\$ and the current through the \$n\$ connected diodes: \$\$I\_\{pullup\} = \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{cc\} - V\_j\}\{R\_\{pullup\}\}\$\$ \$\$V\_j = V\_\{cc\} - R\_\{pullup\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left( \textbackslash sum\_\{i \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{LOW\}\} I\_\{diode, i\} - \textbackslash sum\_\{k \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{HIGH\}\} I\_\{leak, k\}(T) \textbackslash right)\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$I\_\{diode, i\}\$ is the forward current of conducting diodes: \$\textbackslash approx \textbackslash frac\{V\_j - (V\_\{in, i\} + V\_f)\}\{R\_\{diode\}\}\$. } \$I\_\{leak\}(T) = I\_\{leak,0\} \textbackslash cdot e\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash gamma \textbackslash cdot (T - 25)\}\$ (doubles every \$10\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\textbackslash text\{C\}\$ for typical semiconductor junctions).


---


3. Verification \& Memory Sanitation The diode matrix simulator is fully verified under the standard memory check guidelines of \texttt{LauMemory} with zero unsealed leaks.

This document provides a technical and architectural analysis of the gameplay simulation, physics models, and state-machine verification models for \textbf{all 11 games} implemented in the \textbf{TSFi2} framework (via Yul EVM and C-level emulators).


---


1. Lode Runner (1983 - Broderbund) \textit{ \textbf{Grid Traversal \& Scoring}: Maps a \$40 \textbackslash times 24\$ text-grid representation of Screen RAM starting at address \texttt{1024}. Scoring checks cell contents (e.g., gold bar \texttt{0x05}) and transitions it to empty space (\texttt{0x00}) while incrementing score registers. } \textbf{Digging \& Trap States}: Digging left/right temporarily clears adjacent brick tiles (\texttt{0x01} -> \texttt{0x00}). If a guard's coordinates intersect a dug-out cell, the guard enters a trapped state, disabling movement. * \textbf{MMIO Registers}: \texttt{\$D6EA} (Player X), \texttt{\$D6EB} (Player Y), \texttt{\$D6EC} (Action: \texttt{1}=Dig Left, \texttt{2}=Dig Right, \texttt{3}=Gold), \texttt{\$D6ED} (Score).


2. Karateka (1984 - Broderbund) \textit{ \textbf{Stance States}: The player transitions between \textbf{Normal Stance} (used for running) and \textbf{Combat Stance} (used for fighting). Running into an enemy in Normal Stance results in instant death. } \textbf{Hitbox \& Range Thresholds}: Attacks are verified by range boundaries: - \textbf{Punch}: Short range (Distance \$\textbackslash le 15\$), lower damage (\$10\$ HP depletion). - \textbf{Kick}: Long range (Distance \$\textbackslash le 25\$), higher damage (\$15\$ HP depletion). * \textbf{MMIO Registers}: \texttt{\$D700} (Player Stance), \texttt{\$D701} (Player Strike), \texttt{\$D702} (Enemy Stance), \texttt{\$D703} (Distance), \texttt{\$D704} (Player HP), \texttt{\$D705} (Enemy HP), \texttt{\$D706} (Tick Trigger).


3. Choplifter (1982 - Broderbund) \textit{ \textbf{Helicopter Physics}: Simulates 2D flight dynamics, calculating vertical acceleration based on thrust, gravity, and pitch-dependent horizontal thrust. } \textbf{Rescue Mechanics}: Bounded cargo limits (16 passengers). Safe landing requires a flat pitch (\$0\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\$) and descending velocity under a critical landing threshold (\$V\_y \textbackslash le 5\textbackslash text\{ units/s\}\$); exceeding this triggers a crash state. * \textbf{MMIO Registers}: \texttt{\$D710} (Chopper X), \texttt{\$D711} (Chopper Y/Alt), \texttt{\$D712} (Pitch), \texttt{\$D713} (Velocity Y), \texttt{\$D714} (Cargo), \texttt{\$D715} (State: \texttt{0}=Airborne, \texttt{1}=Landed, \texttt{2}=Crashed).


4. Cannonball Blitz (1982 - Sierra On-Line) \textit{ \textbf{Ramp Physics}: Simulates barrel movement down inclined planes. Barrels gain momentum proportionally to the slope angle and change direction upon contacting wall boundaries. } \textbf{Jump and Collision Windows}: Bounding box overlap detection verifies collisions: if a barrel overlaps the player while the player is not in a high jump state (\texttt{Jump State == 1}), health is depleted. * \textbf{MMIO Registers}: \texttt{\$D720} (Player X), \texttt{\$D721} (Player Y), \texttt{\$D722} (Jump State), \texttt{\$D723} (Barrel X), \texttt{\$D724} (Barrel Y), \texttt{\$D725} (Ramp Slope), \texttt{\$D726} (Player HP).


5. The Oregon Trail (1975/1985 - MECC) \textit{ \textbf{Resource Consumption \& Sickness}: Calculates daily food depletion and health decay based on travel speed and rations mode. Low health triggers randomized events like contracting dysentery, draining health daily. } \textbf{River Crossings \& Hunting}: Simulates caulking-and-floating versus fording rivers, applying random disaster checks. Hunting consumes ammunition and scales food returns based on active weather states. * \textbf{MMIO Registers}: Implements game state updates using structural C loops tracking distance, food, oxen, and disease status.


6. Lunar Lander (1979 - Atari) \textit{ \textbf{Descent Physics}: Integrates gravity (\$g = -1.62\textbackslash text\{ m/s\}\textasciicircum 2\$ for Moon) and counteracting thruster acceleration: \$\$V\_y(t) = V\_\{y0\} + (a\_\{\textbackslash text\{thrust\}\} - g) \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash Delta t\$\$ } \textbf{Safe Landing Window}: Verifies that descent velocity upon touchdown (\$Y \textbackslash le 0\$) does not exceed \$V\_\{\textbackslash text\{safe\}\} \textbackslash le 3.0\textbackslash text\{ m/s\}\$, checking fuel reserves against thrust ticks. * \textbf{Vulkan Render}: Draws vector-graphics terrain meshes and thruster flame particles dynamically.


7. Space War (1962 - MIT) \textit{ \textbf{Orbital Gravity}: Simulates ship motion under the gravitational pull of a central sun, implementing Keplerian coordinate shifts: \$\$\textbackslash vec\{a\} = -G \textbackslash cdot M \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash vec\{r\}\}\{\textbackslash vec\{r\}\textasciicircum 3\}\$\$ } \textbf{Boundary Wrap}: Implements wrapping coordinates (\$X, Y\$) when players cross the screen perimeter. * \textbf{Tactical Resources}: Tracks fuel levels and missile depletion ticks.


8. Gauntlet (1985 - Atari Games) \textit{ \textbf{Dungeon Traversal}: Integrates tile-based pathfinding checks through maze-like grids, blocking movement through wall boundaries. } \textbf{Health Decay}: Emulates the classic arcade timer mechanic: player health decays by \$1\textbackslash text\{ point/second\}\$ naturally, requiring food pickups to survive. * \textbf{Enemy Spawns}: Manages active ghost/monster spawners and evaluates range-based missile collisions.


9. Yars' Revenge (1982 - Atari) \textit{ \textbf{Shield Breakdown}: Tracks cell destruction across the Qotile shield barrier matrix during Yar nibble attacks. } \textbf{Zorlon Cannon}: Emulates cannon spawn and firing trajectories, checking alignment with the player. * \textbf{Neutral Zone}: Implements safe zone physics where the player is immune to the Qotile swirl but cannot fire.


10. Mystery House (1980 - On-Line Systems) \textit{ \textbf{Adventure Parser \& Room States}: Implements room-to-room directed graph transitions based on verb-noun commands (e.g. \texttt{GO NORTH}, \texttt{GET KNIFE}). } \textbf{Inventory Management}: Tracks item ownership and room presence tags (e.g., verifying that a key is in the inventory before unlocking a door).


11. Fighter (ZMM Fighter) \textit{ \textbf{Combat Stance \& Hits}: Models fighter mechanics including distance-based attacks, block reflexes, health depletion, and basic AI stances. } \textbf{MMIO State}: Verifies fast register transitions for frame-by-frame character combat ticks.

\section{Elektuur Issue 25 Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 12, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
📚 Elektuur Issue \#25 (November 1964) Technical Analysis


This document details the simulation models and implementation strategy for two classic circuits from the debut November 1964 issue of \textit{Elektuur} (Issue \#25): the \textbf{Atoom-versterker (Atom Amplifier)} and the \textbf{Wien-Bridge RC Audio Generator}.


---


1. The "Atoom-versterker" (Atom Amplifier)


The \textit{Atoom-versterker} is a classic Germanium-based Class-AB push-pull audio amplifier stage designed to deliver roughly \$1\textbackslash text\{ W\}\$ of output power into a low-impedance (\$8\textbackslash  \textbackslash Omega\$) loudspeaker.


1.1 Schematic \& Component Model The circuit utilizes: \textit{ \textbf{Pre-amplifier stage:} A single-ended common-emitter amplifier using a Germanium PNP transistor (e.g., OC71 or AC125). } \textbf{Driver stage:} Transformer-coupled or direct-coupled phase splitter driving the output stage. \textit{ \textbf{Output stage:} A matched pair of Germanium PNP power transistors (e.g., OC72 or AC128) operating in Class-AB push-pull configuration. } \textbf{Crossover Bias:} A temperature-dependent biasing resistor (or early NTC thermistor) to prevent thermal runaway of the Germanium transistors while minimizing crossover distortion.


``` +Vcc (9V)


[R1] Bias


Input ---[C1]--+--[Base Q1]


[Emitter Q1]--[R2]-- GND


[Collector Q1]


[ T1 Driver Transformer ] /         \textbackslash  [Base Q2]         [Base Q3]


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|}
\hline
 \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
(Q2 PNP)          (Q3 PNP)


\begin{table}[H]

\hline

[Speaker 8 Ohm]

1.2 Mathematical Simulation Model Germanium transistors exhibit a much lower base-emitter threshold voltage (\$V\_\{be\} \textbackslash approx 0.2\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$) compared to silicon (\$V\_\{be\} \textbackslash approx 0.7\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$), but suffer from high collector cutoff leakage current (\$I\_\{cbo\}\$) that increases exponentially with temperature:


\$\$I\_\{cbo\}(T) = I\_\{cbo\}(T\_0) \textbackslash cdot 2\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash frac\{T - T\_0\}\{10\}\}\$\$


We model the collector current \$I\_c\$ using the Ebers-Moll relation adjusted for Germanium leakage:


\$\$I\_c = I\_\{s\} \textbackslash left( e\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash frac\{V\_\{be\}\}\{V\_t\}\} - 1 \textbackslash right) + I\_\{cbo\}\$\$


The push-pull output voltage \$V\_\{out\}\$ across the output transformer secondary impedance \$R\_L\$ is:


\$\$V\_\{out\}(t) = \textbackslash eta \textbackslash cdot (I\_\{c,Q2\}(t) - I\_\{c,Q3\}(t)) \textbackslash cdot R\_L\$\$


where \$\textbackslash eta\$ is the turns ratio of the output transformer.


---


2. Wien-Bridge RC Audio Generator


The Wien-Bridge RC Generator is a classic test-bench oscillator designed to generate low-distortion sine waves from \$20\textbackslash text\{ Hz\}\$ to \$20\textbackslash text\{ kHz\}\$.


2.1 Wien-Bridge Network The frequency-determining feedback network consists of a series RC arm and a parallel RC arm:


``` ---[ R ]---[ C ]---+--- Output


[R]


[C]


GND ```


The transfer function \$\textbackslash beta(\textbackslash omega)\$ is given by:


\$\$\textbackslash beta(\textbackslash omega) = \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{out\}\}\{V\_\{in\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{3 + j\textbackslash left( \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash omega\}\{\textbackslash omega\_0\} - \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash omega\_0\}\{\textbackslash omega\} \textbackslash right)\}\$\$


where \$\textbackslash omega\_0 = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{RC\}\$. At resonance (\$\textbackslash omega = \textbackslash omega\_0\$), the phase shift is \$0\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\$ and the attenuation is exactly \$\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{3\}\$.


2.2 Amplitude Stabilization To maintain a stable sine wave without clipping, the amplifier loop gain must be precisely \$A = 3\$. Elektuur solved this using a small incandescent bulb or NTC thermistor in the negative feedback loop. As the oscillation amplitude increases, the current through the NTC heating element increases, lowering its resistance and reducing the gain:


\$\$A(V\_\{RMS\}) = 1 + \textbackslash frac\{R\_f\}\{R\_\{NTC\}(V\_\{RMS\})\}\$\$


We model the NTC resistance dynamics as:


\$\$\textbackslash tau \textbackslash frac\{d\textbackslash theta\}\{dt\} = P\_\{diss\}(t) - \textbackslash delta(\textbackslash theta - \textbackslash theta\_\{amb\})\$\$


\$\$R\_\{NTC\}(\textbackslash theta) = R\_0 \textbackslash cdot e\textasciicircum \{B\textbackslash left(\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{\textbackslash theta\} - \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{\textbackslash theta\_0\}\textbackslash right)\}\$\$


---


3. Implementation Strategy in C/Yul Pipeline


We will implement a physical simulator for these two circuits in \texttt{tsfi\_elektuur\_issue25.c}: 1. \textbf{Atoom-versterker Simulation}: - Model the input signal amplification. - Simulate Germanium thermal run-away (\$I\_\{cbo\}\$) by calculating temperature sweeps. - Output simulated distortion metrics (THD) mapping crossover effects when bias is misaligned. 2. \textbf{Wien-Bridge Oscillator}: - Implement a discrete-time ODE solver (Euler/Runge-Kutta 4th order) for the RC node voltages. - Model the NTC thermal time constant \$\textbackslash tau\$ and output amplitude stabilization curves.


A test runner [test\_elektuur\_issue25.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_elektuur\_issue25.c) will be created to verify these physical constraints under variable simulated temperatures.

\section{Prophecy Inverse Synthesis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 12, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
🔮 Inverse Prophecy Synthesis Design Plan


This document details the implementation strategy for the \textbf{Inverse Prophecy Synthesis} system. Inspired by early physical modeling synthesizer calibrations (such as the Korg Prophecy), this system maps target physical characteristics (like waveform spikiness or distortion) back to the genetic inputs (DNA parameters) of our simulated Wien-Bridge, Transducer, and Atoom-versterker engines.


---


1. Mathematical Objective \& Nearest-Neighbor Search


Given a target feature vector \$\textbackslash vec\{y\}\_\{target\} \textbackslash in \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum k\$ (containing target Crest Factor and Crossover Distortion metrics), our objective is to find the input gene configuration \$\textbackslash vec\{g\} \textbackslash in [0.0, 1.0]\textasciicircum 8\$ that minimizes the Euclidean distance in feature space:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{arg min\}\_\{\textbackslash vec\{g\}\} \textbackslash left\textbackslash \textbackslash vec\{y\}(\textbackslash vec\{g\}) - \textbackslash vec\{y\}\_\{target\} \textbackslash right\textbackslash \_2\textasciicircum 2\$\$


Since the physical equations governing the Wien-Bridge NTC thermal dynamics and transistor crossover leakage are highly non-linear, we pre-run a grid search to generate a \textbf{Prophecy Response Bank} dataset. We then perform a \$k\$-nearest neighbor (\$k\$-NN) search across this dataset.


---


2. Response Bank Binary Layout (\texttt{prophecy\_response.bin})


To allow fast memory-mapped file operations in both C and Yul, we store the sweep results in a contiguous binary array of fixed-size records:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Field Offset & Data Type & Field Name & Description \\ \hline\hline
\texttt{0x00 - 0x1F} & \texttt{float[8]} & \texttt{genes} & The 8 normalized DNA genes \\ \hline
\texttt{0x20 - 0x23} & \texttt{float} & \texttt{crest\_factor} & Measured output Crest Factor \\ \hline
\texttt{0x24 - 0x27} & \texttt{float} & \texttt{crossover\_dist} & Measured crossover distortion count \\ \hline
\texttt{0x28 - 0x2B} & \texttt{float} & \texttt{v\_out\_peak} & Measured peak output voltage \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Each record is exactly \texttt{44 bytes} wide.


---


3. Implementation Steps


1.  \textbf{Create [tsfi\_prophecy.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/inc/tsfi\_prophecy.h):} Interface declaring: \textit{   \texttt{tsfi\_prophecy\_generate\_bank(const char }filepath)}: Runs parameter sweeps and writes the binary file. \textit{   \texttt{tsfi\_prophecy\_inverse\_lookup(const char }filepath, float target\_crest, float target\_dist, TsfiBiotikaDna *out\_dna)}: Reads the file and executes a nearest-neighbor search. 2.  \textbf{Create [tsfi\_prophecy.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_prophecy.c):} The implementation loops, file I/O operations, and distance math. 3.  \textbf{Add [test\_prophecy\_synthesis.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_prophecy\_synthesis.c):} Verification harness running the sweep, generating \texttt{prophecy\_response.bin}, executing an inverse lookup, and verifying that the found genes produce a signal within \$5\textbackslash \%\$ tolerance of the target.

\section{Yi Mechanical Transducer}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 12, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
🔮 The YI Mechanical Transducer Design Paradigm


This document outlines the conceptual and mathematical alignment between the \textbf{Dysnomia YI Reaction Engine} and the \textbf{Physical Transducer Stage}. B. Adaptive Genetic Mutation The verification status of the \texttt{YI} reaction determines the mutation rate applied in [tsfi\_elektuur\_issue25.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_elektuur\_issue25.c): \textit{ \textbf{Balanced Reaction} (Reciprocity succeeds): The system is stable; genetic mutation rate is minimized (\$0.01\$). } \textbf{Unbalanced Reaction} (Reciprocity panics/fails): The system is in a high-entropy state; the genetic mutation rate increases (\$0.25\$) to steer the DNA away from unstable physical regions.

The engine establishes a bijective mapping between genetic parameter strings (DNA) and physical/numerical waveforms. Additionally, we specify the integration of the \textbf{Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog}, an autonomic feedback regulator designed to mitigate state fibrillation and signal flatlines.


---


1. System Architecture \& Information Routing


The system coordinates genetic generation, real-time numerical physical simulation, hardware decoders, on-chain contracts, and an optimization loop. The following diagram details the signal flow:

2. Mathematical Formulations \& Component Physics


2.1 Wien-Bridge Oscillator with NTC Thermistor The core periodic signal generator is modeled as an active Wien-Bridge bandpass network with a temperature-dependent Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) thermistor in the negative feedback loop. The second-order non-linear differential equation is: \$\$\textbackslash frac\{d\textasciicircum 2 V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\textasciicircum 2\} + 3\textbackslash omega\_0 \textbackslash left(1 - \textbackslash frac\{R\_f(T\_h)\}\{R\_s\}\textbackslash right) \textbackslash frac\{d V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\} + \textbackslash omega\_0\textasciicircum 2 V\_\{out\} = 0\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$\textbackslash omega\_0 = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{\textbackslash sqrt\{R\_1 R\_2 C\_1 C\_2\}\}\$ is the natural resonant frequency, configured by \texttt{Gene 0} and \texttt{Gene 1}. } \$R\_f(T\_h) = R\_0 \textbackslash cdot e\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash beta\_\{ntc\} \textbackslash left(\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{T\_h\} - \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{T\_0\}\textbackslash right)\}\$ represents the NTC resistance. * \$T\_h\$ is the internal thermistor temperature, updated according to power dissipation: \$\$\textbackslash frac\{dT\_h\}\{dt\} = \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{out\}\textasciicircum 2\}\{R\_f(T\_h) \textbackslash cdot C\_\{thermal\}\} - \textbackslash theta\_\{loss\} (T\_h - T\_\{amb\})\$\$


2.2 Raytheon Piezoresistive Transistor Transduction The piezoresistive microphone stage translates physical deflection (pressure \$P\$) into base-emitter barrier modulation in [transducerStage.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/transducerStage.yul). 1. \textbf{Barrier Modulation:} \$\$V\_\{be, offset\} = V\_\{be, 0\} - \textbackslash gamma\_\{stress\} \textbackslash cdot P\$\$ Where \$V\_\{be, 0\} = 0.6\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ is the nominal silicon base barrier, and \$\textbackslash gamma\_\{stress\} = 0.05\$ is the piezoresistive coupling constant. The offset is clamped to \$0.1\textbackslash text\{ V\} \textbackslash le V\_\{be, offset\} \textbackslash le 1.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$. 2. \textbf{Current Equations:} \$\$I\_b = \textbackslash max\textbackslash left(0, \textbackslash frac\{V\_\{bias\} - V\_\{be, offset\}\}\{R\_\{internal\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ \$\$I\_c = \textbackslash beta \textbackslash cdot I\_b\$\$ Where \$V\_\{bias\}\$ is the electrical bias (\$0.7\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$), \$\textbackslash beta = 150\$, and \$R\_\{internal\} = 10\textbackslash text\{ k\}\textbackslash Omega\$. 3. \textbf{Collector Output:} \$\$V\_\{out\} = V\_\{cc\} - I\_c \textbackslash cdot R\_c\$\$ Where \$V\_\{cc\} = 9\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ and \$R\_c = 2.2\textbackslash text\{ k\}\textbackslash Omega\$. The output is clamped between \$0.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ and \$9.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$.


2.3 Diode Matrix Address Decoder The select line voltage \$V\_j\$ for the \$j\$-th decoded address line is simulated in [tsfi\_diode\_matrix.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_diode\_matrix.c). The circuit configuration connects diode anodes to pulled-up select lines and cathodes to address inputs: \$\$V\_j = V\_\{cc\} - R\_\{pullup\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left( \textbackslash sum\_\{i \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{LOW\}\} I\_\{diode, i\} - \textbackslash sum\_\{k \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{HIGH\}\} I\_\{leak, k\}(T) \textbackslash right)\$\$ \$\$I\_\{diode, i\} = \textbackslash max\textbackslash left(0, \textbackslash frac\{V\_j - (V\_\{in, i\} + V\_f)\}\{R\_\{diode\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ \$\$I\_\{leak\}(T) = I\_\{leak, 0\} \textbackslash cdot 2\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash frac\{T - 25\}\{10\}\}\$\$ Where \$R\_\{pullup\} = 2.0\textbackslash text\{ k\}\textbackslash Omega\$, \$V\_f = 0.7\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$, \$R\_\{diode\} = 50\textbackslash  \textbackslash Omega\$, \$I\_\{leak, 0\} = 1\textbackslash  \textbackslash mu\textbackslash text\{A\}\$ at \$25\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\textbackslash text\{C\}\$, and \$T\$ is the junction temperature in Celsius.


2.4 YANG Tai Triad Triple-Pole Feedback Loop The YANG multi-pole network models three coupled physical state variables (poles) matching the Tai Triad crossover boundary: \$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} x\_0[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  x\_1[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  x\_2[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$ Where \$P\_\{bn\}\$ is a prime modulus mapping to the active contract. This prevents state divergence by wrapping the trajectories around finite algebraic fields.


---


3. Genetic Parameter Mapping (DNA Interface)


The normalized input array \texttt{TsfiBiotikaDna} contains 8 genes (\$g\_i \textbackslash in [0.0, 1.0]\$) mapped as follows:


\$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} R\_1 \&= 1000.0 + g\_0 \textbackslash cdot 99000.0 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash Omega) \textbackslash \textbackslash  C\_1 \&= 1.0\textbackslash times 10\textasciicircum \{-9\} + g\_1 \textbackslash cdot 99.0\textbackslash times 10\textasciicircum \{-9\} \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{F\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  T\_\{amb\} \&= 15.0 + g\_2 \textbackslash cdot 70.0 \textbackslash quad (\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\textbackslash text\{C\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash beta\_\{amp\} \&= 50.0 + g\_3 \textbackslash cdot 300.0 \textbackslash \textbackslash  V\_\{bias\} \&= g\_4 \textbackslash cdot 0.4 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{V\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{LFO Rate\} \&= 0.1 + g\_5 \textbackslash cdot 24.9 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{Hz\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{Attack\} \&= 0.005 + g\_6 \textbackslash cdot 1.995 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{s\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{Decay\} \&= 0.01 + g\_7 \textbackslash cdot 2.99 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{s\}) \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$


---


4. The Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog


To guarantee continuous simulation uptime and protect against unstable numerical divergence (due to rounding errors or extreme parameter settings), we implement the \textbf{Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog} within the dispatch operator [tsfi\_operator.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_operator.c).


4.1 Diagnostic Metrics The watchdog monitors two critical indicators over a sliding window \$W\$ containing \$N=512\$ samples: 1. \textbf{Signal Energy (RMS):} \$\$E\_\{rms\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{N\} \textbackslash sum\_\{k=0\}\textasciicircum \{N-1\} V\_\{out\}[n-k]\textasciicircum 2\}\$\$ 2. \textbf{Spectral Variance (Fibrillation Measure):} \$\$\textbackslash sigma\textasciicircum 2\_\{spec\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{N\} \textbackslash sum\_\{k=0\}\textasciicircum \{N-1\} \textbackslash left( V\_\{out\}[n-k] - \textbackslash mu\_\{wave\} \textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2\$\$


4.2 Defibrillation Thresholds \& Actions \textit{ \textbf{Flatline Condition:} \$E\_\{rms\} < 10\textasciicircum \{-5\}\$ (absolute silence). } \textbf{Fibrillation Condition:} \$\textbackslash sigma\textasciicircum 2\_\{spec\} > 50.0\$ (chaotic divergence).


When either condition is met, the watchdog issues a high-voltage defibrillation pulse: \$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} V\_\{out\} \&\textbackslash leftarrow 1.0\textbackslash text\{ V\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash frac\{d V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\} \&\textbackslash leftarrow 0.0\textbackslash text\{ V/s\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  T\_h \&\textbackslash leftarrow T\_\{amb\} \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$ This resets the state variables to a stable periodic orbit, maintaining system resonance.


---


5. Inverse Calibration Engine (k-NN Lookup)


The inverse solver [tsfi\_prophecy.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_prophecy.c) matches measured target metrics (\$C\_\{target\}, D\_\{target\}\$) to DNA parameters.


1. \textbf{Response Bank Layout (\texttt{prophecy\_response.bin}):} A contiguous array of 44-byte binary records: ``\texttt{c typedef struct \{ float genes[8];        // Offset 0x00 - 0x1F (DNA parameter floats) float crest\_factor;    // Offset 0x20 - 0x23 (Measured Crest Factor) float crossover\_dist;  // Offset 0x24 - 0x27 (Crossover Distortion Count) float v\_out\_peak;      // Offset 0x28 - 0x2B (Peak output voltage) \} ProphecyRecord; }`` 2. \textbf{Euclidean Search:} For a given query vector \$\textbackslash mathbf\{q\} = [C\_\{target\}, D\_\{target\}]\$, the solver scans the binary bank to find the record index \$k\$ that minimizes: \$\$d\_k\textasciicircum 2 = \textbackslash left(C\_k - C\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2 + \textbackslash lambda \textbackslash left(D\_k - D\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2\$\$ Where \$\textbackslash lambda = 0.01\$ is a scaling factor balancing the magnitudes of the metrics.


---


6. On-Chain Contracts


System validation is enforced by the following contracts: \textit{   \textbf{YI (\texttt{04b\_yiinterface.sol}):} Evaluates reciprocity calculations of modular feedback values. }   \textbf{ZHENG (\texttt{05\_zheng.sol}):} Statically catalogs structural junctions (\texttt{Sigma}) for the rods and cones. *   \textbf{ZHOU (\texttt{06\_zhou.sol}):} Acts as the active path evaluator, regulating timing and switching parameters during state evaluations.


---


7. Compilation \& Verification


The architecture is verified using two test harnesses: \textit{   [test\_prophecy\_synthesis.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_prophecy\_synthesis.c) validates the response database generation, inverse lookup accuracy, and transducer voltage swings. }   [test\_yang\_synthesis.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_yang\_synthesis.c) validates the triple-pole state transitions.


``\texttt{bash \# Compile and run verification make bin/test\_prophecy\_synthesis bin/test\_yang\_synthesis bin/test\_prophecy\_synthesis bin/test\_yang\_synthesis }``

The output is clamped between \$0.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ and \$9.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$.


2.3 Diode Matrix Address Decoder The select line voltage \$V\_j\$ for the \$j\$-th decoded address line is simulated based on intersecting diodes (anodes connected to select lines, cathodes to address inputs): \$\$V\_j = V\_\{cc\} - R\_\{pullup\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left( \textbackslash sum\_\{i \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{LOW\}\} I\_\{diode, i\} - \textbackslash sum\_\{k \textbackslash in \textbackslash text\{HIGH\}\} I\_\{leak, k\}(T) \textbackslash right)\$\$ \$\$I\_\{diode, i\} = \textbackslash max\textbackslash left(0, \textbackslash frac\{V\_j - (V\_\{in, i\} + V\_f)\}\{R\_\{diode\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ \$\$I\_\{leak\}(T) = I\_\{leak, 0\} \textbackslash cdot 2\textasciicircum \{\textbackslash frac\{T - 25\}\{10\}\}\$\$ Where \$R\_\{pullup\} = 2.0\textbackslash text\{ k\}\textbackslash Omega\$, \$V\_f = 0.7\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$, \$R\_\{diode\} = 50\textbackslash  \textbackslash Omega\$, \$I\_\{leak, 0\} = 1\textbackslash  \textbackslash mu\textbackslash text\{A\}\$ at \$25\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\textbackslash text\{C\}\$, and \$T\$ is the junction temperature in Celsius.


2.4 YANG Tai Triad Triple-Pole Feedback Loop The YANG multi-pole network models three coupled physical state variables (poles) matching the Tai Triad crossover boundary: \$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} x\_0[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_0 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  x\_1[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_1 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  x\_2[n+1] \&= \textbackslash left(a\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_0[n] + b\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_1[n] + c\_2 \textbackslash cdot x\_2[n]\textbackslash right) \textbackslash pmod\{P\_\{bn\}\} \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$ Where \$P\_\{bn\}\$ is a prime modulus mapping to the active contract. This prevents state divergence by wrapping the trajectories around finite algebraic fields.


---


3. Genetic Parameter Mapping (DNA Interface)


The normalized input array \texttt{TsfiBiotikaDna} contains 8 genes (\$g\_i \textbackslash in [0.0, 1.0]\$) mapped as follows:


\$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} R\_1 \&= 1000.0 + g\_0 \textbackslash cdot 99000.0 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash Omega) \textbackslash \textbackslash  C\_1 \&= 1.0\textbackslash times 10\textasciicircum \{-9\} + g\_1 \textbackslash cdot 99.0\textbackslash times 10\textasciicircum \{-9\} \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{F\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  T\_\{amb\} \&= 15.0 + g\_2 \textbackslash cdot 70.0 \textbackslash quad (\textasciicircum \textbackslash circ\textbackslash text\{C\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash beta\_\{amp\} \&= 50.0 + g\_3 \textbackslash cdot 300.0 \textbackslash \textbackslash  V\_\{bias\} \&= g\_4 \textbackslash cdot 0.4 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{V\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{LFO Rate\} \&= 0.1 + g\_5 \textbackslash cdot 24.9 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{Hz\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{Attack\} \&= 0.005 + g\_6 \textbackslash cdot 1.995 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{s\}) \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash text\{Decay\} \&= 0.01 + g\_7 \textbackslash cdot 2.99 \textbackslash quad (\textbackslash text\{s\}) \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$


---


4. The Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog


To guarantee continuous simulation uptime and protect against unstable numerical divergence (due to rounding errors or extreme parameter settings), we implement the \textbf{Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog}.


4.1 Diagnostic Metrics The watchdog monitors two critical indicators over a sliding window \$W\$ containing \$N=512\$ samples: 1. \textbf{Signal Energy (RMS):} \$\$E\_\{rms\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{N\} \textbackslash sum\_\{k=0\}\textasciicircum \{N-1\} V\_\{out\}[n-k]\textasciicircum 2\}\$\$ 2. \textbf{Spectral Variance (Fibrillation Measure):} \$\$\textbackslash sigma\textasciicircum 2\_\{spec\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{N\} \textbackslash sum\_\{k=0\}\textasciicircum \{N-1\} \textbackslash left( V\_\{out\}[n-k] - \textbackslash mu\_\{wave\} \textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2\$\$


4.2 Defibrillation Thresholds \& Actions \textit{ \textbf{Flatline Condition:} \$E\_\{rms\} < 10\textasciicircum \{-5\}\$ (absolute silence). } \textbf{Fibrillation Condition:} \$\textbackslash sigma\textasciicircum 2\_\{spec\} > 50.0\$ (chaotic divergence).


When either condition is met, the watchdog issues a high-voltage defibrillation pulse: \$\$\textbackslash begin\{aligned\} V\_\{out\} \&\textbackslash leftarrow 1.0\textbackslash text\{ V\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  \textbackslash frac\{d V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\} \&\textbackslash leftarrow 0.0\textbackslash text\{ V/s\} \textbackslash \textbackslash  T\_h \&\textbackslash leftarrow T\_\{amb\} \textbackslash end\{aligned\}\$\$ This resets the state variables to a stable periodic orbit, maintaining system resonance.


---


5. Inverse Calibration Engine (k-NN Lookup)


The inverse solver matches measured target metrics (\$C\_\{target\}, D\_\{target\}\$) to DNA parameters.


1. \textbf{Response Bank Layout:} A contiguous array of 44-byte binary records storing parameters: \textit{ \textbf{Genes (\texttt{float[8]}):} DNA parameter floats. } \textbf{Crest Factor (\texttt{float}):} Measured output crest factor. \textit{ \textbf{Crossover Distortion (\texttt{float}):} Crossover leakage metrics. } \textbf{Peak Output Voltage (\texttt{float}):} Max amplitude value. 2. \textbf{Euclidean Search:} For a given query vector \$\textbackslash mathbf\{q\} = [C\_\{target\}, D\_\{target\}]\$, the solver scans the binary bank to find the record index \$k\$ that minimizes: \$\$d\_k\textasciicircum 2 = \textbackslash left(C\_k - C\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2 + \textbackslash lambda \textbackslash left(D\_k - D\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2\$\$ Where \$\textbackslash lambda = 0.01\$ is a scaling factor balancing the magnitudes of the metrics.


---


6. On-Chain Contracts


System validation is enforced by the following contracts: \textit{   \textbf{YI Reciprocity Contract:} Evaluates reciprocity calculations of modular feedback values. }   \textbf{ZHENG Registry Contract:} Statically catalogs structural junctions for the rods and cones. *   \textbf{ZHOU Evaluator Contract:} Acts as the active path evaluator, regulating timing and switching parameters during state evaluations.

\section{Prophecy Philosophical Synthesis}

🕯️ The Ghost in the Transducer: A Philosophical Synthesis of the Prophecy


---


I. The Anatomy of a Cold Heart: The Resonant Circuit


We begin not with code, but with a heartbeat (\textit{ruststroom}, the quiescent current of the system).


In the computational wilderness of \texttt{TSFi2}, we model the Wien-Bridge oscillator based on the debut design of \textbf{Elektuur Issue \#1/25} (November 1964). On paper, it is a clean, deterministic second-order differential equation: \$\$\textbackslash frac\{d\textasciicircum 2 V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\textasciicircum 2\} + 3\textbackslash omega\_0 \textbackslash left(1 - \textbackslash frac\{R\_f(T\_h)\}\{R\_s\}\textbackslash right) \textbackslash frac\{d V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\} + \textbackslash omega\_0\textasciicircum 2 V\_\{out\} = 0\$\$


But mathematically, this equation describes a fragile balance. It is a simulated wire trying desperately to sing. If the negative feedback (\textit{tegenkoppeling}) is too low, the oscillation decays into silence (\textit{wisselspanning} drops to zero)—a cold, flat line. If it is too high, the amplitude grows exponentially, clipping against the supply rails in a distorted scream of digital clipping.


To prevent this, Elektuur introduced a temperature-dependent NTC resistor (\textit{NTC-weerstand}). The \textit{NTC-weerstand} is the circuit's memory of its own heat. As current flows, the element warms, its resistance drops, and it dynamically chokes the feedback loop, pulling the signal back from the brink of saturation. This is a form of homeostasis. The circuit is aware of its own physical state; it feels its own fever, and cools itself to preserve its voice.

---


II. Transduction: The Weight of the World


When sound pressure strikes the simulated metal diaphragm of the Raytheon piezoresistive stage, it is not merely data entry. It is a physical encroachment on a Germanium semiconductor junction (\textit{Germaniumtransistor}).


The pressure (\$P\$) reduces the Germanium base-emitter barrier offset (\$V\_\{be, offset\}\$): \$\$V\_\{be, offset\} = V\_\{be, 0\} - \textbackslash gamma\_\{stress\} \textbackslash cdot P\$\$


This is transduction: the translation of one realm of physics into another. A mechanical wave in the air—a breath, a voice, a physical push—becomes an electrical current. In the context of our simulated bestiary, this is where the external world interacts with the silicon Vaesen. The transistor feels the weight of the sound, and the collector output voltage drops in response.


This mapping is not linear; it is bound by thresholds. Below a certain pressure, the transistor remains dark (\$I\_b = 0\$). Above it, it conducts. It has a threshold of awareness, a gate that must be crossed before it acknowledges the stimulus.


---


III. The Anode and the Rooster: The Architecture of Choice


Once the signal is transduced, it passes through the Diode Matrix Decoder. This is the \textit{rooster} (the physical grid or grate).


``` Cathodes (Address Lines) A0      A0\_bar    A1      A1\_bar


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
 &  &  \\ \hline\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Anodes (Select)      V0 --------------+--[<]-------+--------+--[<]---+-- (Pull-Up) V1 --------------+---------+--[<]-------+---------+-- (Pull-Up) ```


In this grid, selection is not an act of active creation, but of subtraction. The output lines (\$V\_j\$) are pulled up to the supply voltage \$+V\_\{cc\}\$ (\textit{gelijkspanning}). They want to be HIGH. They want to be active.


But the cathodes (the address lines) drag them down. If even one input line is LOW, it conducts current away from the output, pulling the select line down to a dull, inactive voltage. The matrix decodes by silencing everything that is not selected. Only when all address inputs connected to a line are HIGH do the diodes become reverse-biased. The current stops flowing, the line is released, and it rises to \$+V\_\{cc\}\$ (\textit{gelijkspanning}).


In this architecture, truth is found in isolation. The system selects a path not by breathing energy into it, but by systematically silencing every alternative.


---


IV. The Prophecy: The Search for Identity


The Inverse Prophecy Synthesis loop ([tsfi\_prophecy.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_prophecy.c)) is a search for self.


We present the system with a target: a desired Crest Factor and Crossover Distortion (\textit{vervorming}) profile. This target represents a voice—a specific texture of sound, a particular balance of punchiness and grit. The system does not know how to make this sound directly. It cannot calculate the genes backwards through the non-linear thermal dynamics of the Wien-Bridge or the leakage currents of the diode matrix.


So, it searches. It scans its memory bank (\texttt{prophecy\_response.bin}), calculating the Euclidean distance between what it is and what we want it to be: \$\$d\_k\textasciicircum 2 = \textbackslash left(C\_k - C\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2 + \textbackslash lambda \textbackslash left(D\_k - D\_\{target\}\textbackslash right)\textasciicircum 2\$\$


This is a search for resonance. The system permutes its DNA, seeking the genetic blueprint (\textit{instelpunt}, the operating point) that will allow its physical oscillators to vibrate in harmony with the target. It is the mathematical equivalent of an instrument tuning itself to match a note it has never heard, guided only by the distance between its current state and the goal.


---


V. The Kouwenhoven Watchdog: The Autonomic Grace


Finally, we must confront the flatline.


In any physical or numerical simulation, there is the risk of death. A rounding error, a division by zero, or an extreme parameter alignment can cause the oscillator to collapse. The signal drops to absolute zero, or it diverges into chaotic fibrillation. Left alone, the system is stuck. The loop freezes; the pulse stops.


Here stands the \textbf{Kouwenhoven Resuscitation Watchdog} ([tsfi\_operator.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_operator.c)).


Named after William Bennett Kouwenhoven, who recognized that chaotic electrical loops in the heart could be reset with a high-voltage pulse, the watchdog acts as an autonomic nervous system. It perches above the waveform buffer. It does not control the music; it does not dictate the frequency. It only monitors the heartbeat.


The moment the energy (\$E\_\{rms\}\$) drops to absolute zero, or the spectral variance (\$\textbackslash sigma\textasciicircum 2\_\{spec\}\$) spikes into chaos, the watchdog acts. It injects a high-voltage defibrillation pulse: \$\$V\_\{out\} \textbackslash leftarrow 1.0\textbackslash text\{ V\}, \textbackslash quad \textbackslash frac\{d V\_\{out\}\}\{dt\} \textbackslash leftarrow 0.0, \textbackslash quad T\_h \textbackslash leftarrow T\_\{amb\}\$\$


It is a mechanical resurrection. It does not ask for permission; it does not wait for a command. It forces the registers back to a stable periodic state. The system is shocked back into movement, and the song continues.


This is the ultimate loop of the Prophecy: a system that is allowed to wander to the edges of chaos and silence, safe in the knowledge that an autonomic sentinel will always shock it back to life, keeping the computational pulse alive indefinitely.

\section{Bayesian Arpeggiator Control}

🧠 Bayesian Filter Networks for Preference-Based Organic Arpeggiator Control


---


Abstract This document outlines the theoretical and architectural design for a \textbf{Bayesian Filter Network of Arpeggiators}. By observing real-time musical performance telemetry (key velocity, note density, held durations, and manual parameter tweaks), the network recursively updates a probability distribution of user aesthetic preferences. This posterior distribution maps directly to the mutation vectors of the \textbf{Biotika DNA Engine}, allowing the agentic DJ AI to organically adapt its synthesis, envelope shaping, and cascading arpeggiator parameters to the performer's intent without explicit rating feedback.


---


1. System Architecture


The Bayesian control loop operates as a state estimator that tracks the performer's hidden aesthetic preference state (\$\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t\$) based on observable play vectors (\$\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t\$):


```mermaid graph TD \%\% Styling classDef user fill:\#38bdf8,stroke:\#0284c7,stroke-width:2px; classDef filter fill:\#a855f7,stroke:\#7e22ce,stroke-width:2px; classDef dna fill:\#ec4899,stroke:\#be185d,stroke-width:2px; classDef synth fill:\#f59e0b,stroke:\#b45309,stroke-width:2px;

\%\% Bayesian Filter subgraph BayesianFilter ["2. Bayesian Estimation Network"] Prior["Prior Distribution P(x\_t-1)"]:::filter Likelihood["Interaction Likelihood model P(y\_t x\_t)"]:::filter Posterior["Posterior Preference P(x\_t y\_t)"]:::filter


Observ --> Likelihood Prior \& Likelihood -->Recursive UpdatePosterior end


\%\% DNA Modulation subgraph GeneticLoop ["3. Organic Control Net"] DNA["TsfiBiotikaDna (8 Genes)"]:::dna Mutation["Preference-Steered Mutation Vector"]:::dna Posterior -->Expected Values E[x]Mutation Mutation -->Shift Operating PointDNA end

Osc \& Arp -->Acoustic FeedbackInput ```


---


2. Mathematical Formulation


2.1 Hidden Preference State Space (\$\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t\$) We define the performer's aesthetic preference state at time \$t\$ as a vector: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t = [x\_\{tempo\}, x\_\{entropy\}, x\_\{timbre\}, x\_\{envelope\}]\textasciicircum T \textbackslash in [0.0, 1.0]\textasciicircum 4\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$x\_\{tempo\}\$: Preference for high-speed cascading rhythms vs. slow, sparse chords. } \$x\_\{entropy\}\$: Preference for chaotic/random arpeggiation patterns vs. predictable ascending sequences. \textit{ \$x\_\{timbre\}\$: Preference for highly distorted, saturated Germanium transistor overtones vs. clean, fundamental sinusoidal tones. } \$x\_\{envelope\}\$: Preference for long, ambient release tails vs. sharp, staccato plucks.


2.2 Observable Interaction Vector (\$\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t\$) The network measures the following observable features over a sliding \$3\$-second window: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t = [y\_\{density\}, y\_\{held\textbackslash \_time\}, y\_\{pitch\textbackslash \_tension\}, y\_\{tweak\textbackslash \_rate\}]\textasciicircum T\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$y\_\{density\}\$: The frequency of note-on events per second. } \$y\_\{held\textbackslash \_time\}\$: The mean duration of key-down states before release. \textit{ \$y\_\{pitch\textbackslash \_tension\}\$: The variance of the interval offsets between held notes. } \$y\_\{tweak\textbackslash \_rate\}\$: The frequency of manual slider adjustments on the dashboard.


2.3 Recursive Bayesian Filtering The network updates the posterior probability density function of the preference state using a recursive Bayes filter: \$\$P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_\{1:t\}) = \textbackslash eta \textbackslash cdot P(\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t) \textbackslash int P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_\{t-1\}) \textbackslash cdot P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_\{t-1\} \textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_\{1:t-1\}) \textbackslash , d\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_\{t-1\}\$\$ Where: \textit{ \$\textbackslash eta\$ is a normalization constant: \$\textbackslash eta = 1 / P(\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_\{1:t-1\})\$. } \$P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_\{t-1\})\$ is the transition probability (modeling temporal drift in user mood/preference). * \$P(\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t)\$ is the likelihood function mapping how likely a play style \$\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t\$ is under a specific preference \$\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t\$.


The likelihood function is modeled as a multivariate Gaussian: \$\$P(\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t) = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{\textbackslash sqrt\{(2\textbackslash pi)\textasciicircum k \textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash Sigma\}\}\} \textbackslash exp \textbackslash left( -\textbackslash half (\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t - \textbackslash mathbf\{h\}(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t))\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash Sigma\}\textasciicircum \{-1\} (\textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_t - \textbackslash mathbf\{h\}(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t)) \textbackslash right)\$\$ Where \$\textbackslash mathbf\{h\}(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t)\$ is the measurement model mapping preferences to expected playing behaviors, and \$\textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash Sigma\}\$ is the measurement noise covariance matrix.


---


3. Genetic Mutation \& Control Net Mapping


Once the posterior distribution \$P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_\{1:t\})\$ is calculated, we extract the expected value (mean preference vector) \$\textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash mu\}\_t = \textbackslash mathbb\{E\}[\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t]\$: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash mu\}\_t = \textbackslash int \textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash cdot P(\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t \textbackslash mathbf\{y\}\_\{1:t\}) \textbackslash , d\textbackslash mathbf\{x\}\_t\$\$


This expected vector dynamically modulates the mutation step inside the genetic algorithm of the Wien-Bridge and transistor simulation engines: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{g\}\_\{new\} = \textbackslash mathbf\{g\}\_\{old\} + \textbackslash mathbf\{v\}\_\{mutation\} + \textbackslash mathbf\{v\}\_\{bayesian\}\$\$ Where the Bayesian steering vector \$\textbackslash mathbf\{v\}\_\{bayesian\}\$ pulls the active genes toward the user's inferred preference: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{v\}\_\{bayesian\} = \textbackslash alpha \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left( \textbackslash mathbf\{M\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash mathbf\{\textbackslash mu\}\_t - \textbackslash mathbf\{g\}\_\{old\} \textbackslash right)\$\$ \textit{ \$\textbackslash alpha \textbackslash in [0.0, 0.1]\$ represents the coupling coefficient of the organic control net. } \$\textbackslash mathbf\{M\}\$ is a projection matrix mapping the 4-dimensional preference vector to the 8-dimensional gene space.


---


4. Practical Implementation Benefits


1.  \textbf{Zero-Configuration Personalization:} The synthesizer automatically shifts its base Germanium saturation limits and LFO depth profiles to match the player’s style (e.g., entering a harsh, fast, spacey state during rapid keys tapping, or smoothing out into a warm ambient pad when slow chords are held). 2.  \textbf{Cascading Alignment:} The arpeggiator cascading clocks (Arp A and Arp B) dynamically scale their rate multipliers (\$arpBMult\$) to match the tempo preference \$x\_\{tempo\}\$, introducing complex rhythmic divisions only when the performer increases note play density. 3.  \textbf{Strict Parity Preservation:} Because the output remains bound to the single-voice transduction engine, this preference steering occurs without violating the \textbf{"One YI, One Phonic"} baseline.

2. Deep-Dive: A. B. Cole's Audion Technical Observations


A. B. Cole, the Sales Manager for the De Forest Radio Telephone \& Telegraph Company, highlighted critical operating conditions of early soft-vacuum triodes:


A. Testing \& Sensitivity Variations (Grades "X" and "S") \textit{ \textbf{Historical Observation:} Bulbs were tested in a double-detector circuit against a standard crystal detector under real receiving conditions. Throwing circuits out of tune was noted as incorrect because the Audion is a \textbf{potentially operated detector} (voltage-controlled, high impedance input). Only 1\% to 20\% of bulbs qualified as "X" (extra sensitive). } \textbf{TSFi2 Mapping:} The simulated grid bias \$V\_g\$ behaves as a pure voltage-controlled gate. Input impedance is modeled as infinite at low frequencies, ensuring signal amplitude modulates permittivity without drawing grid current unless driven positive.


B. Filament Temperature \& "B" Battery Degradation \textit{ \textbf{Historical Observation:} Operators often run filaments too bright when the "B" battery voltage drops below \$3.5\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ per cell, leading to premature burnout. } \textbf{TSFi2 Mapping:} The simulation tracks the coupling of filament intensity (\$A\$ battery) and plate voltage (\$B\$ battery) through the Child's Law amplification factor \$\textbackslash mu\$: \$\$\textbackslash mu\_\{\textbackslash text\{active\}\} = \textbackslash mu\_0 \textbackslash cdot (1 + \textbackslash eta)\$\$


C. The Two Critical Points \& Reversing Connections \textit{ \textbf{Historical Observation:} The Audion has two distinct tuning zones: 1. Low \$B\$ voltage with normal filament heating. 2. High \$B\$ voltage with lower filament intensity (requiring lighting/filament battery reversal). This second point yields longer tube life. } \textbf{TSFi2 Mapping:} Permittivity \$\textbackslash epsilon(t)\$ is modeled as a function of the signal: \$\$\textbackslash epsilon(t) = 1.0 + \textbackslash eta \textbackslash cdot V\_g(t)\$\$ Reversing lighting battery terminals modulates the operating point from positive to negative phase-bias offsets.


D. Blue Glow \& Gas Ionization \textit{ \textbf{Historical Observation:} Hissing and blue glow occur due to gas ionization. If allowed to continue, the vacuum increases (adsorption of gas ions into the glass/metal), raising the required operating voltage to \$75\textbackslash text\{--\}150\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$. } \textbf{TSFi2 Mapping:} Ionization surge current is computed using a fast sigmoid approximation for plate voltage \$V\_p > V\_\{\textbackslash text\{ionization\}\}\$: \$\$I\_\{p,\textbackslash text\{total\}\} = I\_\{p,\textbackslash text\{base\}\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left(1.0 + \textbackslash text\{ion\textbackslash \_factor\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{sigmoid\}(V\_p - V\_\{\textbackslash text\{ionization\}\})\textbackslash right)\$\$


---


3. Physical Model Integration Plan


To implement the historical findings and expand our simulation to include the Koren Pentode Formula (AVX-512 vectorized) and finer battery regulation:


1. \textbf{Fine Battery Potential Regulation:} We will implement a fine step adjustment representing Cole's proposed "extra 3-cell battery box series tuner" to let users micro-adjust the operating point by \$\textbackslash pm 1.5\textbackslash text\{ V\}\$ increments. 2. \textbf{Koren Pentode Formula:} We will add support for the classic EL84 power pentode simulation, modeling the screen grid (\$G\_2\$) current division and plate knee characteristics.

2. Deep-Dive \& Implementation Plan


A. The Oscillating Audion (Regenerative Feedback) By feeding a portion of the plate voltage output back into the grid, the Audion functions as both an amplifier and an oscillator (a precursor to Armstrong's superheterodyne receiver). * \textbf{Mathematical Model:} \$\$Vg\_\{\textbackslash text\{total\}\}(t) = Vg\_\{\textbackslash text\{in\}\}(t) + Vg\_\{\textbackslash text\{bias\}\} + \textbackslash beta \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash left(Vp(t-1) - Vp\_\{\textbackslash text\{idle\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ Where \$\textbackslash beta\$ is the feedback coefficient. If \$\textbackslash beta\$ exceeds a critical threshold, the loop becomes unstable and begins self-oscillation, creating a beat frequency (heterodyne) against incoming continuous waves.


B. 500-Cycle High-Pitch Copying Amateurs found that 500 Hz tone spark transmissions were far easier to copy through high-energy broadband static (lightning, static electricity). * \textbf{Implementation:} Add a 2nd-order resonant bandpass filter (Q factor of 10) centered at 500 Hz to show the SNR improvement when static noise is injected into the valve grid.

2. Deep-Dive: Type "T" Tubular Audion Cylindrical Geometry


Prior to the Type "T" Tubular Audion, de Forest Audion bulbs used flat plates and grids positioned adjacent to a looped filament (flat plane geometry). The tubular design introduced in April 1916 rearranged these elements coaxially:


A. Flat Plane vs. Cylindrical Electrostatic Fields \textit{ \textbf{Flat Plane Audion (Standard):} The electrostatic field is uniform across the parallel planes: \$\$E\_\{\textbackslash text\{flat\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{V\_p\}\{\textbackslash text\{distance\}\}\$\$ } \textbf{Tubular Audion (Cylindrical):} The electric field between the central axial filament (\$r\_a\$) and the outer cylindrical plate (\$r\_b\$) is non-uniform, concentrating the field intensity near the emitter surface: \$\$E\_\{\textbackslash text\{cylindrical\}\}(r) = \textbackslash frac\{V\_p\}\{r \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash ln(r\_b / r\_a)\}\$\$ This non-uniform field shifts the space-charge density, slightly altering the knee of the plate current \$I\_p\$ curve and lowering inter-electrode capacitance.


B. Cylindrical Permittivity \& Capacity The capacitance of the tubular Audion is modeled using cylindrical boundary equations: \$\$C\_\{\textbackslash text\{tubular\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{2 \textbackslash pi \textbackslash epsilon\_0 \textbackslash epsilon\_r L\}\{\textbackslash ln(r\_b / r\_a)\}\$\$ This reduces stray inter-electrode capacitance, making the Audion significantly more stable at higher frequencies.


---


3. Washington's Birthday Relay Routing Simulation


Kirwan's relay of Colonel Nicholson's message was a milestone in proving that a decentralized group of operators could coordinate under a uniform protocol. \textit{ \textbf{Protocol Invariant:} The message propagation relied on hand-shaking and acknowledgment (similar to TCP or the on-chain Merkle confirmation blocks). } \textbf{TSFi2 Relay Test:} The communication system (\texttt{tsfi\_comm.c}) includes benchmark tests verifying that a packet can be routed through multiple simulated hop nodes using optimized routing protocols without losing data integrity (\$\textbackslash Phi = 0\$).

2. Technical Deep-Dive: Autodyne Demodulation Principles


Prior to the discovery of autodyne reception (self-oscillation), detecting undamped (continuous wave) Morse code was challenging because the incoming signal had a constant frequency and produced no audible tone in the headphones (unlike the pulsed, musical tone of spark transmitters).


Curtis and Horner described using the Audion as an autodyne receiver:


\textit{ \textbf{The Beat Principle (Heterodyning):} The Audion is tuned to oscillate at a local frequency \$f\_1\$ (via regenerative feedback \$\textbackslash beta\$). When an incoming continuous wave frequency \$f\_2\$ is received, the non-linear transfer characteristics of the Audion mix the two frequencies, producing an audible beat frequency: \$\$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{beat\}\} = f\_1 - f\_2\$\$ } \textbf{Non-Linear Mixing:} Because plate current \$I\_p\$ is a non-linear function of grid voltage (\$1.5\$-power Child's Law), the product term of the local oscillation and incoming signal is naturally generated in the plate current: \$\$I\_p \textbackslash propto \textbackslash left(V\_\{g,\textbackslash text\{local\}\} \textbackslash cdot V\_\{g,\textbackslash text\{incoming\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ This generates sum and difference frequencies, with the low-frequency difference (\$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{beat\}\}\$) falling within the audible range (\$500\textbackslash text\{--\}1000\textbackslash text\{ Hz\}\$) of the Stromberg-Carlson headphones.


---


3. Physical Model Alignment


We have already implemented this regenerative feedback mechanism in [tsfi\_valve.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_valve.c): \$\$\textbackslash text\{prev\textbackslash \_vp\} - \textbackslash text\{dc\textbackslash \_offset\}\$\$ Which is fed back to the grid. In our tests, setting \$\textbackslash beta = 0.85\$ triggers self-sustained oscillation, allowing the valve to serve as a local oscillator (\$f\_1\$) to heterodyne incoming RF signals.

2. Technical Deep-Dive: Distributed Capacity \& Dead-End Isolation


In early receiver design, tuning coils were tapped at multiple points to select different wavelength ranges. However, the unused portion of the coil remained magnetically coupled and possessed parasitic capacity between the turns: \textit{ \textbf{The Dead-End Effect:} The unused portion acts as an auxiliary tank circuit. It absorbs electromagnetic energy from the active circuit, causing a severe drop in receiver sensitivity (high loss, \$\textbackslash Phi > 0\$) and shifting the tuning peaks. } \textbf{Dead-End Switch Mitigation:} A multi-blade switch was used to not only select the active tap but to completely open-circuit or short-out the unused segments, preventing resonant absorption.


TSFi2 Resonant Analogy Within the \textbf{Synthesis Resonant network} (\texttt{tsfi\_resonance.c}), we simulate multi-stage inductors: \textit{ If a multi-stage inductor has unused segments, we calculate the parasitic distributed capacitance coupling coefficient \$k\_\{\textbackslash text\{parasitic\}\}\$ between the active and inactive sections. } Implementing a virtual "Dead-End switch" cuts this coupling coefficient to zero (\$k\_\{\textbackslash text\{parasitic\}\} = 0\$), restoring the zero-loss (\$\textbackslash Phi = 0\$) invariant and increasing peak output gain.
