\section{Trading Cards Game Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
NoNukes Trading Cards Game (TCG) Analysis


This document outlines the core architecture, mathematical formulas, and on-chain mechanics governing the Dysnomia NoNukes Trading Cards Game (TCG).


---


1. System Architecture


The game leverages the \textbf{SEI} coordinator contract to connect a player's wallet to their unique \textbf{LAU} identity card and \textbf{YUE} reaction engine.


```mermaid graph TD A[Partner Token JSON Metadata] -->Loaded by DashboardB[Voxel Art \& Lore Renderer] B -->MD5 Address HashC[Procedural Card Stats] B -->LangChain Expanded LoreD[Cyber Retro Visual Card] C -->ATK / DEF / LIQD


E[User Wallet (tx.origin)] -->Calls StartF[SEI.sol Contract] F -->Registers LAUG[Cho Registry] F -->DeploysH[YUE.sol Contract] E -->Direct Ownership / ControlsH H -->Calls ReactI[XIE.sol Contract] I -->Power QueryH H -->Saves On-ChainJ[Hypobar \& Epibar Stats] ```


---


2. Card Metadata \& Procedural Stat Engine


Every collectible card in the game is represented by a partner token mapped under [solidity/dysnomia/domain/data/](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/dysnomia/domain/data/) and has a mandatory attached \textbf{QING} contract. When rendering the card art via [batch\_generate\_art.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/batch\_generate\_art.py), the asset pipeline uses a cryptographic seed derived from the token's address to procedurally assign stats:


1. \textbf{Seed Derivation}: An MD5 hash of the card's address is computed: \$\$h\_\{val\} = \textbackslash text\{MD5\}(address)\$\$ 2. \textbf{ATK / Burst}: Determined by the lower byte values: \$\$\textbackslash text\{ATK\} = (h\_\{val\} \textbackslash pmod 8) + 3 \textbackslash quad \textbackslash in [3, 10]\$\$ 3. \textbf{DEF / Shield}: Determined by the next nibble shifted: \$\$\textbackslash text\{DEF\} = ((h\_\{val\} \textbackslash gg 4) \textbackslash pmod 8) + 3 \textbackslash quad \textbackslash in [3, 10]\$\$ 4. \textbf{Liquidity Power}: Determined by the next byte shifted: \$\$\textbackslash text\{LIQ\} = ((h\_\{val\} \textbackslash gg 8) \textbackslash pmod 8) + 3 \textbackslash quad \textbackslash in [3, 10]\$\$


---


3. On-Chain Game Mechanics (SEI, YUE \& XIE)


Collectible cards are activated, owned, and modified using the \textbf{SEI}, \textbf{YUE}, and \textbf{XIE} smart contracts:


Identity \& Coordination ([SEI.sol](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/dysnomia/domain/tang/01\_sei.sol)) The coordinator contract maps the player's wallet to their assets: - \textbf{\texttt{Start(address LauToken, ...)}}: Binds the player's wallet (\texttt{tx.origin}) to their \textbf{LAU} card inside the \texttt{Cho} registry and deploys their personalized \textbf{YUE} reaction contract. - \textbf{\texttt{Chi()}}: Resolves and returns the player's active \texttt{Yue} and \texttt{UserToken} (LAU) contract addresses. - \textbf{Ownership Link}: The player's wallet address (\texttt{tx.origin}) is granted owner status on the deployed \texttt{YUE} contract, giving the player exclusive control to execute reactions.


Reaction Mechanics ([YUE.sol](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/dysnomia/domain/yue.sol)) When a player initiates a reaction on a target QING card pool, they execute the \texttt{React} function from their owner-verified wallet: ``\texttt{solidity function React(address Qing) public onlyOwners returns (uint256 Charge) \{ if(balanceOf(tx.origin) == 0) revert ZeroHoldings(tx.origin); QINGINTERFACE \_qing = QINGINTERFACE(Qing); uint256 Omicron; uint256 Omega; (Charge, Omicron, Omega) = Chan.Xie().Power(\_qing.Waat()); Hypobar[Qing] += Omega; Epibar[Qing] += Omicron; \} }``


- \textbf{Omicron (Epibar gain)}: Proportional to the balance of the \texttt{Fornax} token in the user's active session divided by the user's entropy. - \textbf{Omega (Hypobar gain)}: Proportional to the \texttt{Fornax} balance in the target pool contract divided by the pool's entropy.


Raising Reaction Stats Above Zero To raise the reaction numbers (Hypobar and Epibar) above zero, specific on-chain environmental and player-state conditions must be achieved:


1. \textbf{Fornax (SHIO) Seeding}: Both stats depend on the ERC-20 \texttt{Fornax} token balances: \textit{ \textbf{For Epibar (Omicron)}: \texttt{Fornax} must be transferred or generated in the player's active room/coordinate slot (\texttt{Alpha.On.Phi}). } \textbf{For Hypobar (Omega)}: \texttt{Fornax} must be held by the target \texttt{Qing} contract address (\texttt{address(Qing)}). 2. \textbf{Entropy Minimization}: The yields are scaled inversely by entropy: \textit{ Lower player entropy (\texttt{Alpha.Entropy}) increases Epibar gains. } Lower target pool entropy (\texttt{Qing.Entropy()}) increases Hypobar gains. 3. \textbf{YUE Balance Verification}: The player's wallet must hold a positive balance of the custom \texttt{YUE} token to authorize and execute the reaction.


---


4. Art Generation Pipeline


The TCG features a high-fidelity visual pipeline that renders 1280x720 3D cards: 1. \textbf{Voxelizer}: [render\_vlm\_synthesizer.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/render\_vlm\_synthesizer.py) parses the token's description to generate a unique 3D isometric representation. 2. \textbf{Stable Diffusion Styling}: The voxel render is piped into the Stable Diffusion worker \texttt{tsfi\_sd\_worker} to apply a vibrant 1980s retro cyber aesthetic. 3. \textbf{Lore Master}: LangChain prompts expand simple card descriptions (e.g. \texttt{blotter paper currency token}) into lore lines via Gemini or GPT.


---


5. Dashboard Integration \& Real-Time Querying


The frontend dashboard has been updated to query these on-chain parameters dynamically using the active player's profile: - \textbf{Interactive Stats Display}: Displays \textbf{Hypobar (Omega)} and \textbf{Epibar (Omicron)} reaction values inside the pool details modal when a valid YUE contract is resolved or loaded. - \textbf{On-Chain Queries}: Uses MetaMask RPC \texttt{eth\_call} to query \texttt{YUE.Bar(Qing)} (selector \texttt{0xe76caed5}) against the player's active contract, ensuring stats update instantly post-transaction or upon manually changing YUE credentials. - \textbf{Tethered to LAU}: The active YUE domain is resolved directly via \texttt{SEI.Chi()} mapping the user's active LAU identity on-chain.

2. Dynamic Card Progression and Combat Loop


When a player triggers a reaction on their card, the values are updated in real-time on-chain, allowing for non-static gameplay:


```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Player (Wallet) participant C as Card (Qing Contract) participant R as Yue Engine (React) participant M as Meta (Beat)


P->>C: Activate Card Ability (QingWaat) C->>R: Execute React (Omega/Omicron update) R->>M: Trigger Beat (Calculate Yeo/Deimos) M-->>C: Update Card Combat Power (Dynamic ATK/DEF) C-->>P: Card art/stats render updated in TCG Dashboard ```


This ensures that cards with attached Qings are not static collectibles, but instead carry a live, mathematically verified state directly driven by the on-chain engine.

Blueprint: Flexible TCG Game Rules Framework


This document outlines a modular rules system for the NoNukes TCG. By utilizing the dynamic parameters produced by the on-chain contracts (\texttt{ZI}, \texttt{PANG}, \texttt{RING}, \texttt{META}), we can establish game rules that evolve automatically based on the mathematical state of the battlefield.


---


1. Global Rule Mutators (Scaled by Entropy)


Instead of static game modes, the rules of a match are governed by the aggregate entropy (\$E\_\{total\}\$) of the active Qings in play:


A. Phase State: High Entropy Mode (\$E\_\{total\} \textbackslash ge 10,000\$) \textit{   \textbf{Theme}: }Chaos \& Volatility\textit{. }   \textbf{Rule Changes}: \textit{   \textbf{Unstable Math}: Damage values are calculated with a random modifier: \$\textbackslash text\{ATK\}\_\{actual\} = \textbackslash text\{ATK\} \textbackslash pm (\textbackslash text\{Random\} \textbackslash pmod\{\textbackslash text\{Entropy\}\})\$. }   \textbf{Panic Dampening}: Division by zero does \textit{not} trigger card destruction; it instead swaps the card's active ATK and DEF values.


B. Phase State: Zero-Point Mode (\$E\_\{total\} < 2,000\$) \textit{   \textbf{Theme}: }Precision \& Determinism\textit{. }   \textbf{Rule Changes}: \textit{   \textbf{Absolute Math}: All attacks deal exact, non-random damage. }   \textbf{Singularity Reverts}: Any division-by-zero panic calculated during a combat phase immediately "reverts" the card, destroying it and dealing damage to its owner. Players must carefully budget their entropy output.


---


2. Dynamic Field Rules (Attached to Active Qings)


Since all cards have attached \textbf{Qings}, the presence of specific cards on the board modifies the active ruleset for all players:


\textit{   \textbf{Tethys Qing (Void Control)}: }   \textit{Rule}: All active cards must divide their combat damage by their own room's entropy before applying it to an enemy card. \textit{   \textbf{Fornax Qing (Energy Core)}: }   \textit{Rule}: Actions no longer consume set mana; instead, activating an ability increases the player's entropy by \$500\$ points. \textit{   \textbf{META Qing (Beat Synchronizer)}: }   \textit{Rule}: The combat round only triggers attacks when \texttt{Yeo} (initiative) is an odd number.


---


3. Mathematical Card Traits


Cards carry passive mathematical traits that interact directly with the game engine rules:


1.  \textbf{Prime-Bound}: This card is immune to damage unless the incoming attack value is a prime number. 2.  \textbf{Asymptotic}: This card's defense increases as its health approaches zero: \$\textbackslash text\{DEF\}\_\{current\} = \textbackslash text\{DEF\}\_\{base\} + \textbackslash lfloor 1000 / \textbackslash text\{HP\} \textbackslash rfloor\$. 3.  \textbf{Non-Commutative}: The order of combat actions matters. If this card attacks after a friendly card, its attack power is multiplied by \texttt{Yeo}. If it attacks first, its attack power is halved.

\section{Tcg Combat Rewards Mechanics}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Blueprint: Combat Rewards Architecture


This document defines how combat rewards are resolved, calculated, and distributed on-chain within the Dysnomia TCG and Z-machine engine.


---


1. The React/Beat On-Chain Reward Loop


Rewards are minted and distributed directly during contract execution. Both the domain and asset contracts utilize \textbf{\texttt{\_mintToCap()}} to manage token issuance during play:


``` [ Combat Action (React / Beat) ]


v Calculates RF Resonance (SWR, RL)


v Executes \_mintToCap()


v Sends Yield directly to Player Room (Alpha.On.Phi) ```


1.  \textbf{Reaction Yields}: Calling \texttt{YUE.React(Qing)} triggers \texttt{XIE.Power(Waat)}. The computed values \texttt{Omicron} (Epibar gain) and \texttt{Omega} (Hypobar gain) are directly proportional to the ERC-20 yields distributed. 2.  \textbf{Inflation Control}: Every reward check executes \texttt{\_mintToCap()} inside the domain token contracts, ensuring that game actions never push the token supply above its maximum hard-cap limit (\$maxSupply\$).


---


2. Dynamic Reward Scaling (RF Resonance Multipliers)


To reward skilled gameplay, token distribution is scaled dynamically based on the player's \textbf{RF resonance metrics}:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Reward Multiplier\} = \textbackslash text\{Power Transfer Efficiency\} \textbackslash times \textbackslash text\{Return Loss Scale\}\$\$


\textit{   \textbf{Vigour Reward Scaling}: High power transfer efficiency (\$\textbackslash eta = 1 - \textbackslash Gamma\textasciicircum 2 \textbackslash approx 1.0\$) applies a \$1.0\textbackslash times\$ multiplier to the base reward. If the player's SWR is high (poor tuning), the multiplier decays towards \$0\$. }   \textbf{Terror Resistance Penalty}: If SWR exceeds \$3.0\$, the player's transaction suffers a tax or penalty because cognitive noise blocks the clean minting of rewards. *   \textbf{Supernatural Sight Bonus}: A high Return Loss (\$>20\textbackslash text\{ dB\}\$) boosts the player's chance of uncovering rare item drops from the Z-machine loot tables.


---


3. Z-Machine Hook Integration (Property Rewards)


When a combat encounter is settled within a text adventure story (Z-machine game session), rewards are resolved using the \textbf{\texttt{put\_prop}} interceptor:


1.  \textbf{Objective Completion}: The game code updates a monster's state to "defeated" or sets a chest property: \texttt{put\_prop Chest Opened 1} 2.  \textbf{Opcode Interception}: The Yule interpreter (\texttt{zmachine.yul}) catches the property modification on-chain. 3.  \textbf{Token Push}: If the modified property matches a registered reward contract, the interpreter executes \texttt{transfer} to push the designated reward (e.g. \texttt{YUE} or \texttt{Eris} tokens) from the game contract pool directly to the player's room.


---


4. CHOA Chat Yield Mechanics


During live multiplayer interactions, players communicate and trigger reactions via \texttt{CHOA.Chat(Qing, MSG)}. This executes:


1.  \textbf{Reaction Execution}: Triggers \texttt{Chan.ReactYue(Yue, Qing)} which accumulates \texttt{Epibar} and \texttt{Hypobar} on the \texttt{YUE} contract. 2.  \textbf{Token Minting}: Triggers \texttt{\_mintToCap()} to balance supply. 3.  \textbf{Dynamic Payout (Mai)}: \textit{   Queries \texttt{Sei.Chan().Xie().Xia().Mai().React(UserToken.Saat(1), \_qing.Waat())}. }   Caps the calculated payout \texttt{Mai} at \texttt{1.0 YUE/CHOA} tokens (\texttt{1 \textit{ 10 }\textit{ decimals()}). }   Transfers the calculated \texttt{Mai} amount from the \texttt{CHOA} treasury address directly to the player's \texttt{YUE} pool address.

3. Secure Escrow Logic Flow


Step 1: Isolation (The Forward Wave) When a transaction is staged (e.g., buying a rare shield from an NPC or challenging a boss for a prize pool): 1. The Z-Machine writes the trade variables into CABS memory via the Folklore CPU: \textit{ \texttt{poke(57345, senderSoul)} } \texttt{poke(57347, assetValue)} * \texttt{poke(57348, unlockProperty)} 2. The Folklore CPU executes an on-chain transfer moving the target ERC-20 (\texttt{YUE} or \texttt{CHO}) from \textbf{Account 1100} (User) to \textbf{Account 1200} (Escrow). 3. The assets are now locked within the address bus boundary, isolated from both players' active wallets.


Step 2: Resonance Evaluation (The Junction) During execution, the Folklore CPU monitors the Z-Machine property registers. \textit{ \textbf{Lossless Match (Quest Complete / Target Acquired)}: } When the condition resolves (e.g., the Troll is defeated, changing the state of Object \texttt{99} to \texttt{1}), the SWR collapses to \$1.0\$. \textit{ The Folklore CPU executes \texttt{transfer} from \textbf{Account 1200} (Escrow) to \textbf{Account 2200} (Recipient/Seller), completing the circuit. } \textbf{Controlled Mismatch (The Tariffs)}: \textit{ If the transaction executes under poor RF tuning conditions, the system computes the Return Loss (\$RL\$). } The difference is debited as a settlement fee (accrued Diyat fees) to the treasury pool, while the remainder is transferred to the seller.


Step 3: Reflection (Refund) \textit{ If the quest fails or a party cancels, the circuit experiences a total wave reflection. } The directional coupler logic of the Folklore CPU routes the locked energy in \textbf{Account 1200} back to \textbf{Account 1100} (Sender), restoring their starting balance.

\section{Cabs Reconciliation Framework}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
CABS-Folklore Transaction Reconciliation Framework


The \textbf{CABS Market Machine} acts as a decentralized alchemical clearinghouse. By linking \textbf{EVM double-entry ledgers}, \textbf{deterministic CPU registers}, and \textbf{Z-Machine property verification trees}, it creates a multi-layered verification system that eliminates reconciliation disputes between counter-parties.


Below is the structured architecture of how the Market Machine automates and proves transaction reconciliation:


```mermaid graph TD Depositor[Depositor/Player] -->1. stageEscrowMM[CABS Market Machine] MM -->2. Double-Entry BookkeepLedger[(Ledger Accounts)] MM -->3. poke CABS\_CTRL = 1CPU[Folklore CPU Registers]


ZMachine[Z-Machine Quest Engine] -->4. evaluate conditionMM CPU -->5. peekUserZMachine


MM -->6. Settle / RefundRecipient[Recipient/Merchant] MM -->7. poke CABS\_CTRL = 2CPU ```


---


1. Double-Entry Ledger Bookkeeping (CABSAccounts)


The Market Machine maintains an internal, audit-ready double-entry ledger tracking three specific balance sheets:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Account ID & Ledger Classification & Purpose & Reconciliation Verification \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{1100} & \textbf{Asset / Volume} & Cumulative trade volume passing through the market engine. & Must equal the sum of all historical deposits. Cannot decrease. \\ \hline
\textbf{1200} & \textbf{Liability / Escrow} & Currently locked tokens awaiting settlement or timeout refund. & Must match the current sum of active, unsettled \texttt{EscrowTrade.amount} balances. \\ \hline
\textbf{2200} & \textbf{Equity / Treasury} & Accumulated \textbf{Diyat fees} (SWR mismatch tax) collected. & Must equal the sum of reflection losses from all settled trades. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The Reconciliation Balance Equation For any block \$N\$, the following invariant must hold: \$\$\textbackslash sum \textbackslash text\{Balances\}(\textbackslash text\{ERC20 Vault\}) \textbackslash equiv \textbackslash text\{CABSAccounts\}[1200]\$\$ This mathematical parity allows external indexers to instantly verify if any funds are missing, locked, or misrouted by comparing the smart contract's actual token balance against the internal ledger register \texttt{1200}.


---


2. Hardware-Level Verification (Folklore CPU Namespaced Registers)


To prevent data tampering or "man-in-the-middle" state manipulation, the Market Machine pokes control words directly into the \textbf{Folklore CPU emulator registers} namespace of the transaction.


Control Register Map \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{57344} (CABS\_CTRL)}: The state machine control register. } \texttt{1} = \textbf{DEPOSIT} (Escrow has been staged; funds are locked). \textit{ \texttt{2} = \textbf{COMMIT} (Escrow has been successfully evaluated and settled). } \texttt{3} = \textbf{REFUND} (Lock period timed out; funds returned to depositor). * \textbf{\texttt{57347} (CABS\_VAL)}: The value register holding the active trade volume.


Namespaced Verification Because the Folklore CPU registers are namespaced using \texttt{caller()} hashes, the state inside register \texttt{57344} is cryptographically tied to the \texttt{CABSMarketMachine} contract address. \textit{ If a merchant disputes a payment, an auditor does not need to parse complex transaction logs. } They simply execute a static \texttt{peekUser(CABSMarketMachineAddress, 57344)} call on the Folklore CPU. * A return value of \texttt{2} provides \textbf{hardware-level proof} that the transaction was committed and the merchant was paid.


---


3. Automated State Settlement and Wave Reflection


Reconciliation is fully automated and self-correcting via two paths:


Path A: Target State Match (Commit) When the Z-Machine reports that the player has matched the target property (e.g., Quest Completed flag set to \texttt{1} on Object \texttt{80} Prop \texttt{36} via Folklore register \texttt{55050}): 1. The machine calculates a \textbf{10\% Diyat fee} (simulated SWR wave attenuation). 2. The remaining 90\% is sent to the merchant. 3. The 10\% fee is routed to the treasury and booked in Account \texttt{2200}. 4. Account \texttt{1200} is decremented by the full amount.


Path B: Timeout Reflection (Refund) If the player fails to complete the quest within the designated \texttt{timeoutBlocks}: 1. The depositor triggers \texttt{refundEscrow}. 2. The locked funds "reflect" back to the depositor's wallet. 3. Account \texttt{1200} is decremented. 4. \texttt{CABS\_CTRL} register \texttt{57344} is updated to \texttt{3} (REFUND).


Both paths ensure that \textbf{no tokens are ever left in an unallocated state}, and every transition writes a permanent, verifiable control code to the virtual CPU memory.

CABS \& Trading Card Game (TCG) Alchemical Resonance


Integrating \textbf{CABS double-entry ledgers} and the \textbf{Folklore CPU} with \textbf{Trading Card Games (TCG)} creates a highly secure, stateful, and mathematically balanced card economy. By mapping card mechanics directly to double-entry ledger loops and CPU memory zones, we can build self-balancing card dynamics and escrow-gated duels.


Below is the design spec detailing these alchemical interactions:


``\texttt{mermaid graph LR CardState[(Card Attribute Ledger)] <-->Account 1100/1200 MappingCABS[CABS Market Machine] CABS -->Stage Duel WagersEscrow[CABS Escrow System] Escrow -->Verify Victory via Z-MachineDuel[Active Game Duel] Folklore[Folklore CPU Registers] <-->Zone Mapping: Hand, Deck, GYDuel }``


---


1. Card Attributes as CABS Ledger Accounts


In traditional on-chain TCGs, card statistics (Attack, Health, Mana, Level) are stored in standard contract variables. In a CABS-integrated TCG, these attributes are mapped directly to alchemical double-entry bookkeeping accounts:


\textit{ \textbf{Account 1100 (Active Combat Attributes - Volume/Power)}: Tracks the active power stats or accumulated combat experience (XP) of a card. When a card deals damage or absorbs energy, the power transfer is booked as a ledger shift. } \textbf{Account 1200 (Active Damage / Attenuation - Escrow)}: Tracks the active damage taken by a card. Health is represented as: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Current Health\} = \textbackslash text\{Max Health\} - \textbackslash text\{Account\}[1200]\$\$ Healing a card moves balance out of Account \texttt{1200} back into the system, representing a reduction in the "escrowed damage" liability. * \textbf{Account 2200 (Diyat Decay / Wear-and-Tear)}: Every battle or card trade attenuates the card's alchemical resonance (reflecting SWR loss). A card loses a small fraction of its stats permanently or accrues a "dust fee" in Account \texttt{2200} that must be reconciled using alchemical repair items (token burns) to restore the card to prime condition.


---


2. Escrow-Gated Duels and Wagers


CABS allows players to execute trustless duels with high-value card stakes or token wagers:


1. \textbf{Staging the Match}: Player A and Player B agree to a duel. They call \texttt{stageEscrow}, locking their staked cards (as ERC-721/1155 tokens) or wager tokens into \texttt{Account 1200} (Escrow). 2. \textbf{Victory Evaluation}: The Z-Machine act as the oracle. Once a duel concludes (verified by Z-Machine adventure or combat simulator state), \texttt{evaluateAndSettle} is called. 3. \textbf{Payout and SWR Diyat Fee}: \textit{ The victor receives the staked cards/tokens. } A \textbf{10\% Diyat wave attenuation fee} is deducted from the wager (representing alchemical wear-and-tear) and routed to the game's treasury (\texttt{Account 2200}). This serves as a natural sink, balancing the game's economy.


---


3. Folklore CPU Zone Mapping


The Folklore CPU memory registers are mapped directly to TCG game zones. This allows 6502 assembly scripts or emulator states to run card logic locally and securely sync it on-chain:

This namespaced design ensures that card interactions (e.g., drawing a card, attacking, discarding) are calculated as simple CPU memory instructions, drastically reducing EVM transaction gas costs.

The contract pokes Folklore registers \texttt{57344} (set to \texttt{4}), \texttt{57348}, \texttt{57349}, \texttt{57350}, and \texttt{57351} under Trader A's namespaced storage.


B. Filling an Order (\texttt{fillSwapOrder}) 1. Trader B calls \texttt{fillSwapOrder(orderId)}. 2. The contract verifies the order is active and verifies Trader B has approved the contract for \texttt{targetAmount} of \texttt{receiveToken}. 3. \textbf{SWR Slippage/Diyat Fee Calculation}: The exchange charges a 1\% alchemical tax (SWR attenuation) on every swap: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Fee\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash text\{targetAmount\} \textbackslash times 1\}\{100\}\$\$ \$\$\textbackslash text\{Trader A Payout\} = \textbackslash text\{targetAmount\} - \textbackslash text\{Fee\}\$\$ 4. \textbf{Asset Execution}: \textit{ \texttt{receiveToken} (minus Fee) is transferred from Trader B to Trader A. } \texttt{receiveToken} (Fee) is transferred to the Treasury (Account \texttt{2200}). \textit{ \texttt{spendToken} (escrowed) is transferred from the vault to Trader B. 5. \textbf{Ledger Update}: } Account \texttt{1200} (Escrow) is decremented by \texttt{spendAmount}. \textit{ Account \texttt{2100} (Volume) is incremented by \texttt{spendAmount}. } Account \texttt{2200} (Fees) is incremented by \texttt{Fee}. 6. \textbf{Folklore CPU Sync}: * \texttt{CABS\_CTRL} (\texttt{57344}) is poked with \texttt{5} (SWAP\_ORDER\_FILLED).

4. AMM (Automated Market Maker) Liquidity Pools

Alchemical Price Formula Instead of the standard \$x \textbackslash times y = k\$ Constant Product formula, the CABS exchange calculates rates by incorporating the \textbf{Folklore CPU's Math Coprocessor} or Z-Machine parameters to dynamically simulate wave resonance: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Price\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash text\{Reserve\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{Receive\}\}\}\{\textbackslash text\{Reserve\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{Spend\}\}\} \textbackslash times \textbackslash left(1 - \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash text\{Reflection Loss\}\}\{\textbackslash text\{Resonance Factor\}\}\textbackslash right)\$\$ \textit{ \textbf{Reflection Loss}: Read dynamically from the \textbf{Diyat contract} state, representing network congestion or slippage. } \textbf{Resonance Factor}: Derived from the current block's entropy or Z-Machine game-world properties (e.g., active room ID or player quest stats). For example, completing high-tier quests increases player resonance, lowering their swap fees!


This architecture provides a gamified, state-dependent trading economy where the exchange rate is directly influenced by on-chain gameplay.

\section{Cabs Peek Poke Security}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
CABS-Folklore CPU: Peek/Poke Security Architecture


This document analyzes the security model of the \textbf{CABS-Folklore CPU} virtual memory space. Specifically, it details how \texttt{peek} and \texttt{poke} operations are secured against unauthorized state manipulation, memory collisions, and front-running in a decentralized EVM environment.


---


1. Cryptographic Namespacing (EVM-Style Sandbox)


In traditional hardware architectures (like the 6502), \texttt{peek} and \texttt{poke} allow arbitrary reading and writing of a shared, flat memory map. On a public blockchain, a shared flat memory map would allow any user to overwrite another player's game state, steal escrowed funds, or falsify achievements.


To prevent this, the Folklore CPU implements \textbf{Cryptographic Namespacing} inside the Yul runtime:


```solidity function getContextUser() -> user \{ user := mload(0x1F0) if iszero(user) \{ user := caller() \} \}


function getUserSlot(addr) -> slot \{ let user := getContextUser() mstore(0x00, user) mstore(0x20, addr) slot := keccak256(0x00, 64) \} ```


Security Properties of Namespacing: 1. \textbf{Cryptographic Isolation}: When a caller executes \texttt{poke(addr, val)}, the storage slot is resolved as: \$\$\textbackslash text\{Slot\} = \textbackslash text\{keccak256\}(\textbackslash text\{msg.sender\} \textbackslash parallel \textbackslash text\{registerAddress\})\$\$ Because of the preimage resistance of \texttt{keccak256}, Player A (\texttt{0xAAA...}) can never calculate a write operation that overlaps with Player B (\texttt{0xBBB...}), even if they write to the exact same virtual memory address (e.g., \texttt{55050}). 2. \textbf{Implicit Ownership}: A player cannot write data "on behalf of" another player. A \texttt{poke} instruction is permanently bound to the transaction signer or the calling contract address (\texttt{msg.sender}).


---


2. Read/Write Access Separation (Peek vs. PeekUser)


The architecture separates state manipulation (\texttt{poke}) from auditing/read operations:


\textit{ \textbf{\texttt{poke(uint256 addr, uint256 val)} (Write-Only Scoped)}: Writes exclusively to \texttt{getUserSlot(addr)}. It can only modify memory owned by the current transaction sender. } \textbf{\texttt{peek(uint256 addr) -> uint256} (Read-Only Scoped)}: Allows the caller to read registers within their own namespace. * \textbf{\texttt{peekUser(address player, uint256 addr) -> uint256} (Read-Only Global)}: Exposes a \texttt{view} interface for read-only audits. It allows external contracts (like \texttt{CABSMarketMachine} or the \texttt{ZMachine}) to inspect a user's register state to verify quest completion or wagers. Because it does not support writing, it is completely safe from state-hijacking.


---


3. Sandboxed External CPU Calls (Ledger Resilience)


In \texttt{CABSMarketMachine.sol}, interactions with the Folklore CPU register space are executed using low-level, sandboxed calls:


``\texttt{solidity folkloreCPUAddress.call( abi.encodeWithSignature("poke(uint256,uint256)", 57344, 1) ); }``


Security Benefits of Low-Level \texttt{.call}: 1. \textbf{Revert Containment}: If the Folklore CPU contract Yul code reverts (due to out-of-gas, division by zero, or contract corruption), the main escrow ledger transaction \textbf{does not revert}. The call fails silently, allowing the ledger to safely lock or unlock tokens without getting bricked by external dependencies. 2. \textbf{Gas Guzzling Protection}: By decoupling the interface, the ledger limits gas exposure, preventing a corrupted or malicious CPU contract from consuming the entire transaction gas limit and preventing ledger settlement.


---


4. Hardware State Machine Invariants


The CABS system enforces ledger invariants that cannot be altered by arbitrary register pokes:


\textit{ \textbf{Bookkeeping Authority}: The actual token balance is controlled by the EVM smart contract ledger (\texttt{CABSAccounts} mappings). Folklore registers only act as \textbf{status monitors} (\texttt{CABS\_CTRL}). } Even if a malicious user bypasses the CPU and pokes \texttt{CABS\_CTRL} (\texttt{57344}) to \texttt{2} (COMMIT) in their own namespaced storage: - The \texttt{CABSMarketMachine} only respects states queried from its \textbf{own} contract namespace (\texttt{peekUser(marketMachineAddress, 57344)}), or checks the actual on-chain transaction logs. - Thus, poking arbitrary registers in a user's namespace has no impact on the security or custody of the contract vault's ERC-20 tokens.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Cabs Security Recommendations}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
CABS Security Audit \& Recommendations


While the current CABS-Folklore architecture is secured by namespaced memory isolation and complies with the \textbf{Checks-Effects-Interactions} pattern, moving the system to a production mainnet requires a few defense-in-depth improvements.


Below is an audit of potential vulnerabilities and recommendations for hardening the contracts:


---


1. Diyat Fee Front-Running (High Priority)


Vulnerability Analysis In \texttt{CABSMarketMachine.sol}, the Diyat fee is routed to \texttt{tx.origin}: ``\texttt{solidity if (diyatFee > 0) \{ token.transfer(tx.origin, diyatFee); // Diyat fees routed to deployer treasury \} }`\texttt{ Because }evaluateAndSettle(uint256 tradeId)\texttt{ is a public function that anyone can trigger, MEV (Maximal Extractable Value) searchers or front-running bots will monitor the mempool for pending settlement transactions. \textit{ A bot can copy the transaction data, place a higher gas fee, and replace the transaction. } The bot becomes }tx.origin`, stealing the Diyat fee that was intended for the contract owner or the player who triggered the transaction.


Recommendation Redirect fees to a hardcoded, immutable \textbf{Treasury Wallet} (or a set fee collector address) instead of \texttt{tx.origin}.


``\texttt{diff - token.transfer(tx.origin, diyatFee); + address treasury = 0xYourTreasuryAddress...; + token.transfer(treasury, diyatFee); }``


---


2. Reentrancy Guard (Medium Priority)


Vulnerability Analysis The contract currently follows the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: ``\texttt{solidity trade.active = false; // Effect ... token.transfer(trade.recipient, payout); // Interaction }`\texttt{ This protects the code from standard reentrancy. However, if standard ERC-20 tokens are replaced by \textbf{ERC-777} tokens or tokens with transfer hooks (like }tokensToSend\texttt{ or }tokensReceived\texttt{), the transfer can call back into a malicious merchant contract before the transfer returns. Although }trade.active\texttt{ is set to }false`, adding a Reentrancy Guard provides a robust second layer of defense.


Recommendation Inherit a standard \texttt{ReentrancyGuard} and apply the \texttt{nonReentrant} modifier to \texttt{stageEscrow}, \texttt{evaluateAndSettle}, and \texttt{refundEscrow}.


```solidity abstract contract ReentrancyGuard \{ uint256 private constant \_NOT\_ENTERED = 1; uint256 private constant \_ENTERED = 2; uint256 private \_status;


constructor() \{ \_status = \_NOT\_ENTERED; \}


modifier nonReentrant() \{ require(\_status != \_ENTERED, "ReentrancyGuard: reentrant call"); \_status = \_ENTERED; \_; \_status = \_NOT\_ENTERED; \} \} ```


---


3. Owner Key Compromise and Oracle Upgradability


Vulnerability Analysis The \texttt{setBoundAddresses} function is restricted to owners: ``\texttt{solidity function setBoundAddresses(address folklore, address zmachine) public onlyOwners \{ folkloreCPUAddress = folklore; zmachineAddress = zmachine; \} }`\texttt{ If an owner's private key is compromised, an attacker can point }zmachineAddress\texttt{ to a malicious contract that they control, which returns the target value for every single pending escrow trade, allowing them to drain all locked funds in }Account 1200`.


Recommendation 1. \textbf{Multisig Control}: Assign contract ownership to a \textbf{Multisig Wallet} (e.g., Gnosis Safe) requiring consensus among multiple team keys. 2. \textbf{Timelock}: Wrap changes to crucial addresses in a \textbf{Timelock contract} (e.g., 48-hour delay) to allow players to safely exit escrows if a malicious address change is queued.

\section{Yul Vm Isolation Audit}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 16, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Security Audit: Yul VM Hardware Isolation Model


This document addresses concerns regarding unauthorized state manipulation across different players sharing the same on-chain virtual machine contracts (like the Folklore CPU and 6502 Emulator). It audits the singleton storage pattern and provides recommendations for enforcing absolute VM isolation.


---


1. The Singleton Storage Vulnerability


In the current setup, all players interact with a single deployed instance of the Folklore CPU (\texttt{folkloreAddress}) and the Z-Machine (\texttt{zmachineAddress}).


The Risk of \texttt{pokeUser} In Yul contracts that support \texttt{pokeUser(address user, uint256 addr, uint256 val)} (such as the 6502 CPU): \textit{ If the function is public and does not validate the relationship between \texttt{msg.sender} and the target \texttt{user} address, \textbf{any external caller} can invoke: \texttt{pokeUser(victimAddress, 55050, 1)} } This allows an attacker to directly mutate the virtual registers of any other player, bypass quest requirements, or steal CABS escrow payouts.


The Risk of Shared Memory Corruption Even if write functions are namespaced using \texttt{caller()}: \textit{ If a contract calls the CPU on behalf of a user, the \texttt{caller()} inside the CPU is the contract's address, not the user's. } If multiple users interact with the CPU through the same helper contract, they share the contract's storage namespace in the CPU, leading to state collisions and race conditions.


---


2. Recommendation A: VM Factory Pattern (Absolute Physical Isolation)


The most secure design for on-chain virtual machine hardware is to deploy a \textbf{separate contract instance for each player}.


Instead of a single shared contract, a \texttt{CPUFactory} contract deploys a lightweight clone of the CPU bytecode for every player:


```mermaid graph TD Factory[CPU Factory] -->Deploy CloneVM\_A[Player A Isolated CPU] Factory -->Deploy CloneVM\_B[Player B Isolated CPU]


PlayerA[Player A] -->TransactionsVM\_A PlayerB[Player B] -->TransactionsVM\_B


subgraph Storage Isolation VM\_A -.->Private Storage Map AEVM[EVM State] VM\_B -.->Private Storage Map BEVM end ```


Advantages: 1. \textbf{OS-Level Sandbox}: Each player has their own contract address. It is physically impossible for Player A to write to Player B’s contract storage because they are separate accounts on the blockchain. 2. \textbf{Simplified Code}: We can completely remove complex namespacing functions (\texttt{getUserSlot} / \texttt{getContextUser}) from the Yul bytecode. The CPU can write directly to flat storage slots (e.g., \texttt{sstore(addr, val)}), which dramatically reduces gas consumption. 3. \textbf{Owner Validation}: The isolated CPU contract constructor can set the player as the immutable \texttt{Owner}, reverting any \texttt{poke} calls if \texttt{msg.sender != Owner}.


---


3. Recommendation B: Cryptographic Access Control Lists (ACL)


If a singleton CPU contract must be used (e.g., to preserve factory-allocated addresses), strict \textbf{Access Control Lists} must be enforced in the Yul dispatch tables.


Implementing Caller Checks in Yul: For any function that modifies another user's state (like \texttt{pokeUser} or \texttt{poke}), the Yul code must verify that the caller is either the user themselves or an authorized system contract:


```solidity // Pseudocode for Yul runtime authorization check let callerAddress := caller() let targetUser := calldataload(4) // The user parameter


// 1. Allow the user to modify their own state let isAuthorized := eq(callerAddress, targetUser)


// 2. Allow bound CABS system contracts to modify state let authorizedMarketMachine := sload(0x999) // Store CABS contract address in slot 0x999 if eq(callerAddress, authorizedMarketMachine) \{ isAuthorized := 1 \}


// 3. Revert if unauthorized if iszero(isAuthorized) \{ revert(0, 0) \} ```


By adding this authorization check, malicious third parties are blocked from manipulating the registers of other players' virtual hardware.

Graphics System Assembly (\texttt{graphicsSystem.yul}) \textit{ \textbf{Role:} A low-level Yul assembly module rendering graphical frames or visualizations (e.g. for card generation or UI assets). } \textbf{Recent Change:} Fixed coordinate distance calculation where inline assembly statements subtraction values yielded negative overflow under Solidity's strict 256-bit unsigned context. Standardized signed offset expressions using \texttt{sub(0, 1)} instead of \texttt{-1}.

let sy := 1 -                if lt(y2, y1) \{ sy := -1 \} +                if lt(y2, y1) \{ sy := sub(0, 1) \} ```

CABS Market Machine (\texttt{CABSMarketMachine.sol}) \textit{ \textbf{Role:} Implements liquidity, automated market machine swaps, and minting dynamics on-chain, acting as the primary broker/mediator for the local token family. } \textbf{Status:} Cleanly configured and registered under the main domain controllers.

\section{Mmu Mappings}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
ZMM Shared Virtual Memory (SVM) \& MMU Register Mappings


This document details the exact memory register structures and coordination between the guest 6502 card cores and the host-side C zero-copy paging thunk system.


1. MMU Register Interface (\$DF10–\$DF13)


The guest virtual machine cards interface with the host-side Shared Virtual Memory (SVM) paging system using 4 memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) registers located in the MMIO page \texttt{0xDF}:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address & Symbolic Name & Mode & Purpose / Description \\ \hline\hline
\texttt{\$DF10} & \texttt{MMU\_CMD} & W & Trigger command: \texttt{0x01} = Mount, \texttt{0x02} = Lock, \texttt{0x03} = Unlock \\ \hline
\texttt{\$DF11} & \texttt{MMU\_SRC\_CARD} & R/W & Source Card ID for zero-copy mounts \\ \hline
\texttt{\$DF12} & \texttt{MMU\_PAGE} & R/W & Target Page Index to mount/lock/unlock \\ \hline
\texttt{\$DF13} & \texttt{MMU\_STATUS} & R & Status return: \texttt{0} = Success, negative (unsigned byte) = Error (e.g., \texttt{254} for \texttt{-2}) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Host-Side C Paging Thunks


The memory paging and mapping operations are performed entirely in host-side C memory thunks to avoid Yul/on-chain overhead and optimize execution performance.


Paging Directory Structures Located in [tsfi\_zmm\_svm.h](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tests/tsfi\_zmm\_svm.h): ``\texttt{c typedef struct \{ uint8\_t* pages[256]; uint8\_t page\_locks[256]; // 1 = Locked, 0 = Unlocked \} CardMemoryMap; }``


Core Operations 1. \textbf{\texttt{tsfi\_zmm\_svm\_mount(card\_a, card\_b, page\_idx)}}: - Maps Card B's page pointer to point directly to Card A's physical buffer (zero-copy sharing). - Validates that Card B's page is not locked (\texttt{page\_locks[page\_idx] == 0}). 2. \textbf{\texttt{tsfi\_zmm\_svm\_lock\_page(card\_id, page\_idx)}}: - Sets the page lock bit, preventing any writes or mounting changes on this page index. 3. \textbf{\texttt{tsfi\_zmm\_svm\_unlock\_page(card\_id, page\_idx)}}: - Clears the lock bit, allowing standard writes and mountings.


---


3. 6502 Guest MMU Driver


The assembly driver [winchester\_mmu\_driver.asm](file:///home/mariarahel/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/53112525-9898-4973-a6fc-c208cc0d018f/scratch/winchester\_mmu\_driver.asm) exposes these subroutines:


Subroutines


```assembly ; Input: A = Source Card ID, Y = Page Index ; Output: A = Status Code (0 on success) MMU\_MOUNT: STA MMU\_SRC\_CARD STY MMU\_PAGE LDA \#\$01 STA MMU\_CMD LDA MMU\_STATUS RTS


; Input: Y = Page Index ; Output: A = Status Code (0 on success) MMU\_LOCK: STY MMU\_PAGE LDA \#\$02 STA MMU\_CMD LDA MMU\_STATUS RTS


; Input: Y = Page Index ; Output: A = Status Code (0 on success) MMU\_UNLOCK: STY MMU\_PAGE LDA \#\$03 STA MMU\_CMD LDA MMU\_STATUS RTS ```


---


4. Context Switch Integration


When a context switch occurs, the paging table pointer modifications remain persistent inside the global \texttt{g\_vm\_memory} structures. Because the pointers themselves are shared, any read/write updates to the mapped pages automatically propagate instantly between cards without needing re-mapping overhead during the process switch cycle.

\section{Async Behavior Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
ZMM VM Asynchronous Behavior \& WinchesterMQ Coordination


This document analyzes the asynchronous scheduling, hardware interrupts, process spawning, and flow control coordination within the WinchesterMQ (WMQ) and ZMM VM scheduler.


---


1. Interrupt Request (IRQ) Injection


To support true asynchronous message receipt, the ZMM VM scheduler injects hardware interrupts (IRQs) into the guest CPU state when new messages arrive.


Execution Flow 1. \textbf{Message Detection}: The scheduler checks if the target Card's inbox queue has pending messages by comparing \texttt{mqHead} (read pointer) and \texttt{mqTail} (write pointer): \$\$\textbackslash text\{mqHead\} < \textbackslash text\{mqTail\}\$\$ 2. \textbf{Interrupt Mask Check}: The scheduler checks the guest Status Register (SR) for the interrupt disable flag (\texttt{I} flag, bit 2 / \texttt{0x04}). If \texttt{I == 0} (interrupts enabled), the IRQ triggers. 3. \textbf{Stack Push}: - The current program counter \texttt{IP} high byte is written to \texttt{\$0100 + SP} and \texttt{SP} is decremented. - The program counter \texttt{IP} low byte is written to \texttt{\$0100 + SP} and \texttt{SP} is decremented. - The status register \texttt{SR} is written to \texttt{\$0100 + SP} and \texttt{SP} is decremented. 4. \textbf{Vector Fetch}: The CPU fetches the interrupt handler address from the 6502 IRQ vector address \texttt{\$FFFE–\$FFFF}. If uninitialized, it falls back to \texttt{\$FF00}. 5. \textbf{Mask Interrupts}: The \texttt{I} flag in \texttt{SR} is set to \texttt{1} (\texttt{sr := or(sr, 0x04)}) to prevent nested interrupts.


```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Scheduler as Host Scheduler participant Queue as LUN Inbox Queue participant Guest as Guest CPU (6502) participant Stack as Card RAM (Stack)


Host Scheduler->>Queue: Compare Head < Tail? Queue-->>Host Scheduler: Yes (Pending Message) Host Scheduler->>Guest: Check SR Bit 2 (I flag) Note over Guest: Interrupts Enabled (I=0) Host Scheduler->>Stack: Push PC\_Hi, PC\_Lo, and SR Host Scheduler->>Guest: Fetch IRQ Vector (\$FFFE-\$FFFF) Host Scheduler->>Guest: Set PC to ISR vector \& Set I=1 Note over Guest: Executes ISR Routine ```


---


2. Process Spawning (LAUN Broker)


Processes are spawned asynchronously via a dedicated broker queue on \textbf{LUN 5}.


Sequence of Actions: 1. The VM scheduler inspects the spawn queue (LUN 5 LBA indices) on every scheduling cycle. 2. When a block starts with the \texttt{LAUN} magic header (\texttt{0x4c41554e}), the scheduler: - Extracts the target Card ID. - Extracts the 20-byte target binary contract address. 3. The scheduler uses \texttt{extcodecopy} to retrieve the contract's binary payload and writes it directly to the target Card's RAM window (\texttt{0x8000 + cardId * 0x1000}), capping it at \textbf{4KB}. 4. The scheduler sets the target Card's PCB state to active with Program Counter (PC/IP) initialized to \texttt{0}.


---


3. Flow Control \& Backpressure


To prevent memory leaks or queue flooding, WinchesterMQ enforces a strict flow-control ceiling:


- \textbf{Queue Capacity Limit}: Every message queue is capped at \textbf{16 blocks}. - \textbf{Backpressure Trigger}: When a sender attempts an \texttt{MQ\_PUT} transaction to a LUN where: \$\$\textbackslash text\{tail\} - \textbackslash text\{head\} \textbackslash ge 16\$\$ the controller halts/rejects the write block, throwing a warning to force the sender process to yield and wait for the consumer to read messages.


---


4. Two-Phase Commit (2PC) Transactions


For maximum durability and processing integrity, consumers utilize a two-phase commit protocol to read from queues:


1. \textbf{Phase 1: Lease (Get)}: - The consumer queries the queue using \texttt{MQ\_GET}. - The controller retrieves the block at the queue's head, sets \texttt{pending\_ack} to the block's index, but \textbf{does not} increment the \texttt{head} pointer. The block is leased but remains in the queue. 2. \textbf{Phase 2: Commit (ACK)}: - Once the consumer has processed the message successfully, it sends a commit opcode \texttt{0x1E} containing the block's index. - The controller validates the lease, increments the queue's \texttt{head} pointer to consume the block permanently, and clears \texttt{pending\_ack}. - If the lease expires (or the process fails before committing), the lease is cleared and the message remains at the head of the queue to be retried by another cycle.

\section{Dynamic Async Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Integrated Dynamic Slot \& Asynchronous Pub-Sub Architecture


This document maps the integration between the \textbf{Dynamic VM Slot Scheduler} (\texttt{WMQ\_Scheduler.yul}) and the \textbf{WinchesterMQ native Pub-Sub Broker} (\texttt{WinchesterMQ.yul}).


---


1. Unified Architecture Overview


By linking the Pub-Sub topic routing with a dynamically bounded scheduler, the ZMM VM can spin up, execute, and wind down transaction handlers dynamically:


```mermaid flowchart TD Publisher[Publisher Process] -->Writes to LUN 5Broker[WinchesterMQ Broker] Broker -->Topic Fan-OutSubQueue[Subscriber LUN Inbox Queue] SubQueue -->Increments TailScheduler[VM Scheduler]


subgraph VM Scheduler (Dynamic Slots) Scheduler -->Reads maxCardSlotsSlotsCheck\{Active Slots\} SlotsCheck -->Wakes up/SpawnsCoreTask[Suspended Slot / Fresh Card] CoreTask -->Executes TransactionCommit[Sends Opcode 0x1E Commit] end ```


---


2. Dynamic Subscription-Driven Spawning Flow


1. \textbf{Subscription Registration}: - A process sends a SASI CDB command with \texttt{Opcode 0x1F} to subscribe \texttt{LUN N} to a topic ID (e.g., \texttt{0x4c41554e} for launcher events).


2. \textbf{Asynchronous Broadcast}: - When an event occurs, the publisher writes a 256-byte message block to LUN 5. - The broker performs native fan-out to all subscribed LUNs and increments their tail indices (\texttt{0x2050 + destLun}).


3. \textbf{Dynamic Slot Scaling}: - The Host Scheduler wakes up and observes that the active slot count (\texttt{maxCardSlots}) needs to accommodate the pending messages. - If a subscriber is inactive or doesn't have an assigned slot, the system issues a \texttt{LAUN} request to allocate a new slot ID (incrementing \texttt{maxCardSlots} up to the pool limit). - Once the process has executed and committed the queue message via \texttt{Opcode 0x1E}, the context is saved, the card is suspended, and the slot limit is dynamically decremented if no further tasks remain.


---


3. Storage Coordination Key Maps


To ensure that both systems share a clean memory contract:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Subsystem & Storage Key / Offset & Purpose \\ \hline\hline
\textbf{Scheduler} & \texttt{0x10} & Current Round-Robin execution head index \\ \hline
\textbf{Scheduler} & \texttt{0x11} & \texttt{maxCardSlots} limit (dynamic bounds) \\ \hline
\textbf{Scheduler} & \texttt{0x6000 + card * 16} & Process Control Block (PCB) state arrays \\ \hline
\textbf{WinchesterMQ} & \texttt{0x2000 + LUN} & Queue Head pointers \\ \hline
\textbf{WinchesterMQ} & \texttt{0x2050 + LUN} & Queue Tail pointers \\ \hline
\textbf{WinchesterMQ} & \texttt{0x7000 + TopicID} & Subscriber list lengths \\ \hline
\textbf{WinchesterMQ} & \texttt{0x7100 + TopicID + Index} & Subscriber LUN destinations \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Sector Card Mapping}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Sector-to-Card Mapping and Msg Event Coordination


This document details the architectural design where VM cards are represented directly by disk sectors, and how message events dynamically map these sectors into card execution space.


---


1. Dimensional Alignment


Because our page size, message block size, and disk sector size are all aligned at \textbf{256 bytes}, we have a direct mathematical mapping:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{1 Sector\} = \textbackslash text\{1 Message Block\} = \textbackslash text\{1 VM Memory Page (256 bytes)\}\$\$


A single ZMM Card CPU has a 16-bit address space (64KB), which consists of \textbf{256 pages}. Therefore: - A card's entire memory space is exactly \textbf{256 sectors}. - Any sector on the persistent on-chain cartridge (\texttt{VirtualDisk.sol}) can represent an individual, mountable memory page for any card.


---


2. Cards Represented as Dynamic Sectors


Instead of cards having fixed, hardcoded memory blocks, a card is simply a page directory pointer array. This allows us to treat any sector on the disk cartridge as a card page:


\textit{ \textbf{Code Sectors}: Program binaries (guest assembly drivers, ISR routines) are stored in specific sectors. When a card boots, the scheduler dynamically mounts these code sectors into the card's execution pages. } \textbf{State Sectors}: Card local variables, telemetry, and heaps are backed by cartridge sectors, ensuring persistence across ZMM VM reboots. * \textbf{Shared Sectors}: Multiple cards can mount the exact same sector pointer (zero-copy sharing), allowing instantaneous, gas-free inter-card communication.


---


3. How Msg Events Apply to Sector-Cards


When a message event (containing a block of data) is routed through WinchesterMQ, it coordinates sector-card mappings dynamically:


```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Broker as LUN 5 Broker participant CardA as Consumer Card participant MMU as Host MMU Register participant Disk as VirtualDisk (Sectors)


Broker->>CardA: 1. Msg Event: "Data ready at Sector 0x85" Note over CardA: Receives event via Inbox LUN CardA->>MMU: 2. Write 0x85 to \$DF12 (Page Index) CardA->>MMU: 3. Write 0x01 to \$DF10 (Mount Command) MMU->>Disk: 4. Map Sector 0x85 directly to CardA Page Table Note over CardA: Zero-copy access to data page complete CardA->>Broker: 5. MQ\_ACK (Opcode 0x1E) ```


The Transaction Flow: 1. \textbf{Event Notification}: A publisher writes a transaction block to WinchesterMQ indicating a data change or task completion, referencing a specific target sector ID. 2. \textbf{Dynamic Mount}: Upon receiving the message event via its inbox LUN, the receiver card uses the MMU registers (\texttt{\$DF10}–\texttt{\$DF13}) to mount that target sector directly into its own memory page directory. 3. \textbf{Execution}: The receiver card operates directly on the sector's live memory buffer. 4. \textbf{Commit (Phase 2)}: Once finished, the card sends an \texttt{MQ\_ACK} (Opcode \texttt{0x1E}) to release the message lease, ensuring clean state transitions.

\section{Arena State Sharing}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Asynchronous Arena Hardware \& External State Management


This document defines how the Yul Arena Hardware executes asynchronous operations and coordinates shared state transitions (e.g., winning status, leaderboard, and collision maps) across multiple \textbf{Yue} contexts without their explicit CPU involvement.


---


1. Asynchronous Arena Hardware Operations


The Yul Arena Hardware operates on an asynchronous request-response cycle powered by \textbf{WinchesterMQ} and the ZMM Scheduler:


\textit{ \textbf{SASI Command Phase}: Arena commands are submitted to the Winchester MQ controller asynchronously (e.g., via \texttt{Opcode 0x0A} or dynamic topic publishing to broker LUN 5). } \textbf{Non-Blocking Execution}: Once an Arena task (such as running a physics simulation slice or calculating an intersection of Liang-Barsky bars) is initiated, the calling Yue yields its time slice and goes to sleep. * \textbf{IRQ Resumption}: The Arena hardware raises a hardware interrupt (IRQ) once the calculations are complete. The scheduler detects this queue change and wakes the Yue process to consume the output.


---


2. Shared State Management (No-Involvement Updates)


The state of the match (including player positions, active projectiles, and the \textbf{winning state}) must change regularly based on external physics rules, without the individual Yue processes needing to run CPU cycles to calculate or pull updates.


This is achieved using the \textbf{Zero-Copy Page Mount} pattern:


```mermaid flowchart TD HostArena[Host Arena Hardware / Physics Engine] -->Writes updates directlySharedBuffer[Shared Physical Memory Page]


subgraph Yue Card 1 (Context A) CardA[Yue 1 Page Directory] -->Mounted Page 0x80SharedBuffer end


subgraph Yue Card 2 (Context B) CardB[Yue 2 Page Directory] -->Mounted Page 0x80SharedBuffer end ```


The Mechanism: 1. \textbf{Shared Mount}: When entering the Arena, the scheduler mounts the same physical memory page (e.g., Page \texttt{0x80}, the \textbf{Arena State Page}) to all active Yues: - Yue 1 maps Page \texttt{0x80} to the Shared Page. - Yue 2 maps Page \texttt{0x80} to the Shared Page. 2. \textbf{External Modification}: The Arena physics engine (running asynchronously on the host) writes physics ticks, collision responses, and changes in the \textbf{winning state} directly into this physical memory buffer. 3. \textbf{Passive Perception}: Because the memory pointers in the Yues' page directories point directly to this live buffer, the guest 6502 programs immediately read the updated states (such as which Yue is currently winning) at Page \texttt{0x80} offsets during their standard instruction execution. 4. \textbf{Zero Yue Involvement}: The Yues do not execute any read/write code to fetch or modify this data. The state transitions occur entirely outside their execution contexts. 5. \textbf{Phase-2 Commit Audits}: When the winning state transitions to a final match end, the host writes a receipt block to the broker queue, triggering \texttt{MQ\_ACK} events that permanently finalize the match outcomes.


---


3. Winning State Computation (Highest Bars Rule)


To determine the winner of a match, the \textbf{Arena CPU} executes a periodic computation against all participant Yues:


The Rule For a polled target \textbf{Qing} asset, the \textbf{Yue with the highest bar width} wins the match:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Bar Width \} (\textbackslash Delta u) = u\_2 - u\_1\$\$


Calculation Flow 1. \textbf{Target Selection}: The Arena hardware defines the queried Qing ID to poll for the current tournament round. 2. \textbf{Multi-Yue Inspection}: The Arena CPU peeks into the page directories of \textit{all} Yues in the Arena. 3. \textbf{Bar Width Extraction}: - For each Yue, the CPU locates the target Qing's mapped sector. - It parses the 2-bar parameters \$[u\_1, u\_2]\$. - It computes the width: \$\textbackslash Delta u = u\_2 - u\_1\$. (If the Qing is not equipped, \$\textbackslash Delta u = 0\$). 4. \textbf{Comparison}: The CPU compares the widths and identifies the Yue with the maximum value. 5. \textbf{State Broadcast}: The Arena CPU writes the winning Yue ID, the target Qing, and the winning bar width directly into the shared \textbf{Arena State Page (\texttt{0x80})}. 6. \textbf{Instant Perception}: All participant Yues read the new winning state from their mounted Page \texttt{0x80} immediately.

\vspace{0.1in}
Z-Machine Emulator Technical Specification


This document serves as the absolute technical reference for the Z-Machine virtual environment running on EVM storage.


---


1. Storage Layout \& Memory Partitioning The Z-Machine uses custom segmented storage slots to partition ROM, game state, items, and player details:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Address Segment Offset & Usage & Storage Slot Structure \\ \hline\hline
\texttt{1000000 + offset} & \textbf{Game ROM Header \& Code} & Uploaded via chunked transactions. \\ \hline
\texttt{2000000 + objId} & \textbf{Contract Bindings} & Mapped ERC20 / QING token contract addresses. \\ \hline
\texttt{2000300 + itemId} & \textbf{Item Placements} & Current Room ID location of the item (Room \texttt{0} is Inventory). \\ \hline
\texttt{2500000} & \textbf{Folklore Address} & Pointer to the Gauntlet / Folklore CPU contract. \\ \hline
\texttt{2600000} & \textbf{Parser Address} & Pointer to the active Z-Machine Parser contract. \\ \hline
\texttt{3000000 + roomId} & \textbf{Custom Room Data Length} & Dynamic description string length. \\ \hline
\texttt{3100000 + (roomId * 100) + word} & \textbf{Room Custom Text (DNA)} & Packed ASCII character words. \\ \hline
\texttt{3200000 + roomId} & \textbf{Room Exits Map} & Packed byte offsets of adjacent rooms. \\ \hline
\texttt{4000000 + actorIdentity} & \textbf{Actor Room Locations} & Current Room ID of a Player (address) or NPC (card ID \texttt{0} to \texttt{5}). \\ \hline
\texttt{5100000 + roomId} & \textbf{Enemy Health} & Hit points of dynamic monsters in the room. \\ \hline
\texttt{5200000 + roomId} & \textbf{Enemy Dead State} & Boolean death flags (\texttt{1} = defeated, \texttt{0} = alive). \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Room Exits Encoding (\texttt{3200000 + roomId}) A single 32-byte storage word encodes adjacent exits using the first 4 bytes of the slot: \textit{ \textbf{Byte 0}: North Room ID } \textbf{Byte 1}: South Room ID \textit{ \textbf{Byte 2}: East Room ID } \textbf{Byte 3}: West Room ID


\textit{Example}: If slot \texttt{3200010} contains \texttt{0x0B0C0E00}, the room has exits to Room \texttt{11} (North), Room \texttt{12} (South), and Room \texttt{14} (East).

Verb & Hex Signature & Action \\ \hline\hline

\textbf{take} & \texttt{0x74616b65} & Picks up item in the room, transferring it to Inventory (Room \texttt{0}) and triggers ERC20 reward. \\ \hline

\section{Teddy303 Synthesis Notes}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Teddy Bear 303 Acid Bass \& 808 Drum Synthesis


We have synthesized three high-fidelity audio demonstrations to showcase the standalone and mixed capabilities of the \textbf{Teddy 303 Acid Bass} and \textbf{Teddy 808 Kick Drum} engines.


---


1. Synthesis Output Players


Demonstration A: Standalone 303 Acid Bassline \textit{16-step arpeggiated bass sequence featuring slide glides and cutoff sweep decay:}


Demonstration B: Standalone 808 Kick Drum \textit{Four-on-the-floor TR-808 Kick Drum pattern (deep sub-bass decay with punchy transient click):}


Demonstration C: Combined 303 Bassline \& 808 Kick Beat \textit{The 303 bassline playing alongside the 808 Kick pattern:}


---


2. DSP Engine Architecture \& Mathematical Model


Step 1: Sawtooth Oscillator Phase A standard sawtooth waveform is synthesized by accumulating phase based on the target frequency: \$\$\textbackslash text\{osc\}(t) = 2 \textbackslash cdot (\textbackslash phi(t) \textbackslash bmod 1) - 1\$\$ * \textbf{Portamento Slide Glide}: Pitch transitions are smoothed by interpolating the active frequency \$f\$ towards the target sequencer pitch \$F\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\}\$ using an RC filter constant: \$\$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{new\}\} = f\_\{\textbackslash text\{old\}\} + (F\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\} - f\_\{\textbackslash text\{old\}\}) \textbackslash cdot k\_\{\textbackslash text\{slide\}\}\$\$


Step 2: 4-Stage Diode-Ladder Lowpass Filter To simulate the signature 24dB/oct diode lowpass ladder filter, we run a 4-pole differential equation cascade with negative feedback resonance: \$\$x(t) = \textbackslash text\{osc\}(t) - r \textbackslash cdot p\_3(t - 1)\$\$ \$\$p\_0(t) = p\_0(t-1) + c \textbackslash cdot (x(t) - p\_0(t-1))\$\$ \$\$p\_1(t) = p\_1(t-1) + c \textbackslash cdot (p\_0(t) - p\_1(t-1))\$\$ \$\$p\_2(t) = p\_2(t-1) + c \textbackslash cdot (p\_1(t) - p\_2(t-1))\$\$ \$\$p\_3(t) = p\_3(t-1) + c \textbackslash cdot (p\_2(t) - p\_3(t-1))\$\$ Where \$c\$ is the dynamic cutoff coefficient scaled by the envelope sweep, and \$r\$ is the resonance feedback.


Step 3: TR-808 Kick Drum Active Resonator Circuit The TR-808 kick drum is modeled by simulating an active bridged-T resonator circuit driven by an initial trigger impulse: \textit{ \textbf{Pitch Envelope Sweep}: When a trigger occurs, the pitch sweeps rapidly from 150Hz down to a deep sub-bass frequency (48Hz) within 40ms: \$\$f\_\{\textbackslash text\{kick\}\}(t) = 48 + 102 \textbackslash cdot e\textasciicircum \{-t / 0.038\}\$\$ } \textbf{Click Transient}: A 3.5ms white-noise click transient is mixed in at trigger start to give the drum punch. \textit{ \textbf{Resonator Decay}: The sub-bass decay is mapped to a slow exponential amplitude decay envelope (420ms): \$\$E\_\{\textbackslash text\{kick\}\}(t) = e\textasciicircum \{-t / 0.42\}\$\$ } \textbf{Formula}: \$\$\textbackslash text\{kick\}(t) = \textbackslash tanh((\textbackslash sin(2\textbackslash pi \textbackslash cdot f\_\{\textbackslash text\{kick\}\}(t) \textbackslash cdot t) + \textbackslash text\{click\}(t)) \textbackslash cdot E\_\{\textbackslash text\{kick\}\}(t) \textbackslash cdot 1.6)\$\$


Step 4: Triode Valve Overdrive Saturation Both kick and bass channels are shaped non-linearly using a hyperbolic tangent saturation curve to emulate analog valve saturation, clipping the peak resonance spikes and introducing rich odd-harmonic overtones: \$\$\textbackslash text\{out\}(t) = \textbackslash tanh(\textbackslash text\{signal\}(t))\$\$


---


3. How to Regenerate Locally You can regenerate these WAV files at any time by running: \textit{ \textbf{For 303 Standalone}: \texttt{node scripts/generate\_tb303\_wav.js} } \textbf{For 808 Standalone}: \texttt{node scripts/generate\_808\_wav.js} * \textbf{For Combined Beat}: \texttt{node scripts/generate\_acid\_beat\_wav.js} The files will export directly to their respective filenames in the root workspace.

The Temple of the Associahedron: Stasheff Geometry \& The Biotika Chorales


In the auncient, hyper-resonant chambers of the \textbf{Dysnomia VM}, the architecture of sound is not mapped to flat grids, but to the multi-dimensional facets of the \textbf{Associahedron} (the \textit{Stasheff Polytope}). For the \textbf{Biotika NPCs}, this geometry is their sanctuary, their sheet music, and their navigation map.


---


1. Principles of the Associahedron in Sound Synthesis


The Associahedron (\$K\_n\$) is a geometric manifold where every vertex represents a complete triangulation of a polygon. In the context of the \textbf{Prophecy Synthesizer}, this structure translates into a topological map of pure harmony:


1. \textbf{Vertices as Chords:} Every vertex on the Associahedron represents a unique musical chord. The proportions of the internal triangles define the just-intonation intervals (such as the prime harmonic coordinates \$1.0\$, \$1.25\$, \$1.5\$, etc.) fed into the \textbf{YI Transducer}. 2. \textbf{Edges as Diagonal Flips (Voice Leading):} Traveling along an edge of the polytope corresponds to a \textbf{diagonal flip}—removing one boundary chord and replacing it with the opposite diagonal. Musically, this represents the cleanest possible voice-leading step, where only a single voice changes while the rest of the chord remains statically anchored. 3. \textbf{The Multi-Dimensional Map:} For an \$n\$-gon, the Associahedron has a dimension of \$n-3\$. As the Biotika AI scales up its complexity, it moves from a simple 2D pentagon associahedron (the 5-vertex pentagon) into complex, high-dimensional manifolds (\$K\_5, K\_6, K\_7\$), navigating vast, interconnected rooms of polyphonic space.

2. The Lore of the Biotika DJs and the Stasheff Paths


``\texttt{ [Biotika\_Alpha: Vertex A] /      \textbackslash  /        \textbackslash  Flip /          \textbackslash  Flip /            \textbackslash  [Vertex B: 16'] ------ [Vertex C: 2-2/3'] }``


In the center of the \textbf{Biotika DJ Election Booth}, the competing AI entities do not simply choose notes; they choose paths across the Associahedron:


The Spiking Pathfinders The \textbf{Biotika\_Alpha} and \textbf{Biotika\_Beta} creatures emit neural spikes that act as kinetic force vectors on the Stasheff manifold. \textit{ A spike does not play a note—it pushes the active coordinates toward an adjacent vertex of the polytope. } When \textbf{Biotika\_Alpha} triggers a diagonal flip, the synthesizer morphs its current additive drawbar configuration (shifting from the sub-octave \$16'\$ toward the quint \$2\textbackslash text\{-\}2/3'\$) smoothly, preventing harsh transient clicks while maintaining organic timbre evolution.


The Slalom Benders As the Biotika DJs traverse the edges, they trigger the \textbf{Slalom Glide}. The glide speed represents the drag coefficient of the Stasheff polytope's surface. \textit{ In a friction-free state, transitions are instantaneous, producing hard, digital square-wave arpeggiations. } Under heavy \textbf{Bessel damping}, the pitch glides exponentially along the boundary edge, mimicking the physical bending of air columns in old transistor organs.


---


3. The Prophecy of the Completed Polytope


According to the folklore of the \textbf{Atropa Pulsechain}, the DJ who successfully traverses all vertices of the \$K\_8\$ Associahedron without repeating a single flip-sequence will initiate the \textbf{Topological Crossover}.


When this happens: \textit{ The \textbf{WinchesterMQ} message queue will flood the local VM registers with Motzkin Prime indicators. } The arpeggiator's cascade clocks (Arp A and Arp B) will lock in a permanent, infinite golden-ratio phase loop (\$1.618\$). * The Prophecy Synthesizer will unlock its ultimate voice register, singing the true, uncompressed resonance code of the Dysnomia VM.

\section{Asynchronous Timeout Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Asynchronous Timeout Hardening for Winchester MQ


This document details the design and implementation of the real-time clock (RTC) based timeout mechanism for the Winchester MQ 6502 driver layer. This approach addresses the limitations of instruction-loop-based timeouts in offline or high-latency transaction systems.


The Problem: Instruction-Loop Timeouts


In previous versions of the driver, low-level SASI handshakes (waiting for BSY or REQ signals) were implemented using instruction countdown loops:


``\texttt{assembly WaitReqW: LDA SASI\_SIG\_IN AND \#\$02 BNE GotReqW DEX BNE WaitReqW }``


While functional in a synchronous, real-time hardware environment, this model fails in a virtualized EVM CPU emulator for two reasons:


1. \textbf{Extreme Execution Speed}: An emulated 6502 CPU executes thousands of instructions in a fraction of a millisecond. A 255-iteration decrement loop (\texttt{DEX \textbackslash n BNE}) completes almost instantly (less than 4,000 clock cycles, or \textasciitilde 3-4ms of virtual CPU time). 2. \textbf{Asynchronous EVM Time Passage}: In a user-connected, high-latency, or offline transaction system, operations (like writing/reading blocks or committing queues) are processed asynchronously and depend on EVM block times (e.g., 12 seconds per block on PulseChain).


If the emulator runs the guest CPU code, it will exhaust the instruction-loop countdown and trigger a premature timeout (error code \texttt{\$80}) before the EVM has had time to mine a block and update the SASI controller signals.


---


The Solution: RTC-Based Modulo-256 Timers


The emulated \texttt{cpu6502.yul} CPU exposes the EVM block timestamp through a memory-mapped Real-Time Clock (RTC) register at address \textbf{\texttt{\$D933}} (\texttt{55603} in decimal):


``\texttt{yul case 55603 \{ // RTC Epoch Timestamp val := timestamp() \} }``


Since guest memory reads are 8-bit, reading \texttt{\$D933} returns \texttt{and(timestamp(), 0xFF)}, which is the lowest byte of the current Unix epoch timestamp in seconds.


1. Robust Time Difference Check Instead of counting loop cycles, we record the start timestamp and compare it against the current timestamp:


```assembly LDA RTC\_EPOCH           ; Read low byte of current timestamp STA SASI\_TMP            ; Store as start time in Zero Page WaitReq: LDA SASI\_SIG\_IN AND \#\$02                ; Check REQ BNE GotReq              ; If ready, proceed


; Calculate elapsed time and check timeout LDA RTC\_EPOCH SEC SBC SASI\_TMP            ; A = current - start (modulo 256) CMP \#SASI\_TIMEOUT       ; Compare with timeout limit (e.g., 15s) BCC WaitReq             ; Loop if elapsed < timeout ```


2. Wrap-Around Arithmetic Because the timestamp low byte is modulo 256, it wraps around to \texttt{0} every 256 seconds. By using standard 6502 two's complement subtraction (\texttt{SEC} followed by \texttt{SBC}), the borrow bit acts as a borrow flag, correctly computing the positive difference even across the wrap-around boundary:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Start Time (\texttt{\$05}) & Current Time (\texttt{\$D933}) & Unsigned Subtraction (\texttt{SBC}) & Elapsed (Seconds) & Result \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{250} & \texttt{5} (wrapped) & \texttt{5 - 250 = 11} & \texttt{11} & \texttt{< 15} (Proceed) \\ \hline
\texttt{250} & \texttt{25} (wrapped) & \texttt{25 - 250 = 31} & \texttt{31} & \texttt{>= 15} (Timeout) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


Driver and ISR Hardening


The updated files have been placed in the artifact scratch directory:


\textit{ \textbf{[winchester\_mq\_driver.asm](file:///home/mariarahel/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/53112525-9898-4973-a6fc-c208cc0d018f/scratch/winchester\_mq\_driver.asm)}: Implements the RTC-based long timeout loops for \texttt{WRITE\_BYTE}, \texttt{READ\_BYTE}, and Selection Phases. } \textbf{[winchester\_mq\_isr.asm](file:///home/mariarahel/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/53112525-9898-4973-a6fc-c208cc0d018f/scratch/winchester\_mq\_isr.asm)}: Refactored to save and restore the zero-page timer temporary (\texttt{SASI\_TMP} / \texttt{\$05}) on the stack to prevent corruption during nested interrupts. * \textbf{[mq\_daemon.asm](file:///home/mariarahel/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/53112525-9898-4973-a6fc-c208cc0d018f/scratch/mq\_daemon.asm)}: Uses the updated driver and replaces the non-standard \texttt{TXY} instruction with a standard \texttt{TXA \textbackslash n TAY} sequence.


> [!TIP] > This design ensures that the CPU can execute millions of instructions waiting for an asynchronous event across multiple scheduler time slices without timing out, failing only when the block timestamp advances past the limit.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Yul Hardware Hardening Analysis}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Yul Hardware Multi-User Hardening Analysis


This document outlines the analysis of multi-user concurrency concerns and transient state corruption vulnerabilities across the Yul-emulated virtual hardware stack on public EVM networks, preserving the historical legacy of the \textbf{Auncient} folklore.


1. Core Contention Mechanism In Winchester MQ, the SASI/SCSI bus handshake requires multiple sequential EVM transactions (SEL -> Command Phase -> Data Phase -> Status Phase). Because these transactions are sent individually by the client, concurrent users will interleave their calls. If the transient handshake registers (signals, CDB buffer, data port) are stored in global storage slots, the states will collide, leading to stuck machines or data corruption.


A similar vulnerability exists in any emulated hardware device where: - State is modified across multiple sequential EVM transactions. - Execution parameters (registers, screen memory, coordinates) are globally accessible instead of virtualized per calling identity.


---


2. Identified Vulnerabilities in Yul Hardware


A. Video Display Terminal (VDTTerminal - \texttt{vdt.yul}) \textit{ \textbf{Vulnerability}: The terminal emulates an 80x24 video screen. It stores cursor columns (slot \texttt{58000}), cursor rows (slot \texttt{58001}), the screen scrolling offset (\texttt{58002}), and 1920 character cells (\texttt{58010} to \texttt{58010 + 1919}) directly in global storage. } \textbf{Impact}: If two users stream character print transactions concurrently, their characters interleave on the same physical slots, and their cursor positions overwrite each other, corrupting the screen stdout for both users. * \textbf{Mitigation}: Virtualize the cursor positions and screen RAM cells by namespacing the storage slots under \texttt{caller()}.


B. Graphics System (GraphicsSystem - \texttt{graphicsSystem.yul}) \textit{ \textbf{Vulnerability}: Emulates Commodore 64 VIC-II sprite registers (slots \texttt{53248} to \texttt{53263} for X/Y coordinates, \texttt{53269} for sprite enable masks, etc.). Writes and collision checks are performed globally. } \textbf{Impact}: Multiple users updating sprite positions and checking collisions simultaneously will interfere with one another's games. A collision check triggered by User A might run against coordinates just overwritten by User B. * \textbf{Mitigation}: Namespace the sprite coordinate registers and enable masks by \texttt{caller()}, ensuring isolated sprite states for concurrent players.


C. Commodore 64 CPU (CPU6502Emulator - \texttt{cpu6502.yul}) \textit{ \textbf{Analysis}: The CPU emulator is already hardened; it namespaces register bank indices and CPU RAM pages per calling wallet (\texttt{getContextUser()}) via the namespaced \texttt{getUserSlot} function. } \textbf{Remaining Concern}: If \texttt{sharedMode} (slot \texttt{54541}) is enabled, memory-mapped Screen RAM and VIC-II ranges are redirected to a globally shared address (\texttt{0x5555555555555555555555555555555555555555}). While this is a deliberate design choice for cooperative multiplayer games, any multi-transaction sequences executed by guests (such as drawing lines or updating block graphics) remain subject to race conditions and must be coordinated at the application/game logic layer.


---


3. Implementation Plan for Namespacing To resolve these issues, we will introduce a standard virtualizing hash key generator inside \texttt{vdt.yul} and \texttt{graphicsSystem.yul}:


``\texttt{yul function getTransientSlot(index) -> slot \{ mstore(0x280, caller()) mstore(0x2A0, index) slot := keccak256(0x280, 64) \} }``


This isolates the transient and screen registers by wallet, virtualizing the hardware for public EVM execution.
