\section{Star Castle Autopilot Model}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 18, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Star Castle AI Autopilot Steering \& Evasion Model


This document specifies the architecture, mathematical model, and implementation details of the AI Autopilot Model designed to pilot the player ship under the flight physics of the Dysnomia VM and Auncient Wavelet lore.


---


1. Problem Statement \& Previous Limitations


In prior iterations, the autopilot relied on a discrete state machine (\texttt{thrust} vs. \texttt{shoot}) and targeted incoming mines directly: 1. \textbf{State Machine Jitter}: Toggling between aiming at the center (to shoot) and turning 90+ degrees to escape (to thrust) caused high-frequency turning oscillations (jitter). 2. \textbf{Loss of Tangential Velocity}: To face and shoot approaching mines, the ship turned towards them and stopped thrusting tangentially. Without tangential speed, the castle's core gravity pulled the ship inward, leading to collisions with castle bullets and shield rings. 3. \textbf{Spawn-Killing \& Mutation Loops}: Clearing active threat arrays directly within \texttt{resetShip()} mutated variables in the middle of active iteration loops (e.g. mines and castle bullet loops), which threw a \texttt{TypeError} and froze game execution, leaving the ship stuck at \texttt{(300, 520)}.


---


2. Model Architecture


The new model resolves these limitations using a \textbf{single continuous steering controller}, an \textbf{orbit-inflation evasion strategy}, and \textbf{deferred hazard clearing}.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[Threat Proximity Sensors] --> B[Orbit Inflation Engine] B -->targetOrbitC[Continuous Blend Controller] C -->targetAngleD[Steering \& Thrust Execution] E[Core / Mine Alignment] --> F[Smart Active Defense Gunner] G[Ship Death Event] --> H[Set shouldClearHazards Flag] H -->Defer till update endI[Clear active mines/bullets/lasers] }``


A. Orbit Inflation Engine Instead of turning away from threats, the ship expands its desired orbit radius \$R\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\}\$ when threats are close. This naturally guides the ship to spiral outward away from hazards while maintaining its orbital momentum.


The target orbit radius is calculated as: \$\$R\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\} = R\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\} + \textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{mines\}\} + \textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{bullets\}\} + \textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{laser\}\}\$\$


Where: \textit{ \$R\_\{\textbackslash text\{base\}\} = 220 + 15 \textbackslash sin(\textbackslash omega t)\$ (adds a slow, organic \$0.0008\textbackslash text\{ rad/ms\}\$ weaving motion) } \$\textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{mines\}\} = \textbackslash sum \textbackslash max(0, (180 - d\_\{\textbackslash text\{mine\}\}) \textbackslash times 0.75)\$ \textit{ \$\textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{bullets\}\} = \textbackslash sum \textbackslash max(0, (120 - d\_\{\textbackslash text\{bullet\}\}) \textbackslash times 0.45)\$ } \$\textbackslash Delta R\_\{\textbackslash text\{laser\}\} = 60\$ if the ship is within the charging/active laser sector (\$\textbackslash Delta\textbackslash theta\_\{\textbackslash text\{laser\}\}< 0.5\textbackslash text\{ rad\}\$) * Clamped such that \$160\textbackslash text\{px\} \textbackslash le R\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\} \textbackslash le 285\textbackslash text\{px\}\$ to prevent flying off-screen.


B. Continuous Blend Controller To determine the target angle \$\textbackslash theta\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\}\$ without discrete state jumps, we define an interpolation parameter \$t\$ based on the radial deviation \$\textbackslash Delta d = d\_\{\textbackslash text\{ship\}\} - R\_\{\textbackslash text\{target\}\}\$: \$\$t = \textbackslash text\{clamp\}\textbackslash left(\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash Delta d + 40\}\{80\}, 0, 1\textbackslash right)\$\$


\textit{ \textbf{\$t = 0.5\$ (Sweet Spot)}: The ship is at the target orbit. It faces slightly offset from the center (\$\textbackslash pm 0.22\textbackslash text\{ rad\}\$) to maintain orbit speed and keep the core in its firing arc. } \textbf{\$t < 0.5\$ (Too Close)}: The ship is inside the target orbit. The offset smoothly increases to \$\textbackslash pm 1.92\textbackslash text\{ rad\}\$ (pointing outward and tangentially) to push the ship back out. * \textbf{\$t > 0.5\$ (Too Far)}: The ship is outside the target orbit. The offset smoothly decreases to \$0\textbackslash text\{ rad\}\$ (facing the center directly) to pull the ship back in.


C. Deferred Threat Clearing (Anti Spawn-Killing) To prevent spawn-killing upon respawn (when a life is lost), the battlefield is cleared of active mines, bullets, and laser charges. To prevent modifying the arrays while they are being iterated in the main game loops: 1. \texttt{resetShip()} sets a global flag: \texttt{shouldClearHazards = true;} 2. At the very end of the \texttt{update()} loop (safely outside all iteration blocks), the arrays are safely emptied: ``\texttt{javascript if (shouldClearHazards) \{ mines.length = 0; castleBullets.length = 0; bullets.length = 0; laser.active = false; laser.charge = 0; shouldClearHazards = false; \} }``


---


3. Verification \& E2E Simulation Logs


\textit{ \textbf{Survival rate}: The ship successfully survives long sequences containing multiple homing mines, maintaining its lives, destroying multiple shield rings, and vaporizing the central core. } \textbf{Score Achievements}: Reached scores of \textbf{39,500+} during headless Chrome visual verification runs, harvesting 47 Lead, 19 Mercury, and 81 Sulfur before completing execution. * \textbf{Console Logs}: The Selenium automation test verified there are no runtime Javascript errors, crashes, or unhandled exceptions.

\section{Phase Space Formulation}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 19, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
🌀 Auncient Phase Space \& Hamiltonian Mechanics Blueprint


This document details the transition from velocity-rate configurations (tangent space \$TQ\$) to canonical Hamiltonian mechanics in \textbf{Phase Space} (cotangent bundle \$T\textasciicircum *Q\$) for the 6-DOF spacecraft simulation.


---


1. The Configuration Manifold \& Cotangent Bundle


To describe the state of the spacecraft in phase space, we map its position and orientation to a configuration manifold \$Q\$:


\$\$Q = \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 3 \textbackslash times S\textasciicircum 3\$\$


Where: \textit{   \$\textbackslash mathbf\{r\} = (x, y, z)\textasciicircum T \textbackslash in \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 3\$ represents translation. }   \$\textbackslash mathbf\{q\} = (w, x, y, z)\textasciicircum T \textbackslash in S\textasciicircum 3 \textbackslash subset \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 4\$ represents rotation (unit quaternion double cover of \$\textbackslash text\{SO\}(3)\$), satisfying the constraint \$\textbackslash \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\textbackslash \textasciicircum 2 = 1\$.


The \textbf{Phase Space} is defined as the cotangent bundle \$T\textasciicircum *Q\$, where every point is a pair of configuration coordinates and their corresponding canonical conjugate momenta:


\$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{x\} = (\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}, \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}, \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r, \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q) \textbackslash in T\textasciicircum *Q\$\$


---


2. Translation Phase Space


For translation, the canonical coordinates are: \textit{   \textbf{Position:} \$\textbackslash mathbf\{r\} = (x, y, z)\textasciicircum T\$ }   \textbf{Conjugate Linear Momentum:} \$\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r = (p\_x, p\_y, p\_z)\textasciicircum T = m \textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}\}\$


The translation Hamiltonian \$H\_\{\textbackslash text\{trans\}\}\$ is:


\$\$H\_\{\textbackslash text\{trans\}\}(\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}, \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r) = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r\textbackslash \textasciicircum 2\}\{2m\} + V(\textbackslash mathbf\{r\})\$\$


Where \$V(\textbackslash mathbf\{r\})\$ is the external potential field (e.g., gravitational pull of targets or planetary bodies).


---


3. Rotational Phase Space on the \$S\textasciicircum 3\$ Hypersphere


For rotation, we express dynamics directly on the unit quaternion hypersphere \$S\textasciicircum 3\$ rather than mapping to coordinates that introduce gimbal locking.


Conjugate Rotational Momentum Let \$\textbackslash mathbb\{I\}\$ be the \$3 \textbackslash times 3\$ rigid-body inertia tensor in the local body-fixed frame. The angular velocity in the body frame is \$\textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash omega\} \textbackslash in \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 3\$. The quaternion derivative \$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\}\$ relates to \$\textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash omega\}\$ via:


\$\$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{2\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) \textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash omega\}\$\$


Where the \$4 \textbackslash times 3\$ matrix \$E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\$ is defined as:


\$\$E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) = \textbackslash begin\{pmatrix\} -x \& -y \& -z \textbackslash \textbackslash  w  \& -z \&  y \textbackslash \textbackslash  z  \&  w \& -x \textbackslash \textbackslash  -y \&  x \&  w \textbackslash end\{pmatrix\}\$\$


The kinetic energy of rotation is:


\$\$T\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{2\} \textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash omega\}\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbb\{I\} \textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash omega\}\$\$


Defining the canonical conjugate momentum \$\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q \textbackslash in T\textasciicircum *\_\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} S\textasciicircum 3\$ as:


\$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial T\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\}\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\}\} = 4 E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) \textbackslash mathbb\{I\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\textasciicircum T \textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\}\$\$


Using the relation \$E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\textasciicircum T E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) = \textbackslash \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\textbackslash \textasciicircum 2 \textbackslash mathbb\{E\}\_\{3\textbackslash times3\} = \textbackslash mathbb\{E\}\_\{3\textbackslash times3\}\$ (on the unit sphere), the rotational Hamiltonian \$H\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\}\$ is:


\$\$H\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\}(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}, \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q) = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{8\} \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q\textasciicircum T E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) \textbackslash mathbb\{I\}\textasciicircum \{-1\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q\$\$


---


4. Hamilton's Canonical Equations of Motion


The total Hamiltonian of the spacecraft system is \$H = H\_\{\textbackslash text\{trans\}\} + H\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\}\$. Hamilton's equations dictate the phase flow:


\$\$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial H\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r\}\{m\}\$\$


\$\$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\}\_r = -\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial H\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{r\}\} = -\textbackslash nabla V(\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}) + \textbackslash mathbf\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{ext\}\}\$\$


\$\$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} = \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial H\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q\} = \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{4\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) \textbackslash mathbb\{I\}\textasciicircum \{-1\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q\$\$


\$\$\textbackslash dot\{\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\}\_q = -\textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial H\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} = -\textbackslash frac\{1\}\{8\} \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} \textbackslash left( \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q\textasciicircum T E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}) \textbackslash mathbb\{I\}\textasciicircum \{-1\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\})\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q \textbackslash right) + \textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash tau\}\_q\$\$


Where \$\textbackslash mathbf\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{ext\}\}\$ and \$\textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash tau\}\_q\$ are external non-conservative forces and thruster torques mapped into conjugate coordinates.


---


5. Symplectic Integration (Phase-Volume Preservation)


A standard Euler integrator violates Liouville's theorem, causing artificial energy drift and orbital decay. To maintain the \textbf{Auncient} geometric properties of the Phase Space, we must implement a \textbf{Symplectic Integrator} (such as a Semi-Implicit Euler or Stormer-Verlet scheme):


Symplectic Euler Step (\$\textbackslash Delta t\$): 1. Update momentum using current configuration: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r(t + \textbackslash Delta t) = \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r(t) - \textbackslash nabla V(\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}(t)) \textbackslash Delta t + \textbackslash mathbf\{F\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{thruster\}\} \textbackslash Delta t\$\$ \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q(t + \textbackslash Delta t) = \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q(t) - \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash partial H\_\{\textbackslash text\{rot\}\}\}\{\textbackslash partial \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}\} \textbackslash Delta t + \textbackslash boldsymbol\{\textbackslash tau\}\_\{\textbackslash text\{thruster\}\} \textbackslash Delta t\$\$


2. Update configuration using new momentum: \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{r\}(t + \textbackslash Delta t) = \textbackslash mathbf\{r\}(t) + \textbackslash frac\{\textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_r(t + \textbackslash Delta t)\}\{m\} \textbackslash Delta t\$\$ \$\$\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}(t + \textbackslash Delta t) = \textbackslash text\{Normalize\}\textbackslash left( \textbackslash mathbf\{q\}(t) + \textbackslash frac\{1\}\{4\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}(t)) \textbackslash mathbb\{I\}\textasciicircum \{-1\} E(\textbackslash mathbf\{q\}(t))\textasciicircum T \textbackslash mathbf\{p\}\_q(t + \textbackslash Delta t) \textbackslash Delta t \textbackslash right)\$\$


---


Next Steps We can map these equations into a symplectic update loop inside [quaternion\_fighter.html](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/frontend/quaternion\_fighter.html) to transition the simulator from simple angular rate inputs to a complete phase space dynamic model tracking coordinate-momentum trajectories.

\section{Mozilla Integration Plan}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Mozilla Vulkan/Wayland Integration Plan


This document outlines the architecture for integrating our native \textbf{Auncient} Wayland Vulkan technologies directly inside the Mozilla Firefox rendering pipeline.


1. Current Technologies to Port Our existing native rendering demos located in \texttt{tsfi2-deepseek} include: \textit{   \textbf{Wayland Terminal Shell (\texttt{test\_wayland\_terminal\_shell.c}):} Renders an interactive shell interface directly using raw pixel buffers. }   \textbf{Vulkan Teddy Bear Generator (\texttt{test\_vulkan\_teddy.c}):} Headless and windowed 3D mesh rendering using Vulkan pipelines. *   \textbf{Gauntlet / Lunar Lander / Space War:} Standard 2D vector game loops.


2. Mozilla Integration Architecture


Since the Firefox compositor (\textbf{WebRender}) is written in Rust and manages the GPU swapchain natively, we can integrate our custom Vulkan pipeline at two distinct levels:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[Firefox HTML/CSS Parser] --> B[WebRender Layout Tree] B --> C[Rust WebRender Compositor] D[Our Custom Vulkan Pipeline: Teddy, Terminal, Gauntlet] --> E[Shared Vulkan Device \& Command Buffer] C --> F\{Vulkan Blend Stage\} E --> F F --> G[Wayland WSI Swapchain] }``


Level 1: WebRender Custom Render Tasks (Texture Injection) We can inject our Vulkan drawing passes directly into WebRender's pipeline as external textures: 1. \textbf{Shared Vulkan Context:} Initialize our Vulkan resources (Teddy pipeline, Terminal buffers) using the same Vulkan Logical Device (\texttt{VkDevice}) as WebRender. 2. \textbf{External Image Rendering:} Render the 3D teddy bear or terminal grid to a Vulkan offscreen texture. 3. \textbf{Texture Mapping:} Pass the texture handle (\texttt{VkImage}) to WebRender via its External Image API (\texttt{wr\_notifier} and \texttt{ExternalImageHandler} in Rust/C++ glue). The browser then renders our content inside a standard HTML element container.


Level 2: Compositor Blending (Direct Window Overlay) If we want our terminal or gauntlet to overlay the entire browser window: 1. \textbf{Intercept Present Pass:} Hook into Firefox's Wayland Windowing System Integration (\texttt{nsWindowWayland.cpp}). 2. \textbf{Command Buffer Recording:} Record our Vulkan draw commands (drawing the terminal border or gauntlet UI) directly into the main render command buffer before presenting to the Wayland surface.


3. Implementation Steps 1. \textbf{Await Clone Completion:} Wait for the shallow clone of \texttt{gecko-dev} to finish. 2. \textbf{Locate GFX Integration Points:} Map out the exact C++/Rust files in Firefox handling Vulkan instance creation (\texttt{gfx/thebes/}, \texttt{gfx/webrender/}). 3. \textbf{Write Vulkan Compositor Hook:} Implement the Vulkan texture sharing and drawing calls within the layout loops.

\section{Tsfi2 Mozilla Efficiency Plan}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
TSFi2 Integration \& Mozilla Engine Reduction Plan


This plan details the implementation strategy for building TSFi2's high-efficiency C-based components directly into the Mozilla Firefox source tree, tracing optimization candidates, and replacing Rust-based modules.


1. Trace and Profiling Framework


To understand Gecko's runtime bottlenecks, we will use profiling tools on the newly compiled baseline binary:


``\texttt{mermaid flowchart TD A[Launch Firefox on Wayland-1] --> B[Profile with perf / GeckoProfiler] B --> C\{Identify Hotspots\} C -->IPC/VRAM CopyD[Inject TSFi2 Zero-Copy Shm] C -->Math/Coord TransformsE[Replace with ZMM/AVX-512 Loops] C -->WebRender RasterizationF[Map directly to C-based Vulkan renderer] }``


Hotspot Tracing Targets: 1. \textbf{GPU Texture Uploads (\texttt{gfx/layers/ipc/}):} Track the pipeline rendering YouTube video frames. We will trace the allocation path of \texttt{DMABufSurface} and verify if it matches our VRAM zero-copy models (\texttt{lau\_vram.c}). 2. \textbf{Layout Math Calculations (\texttt{gfx/2d/}):} Profile vector transformations, clipping, and coordinate mappings. These are candidates for acceleration using ZMM register instructions (\texttt{tsfi\_opt\_zmm.c}).


---


2. Porting C-Based TSFi2 Modules into Mozilla


To avoid using any Rust code inside TSFi2 and to ultimately remove Rust dependencies from the browser engine, we can integrate the following C modules directly into Mozilla's C++ entry points:


A. Core Math and Transforming \textit{ \textbf{Module:} \texttt{tsfi\_opt\_zmm.c} / \texttt{tsfi\_vec\_math.c} } \textbf{Gecko Integration Point:} \texttt{gfx/2d/Matrix.h} and transform helpers inside \texttt{gfx/skia/}. * \textbf{Method:} Replace standard CPU matrix multiply loops with AVX-512 ZMM SIMD operations, achieving massive layout computation efficiency.


B. Compositor Blending \& Wavelet Compression \textit{ \textbf{Module:} \texttt{tsfi\_fourier.c} / \texttt{tsfi\_math.c} } \textbf{Gecko Integration Point:} \texttt{RenderThread.cpp} / WebRender bindings. * \textbf{Method:} Route offscreen framebuffers directly through our \textbf{Auncient} Wavelet formulations to perform compressed compositing inside VRAM before swapchain presentation.


C. Direct WSI Client Hooking \textit{ \textbf{Module:} \texttt{vulkan\_init.c} / \texttt{vulkan\_main.c} } \textbf{Gecko Integration Point:} \texttt{widget/gtk/nsWindowWayland.cpp} * \textbf{Method:} Intercept the Wayland surface initialization, passing native file descriptors (DMA-BUF handles) directly to our Vulkan pipeline.


---


3. Road toward a Pure C Minimal Renderer


By using this integration to learn Gecko's layout tree serialization: 1. \textbf{Dumping Display Lists:} Hook into the display list builder (\texttt{nsDisplayList.cpp}) to dump serialized drawing commands. 2. \textbf{Bypassing WebRender:} Write a C-based backend in Mozilla that consumes these commands directly, feeding them into TSFi2's C-based font and shape rasterizers (\texttt{tsfi\_font\_engine.c} / \texttt{tsfi\_pbr.c}). 3. \textbf{Decoupling Rust:} Once the C backend replaces WebRender, we can turn off Rust compilation in \texttt{.mozconfig}, leaving a highly optimized, lean browser engine built upon the pure C foundation of TSFi2.

\section{Automation System Design}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
TSFi Zero-Latency In-Process Automation System Design


This document details the architectural specifications and step-by-step implementation plan for building a Selenium-like browser automation engine using the \textbf{Auncient} Wayland Vulkan compositor, the ZMM Yul execution hardware, and shared memory manifolds.


---


1. Core Architectural Pillars


```mermaid flowchart TD Gecko[Gecko Layout \& DOM Engine] -->nsDisplayList HooksManifold[g\_local\_manifold Registry] Manifold -->Registry LookupZMM[ZMM Yul Thunk Executor] ZMM -->Generate Wayland InputsInputBridge[vulkan\_input.c / wl\_seat] InputBridge -->In-Process Wayland DisplayGecko


Cockpit[Transcendental Cockpit Debugger] <-->/tsfi\_telem\_* SHMManifold ```


1.  \textbf{Direct Layout Introspection (Zero-Copy DOM):} \textit{   Hook into [nsDisplayList.cpp](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/layout/painting/nsDisplayList.cpp) inside the Gecko layout engine. }   During layout cycles, dump key element boundaries (node tags, text content, IDs, classes, and viewport coordinates \texttt{x, y, w, h}) directly into \texttt{g\_local\_manifold} managed by [lau\_registry.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/memory/tsfi2/src/lau\_registry.c). *   This bypasses the standard WebSockets/HTTP serialization overhead of WebDriver.


2.  \textbf{Yul Automation Scripts:} \textit{   Instead of JavaScript/Python drivers, the automation steps are written in \textbf{Yul} (EVM-compatible intermediate logic) and compiled to ZMM thunks. }   The ZMM executor ([tsfi\_zmm\_vm.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/memory/tsfi2/src/tsfi\_zmm\_vm.c)) runs the instructions natively on the CPU register bank, scanning elements and controlling flow.


3.  \textbf{Compositor Event Injection:} \textit{   The browser compositor thread in [tsfi\_browser.cpp](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/browser/app/tsfi/tsfi\_browser.cpp) hosts the \texttt{wayland-tsfi} compositor. }   The ZMM script invokes native thunks that call into the compositor's input processing queue in [vulkan\_input.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/plugins/vulkan/vulkan\_input.c). *   These simulated hardware actions (pointer movement, keyboard press) are delivered to the Gecko event loops over the internal Wayland socket.


---


2. Component Design \& APIs


A. Layout Registry Hook (C++) We define an dynamic mapping inside Gecko to register layout coordinates. In [nsDisplayList.cpp](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/layout/painting/nsDisplayList.cpp): ```cpp extern "C" \{ void tsfi\_register\_layout\_element(const char* element\_id, int x, int y, int w, int h); \}


// In nsDisplayList::Paint: if (mContent \&\& mContent->GetID()) \{ nsCString idStr; mContent->GetID()->ToCString(idStr); nsRect rect = GetBounds(aBuilder); tsfi\_register\_layout\_element(idStr.get(), rect.x, rect.y, rect.width, rect.height); \} ```


B. Yul Automation Script (\texttt{automation.yul}) An EVM-like script compiled to ZMM bytecode. It queries coordinate manifolds and generates input sequences: ```yul object "AutomationScript" \{ code \{ datacopy(0, dataoffset("runtime"), datasize("runtime")) return(0, datasize("runtime")) \} object "runtime" \{ code \{ // Step 1: Query location of button id = "movie\_player" let player\_addr := call\_reg\_lookup("movie\_player") if iszero(player\_addr) \{ revert(0, 0) \}


// Step 2: Retrieve coordinates (first 32-bytes contain X/Y pack) let coords := mload(player\_addr) let click\_x := sar(128, coords) let click\_y := and(0xffffffff, coords)


// Step 3: Trigger Pointer Move \& Click inject\_pointer\_move(click\_x, click\_y) inject\_pointer\_click() \} \} \} ```


C. Input Simulation Bridge (C) In [tsfi\_input.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/plugins/window\_src/tsfi\_input.c): ``\texttt{c void tsfi\_inject\_pointer\_event(uint32\_t button, uint32\_t state, double x, double y) \{ // Deliver Wayland seat pointer event directly to the active surface struct wl\_pointer *pointer = tsfi\_get\_active\_pointer(); if (pointer) \{ wl\_pointer\_send\_motion(pointer, tsfi\_get\_current\_time(), wl\_fixed\_from\_double(x), wl\_fixed\_from\_double(y)); wl\_pointer\_send\_button(pointer, tsfi\_get\_serial(), tsfi\_get\_current\_time(), button, state); wl\_pointer\_send\_frame(pointer); \} \} }``


---


3. Implementation Roadmap


Phase 1: Event Injection Bridge \textit{   Expose C hooks (\texttt{tsfi\_inject\_pointer\_event} and \texttt{tsfi\_inject\_keyboard\_event}) from the Wayland compositor plugin to \texttt{libtsfi2.so}. }   Link these symbols to the ZMM thunk registry ([tsfi\_zmm\_vm.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/memory/tsfi2/src/tsfi\_zmm\_vm.c)) so they can be triggered from Yul contracts.


Phase 2: Layout Manifold Integration \textit{   Implement \texttt{tsfi\_register\_layout\_element} inside \texttt{libtsfi2.so} to map Gecko coordinates to the local manifold registry. }   Hook [nsDisplayList.cpp](file:///home/mariarahel/src/mozilla/layout/painting/nsDisplayList.cpp) to populate the elements manifold on every frame paint.


Phase 3: Cockpit Control Interface \textit{   Extend the Transcendental Debugger (Cockpit) to load and register \texttt{automation.yul} scripts dynamically into the running browser's ZMM engine. }   Monitor telemetry ammeter and execution logs to trace script completion.

\section{Rooted Minimal C Renderer Plan}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
ROOTED: Minimal C-Based Vulkan Renderer Roadmap


This document outlines the architecture for stripping down the Mozilla/Gecko engine to retain only the essential HTML and JS parser layers, while rewriting the rendering, presentation, and input layers entirely in C for our custom Vulkan displays.


1. Architectural Overview


Instead of maintaining the massive Firefox layout/compositing pipelines (WebRender, Rust libraries, GTK/Wayland widgets, and hardware acceleration layers), we intercept the rendering commands at the layout boundary and route them to our custom C-based rasterizers.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[HTML/CSS Input] --> B[Gecko DOM Parser] C[JS Files] --> D[SpiderMonkey JS Engine] B \& D --> E[Layout: nsDisplayList Builder] E -->C Interface HookF[TSFi2 Serializer: nsDisplayList to C-Structs] F -->Zero-Copy Ring BufferG[ROOTED C-Based Vulkan Renderer] G -->Direct WSI PresentationH[Auncient Vulkan Framebuffer] }``


---


2. Core Integration Points


A. Extracting the Display List (C++ to C Boundary) Instead of feeding WebRender, we hook into \texttt{nsDisplayList.cpp} (specifically during \texttt{nsDisplayList::PaintRoot}). - We walk the display tree and serialize each drawing primitive (text runs, rectangles, images, boundaries) into a simplified C-struct format: ``\texttt{c typedef struct \{ uint8\_t type;         // TEXT, RECT, IMAGE, CLIP\_PUSH, CLIP\_POP float x, y, w, h;     // Position \& bounds uint32\_t color;       // HSL / RGBA color data (4:4:4 color support) void* resource;       // Backing texture/font pointer \} RootedDrawItem; }`` - This list is copied directly to a shared memory ring buffer managed by the \textbf{Auncient} compositor.


B. C-Based Rasterization (Bypassing WebRender \& Rust) The serialized \texttt{RootedDrawItem} stream is consumed by our optimized C engines: 1. \textbf{Text Rendering:} Handled by \texttt{tsfi\_font\_engine.c} using subpixel anti-aliasing and AVX-512 acceleration. 2. \textbf{Vector/Shape Drawing:} Rendered via \texttt{tsfi\_pbr.c} and coordinate transformation helpers (\texttt{tsfi\_opt\_zmm.c}). 3. \textbf{Image \& Lensing Composition:} Processed by our \textbf{Auncient} Fourier and Wavelet filters in \texttt{tsfi\_fourier.c} for top plane 77 overlay lensing.


C. Input Routing (Direct Access Layer) Instead of routing events through GTK, Wayland client libraries, and the Firefox Widget loop, we intercept raw inputs from our Vulkan window and feed them directly to Gecko's event queue: - Device file descriptors are read inside the compositor loop. - Inputs are injected via \texttt{nsIWidget::DispatchEvent} bypassing the GTK library layer.


---


3. Step-by-Step Implementation Plan


Step 1: Serialize Display Lists Modify \texttt{layout/painting/nsDisplayList.cpp} to dump drawing primitives to stdout/logs, verifying layout coordinates. Write a C-compatible serialization bridge.


Step 2: Inject the C Vulkan Presentation Layer Route the serialized items to \texttt{libtsfi2.so}'s drawing queue. Bypass the GTK window loop (\texttt{nsWindowWayland.cpp}) by initializing the Vulkan surface directly from our compositor thread.


Step 3: Turn off WebRender \& Rust Compilation Once the C rasterizer handles the serialized display list, disable WebRender and the Rust-dependent subsystems in \texttt{.mozconfig} using: ``\texttt{bash ac\_add\_options --disable-webrender ac\_add\_options --disable-rust }`` This isolates the browser to a lean HTML/CSS parser and SpiderMonkey JS compiler, running entirely on our C-based Vulkan backend.

\section{Transcendent Control Framework}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Transcendent Control Framework Architecture


The \textbf{Transcendent Control Framework} is a unified execution architecture designed to interface low-overhead hardware interfaces, virtualized display compositors, and on-chain state transitions. It facilitates CPU input injection straight to the query fields and filters of nested sub-sessions.


```mermaid graph TD UserInterface["Dashboard SVG Overlay (Browser-in-Browser)"] -->Event: click / move / scrollControlEndpoint["HTTP Server POST /control"] ControlEndpoint -->Encode as hex transactionWinchesterMQ["WinchesterMQ Yul Contract (Anvil EVM)"] WinchesterMQ -->LogPut / Fast Log EventBrowserController["Rooted Browser Controller (Node.js/Puppeteer)"] BrowserController -->Input InjectionChromeBrowser["System Google Chrome (Headless)"] ChromeBrowser -->Screenshot Frame CaptureImageFrame["latest\_frame.jpg"] ImageFrame -->Reload Frame LoopUserInterface


subgraph Presentation Pipeline BrowserController -->STDIN JPEG StreamVulkanPresenter["Vulkan / Wayland Presenter (C executable)"] VulkanPresenter -->Decode JPEG to p72 planeVulkanCompositor["Vulkan Queue Present (tsfi\_vulkan\_cells)"] VulkanCompositor -->Alpha blend to scanout\_bufferWaylandCompositor["Wayland Surface Attach / Commit"] end ```


---


1. Yul On-Chain Logic The underlying communication backbone relies on contract components written in \textbf{Yul} (strict assembly) to bypass standard Solidity compiler overhead. Yul allows precise memory offsets and zero-overhead execution for event emission.


\textit{ \textbf{Target Selector (\texttt{0xccb077a0})}: Fast-path transactions write directly to the hardware-mapped data port. } \textbf{Low Gas Dispatches}: By avoiding high-level EVM abstractions, input routing transactions are executed with minimal gas, bypassing typical SCSI handshakes and allowing high-frequency input updates (up to 60 events/second).


---


2. WinchesterMQ (MQ) Messaging Queue WinchesterMQ acts as the on-chain message broker. Input commands (e.g., mouse movement coordinates, keycodes, clicks, and page scrolls) are dispatched as transaction data payloads targeting the WinchesterMQ deployment address:


\textit{ \textbf{Handshake Mode}: Larger command buffers are stored in contract storage slots starting at offset \texttt{0x1000 + blockId} and emitted via \texttt{LogPut} events. } \textbf{Fast Log Mode}: Emits events using a dedicated log topic hash (\texttt{0xe1dae1da...}) containing the exact ASCII representations of the input command in the transaction body. * \textbf{Listener Module}: The \texttt{rooted\_browser\_controller.js} listens to logs matching these topics, extracts the transaction inputs, and dynamically routes them to the corresponding interactive sub-sessions.


---


3. Browser-in-Browser (Picture-in-Picture) Routing To achieve seamless nesting without layout conflicts, the dashboard uses a \textbf{Browser-in-Browser (BiB)} overlay mechanism:


\textit{ \textbf{Frame Capture}: Headless Puppeteer browser sub-sessions capture screenshot frames at 75\% JPEG quality. } \textbf{Layout Streaming}: The frames are written to a shared directory (\texttt{frontend/latest\_frame.jpg}) and reloaded dynamically inside the SVG viewport of the parent dashboard page. * \textbf{SVG Interactive Overlay}: An SVG overlay intercepts mouse clicks and movements on the client interface and maps local coordinate boxes to Puppeteer viewport coordinates. The mapped events are forwarded back as WinchesterMQ messages.


---


4. Vulkan Virtual Planes For low-level hardware rendering, the presentation pipeline uses \textbf{Auncient} DRM/ZMM virtual planes:


\textit{ \textbf{Virtual Plane Allocation}: Registers a virtual display plane (ID \texttt{72}) using \texttt{tsfi\_drmModeAddPlane}. } \textbf{JPEG Decoder Routing}: The STDIN-piped screenshots are decoded into the raw virtual plane buffer \texttt{p72} (\texttt{tsfi\_drmModeGetVirtualPlaneBuffer(72)}). * \textbf{Mock Presentation}: Calling \texttt{vkQueuePresentKHR} initiates a mock rendering queue. The Vulkan cells compositor performs alpha blending of all registered active planes onto the final \texttt{g\_scanout\_buffer} background.


---


5. Wayland Client Interface The compositor windowing uses Wayland protocols to remain lightweight and platform-independent:


\textit{ \textbf{Configure Resizing}: The presenter handles \texttt{xdg\_toplevel} configure events. When the compositor triggers a resize, the presenter dynamically destroys and reconstructs the shared memory (\texttt{wl\_shm\_pool}) buffer (\texttt{wl\_buffer}) to match the new dimensions. } \textbf{Stability Safeguard}: Re-creation only occurs if the configure dimensions differ from the current layout (\texttt{width != g\_w height != g\_h}). This prevents compositor crashes due to race conditions during configure acknowledge (\texttt{xdg\_surface.ack\_configure}) sequences. \textit{ \textbf{Buffer Allocation Limits}: The shared memory pool is dynamically sized up to \texttt{3840 } 2160 * 4} bytes, ensuring safe buffer allocation on displays up to 4K.


\vspace{0.2in}\hrule\vspace{0.2in}
\section{Resize Verification}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Wayland Compositor Window Resizing Verification


The window resize behavior has been stabilized, and a video capture of the compositor output has been recorded to verify visual transitions.


🎥 Recorded Compositor Output Below is the video capture showing the presenter window resizing and viewport adaptation transitions on the Xwayland display:


---


🛠️ Analysis \& Mitigations Implemented


1. Wayland Buffer ID Collision Race (Resolved) \textit{ \textbf{Problem}: Previously, when a configure resize event was received, the presenter sent a \texttt{wl\_buffer.destroy} call on the buffer ID (\texttt{bid\_val}) and immediately issued a \texttt{wl\_shm\_pool.create\_buffer} call reusing the exact same ID. Under fast resizing operations, the compositor did not finish processing the async destruction before the client created the new buffer with the same ID, causing a fatal Wayland display protocol error. } \textbf{Mitigation}: The code now assigns a fresh, incremental object ID (\texttt{bid\_val = next\_id++}) for every newly created buffer. This allows the compositor to safely clean up the old buffer ID at its own pace without blocking or crashing the client.


2. High-Resolution Scaling Buffer Limits (Resolved) \textit{ \textbf{Problem}: The shared memory pool was originally constrained to \texttt{1920 } 1080 \textit{ 4} bytes. Dragging or maximizing the presenter window on screens larger than 1080p exceeded the check bounds and caused resizing requests to freeze or stutter. } \textbf{Mitigation}: Increased the maximum supported dimensions to \texttt{3840 * 2160} (4K UHD) to support safe buffer allocation limits when maximizing or dragging windows on multi-monitor or high-DPI displays.

\section{Stabilization Runbook}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 20, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Auncient Video Streaming Stabilization \& Diagnostics Runbook


This runbook documents the engineering solutions implemented to resolve the 44-second video streaming crash, setup advanced diagnostics, and leverage the decoupled architecture of the Transcendent Control Framework.


---


1. Resource Exhaustion Crash Resolution (\texttt{/dev/shm})


The Issue Headless Google Chrome crashed consistently at approximately 44 seconds of video playback, logging \texttt{Page crashed!} and network level \texttt{net::ERR\_INSUFFICIENT\_RESOURCES} errors.


Cause The browser was launched with the \texttt{--disable-dev-shm-usage} flag. Under high-frequency screencasting (which streams 20+ JPEG frames per second to the user interface and Vulkan presenter), this flag forced Chrome to write temporary image data and tab memory structures directly to the \texttt{/tmp} disk directory. The excessive disk write operations and inode usage exhausted system resource descriptors under heavy screen capture loads, crashing the browser tab.


The Fix We removed \texttt{--disable-dev-shm-usage} from the Puppeteer launch parameters in [rooted\_browser\_controller.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/rooted\_browser\_controller.js). Chrome now uses the host's \texttt{/dev/shm} shared memory segment (RAM), eliminating disk I/O bottlenecks and ensuring infinite, uninterrupted video playback.


---


2. Advanced Error Diagnostics Framework


To quickly isolate future playback disruptions (such as geoblocking, ad-blocker interference, or network timeouts), we introduced a multi-tier diagnostics listener in [rooted\_browser\_controller.js](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/scripts/rooted\_browser\_controller.js).


A. Network Request Failure Tracking We hook into Puppeteer's \texttt{requestfailed} event to filter and log failures of critical resources (such as \texttt{media}, \texttt{xhr}, or \texttt{fetch} types): ``\texttt{javascript page.on('requestfailed', request => \{ const failure = request.failure(); const errorText = failure ? failure.errorText : 'unknown'; const type = request.resourceType(); if (type === 'media' type === 'xhr' type === 'fetch' errorText.includes('ERR\_')) \{ console.error(}[PUPPETEER REQUEST FAILED] Type: \$\{type\} URL: \$\{request.url()\} Error: \$\{errorText\}\texttt{); \} \}); }``


B. HTML5 Video Element Inspection The monitor query block retrieves low-level error attributes directly from the \texttt{<video>} element's DOM instance: \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{video.error.code}}: Indicates the error class (1 = Aborted, 2 = Network, 3 = Decode, 4 = Source Not Supported). } \textbf{\texttt{video.error.message}}: Provides the engine-level description of the media error.


C. YouTube PlayerState \& Subtext Diagnostics \textit{ We query \texttt{getPlayerState()} from the \texttt{.html5-video-player} DOM container (e.g. \texttt{-1} = unstarted, \texttt{1} = playing, \texttt{3} = buffering, etc.). } We capture the text content of the primary error message (\texttt{.ytp-error-message-text}) and subtext details (\texttt{.ytp-error-message-subtext}) from the player interface.


If any of these error markers are detected, a consolidated log entry is written: ``\texttt{ [VIDEO ERROR DETECTED] ErrorScreen: true, ErrorText: "An error occurred. Please try again later.", ErrorSubtext: "Playback ID: ...", VideoError: \{"code":3,"message":"..."\}, PlayerState: 3 }``


---


3. Decoupled Playback Architecture


The system utilizes an asynchronous design where the control pipeline is fully independent of the web dashboard.


```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant UI as Master Console (Dashboard) participant Back as Python HTTP Server participant Controller as Browser Controller (Node/Puppeteer) participant Chrome as Headless Chrome


Note over Controller, Chrome: Runs persistently in background Chrome->>Controller: Captures screenshot frames (JPEG) Controller->>Back: Saves latest\_frame.jpg to filesystem UI->>Back: Fetches latest\_frame.jpg repeatedly (polling) Note over UI: User reloads dashboard browser tab UI->>UI: Closes connection \& reloads Note over Controller, Chrome: Uninterrupted playback continues UI->>Back: Reconnects \& resumes reading latest\_frame.jpg ```


Key Architectural Benefits 1. \textbf{Console Resilience:} The master console can be reloaded, closed, or crash without impacting active streaming state, video position, or browser state. 2. \textbf{State Recovery:} When the dashboard reconnects, it receives the latest screenshot file and auto-subscribes to status updates emitted via WinchesterMQ logs.

\section{Vulkan Lore Editor Architecture}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 21, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Vulkan Lore Editor Architecture


This document outlines the design and integration model to make the 400+ markdown and lore documentation files in the \texttt{lore/} directory editable and annotateable directly within the headed Vulkan UI workspace.


1. Architectural Concept


Since the \textbf{Auncient Vulkan UI} (\texttt{rooted\_frame\_presenter}) operates as a zero-copy frame compositor streaming viewport buffers from a headless Chrome instance, any editor interface we build in standard HTML/JS is immediately projected onto the headed Vulkan surface. User inputs (clicks, selections, key entries) captured by the Wayland presenter window are automatically routed back to Chrome via the input bridge.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[Vulkan Presenter Window] -- 1. Captures Input Event --> B[Node Controller Input Router] B -- 2. Dispatches Event via CDP --> C[Headless Chrome Instance] C -- 3. Runs Editor UI \& Renders Frame --> D[Shared Memory Bridge] D -- 4. Zero-Copy Blit --> A C -- 5. REST API: GET/POST --> E[Local Node/Python Server] E -- 6. File Operations --> F[Lore Directory] }``


---


2. Interface Design \& Premium Aesthetics


The editor will adopt the curated \textbf{Auncient Vaesen} style system: \textit{ \textbf{Typography}: }Cinzel\textit{ for headers, }Outfit\textit{ for interface widgets and text editors. } \textbf{Palette}: Dark Mode base (\texttt{\#0c0c0e}), vintage gold accents (\texttt{\#d4af37}), and crimson highlight markers (\texttt{\#801818}). \textit{ \textbf{Layout}: Two-column layout: } \textbf{Left Side}: Scrollable sidebar showing the listing of \texttt{lore/} files, sorted by date or name. \textit{ \textbf{Center Pane}: Rich markdown textarea with live preview rendering. } \textbf{Right Side}: Collapsible annotations drawer. Selecting text in the center pane allows linking comments and highlights.


---


3. Data Integration \& API Routes


To support loading and saving files, the local REST server (\texttt{scripts/server.js} or \texttt{dashboard\_server.py}) will be extended with three key API routes:


\texttt{GET /api/lore/list} Scans the \texttt{lore/} folder and returns metadata (filename, size, modification date, Git status, reviewed status, LOU score, and analysis reasons). ``\texttt{json [ \{ "name": "DYSNOMIA\_VM\_LORE.md", "sizeBytes": 5180, "modified": 1782069513, "gitStatus": null, "reviewed": false, "louScore": 85, "louReasons": ["Undefined terms: DYSNOMIA, VM"] \} ] }``


\texttt{GET /api/lore/content} Reads and returns the raw file content and parsed annotations. * \textbf{Query Parameter}: \texttt{?file=DYSNOMIA\_VM\_LORE.md}


\texttt{POST /api/lore/save} Writes the edited text and annotations back to storage. * \textbf{Payload}: ``\texttt{json \{ "file": "DYSNOMIA\_VM\_LORE.md", "content": "\# New Markdown Content...", "annotations": [ \{ "range": [120, 145], "text": "Preserve Auncient spelling of Wavelets.", "author": "Compositor Node" \} ] \} }``


---


4. Annotation Persistence


To ensure annotations persist without corrupting standard markdown parsing, they will be embedded at the end of the markdown files using standard HTML metadata comments:


```markdown \# Dysnomia VM Lore This file contains the historical records of the Auncient VM compiler design.


<!-- AUNCIENT\_ANNOTATIONS\_START [ \{ "range": [45, 62], "comment": "Ensure compiler limits align with EVM transient specs.", "timestamp": 1782069600 \} ] AUNCIENT\_ANNOTATIONS\_END --> ```


This makes annotations fully self-contained in the Markdown files themselves, preserving portability.


---


5. Multi-Phase Lack of Understanding (LOU) Analysis


To allow the user to guide the review process, the workspace supports a \textbf{Gaps Sort Mode} powered by a multi-phase document analyzer:


1. \textbf{Phase 1 (Structural \& Quantitative Analysis):} Extracts raw text, computes word and sentence counts, and flags documents with sparse content (<150 words) or missing markdown headers. 2. \textbf{Phase 2 (Lexical Jargon Extraction):} Scans the text for capitalized words (potential concepts), cross-references them against existing document names and a common terms dictionary, and marks unknown terms as undefined. 3. \textbf{Phase 3 (Graph Linkage):} Maps reference links between lore documents. Documents that are completely isolated (referencing no other defined concepts) or have extremely sparse linkages are penalized. 4. \textbf{Phase 4 (Explicit Draft \& Annotation Audit):} Searches for unresolved question marks (\texttt{?}) in annotations and scans for active placeholders (\texttt{TODO}, \texttt{FIXME}, \texttt{TBD}, \texttt{PLACEHOLDER}, \texttt{DRAFT}).


The LOU weights are updated in real-time upon saving a document and can be sorted descending in the sidebar using the \textbf{Sort: Gaps} button.


---


6. Wayland Clipboard Synchronization


Because the editor runs in a headless browser, standard text selections do not automatically sync with the Wayland host session clipboard. We bridge this gap via two integrated pathways:


1. \textbf{DOM Interception:} A script is injected via \texttt{page.evaluateOnNewDocument()} that listens to the \texttt{copy} event. If the event is fired, it captures either the window's text selection or the active textarea selection boundary content (\texttt{selectionStart} and \texttt{selectionEnd}). 2. \textbf{Host Injection:} The extracted text is passed to the host controller via \texttt{syncHostClipboard()}. The controller pipes a command frame (\texttt{0x80000000} payload) down to the \texttt{rooted\_frame\_presenter} compositor stdin, which triggers local loopback scripts to write directly to the Wayland seat selection buffers.

\vspace{0.1in}
Magic Disk 64 Issue 12/87 (December 1987) — Technical \& Historical Review


Published in December 1987, the inaugural issue of the German diskmag \textbf{Magic Disk 64} introduces automated loader routines, disk diagnostic tools, and custom sprite graphics animations to preserve the \textbf{Auncient} C64 software architecture.


---


1. Program Listings Index


The following programs were featured in the "Program Listings" section of the first floppy disk issue:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Program Title & Target System & Author & Purpose / Architecture \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\textbf{Deadly Rain} & C64 & - & An action game where the player shoots descending rain drops before they flood the screen. \\ \hline
\textbf{Runaway} & C64 & - & A fast-paced arcade game requiring high-speed navigation. \\ \hline
\textbf{Sprite Editor} & C64 & - & A utility for drawing, loading, and animating VIC-II sprites directly in RAM memory. \\ \hline
\textbf{Protector} & C64 & - & A security utility to encrypt and password-protect BASIC programs from cracking. \\ \hline
\textbf{Interrupt Module 1.0} & C64 & - & A machine-language utility adding command extensions utilizing system interrupt vectors. \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
---


2. Deep Dive: Sprite Editor \& Protector


\textit{   \textbf{Sprite Editor}: Allows pixel editing of 24x21 monochromatic or multi-color VIC-II sprites, storing them in memory pages and facilitating real-time animations. }   \textbf{Protector BASIC Security}: Scrambles BASIC pointers (e.g., \texttt{TXTTAB} at \texttt{\$2B-\$2C} or \texttt{VARTAB} at \texttt{\$2D-\$2E}), locking standard listing functions from cracker interception.


---


3. Emulation Integration Path


To integrate these utilities into our virtual environment: 1.  \textbf{Sprite Editor}: Mapped to our virtual [sally\_larsen\_c64.html](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/frontend/sally\_larsen\_c64.html) editor to import and preview custom sprite pages. 2.  \textbf{Protector}: Connected to our [protecto.html](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/frontend/protecto.html) system console to simulate bank-swapped BASIC program locks.

---


1. Program Structure and Layout


As a specialized \textbf{4k diskmag}, \textit{Wilby \#1} does not contain multiple separate software programs, but is rather a single self-contained MS-DOS executable (\texttt{.EXE} or \texttt{.COM}) that fits entirely within 4096 bytes of memory storage:


\begin{table}[H]
\centering

\hline
Component & Target System & Author & Purpose / Architecture \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline

2. Deep Dive: The 4k Diskmag Architecture


\textit{   \textbf{Size Constraint Execution}: Spock utilized optimized assembly language routines to pack text compression algorithms and custom font display logic directly within the 4-kilobyte execution boundary. }   \textbf{Menu and Navigation}: Utilizes low-level keyboard input vectors (similar to BIOS interrupt \texttt{INT 16h} or direct port polling) to navigate pages without requiring high-level OS window managers.


---


3. Emulation Integration Path


To integrate these utilities into our virtual environment: 1.  \textbf{Compact Executable Loading}: Mapped to our low-level DOS emulators to verify how memory limits are handled under constrained resource allocation. 2.  \textbf{BIOS Hooking}: Interfaced with our custom interrupt handlers inside [interrupt\_standards.md](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/frontend/interrupt\_standards.md) to log keyboard scancodes directly.

\section{Hugi 4D Graphics Integration}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 21, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Hugi 4D Graphics Integration — Technical Blueprint


This document details how classical demoscene algorithms from \textbf{Hugi Diskmag} (such as the Coding Section and \textit{Hugi SE \#01}) are integrated into our \textbf{Auncient} 4D tesseract rendering engine inside \texttt{teddy\_bear\_tournament\_3d.html}.


---


1. 6-Axis 4D Rotations


In 3D graphics, rotations occur across three coordinate planes (XY, XZ, YZ). In 4-dimensional space, rotations generalize to six orthogonal planes: \textit{   \textbf{3D Planes}: XY, XZ, YZ }   \textbf{4D Planes}: XW, YW, ZW


Each rotation step executes a standard 2D rotation matrix on the selected coordinate pair while preserving the remaining axes:


``\texttt{javascript // Rotate in the XW plane let xNew = x \textit{ cos(aXW) - w } sin(aXW); let wNew = x \textit{ sin(aXW) + w } cos(aXW); x = xNew; w = wNew; }``


---


2. 4D-to-3D Hyper-Perspective Projection


To render a 4D tesseract onto a 2D viewport, the geometry must first project from 4D space down to 3D space, and then from 3D to 2D.


The 4D-to-3D projection maps the \$w\$ coordinate using a perspective division factor:


\$\$x\_\{3d\} = \textbackslash frac\{x\_\{4d\}\}\{d - \textbackslash frac\{w\}\{r\}\}\$\$ \$\$y\_\{3d\} = \textbackslash frac\{y\_\{4d\}\}\{d - \textbackslash frac\{w\}\{r\}\}\$\$ \$\$z\_\{3d\} = \textbackslash frac\{z\_\{4d\}\}\{d - \textbackslash frac\{w\}\{r\}\}\$\$


Where: \textit{   \$d\$ is the hyper-camera focal distance (e.g., \$2.3\$). }   \$w\$ is the rotated 4D depth value. *   \$r\$ is the local joint radius scale.


This is implemented directly inside our joint-drawing pipeline: ``\texttt{javascript let factor = 1 / (2.3 - rotated.w / (radius \textit{ 0.65 + 0.01)); let p3dLocal = \{ x: rotated.x } factor, y: rotated.y \textit{ factor, z: rotated.z } factor \}; }``


---


3. Depth Sorting \& Painter's Algorithm


Hugi's rasterization guides recommend sorting polygon faces from back-to-front (descending depth) to ensure proper occlusion sorting: 1.  Calculate the 3D projected coordinates for all 16 vertices. 2.  Aggregate the 24 cyclic faces. 3.  Compute the average 3D depth for each face: \$\$Depth\_\{avg\} = \textbackslash frac\{p\_\{1\}.depth + p\_\{2\}.depth + p\_\{3\}.depth + p\_\{4\}.depth\}\{4\}\$\$ 4.  Sort descending and draw faces using alpha-blended strokes and fills: ``\texttt{javascript validFaces.sort((a, b) => b.depth - a.depth); }``

2. Deep Dive: Memory "Combat" \& State "Damage"


In the MS-DOS era, rivalry between diskmag groups (specifically \textit{Scenial} and \textit{Imphobia}) led to low-level software conflicts in system RAM:


\textit{   \textbf{TSR Contamination (State Damage)}: Competing diskmags frequently left Terminate-and-Stay-Resident (TSR) routines or altered interrupt vectors (such as standard mouse or keyboard interrupts) in memory. This contaminated system state and caused subsequent executables to crash upon loading. }   \textbf{Active Saber Code (Combat)}: Executables contained routines to search for specific memory offsets, file signatures, or interrupt handlers associated with rivals, actively disabling execution or corrupting memory blocks to sabotage competitor demos.


---


3. Emulation Integration Path


To adapt these concepts into our virtual system: 1.  \textbf{Memory State Isolation}: The TSR sabotage routines are referenced when testing sandbox boundaries in the Dysnomia VM, ensuring process execution does not cause system state damage. 2.  \textbf{Sabotage Detection}: Emulated process checks inspect registers for signature hooks, preventing memory combat scenarios in local sockets.


---


4. Synthesizer Context: Audio Sabotage \& Register Contamination


When translated to virtual audio synthesis, memory combat and state damage represent deliberate or collision-based disruption of shared synthesizer hardware states:


\textit{   \textbf{Shared Register Overwrites}: In virtual systems (such as \texttt{yulStorage[97]} representing the speaker output latch in [teddy\_bear\_tournament\_3d.html](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/teddy\_bear\_tournament\_3d.html\#L1291)), competing processes can write competing values to the same register index. This causes volume gating dropouts, voice theft, or instant silencing of the channel. }   \textbf{Timer Interrupt \& Frequency Sabotage}: Sabotaging the Programmable Interval Timer (PIT) frequency dividers alters the duty cycle of the generated square waves, translating to pitch distortion, continuous DC offset noise, or complete audio buffer lockups. *   \textbf{ADSR Envelope Corruption}: Forcing decay or release parameters in shared memory segments to extreme limits renders synthesizer outputs either instantaneously muted or stuck in infinite, non-decaying loops.


---


5. Assembly-Level Sound Samples for Damage Modeling


Beyond standard synthesizer envelope configurations, low-level assembly algorithms from diskmags like \textit{Scenial} illustrate how to model physical impact and damage feedback directly through procedural sample generation in Yul:


\textit{   \textbf{Procedural Waveform Synthesis}: Inside [musicMaker.yul](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/solidity/bin/musicMaker.yul\#L242-L260), the smart contract defines lightweight sound clips (such as \texttt{clipId} 1 for impact "Hits" and \texttt{clipId} 3 for phonetic "Ouch!" speech indicators) using pseudo-random seeds and mathematical decay loops instead of loading heavy audio assets. }   \textbf{Bypassing Engine Limits}: Writing 6-bit registers (port \texttt{\$61}/PIT slot 97) sequentially allows the emulator to run high-speed audio pipelines within memory-constrained environments, ensuring that damage indicators are generated in real-time. *   \textbf{Auncient Sound Mapping}: This mirrors PIT/Sound Blaster sample buffer writing techniques from DOS-era games, providing authentic audio spikes upon registering game hits or state changes.

\section{Tessarant Combat Physics}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 21, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Auncient Tessarant Combat Physics and Collision Specification


This document details the mechanics, physics equations, and low-level \textbf{Auncient} WinchesterMQ event routing that govern how 4D tessarant shapes deform, collide, and take damage within the 3D Arena.


---


1. Mathematical Foundation of Tessarant Physics


A tessarant is represented as a 4D hyper-volume defined by 16 vertices in \$\textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 4\$:


\$\$V = \textbackslash left\textbackslash \{ (x, y, z, w) \textbackslash mid x, y, z, w \textbackslash in \textbackslash \{-1, 1\textbackslash \} \textbackslash right\textbackslash \}\$\$


4D Rotational Kinematics Movement and deformation are driven by six independent planes of rotation (\$XY, XZ, XW, YZ, YW, ZW\$). Under nominal conditions, rotation angles evolve smoothly over time \$t\$:


\$\$\textbackslash theta\_\{ij\}(t) = \textbackslash omega\_\{ij\} \textbackslash cdot t + \textbackslash phi\_\{ij\}\$\$


Where: \textit{ \$\textbackslash omega\_\{ij\}\$ is the angular velocity in the \$IJ\$ plane. } \$\textbackslash phi\_\{ij\}\$ is the phase offset mapped from the \textbf{Auncient} DNA sequence.


Perspective Projection Pipeline The 4D coordinates project to the 3D viewport using a dual-perspective camera model: 1. \textbf{4D to 3D Hyper-Projection}: \$\$x' = \textbackslash frac\{x\}\{d - w\}, \textbackslash quad y' = \textbackslash frac\{y\}\{d - w\}, \textbackslash quad z' = \textbackslash frac\{z\}\{d - w\}\$\$ Where \$d\$ is the hyper-perspective focal distance register (stored in \texttt{yulStorage[104]}). 2. \textbf{3D to 2D Screen Projection}: \$\$X\_\{scr\} = X\_\{off\} + \textbackslash frac\{x' \textbackslash cdot f\}\{z'\}, \textbackslash quad Y\_\{scr\} = Y\_\{off\} + \textbackslash frac\{y' \textbackslash cdot f\}\{z'\}\$\$


---


2. WinchesterMQ Damage Mapping \& Joint Sabotage


Tessarant deformation is controlled dynamically by the low-level \textbf{Auncient} WinchesterMQ bus registers. Each physical joint (Head, Ears, Paws, Feet) maps to a dedicated 10-byte segment in the emulated Yul memory map:


\$\$\textbackslash text\{Base Register Offset\} = \textbackslash text\{JointIndex\} \textbackslash times 10\$\$


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
Register Address & Function & Nominal Value & Combat Sabotage Value \\ \hline\hline
:--- & :--- & :--- & :--- \\ \hline
\texttt{103 + Offset} & Clock Divisor (Damping) & \texttt{1000} & \texttt{160} (Hyper-spin) \\ \hline
\texttt{104 + Offset} & Focal Distance (\$d\$) & \texttt{2300} & \texttt{1350} (Warp/Deflate) \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Damage Propagation Flow When a combat hit is registered in the arena: 1. A collision payload is latched to SCSI Data Register \texttt{yulStorage[101]}. 2. The state machine transitions to Phase \texttt{1} (REQ), executing the loopback handshake. 3. The targeted joint offset is mutated instantly, forcing the corresponding tessarant to spin wildly and collapse inward. 4. The register values gradually recover back to nominal state via an envelope decay function, simulating material elasticity.


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A[Combat Strike Event] --> B[Latch SCSI Keycode to Port 101] B --> C[Set SCSI Phase to REQ] C --> D[SCSI Loopback Acknowledge ACK] D --> E[Sabotage targeted Joint Registers] E --> F[Hyper-spin \& Warp Tessarant Projection] F --> G[Elastic Recovery Envelope decay] G --> H[Return to Nominal Values] }``


---


3. Collision Resolution in \$\textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 4\$


Collisions are not merely calculated in 3D screen space; they are verified at the 4D hyper-frustum boundaries.


Hyper-Sphere Bounding Volumes Every joint is enveloped in a 4D hyper-sphere defined by:


\$\$(x - x\_c)\textasciicircum 2 + (y - y\_c)\textasciicircum 2 + (z - z\_c)\textasciicircum 2 + (w - w\_c)\textasciicircum 2 \textbackslash le R\textasciicircum 2\$\$


Collision Detection Algorithm 1. Retrieve the position vectors \$P\_1, P\_2 \textbackslash in \textbackslash mathbb\{R\}\textasciicircum 4\$ of two interacting joints. 2. Calculate the 4D Euclidean distance: \$\$D\_\{4D\} = \textbackslash sqrt\{\textbackslash sum\_\{i \textbackslash in \textbackslash \{x,y,z,w\textbackslash \}\} (P\_\{1,i\} - P\_\{2,i\})\textasciicircum 2\}\$\$ 3. If \$D\_\{4D\} < R\_1 + R\_2\$, a collision is triggered. 4. The overlap magnitude \$\textbackslash Delta = (R\_1 + R\_2) - D\_\{4D\}\$ is written back into the ZMM register bank to calculate kinetic energy transfer and health damage.


---


4. Multi-Tier LOD Integration


To maintain 60 FPS performance during heavy physics calculations, the engine dynamically adjusts simulation complexity:


> [!NOTE] > \textbf{LOD 2 (Far Viewport Depth)}: Flat 2D skeleton rendering. Bypasses 4D rotation math, shadows, and physics entirely. > > \textbf{LOD 1 (Medium Viewport Depth)}: Simplified 3D cube model (8 vertices, 6 faces) with 3D rotational kinematics. > > \textbf{LOD 0 (Near Viewport Depth)}: Full 4D hypercube calculation (16 vertices, 24 cyclic faces) using 6-axis rotation, perspective projection, and joint warping.

\section{Zil Onchain Parser Design}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 21, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
On-Chain ZIL Parser Specification


To fully support ZIL-like parser mechanics on-chain, we will implement a command parser in Yul that reads the player's text command, parses it against the game's dictionary, and routes it to object interactions.


---


1. ZIL Command Parsing Flow


``` User Input: "take gold"


v Tokenization (Split by space/punctuation)


v Dictionary Lookup (Check if word is in Dictionary Table)


v Grammar Matching (Resolve Verb + Object)


v Object Interaction (Check properties, attributes, and ERC-20 balances) ```


---


2. Byte-Level Dictionary Parsing in Yul


To resolve input words: 1.  \textbf{Word Splitting}: The parser walks the input string in memory, splitting at space \texttt{0x20} and punctuation characters. 2.  \textbf{Z-Encoding}: For each parsed word, we compress it into the 5-bit ZSCII format (representing up to 6 characters packed into 4 bytes) so it can be compared directly to the dictionary entries. 3.  \textbf{Dictionary Lookup}: We binary search the Dictionary table base pointer for the matching Z-encoded word. 4.  \textbf{Grammar Matching}: \textit{   If a Verb is matched, we identify the syntax. }   If a Noun is matched, we search the surrounding objects in the room to find the corresponding Object ID.


---


3. ERC-20 Integration Route


Once a Verb and Noun are successfully matched: \textit{   Action: \texttt{take coin} (where \texttt{coin} is Object 50 bound to an ERC-20 contract). }   The parser triggers the transaction wrapper: \textit{   Verifies that the object has the \texttt{TAKEABLE} attribute. }   Verifies/transfers the corresponding ERC-20 token rewards or fees. *   Updates the sibling/parent pointers in the on-chain Object tree state.


---


4. ZIL \& WinchesterMQ Integration for 4D DNA Assets


ZIL commands compile directly into state mutation transactions that govern 4D DNA assets. By mapping packed Z-encoded noun properties to WinchesterMQ register offsets: 1. \textbf{DNA Codification}: Tesseract collection cards store their 4D vertices and rotation vectors in the ZIL object property table. 2. \textbf{MQ Interaction Routing}: Command verbs (e.g., \texttt{sabotage}, \texttt{spin}) write payload data directly to WinchesterMQ register interfaces (such as \texttt{yulStorage[100]} for SCSI phases), initiating low-level hardware state-machine changes and visual deformation feedback loops.


---


Next Steps 1.  \textbf{Implement \texttt{parseCommand} in \texttt{zmachine.yul}}: Add string parsing and dictionary matching loops. 2.  \textbf{Build Integration Test}: Verify inputs like "take coin" on-chain and watch ERC-20 balances update dynamically.

\section{Procedural Integration Report}

\vspace{0.1in}
Auncient Procedural Physics \& Genome Integration Report


This document records the mathematical integration of \textbf{Thomas Jakobsen's Verlet constraint framework} and \textbf{Joar Jakobsson's (TIGSource) procedural Slugcat/Scavenger physics} into the project's DNA compiler, C-based graphics thunks, and Z-machine instruction registers.


---


1. DNA Compiler Customization (Rain World Genome)


The DNA compiler in [compile\_dna.py](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/compile\_dna.py) has been rebuilt to inject Joar Jakobsson's procedural traits directly into the \texttt{atropa.dna} binary asset structure.


Active Genomic Trait Mapping \textit{ \textbf{\texttt{body\_fatness} (segment width multiplier):} Scales target constraint distances and visual circle radii. } \textbf{\texttt{muscle\_stiffness} (Verlet relaxation decay):} Determines how fast physical twitches decay back to resting states. * \textbf{\texttt{walk\_frequency} (kinematic pacing):} Dictates step timing and tail wiggle cycles.


``\texttt{python GENOME = \{ "cranial\_scale": 1.1, "body\_fatness": 1.25, "tail\_length": 0.95, "muscle\_stiffness": 0.90, "walk\_frequency": 0.60 \} }``


---


2. Thunks \& C graphics Integration


We replaced the static circle calculations in [test\_wayland\_teddy\_standalone.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/test\_wayland\_teddy\_standalone.c) with a complete C-based 4D Verlet particle solver using 13 particles and 12 constraints.


The 4D Verlet Update (Implicit Velocity) \$\$\textbackslash vec\{p\}\_\{i, n+1\} = \textbackslash vec\{p\}\_\{i, n\} + (\textbackslash vec\{p\}\_\{i, n\} - \textbackslash vec\{p\}\_\{i, n-1\}) + \textbackslash vec\{a\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash Delta t\textasciicircum 2\$\$


Constraint Relaxation Loop Runs \$N\$ iterations to project particle positions along constraint vectors, maintaining target lengths: \$\$\textbackslash vec\{p\}\_2 \textbackslash leftarrow \textbackslash vec\{p\}\_2 + \textbackslash vec\{d\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{percent\}\$\$ \$\$\textbackslash vec\{p\}\_1 \textbackslash leftarrow \textbackslash vec\{p\}\_1 - \textbackslash vec\{d\} \textbackslash cdot \textbackslash text\{percent\}\$\$


Segment Capsule Rendering Draws connected ellipses using a thick line segment projection algorithm (\texttt{draw\_capsule}), mimicking the organic connected-shapes style of Slugcats.


---


3. Z-Machine Integration Blueprint


To tie these physics properties to the retro game engine, the Z-machine registers (defined in the Yul bytecode and JSON contracts) are mapped to trigger physical forces:


\textit{ \textbf{Z-Machine Object Attributes (\$D68F\$ / \$D716\$):} Poke triggers in the VM call Yul physics routines, transforming retro inputs (such as jumping or attacking) directly into Verlet momentum impulses (\$\textbackslash vec\{a\}\$) in the C animation loop. } \textbf{Tension-to-Audio Mapping:} Average constraint offsets are mapped to the TB303 synthesizer's cut-off frequency, causing the audio to morph dynamically based on limb strain.

\section{Layout Unit Test Scope}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 23, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Phase 2 Layout Engine Unit Test Scope


This plan scopes the verification checks and scenarios required to guarantee the correctness of our layout solver under Phase 2.


---


1. Structural Box Model Tests Validate that margins, padding, borders, and content sizes are calculated correctly. - \textbf{Box Size Invariance}: Verify that for a box with width \$W\$, padding \$P\$, border \$B\$, and margin \$M\$, its computed outer bounding box matches \$W + 2P + 2B + 2M\$. - \textbf{Auto Width/Height Fallbacks}: Ensure elements without explicit widths fill their parent container's width, and elements without explicit heights shrink to wrap their children.


2. Reflow \& Layout Flow Tests Validate element positioning under standard document flow rules. - \textbf{Block Layout (Vertical Stacking)}: Verify that subsequent block elements are positioned below previous block elements (\$y\_2 = y\_1 + h\_1 + \textbackslash text\{margins\}\$). - \textbf{Inline Layout (Line Wrapping)}: Verify that inline text nodes flow horizontally and wrap onto a new line when they exceed the parent container's boundary. - \textbf{Flexbox Constraints (Horizontal \& Vertical)}: Check that children of elements styled with \texttt{display: flex} correctly align, distribute extra space, or shrink when constrained.


3. Style Cascade \& Hidden Elements Validate that computed style flags are honored during box layout tree generation. - \textbf{Display None Exclusion}: Ensure that any DOM node with \texttt{display: none} does not generate a layout box and is excluded from reflow geometry calculations.


---


4. Test Harness Design Since we have not integrated the Vulkan rasterizer yet, the unit tests for Phase 2 will execute \textit{headless structural validations}: - Parse HTML \& style strings. - Run the Layout Reflow solver. - Programmatically assert coordinates (\$x, y, w, h\$) of DOM nodes against expected geometric values.

\section{Layout Engine Roadmap}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 23, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
Custom Browser Layout Engine Roadmap


This roadmap outlines the steps to build a native, lightweight HTML/CSS layout and rendering engine integrated with V8 and our Vulkan presenter (\texttt{rooted\_frame\_presenter}).


---


Phase 1: Core Parsing \& DOM Tree (C/C++) Build the foundations to ingest HTML and CSS into structured memory.


1. \textbf{HTML Parser \& DOM Builder} [COMPLETED] - Implement a robust, non-backtracking tokenizer/parser for HTML5 subsets. - Construct the Document Object Model (DOM) tree with parent/child links and attributes. 2. \textbf{CSS Parser \& Cascade Engine} - Parse CSS rules, properties, and values (colors, units like \texttt{px}, \texttt{\%}, \texttt{em}, \texttt{auto}). - Implement selector matching (tag, class, ID, hierarchical selectors) and cascade/specificity resolution. 3. \textbf{DOM \& Style Integration} - Compute final CSS styles for each DOM node (inheritable properties, defaults).


---


Phase 2: Layout \& Box Model Calculations Calculate spatial coordinates for all visual elements.


1. \textbf{Render/Box Tree Construction} [COMPLETED] - Generate layout boxes (block, inline, inline-block) from the styled DOM tree. - Handle hidden elements (\texttt{display: none}). 2. \textbf{Reflow \& Geometry Solver} [COMPLETED] - Calculate box coordinates (\$x, y\$) and sizes (\$w, h\$) using CSS box model rules. - Implement basic Flexbox and Flow layouts. 3. \textbf{Text Wrapping \& Font Shaping} [COMPLETED] - Wrap inline text within box bounds. - Integrate with the existing text and font parser/rasterizer (e.g. \texttt{tsfi\_font\_engine.o}) to calculate character advancements.


---


Phase 3: Visual Compositing \& Rasterization (Vulkan) Paint the layout tree directly into the presenter's scanout buffer.


1. \textbf{Paint Tree Generation} [COMPLETED] - Gather visual drawing operations (background color, border, text, JPEG/PNG images) sorted by \texttt{z-index}. 2. \textbf{2D Rendering Pipeline} [COMPLETED] - Implement pixel-blitting functions for colored rectangles, borders, and text drawing. - Integrate existing JPEG image loading for thumbnails and assets. 3. \textbf{Vulkan Presenter Integration} [COMPLETED] - Replace the Puppeteer frame loop in \texttt{rooted\_frame\_presenter} with our custom page layout + render engine pipeline.


---


Phase 4: V8 Binding \& DOM API Runtime Expose the DOM to JavaScript so YouTube's frontend scripts can run.


1. \textbf{V8 DOM Bindings} [COMPLETED] - Wrap C++ DOM and style objects into V8 JavaScript classes. - Expose core APIs: \texttt{document.getElementById}, \texttt{window.addEventListener}, etc. 2. \textbf{Event Dispatch Loop} [COMPLETED] - Map low-level input events (mouse move, clicks, keyboard) from our presenter's input loop into JavaScript events (\texttt{mousedown}, \texttt{keydown}). 3. \textbf{HTTPS Client \& Network Stack} - Create a clean C/C++ network transport helper to handle HTTPS requests and feed resources directly to the browser.


---


Phase 5: Media Stream Rendering Support video playback and audio playback.


1. \textbf{HTML5 \texttt{<video>} and \texttt{<audio>} Nodes} - Implement rendering boxes that hold video frame buffers and sync with audio streams. 2. \textbf{Streaming Protocol Support (DASH/HLS)} - Parse and fetch dynamic adaptive media segments. 3. \textbf{Native Media Decoding} - Parse and decode H.264/VP9/AV1 video frames and AAC/Opus audio packets natively using our libraries.


---


Phase 6: Security, Storage \& Sandbox Handle browser storage, security, and sessions.


1. \textbf{Storage APIs} - Implement cookies, \texttt{localStorage}, and \texttt{sessionStorage} backing stores. 2. \textbf{Secure HTTPS \& TLS} - Enforce TLS certificate validation, cookie security flags, and cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules. 3. \textbf{User Authentication} - Ensure secure sign-in states are maintained for YouTube subscriptions and user data.

\section{Rooted Browser Roadmap}
\noindent\textit{Published: June 23, 2026}\\
\vspace{0.1in}
ROOTED Browser Layout Engine Roadmap


This document outlines the architecture, accomplishments, and implementation milestones for developing a high-fidelity Vulkan Wayland \textbf{Auncient} layout engine and painter capable of achieving parity with standard browser rendering.


---


1. Architectural System Overview


The following diagram illustrates the data flow from raw HTML/CSS inputs down to Vulkan rasterization on Wayland scanout buffers:


``\texttt{mermaid graph TD A["Raw HTML \& CSS Source"] --> B["DOM Tree Parser (tsfi\_dom.c)"] B --> C["Style Resolver \& Selector Cascader"] C --> D["Layout Box Constructor (tsfi\_layout.c)"] D --> E["Layout solver (Reflow \& Geometry)"] E --> F["Layout Paint Dispatcher (tsfi\_paint.c)"] F --> G["Rasterization \& Sub-pixel Blender"] G --> H["Wayland Scanout Buffer (tests/rooted\_frame\_presenter.c)"] }``


---


2. Completed Milestones


> [!NOTE] > The current system has transitioned to direct browser frame projection to ensure pixel-perfect fidelity for YouTube.


\textit{ \textbf{Bilinear Font Smoothing:} Replaced blocky character rendering with dynamic sub-pixel alpha blending ([tsfi\_paint.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/src/tsfi\_paint.c\#L242)). } \textbf{Color Space Expansion:} Support for \texttt{rgba(...)}, transparent elements, and standard hex color sheets. * \textbf{Aspect Ratio Optimization:} Automated vision similarity heuristics ([tests/validate\_youtube\_layout.c](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/validate\_youtube\_layout.c\#L162)) to adjust target canvas bounding boxes.


---


3. Phased Layout Engine Roadmap


Phase 1: Comprehensive CSS Solver (Next) - [ ] \textbf{Cascading Sheet Support:} Implement style rules matching class, ID, and attribute selectors. - [ ] \textbf{Inheritance Rules:} Automate default property cascade from root to leaf text elements.


Phase 2: Flow \& Layout Models - [ ] \textbf{Flexbox (CSS Flexible Box Layout):} Add layout solvers handling alignment (\texttt{justify-content}, \texttt{align-items}) and flex-grow metrics. - [ ] \textbf{Inline Formatting Context:} Add inline block wrap calculation and text hyphenation handling.


Phase 3: Text \& Font Rasterization - [ ] \textbf{Vector Font Rendering:} Integrate a lightweight TrueType / OpenType font parser (e.g., stb\_truetype) to replace the 8x8 font. - [ ] \textbf{Kerning \& Shaping:} Utilize shaping maps to correctly align complex typographic sequences.


Phase 4: Dynamic DOM \& Scripting Bindings - [ ] \textbf{DOM Mutations:} Expose C-side DOM modification functions (e.g., \texttt{appendChild}, \texttt{setAttribute}) to the V8 / Node context ([node\_interop.cpp](file:///home/mariarahel/src/tsfi2/atropa\_pulsechain/tsfi2-deepseek/tests/node\_interop.cpp)). - [ ] \textbf{Event Listeners:} Link user input mouse moves/clicks directly into in-memory DOM event callbacks.


---


> [!IMPORTANT] > To comply with the safety rules, synthetic browser automated drivers (e.g., Puppeteer) are banned. All inputs must route through low-level \textbf{Auncient} hardware register maps.
